chapters.title: Introductory Chapter
paragraphs: Of all the new things that caught my attention during my stay in the United States, none struck me more forcibly than the general equality of conditions. I quickly saw the enormous influence this fundamental fact exerts on the whole course of society: it gives a particular direction to public opinion, a particular character to the laws, new principles to those who govern, and distinctive habits to those who are governed. I soon perceived that this fact reaches far beyond the country's politics and laws — it rules civil society just as thoroughly as it rules the government. It creates opinions, generates sentiments, shapes the ordinary practices of daily life, and alters even what it does not itself produce. The further I advanced in the study of American society, the more I recognized that equality of conditions is the fundamental fact from which all others seem to derive, and the central point at which all my observations constantly converged.

I then turned my thoughts to our own hemisphere, where I seemed to detect something analogous to what the New World had shown me. I noticed that equality of conditions is advancing daily toward those extreme limits it appears to have reached in the United States, and that the democracy that governs American communities is rapidly rising toward power in Europe. From this observation came the idea for the book now before the reader.

Everyone agrees that a great democratic revolution is underway among us, but opinions differ on its nature and consequences. Some see it as a recent accident that can still be stopped; others see it as irresistible, because it is the most uniform, the most ancient, and the most enduring tendency found in history. Consider the state of France seven hundred years ago, when the land was divided among a small number of families who owned the soil and ruled its inhabitants. The right to govern descended through family inheritance from one generation to the next; force was the only means by which one person could act upon another, and landed property was the sole source of power. Soon, however, the political power of the clergy was established and began to assert itself. The clergy opened its ranks to all classes — to the poor and the rich, the villein and the lord; equality entered the government through the Church, and the man who as a serf would have vegetated in perpetual bondage took his seat as a priest among nobles, and not infrequently above the heads of kings.

As society gradually became more stable and more civilized, the relations between men grew more complicated and more numerous. From this came the need for civil laws; and soon the order of legal officials rose from the obscurity of tribunals and their dusty chambers to appear at the monarch's court, beside the feudal barons in their ermine and their chain mail. While kings were ruining themselves with grand enterprises and nobles were exhausting their resources in private wars, the lower orders were enriching themselves through commerce. The influence of money began to be felt in affairs of state. Business transactions opened a new road to power, and the financier rose to a position of political influence where he was at once flattered and despised. Gradually the spread of learning and the growing taste for literature and art opened paths of success to talent: science became a means of government, intelligence brought social power, and the man of letters took part in the affairs of state. The value attached to the privileges of birth fell in exact proportion to the new paths opened for advancement. In the eleventh century, nobility was beyond all price; in the thirteenth, it could be purchased; it was first conferred as a grant in 1270 — and so equality was introduced into government by the aristocracy itself.

Over these seven hundred years, the nobles sometimes granted the people a share of political rights in order to resist the authority of the Crown or to weaken their rivals. More often, the king permitted the lower orders to enjoy some measure of power with the aim of suppressing the aristocracy. In France, the kings have always been the most active and the most consistent levelers. When they were strong and ambitious, they spared no effort to raise the people to the level of the nobles; when they were temperate or weak, they let the people rise above themselves. Some helped democracy through their talents, others through their vices. Louis XI and Louis XIV reduced every rank beneath the throne to the same subjection; Louis XV descended, himself and his whole Court, into the dust.

As soon as land was held on some basis other than feudal tenure, and personal property in its turn began to confer influence and power, every improvement in commerce or manufacture became a fresh element of equality. From that point on, every new discovery, every new want it generated, and every new desire demanding satisfaction was a step toward the universal level. The taste for luxury, the love of war, the sway of fashion, and the most superficial as well as the deepest passions of the human heart all cooperated to enrich the poor and impoverish the rich.

Once the exercise of intellect became a source of strength and wealth, every addition to science, every fresh truth, and every new idea had to be regarded as a seed of power placed within the people's reach. Poetry, eloquence, and memory, the grace of wit, the glow of imagination, the depth of thought — all the gifts that Providence bestows with an equal hand — turned to the advantage of democracy. Even when these gifts were held by democracy's adversaries, they still served its cause by throwing into relief the natural greatness of man. Democracy's conquests spread in step with those of civilization and knowledge, and literature became an arsenal where the poorest and weakest could always find weapons to their hand.

Reading through our history, we will hardly find a single great event in the last seven hundred years that has not turned to the advantage of equality. The Crusades and the wars with the English decimated the nobles and divided their possessions; the rise of communes introduced an element of democratic liberty into the heart of the feudal monarchy; the invention of firearms equalized villein and noble on the battlefield; printing gave the same resources to minds of every class; the postal system carried the same information to the poor man's cottage and to the palace gate; and Protestantism proclaimed that all men are equally capable of finding the road to heaven. The discovery of America opened a thousand new paths to fortune, and placed riches and power within reach of the adventurous and the obscure. If we examine what has happened in France at fifty-year intervals since the eleventh century, we will invariably see that a twofold revolution has taken place in society. The noble has descended the social ladder, and the roturier has risen; one falls as the other rises. Every half century brings them closer together, and very soon they will meet.

Nor is this phenomenon unique to France. Wherever we turn our eyes, we will see the same continual revolution throughout all of Christendom. In every nation, the various events of national life have turned to the advantage of democracy; all men have contributed to it by their efforts — those who intentionally worked in its cause and those who served it unwittingly, those who fought for it and those who declared themselves its opponents. All have been driven along the same track, all have labored toward the same end, some ignorantly and some unwillingly — all have been blind instruments in the hands of God.

The gradual development of the equality of conditions is therefore a providential fact, and it has all the characteristics of a divine decree: it is universal, it is enduring, it constantly eludes all human interference, and all events and all men contribute to its progress. Would it then be wise to imagine that a social impulse dating from so far back can be checked by the efforts of a single generation? Can we really believe that the democracy which has annihilated the feudal system and conquered kings will respect the citizen and the capitalist? Will it stop now that it has grown so strong and its adversaries so weak? No one can say where we are going, because all points of comparison are lacking: equality of conditions is more complete in today's Christian countries than it has ever been at any time or in any place in the world — and so the scale of what already exists prevents us from foreseeing what may yet come.

The entire book now offered to the public has been written under the impression of a kind of religious dread, produced in the author's mind by the contemplation of a revolution so irresistible — a revolution that has advanced for centuries in spite of astonishing obstacles, and that is still proceeding amid the ruins it has made. It is not necessary for God himself to speak in order to disclose to us the unquestionable signs of his will; we can discern them in the habitual course of nature, and in the invariable tendency of events. I know, without special revelation, that the planets move in the orbits traced by the Creator's finger. If the men of our time were led by careful observation and sincere reflection to acknowledge that the gradual, progressive development of social equality is at once the past and the future of their history, that single truth would confer the sacred character of a divine decree upon the change. To attempt to check democracy would then be to resist the will of God, and nations would be obliged to make the best of the social lot assigned to them by Providence.

The Christian nations of our age seem to me to present a most alarming spectacle. The impulse that bears them along is so strong that it cannot be stopped, but it is not yet so rapid that it cannot be guided: their fate is still in their hands — but only for a little while longer. The first duty imposed at this moment on those who direct our affairs is to educate the democracy: to warm its faith, if that is possible; to purify its morals; to direct its energies; to substitute knowledge of practical business for its inexperience, and an acquaintance with its true interests for its blind propensities; to adapt its government to time and place, and to modify it in response to the events and actors of the age. A new science of politics is indispensable to a new world. This, however, is what we think of least. Launched into the middle of a rapid stream, we obstinately fix our eyes on the ruins still visible on the shore we have left, while the current sweeps us along and drives us backward toward the gulf.

In no country in Europe has the great social revolution I have been describing made such rapid progress as in France; yet it has always been carried forward by chance. The heads of state have never shown any forethought for its demands, and its victories have been won without their consent or even their knowledge. The most powerful, the most intelligent, and the most moral classes of the nation have never tried to connect themselves with it in order to guide it. The people have consequently been abandoned to their wild propensities, and they have grown up like those outcasts who receive their education in the public streets and who know nothing but the vices and wretchedness of society. The existence of a democracy seemed unknown — until suddenly it took possession of the supreme power. Then everything was submitted to its caprices; it was worshipped as the idol of strength. When it was at last enfeebled by its own excesses, the legislator conceived the rash project of annihilating its power instead of instructing it and correcting its vices. No attempt was made to fit it to govern: all efforts were bent on excluding it from government.

The consequence has been that the democratic revolution has been accomplished only in the material parts of society, without the corresponding change in laws, ideas, customs, and manners that was necessary to make such a revolution beneficial. We have gotten a democracy, but without the conditions that lessen its vices and bring out its natural advantages. And although we already see the evils it brings, we remain ignorant of the benefits it may yet confer.

While the power of the Crown, supported by the aristocracy, peacefully governed the nations of Europe, society possessed — amid its wretchedness — several advantages that can now scarcely be appreciated or imagined. The power of one part of his subjects was an insurmountable barrier to the prince's tyranny; and the monarch, feeling the almost divine character he enjoyed in the eyes of the multitude, drew a motive for the just use of his power from the respect he inspired. As high as they stood above the people, the nobles could not help taking that calm and benevolent interest in the people's fate that a shepherd feels toward his flock; and without acknowledging the poor as their equals, they watched over the destiny of those whose welfare Providence had entrusted to their care. The people, never having conceived of a social condition different from their own and never expecting to rank with their chiefs, received benefits from them without disputing their rights. The people grew attached to them when they were merciful and just, and submitted without resistance or servility to their exactions, as to the inevitable visitations of the arm of God. Custom and the manners of the time had also created a kind of law in the midst of violence, and set certain limits to oppression. Since the noble never suspected that anyone would try to deprive him of the privileges he believed to be legitimate, and since the serf regarded his own inferiority as a consequence of the immutable order of nature, it is easy to imagine that a mutual exchange of goodwill took place between two classes so differently gifted by fate. Inequality and wretchedness existed in society then — but the souls of neither class were degraded. Men are not corrupted by the exercise of power or debased by the habit of obedience; they are corrupted by the exercise of a power they believe to be illegal, and by obedience to a rule they consider to be usurped and oppressive. On one side was wealth, strength, and leisure, accompanied by the refinements of luxury, the elegance of taste, the pleasures of wit, and the religion of art. On the other was labor and a rude ignorance — and yet, amid this coarse and ignorant multitude, it was not uncommon to meet with energetic passions, generous sentiments, profound religious convictions, and independent virtues. A body politic so organized could boast of its stability, its power, and above all its glory.

But the scene has now changed. Gradually the two ranks mingle; the divisions that once separated mankind are lowered, property is divided, power is held in common, the light of learning spreads, and the capacities of all classes are equally cultivated. The state becomes democratic, and the empire of democracy is slowly and peacefully introduced into the institutions and manners of the nation. I can conceive of a society in which all men would profess an equal attachment and respect for the laws of which they are the common authors — in which the authority of the state would be respected as necessary, though not as divine, and the citizen's loyalty to the chief magistrate would not be a passion but a quiet, rational persuasion. Every individual possessing rights he is sure to retain, a kind of manly reliance and reciprocal courtesy would arise between all classes, alike free from pride and meanness. The people, well acquainted with their true interests, would acknowledge that to enjoy the advantages of society it is necessary to meet its demands. In this state of things, the voluntary association of citizens might replace the individual exertions of the nobles, and the community would be equally protected from anarchy and from oppression.

I admit that in a democratic state thus constituted, society will not be stationary — but the impulses of the social body can be regulated and directed forward. If there is less splendor than in the halls of an aristocracy, the contrast of misery will also be less frequent. The pleasures of enjoyment may be less excessive, but those of comfort will be more general. The sciences may be less perfectly cultivated, but ignorance will be less common. The impetuosity of the feelings will be restrained, and the habits of the nation softened; there will be more vices and fewer crimes. In the absence of enthusiasm and ardent faith, great sacrifices may be obtained from the members of a commonwealth by an appeal to their understanding and experience. Each individual will feel the same necessity of uniting with his fellow-citizens to protect his own weakness; and knowing that if they are to help him, he must cooperate with them, he will readily see that his personal interest is identified with the community's. The nation, taken as a whole, will be less brilliant, less glorious, and perhaps less strong; but the majority of citizens will enjoy a greater degree of prosperity, and the people will remain quiet — not because they despair of improvement, but because they are conscious of the advantages of their condition. If not all the consequences of this state of things would be good or useful, society would at least have appropriated those that are good and useful; and having once and for all renounced the social advantages of aristocracy, mankind would enter into possession of all the benefits democracy can offer.

But here it may be asked what we have adopted in place of the institutions, ideas, and customs of our forefathers that we have abandoned. The spell of royalty is broken, but it has not been succeeded by the majesty of the laws. The people have learned to despise all authority — but fear now extorts a larger tribute of obedience than reverence and love once did.

I see that we have destroyed those independent beings which were able to cope with tyranny single-handed — but it is the Government that has inherited the privileges of which families, corporations, and individuals have been deprived. The weakness of the whole community has thus replaced the influence of a small body of citizens, which, if it was sometimes oppressive, was often conservative. The division of property has lessened the distance separating the rich from the poor; but it seems that the nearer they draw to each other, the greater their mutual hatred, and the more vehement the envy and dread with which they resist each other's claims to power. The notion of Right is equally alien to both classes, and Force offers each the only argument for the present and the only guarantee for the future. The poor man keeps the prejudices of his ancestors without their faith, and their ignorance without their virtues; he has adopted the doctrine of self-interest as the rule of his actions without understanding the science that governs it, and his egotism is no less blind than his devotion once was. If society is tranquil, it is not because it relies on its strength and well-being, but because it knows its weakness and infirmities; a single effort may cost it its life. Everyone feels the evil, but no one has courage or energy enough to seek the cure. The desires, regrets, sorrows, and joys of the time produce nothing visible or permanent — like the passions of old men, which end in impotence.

We have, then, abandoned whatever advantages the old state of things offered, without receiving any compensation from our present condition. We have destroyed an aristocracy, and we seem inclined to survey its ruins with complacency, and to take up our abode in the midst of them.

The phenomena of the intellectual world are no less deplorable. The democracy of France, checked in its course or abandoned to its lawless passions, has overthrown whatever crossed its path and has shaken everything it has not destroyed. Its empire over society was not gradually introduced or peaceably established, but has constantly advanced amid disorder and the agitation of conflict. In the heat of the struggle, each partisan is driven beyond the limits of his own opinions by the opinions and excesses of his opponents, until he loses sight of the goal of his exertions and adopts a language that disguises his real sentiments or secret instincts. Hence the strange confusion we are witnessing. I cannot recall a passage in history more worthy of sorrow and pity than the scenes now playing out before our eyes. It is as if the natural bond that once united a man's opinions to his tastes and his actions to his principles has now been broken; the sympathy always acknowledged between human feelings and ideas appears dissolved, and all the laws of moral analogy abolished.

Zealous Christians can be found among us whose minds are nurtured in the love and knowledge of a future life, and who readily embrace the cause of human liberty as the source of all moral greatness. Christianity, which has declared that all men are equal in the sight of God, will not refuse to acknowledge that all citizens are equal in the eye of the law. But by a singular concourse of events, religion has become entangled in the very institutions democracy assails, and so is not infrequently led to reject the equality it loves, and to curse as an enemy a cause of liberty it might instead sanctify by its alliance.

Beside these religious men I see others whose eyes are turned more to the earth than to Heaven. They are partisans of liberty, not only as the source of the noblest virtues, but especially as the root of all solid advantages; and they sincerely want to extend its reach and impart its blessings to mankind. It would be natural for them to hasten to invoke the aid of religion — for they must know that liberty cannot be established without morality, nor morality without faith. But they have seen religion in the ranks of their adversaries, and they inquire no further. Some of them attack it openly, and the rest are afraid to defend it.

In former ages, slavery was advocated by the venal and slavish-minded, while the independent and the warm-hearted struggled without hope to save the liberties of mankind. But now one meets men of high and generous character whose opinions are at odds with their inclinations, and who praise a servility they have themselves never known. Others, by contrast, speak in the name of liberty as if they could feel its sanctity and its majesty, and loudly claim for humanity those rights they have always disowned. There are virtuous and peaceful individuals whose pure morality, quiet habits, affluence, and talents fit them to be leaders of the surrounding population. Their love of country is sincere, and they are prepared to make the greatest sacrifices for its welfare — but they confuse the abuses of civilization with its benefits, and the idea of evil is inseparable in their minds from that of novelty.

Not far from this class is another party, whose aim is to materialize mankind — to hit upon what is expedient without heeding what is just, to acquire knowledge without faith, and prosperity without virtue. They assume the title of champions of modern civilization, and take up a station they usurp with insolence and from which they are driven by their own unworthiness. Where does this leave us? The religionists are the enemies of liberty, and the friends of liberty attack religion; the high-minded and the noble advocate subjection, while the meanest and most servile minds preach independence; honest and enlightened citizens oppose all progress, while men without patriotism and without principles are the apostles of civilization and intelligence. Has such been the fate of the centuries that preceded ours? Has man always inhabited a world like the present, where nothing is linked together, where virtue is without genius and genius without honor — where the love of order is confused with a taste for oppression, and the holy rites of freedom with a contempt for law; where the light that conscience throws on human actions is dim, and where nothing any longer seems forbidden or allowed, honorable or shameful, false or true? I cannot, however, believe that the Creator made man only to leave him in an endless struggle with the intellectual miseries that surround us. God destines a calmer and a more certain future to the communities of Europe. I am unacquainted with his designs, but I shall not stop believing in them because I cannot fathom them; I would rather mistrust my own capacity than his justice.

There is one country in the world where the great revolution I am speaking of seems almost to have reached its natural limits. It has been accomplished there with ease and simplicity — or rather, that country has attained the consequences of the democratic revolution we are undergoing without having gone through the revolution itself. The emigrants who settled on the shores of America at the beginning of the seventeenth century separated the democratic principle from all the principles that repressed it in the old communities of Europe, and transplanted it unalloyed to the New World. There it has been allowed to spread in perfect freedom, and to work out its consequences in the laws by influencing the manners of the country.

It appears to me beyond doubt that sooner or later we shall arrive, as the Americans have, at an almost complete equality of conditions. But I do not conclude from this that we shall necessarily be led to draw the same political consequences the Americans have drawn from a similar social organization. I am far from supposing that they have chosen the only form of government a democracy may adopt; but the shared cause of laws and manners in the two countries is enough to explain the immense interest we have in becoming acquainted with its effects in each of them.

It is not, then, merely to satisfy a legitimate curiosity that I have examined America; my wish has been to find lessons we may ourselves profit from. Anyone who imagines that I have intended to write a panegyric will see that this was not my design. Nor has it been my aim to advocate any particular form of government, for I believe that absolute excellence is rarely to be found in any legislation. I have not even affected to discuss whether the social revolution, which I believe to be irresistible, is advantageous or harmful to mankind. I have acknowledged this revolution as a fact already accomplished or on the eve of its accomplishment; and I have selected the nation, from among those that have undergone it, in which its development has been the most peaceful and complete, in order to discern its natural consequences and, if possible, identify the means by which it may be made profitable. I confess that in America I saw more than America: I sought the image of democracy itself, with its inclinations, its character, its prejudices, and its passions — in order to learn what we have to fear or to hope from its progress.

In the first part of this work I have tried to show the tendency given to the laws by the democracy of America — a democracy abandoned almost without restraint to its instinctive propensities — and to exhibit the course it prescribes to government and the influence it exercises on public affairs. I have sought to discover the evils and the advantages it produces. I have examined the precautions the Americans use to direct it, as well as those they have not adopted, and I have undertaken to point out the causes that enable it to govern society. I do not know whether I have succeeded in making known what I saw in America, but I am certain that this has been my sincere desire, and that I have never knowingly molded facts to ideas, rather than ideas to facts.

Wherever a point could be established from written documents, I had recourse to the original text and to the most authentic and approved works. I have cited my authorities in the notes, and anyone may consult them. Wherever an opinion, a political custom, or a remark on the country's manners was concerned, I tried to consult the most enlightened men I met. If the point was important or doubtful, I was not satisfied with one witness but formed my opinion on the testimony of several. Here the reader must necessarily take me at my word. I could often have quoted names known to him, or deserving to be, in proof of what I claim; but I have carefully abstained from this practice. A stranger often hears important truths at the fireside of his host — truths the host would perhaps hide from the ear of a friend. He consoles himself with his guest for the silence imposed on him, and the shortness of the traveler's stay removes all fear of indiscretion. I carefully noted every conversation of this kind as soon as it occurred, but these notes will never leave my writing-case. I would rather weaken the success of my statements than add my name to the list of strangers who repay generous hospitality with subsequent chagrin and annoyance.

I am aware that, despite my care, nothing will be easier than to criticize this book, if anyone ever chooses to. Readers who examine it closely will discover the fundamental idea that connects its several parts. But the diversity of subjects I have had to treat is exceedingly great, and it will not be hard to oppose an isolated fact to the body of facts I cite, or an isolated idea to the body of ideas I put forward. I hope to be read in the spirit that has guided my labors, and that my book will be judged by the general impression it leaves — for I have formed my own judgment not on any single reason, but on the mass of evidence. It must not be forgotten that an author who wishes to be understood is obliged to push all his ideas to their utmost theoretical consequences, often to the verge of what is false or impracticable. If it is sometimes necessary to depart from the rules of logic in active life, such is not the case in discourse: a man finds that almost as many difficulties arise from inconsistency of language as from inconsistency of conduct.

I conclude by pointing out for myself what many readers will consider the principal defect of the work. This book is written to favor no particular views, and in composing it I have entertained no intention of serving or attacking any party. I have undertaken not to see differently, but to look further than parties; while they are busy with tomorrow, I have turned my thoughts to the Future.

chapters.title: Chapter I — Exterior Form Of North America
paragraphs: North America presents in its external form certain general features that are easy to discern at first glance. A kind of methodical order seems to have governed the separation of land and water, mountains and valleys. A simple but grand arrangement can be seen amid the confusion of objects and the prodigious variety of scenes. This continent is divided, almost equally, into two vast regions. One is bounded on the north by the Arctic Pole and on the east and west by the two great oceans; it stretches southward, forming a triangle whose irregular sides eventually meet below the great lakes of Canada. The second region begins where the first ends and takes in all the rest of the continent. The one slopes gently toward the Pole, the other toward the Equator.

The territory covered by the first region descends toward the north with a slope so imperceptible that it may almost be said to form a level plain. Within the bounds of this immense stretch of country there are neither high mountains nor deep valleys. Streams meander through it irregularly; great rivers mingle their currents, separate and meet again, scatter and form vast marshes, losing all trace of their channels in the labyrinth of waters they themselves have created. Then at length, after innumerable windings, they fall into the Polar Seas. The great lakes that bound this first region are not walled in, like most of those in the Old World, between hills and rocks. Their banks are flat and rise only a few feet above the level of their waters. Each of them thus forms a vast bowl filled to the brim. The slightest change in the structure of the globe would send their waters rushing either toward the Pole or to the tropical sea.

The second region is more varied on its surface and better suited for human habitation. Two long chains of mountains divide it from one end to the other: the Alleghany ridge follows the shape of the Atlantic shore, and the other runs parallel with the Pacific. The space lying between these two chains of mountains contains 1,341,649 square miles. *a Its surface is therefore about six times as great as that of France. This vast territory, however, forms a single valley. One side descends gradually from the rounded summits of the Alleghanies, while the other rises in an uninterrupted course toward the tops of the Rocky Mountains. At the bottom of the valley flows an immense river, into which the various streams issuing from the mountains fall from all sides. In memory of their native land, the French once called this river the St. Louis. The Indians, in their pompous language, have named it the Father of Waters, or the Mississippi.
a [ Darby's "View of the United States."]

The Mississippi takes its source above the line between the two great regions I have spoken of, not far from the highest point of the table-land where they meet. Near the same spot rises another river, *b which empties into the Polar seas. The course of the Mississippi is at first uncertain: it winds several times toward the north, from which it rose, and at length, after being delayed in lakes and marshes, it flows slowly onward to the south. Sometimes gliding quietly along the clay bed nature has assigned to it, sometimes swollen by storms, the Mississippi waters 2,500 miles in its course. *c At a distance of 1,364 miles from its mouth, this river reaches an average depth of fifteen feet, and it is navigated by vessels of 300 tons burden for nearly 500 miles. Fifty-seven large navigable rivers contribute to swell its waters: among others, the Missouri, which covers 2,500 miles; the Arkansas, 1,300 miles; the Red River, 1,000 miles; four whose course runs from 800 to 1,000 miles, namely, the Illinois, the St. Peter's, the St. Francis, and the Moingona; and a countless multitude of smaller streams that unite their tributary waters from every side.
c [ Warden's "Description of the United States."]

The valley watered by the Mississippi seems formed to be the bed of this mighty river, which, like a god of antiquity, dispenses both good and evil along its course. On the banks of the stream nature displays an inexhaustible fertility; but as you move away from its banks, vegetation grows weaker, the soil becomes poor, and the plants that survive grow sickly. Nowhere have the great convulsions of the globe left more evident traces than in the valley of the Mississippi; the whole aspect of the country shows the powerful effects of water, both in its fertility and in its barrenness. The waters of the primeval ocean piled up enormous beds of vegetable soil in the valley, which they leveled as they retreated. On the right bank of the river one sees immense plains, as smooth as if a farmer had passed over them with his roller. As you approach the mountains, the soil becomes more and more uneven and sterile; the ground is pierced, as it were, in a thousand places by primitive rocks that stand out like the bones of a skeleton whose flesh is partly consumed. The surface of the earth is covered with granite sand and huge irregular masses of stone, among which a few plants force their growth, giving the appearance of a green field scattered with the ruins of a vast building. On examination, these stones and this sand show a perfect resemblance to those that form the arid and broken summits of the Rocky Mountains. The flood of waters that washed the soil down to the bottom of the valley afterwards carried off portions of the rocks themselves; and these, dashed and bruised against the neighboring cliffs, were left scattered like wrecks at their feet. *d The valley of the Mississippi is, on the whole, the most magnificent dwelling-place prepared by God for man's abode; and yet at present it may be called a mighty desert.
d [ See Appendix, A.]

On the eastern side of the Alleghanies, between the base of these mountains and the Atlantic Ocean, there lies a long ridge of rocks and sand that the sea appears to have left behind as it retreated. The mean breadth of this territory does not exceed one hundred miles, but it runs about nine hundred miles in length. This part of the American continent has a soil that offers every obstacle to the farmer, and its vegetation is scanty and monotonous.

It was on this inhospitable coast that the first united efforts of human industry were made. That narrow strip of arid land was the cradle of the English colonies that were destined one day to become the United States of America. The center of power still lies here, while in the backwoods the true elements of the great people to whom the future control of the continent belongs are gathering, almost in secret.

When the Europeans first landed on the shores of the West Indies, and afterwards on the coast of South America, they thought themselves transported into those fabled regions of which poets had sung. The sea sparkled with phosphorescent light, and the extraordinary clarity of its waters revealed to the navigator's eye all that had until then been hidden in the deep abyss. *e Here and there appeared little islands perfumed with fragrant plants, looking like baskets of flowers floating on the tranquil surface of the ocean. Every object that met the sight in this enchanting region seemed prepared to satisfy man's wants or contribute to his pleasures. Nearly all the trees were loaded with nourishing fruits, and those that were useless as food delighted the eye with the brilliance and variety of their colors. In groves of fragrant lemon trees, wild figs, flowering myrtles, acacias, and oleanders, hung with festoons of climbing plants covered in flowers, a multitude of birds unknown in Europe displayed their bright plumage, glittering with purple and azure, and mingled their song with the harmony of a world teeming with life and motion. *f Beneath this brilliant exterior, death lay concealed. But the air of these climates had so enervating an influence that man, absorbed in present enjoyment, became heedless of the future.

e [ Malte Brun tells us (vol. v. p. 726) that the water of the Caribbean Sea is so transparent that corals and fish are discernible at a depth of sixty fathoms. The ship seemed to float in air, the navigator became giddy as his eye penetrated through the crystal flood, and beheld submarine gardens, or beds of shells, or gilded fishes gliding among tufts and thickets of seaweed.]
f [ See Appendix, B.]

North America appeared under a very different aspect; there everything was grave, serious, and solemn. It seemed created to be the domain of the intellect, as the South was that of sensual delight. A turbulent and foggy ocean washed its shores. It was girded by a belt of granite rocks, or by wide tracts of sand. The foliage of its woods was dark and gloomy, for they were made up of firs, larches, evergreen oaks, wild olive trees, and laurels. Beyond this outer belt lay the thick shade of the central forest, where the largest trees produced in the two hemispheres grow side by side. The plane, the catalpa, the sugar maple, and the Virginian poplar mingled their branches with those of the oak, the beech, and the lime. In these, as in the forests of the Old World, destruction was perpetually at work. The ruins of vegetation were heaped on one another, but there was no laboring hand to remove them, and their decay was not rapid enough to make room for the continual work of renewal. Climbing plants, grasses, and other herbs forced their way through the mass of dying trees; they crept along their bending trunks, found nourishment in their dusty hollows, and made a passage beneath the lifeless bark. Thus decay lent its aid to life, and their respective products were mingled together. The depths of these forests were gloomy and obscure, and a thousand small streams, undirected by human industry, kept them constantly moist. It was rare to meet with flowers, wild fruits, or birds beneath their shades. The fall of a tree overthrown by age, the rush of a waterfall, the lowing of the buffalo, and the howling of the wind were the only sounds that broke the silence of nature.

East of the great river, the woods almost disappeared; in their place were seen prairies of immense extent. Whether Nature in her infinite variety had denied the seeds of trees to these fertile plains, or whether they had once been covered with forests later destroyed by the hand of man, is a question that neither tradition nor scientific research has been able to resolve.

These immense deserts were not, however, empty of human inhabitants. Some wandering tribes had for ages been scattered among the forest shades and the green pastures of the prairie. From the mouth of the St. Lawrence to the delta of the Mississippi, and from the Atlantic to the Pacific Ocean, these savages shared certain points of resemblance that testified to a common origin; yet at the same time they differed from all other known races of men: *g they were neither white like the Europeans, nor yellow like most of the Asiatics, nor black like the negroes. Their skin was reddish brown, their hair long and shining, their lips thin, and their cheekbones very prominent. The languages spoken by the North American tribes varied greatly in their words, but were subject to the same grammatical rules. These rules differed in several respects from those observed to govern the origin of language elsewhere. The idiom of the Americans seemed the product of new combinations, and bespoke an effort of understanding of which the Indians of our day would be incapable. *h

g [ With the progress of discovery some resemblance has been found to exist between the physical conformation, the language, and the habits of the Indians of North America, and those of the Tongous, Mantchous, Mongols, Tartars, and other wandering tribes of Asia. The land occupied by these tribes is not very distant from Behring's Strait, which allows of the supposition, that at a remote period they gave inhabitants to the desert continent of America. But this is a point which has not yet been clearly elucidated by science. See Malte Brun, vol. v.; the works of Humboldt; Fischer, "Conjecture sur l'Origine des Americains"; Adair, "History of the American Indians."]
h [ See Appendix, C.]

The social state of these tribes also differed in many respects from all that was seen in the Old World. They seemed to have multiplied freely in the midst of their deserts without coming into contact with other races more civilized than their own. Accordingly, they showed none of those vague, incoherent notions of right and wrong, none of that deep corruption of manners that is usually joined with ignorance and coarseness among nations which, after advancing to civilization, have relapsed into a state of barbarism. The Indian was indebted to no one but himself; his virtues, his vices, and his prejudices were his own work; he had grown up in the wild independence of his nature.

If, in polished countries, the lowest of the people are rude and uncivil, it is not merely because they are poor and ignorant, but because, being so, they are in daily contact with rich and enlightened men. The sight of their own hard lot and of their weakness, daily contrasted with the happiness and power of some of their fellow creatures, stirs in their hearts both anger and fear: the consciousness of their inferiority and dependence irritates even as it humiliates them. This state of mind shows itself in their manners and language; they are at once insolent and servile. The truth of this is easily proved by observation: the common people are ruder in aristocratic countries than elsewhere, and in opulent cities than in rural districts. In those places where the rich and powerful gather together, the weak and the poor feel oppressed by their inferior condition. Unable to see a single chance of regaining their equality, they give themselves up to despair and allow themselves to fall below the dignity of human nature.

This unfortunate effect of the disparity of conditions is not to be seen in savage life: the Indians, although ignorant and poor, are equal and free. When Europeans first came among them, the natives of North America had no notion of the value of riches, and were indifferent to the pleasures that civilized man secures for himself through them. Nevertheless there was nothing coarse in their bearing; they practiced a habitual reserve and a kind of aristocratic politeness. Mild and hospitable in peace, though merciless in war beyond any known degree of human ferocity, the Indian would risk dying of hunger to aid the stranger who asked admittance by night at the door of his hut; yet he could tear with his hands the still-quivering limbs of his prisoner. The famous republics of antiquity never gave examples of more unshakable courage, prouder spirits, or more unyielding love of independence than were once hidden among the wild forests of the New World. *i The Europeans made no great impression when they landed on the shores of North America; their presence aroused neither envy nor fear. What influence could they possess over such men as we have described? The Indian could live without wants, suffer without complaint, and pour out his death-song at the stake. *j Like all other members of the great human family, these savages believed in the existence of a better world, and worshiped, under different names, God, the creator of the universe. Their ideas on the great intellectual truths were in general simple and philosophical. *k

i [ We learn from President Jefferson's "Notes upon Virginia," p. 148, that among the Iroquois, when attacked by a superior force, aged men refused to fly or to survive the destruction of their country; and they braved death like the ancient Romans when their capital was sacked by the Gauls. Further on, p. 150, he tells us that there is no example of an Indian who, having fallen into the hands of his enemies, begged for his life; on the contrary, the captive sought to obtain death at the hands of his conquerors by the use of insult and provocation.]

j [ See "Histoire de la Louisiane," by Lepage Dupratz; Charlevoix, "Histoire de la Nouvelle France"; "Lettres du Rev. G. Hecwelder;" "Transactions of the American Philosophical Society," v. I; Jefferson's "Notes on Virginia," pp. 135-190. What is said by Jefferson is of especial weight, on account of the personal merit of the writer, of his peculiar position, and of the matter-of-fact age in which he lived.]
k [ See Appendix, D.]
Although we have here traced the character of a primitive people, there can be no doubt that another people, more civilized and more advanced in every respect, had preceded it in the same regions.

An obscure tradition that prevailed among the Indians north of the Atlantic tells us that these very tribes once dwelt on the west side of the Mississippi. Along the banks of the Ohio, and throughout the central valley, there are still found today tumuli raised by human hands. On exploring these heaps of earth to their center, one commonly finds human bones, strange instruments, arms, and utensils of all kinds, made of metal or intended for purposes unknown to the present race. The Indians of our time can give no information about the history of this unknown people. Nor did those who lived three hundred years ago, when America was first discovered, leave any accounts from which even a hypothesis could be formed. Tradition—that perishable yet ever-renewed monument of the primitive world—throws no light on the subject. It is an undoubted fact, however, that in this part of the globe thousands of our fellow beings once lived. When they came here, what their origin, their destiny, their history were, and how they perished, no one can tell. How strange it seems that nations have existed and then so completely vanished from the earth that the memory of their very names is erased; their languages are lost; their glory has vanished like a sound without an echo—though perhaps there is not one that has not left behind some tomb in memory of its passage. The most lasting monument of human labor is the one that recalls the wretchedness and nothingness of man.

Although the vast country we have been describing was inhabited by many indigenous tribes, it may justly be said that at the time of its discovery by Europeans it formed one great desert. The Indians occupied it without possessing it. It is through agricultural labor that man takes possession of the soil, and the early inhabitants of North America lived by the produce of the hunt. Their implacable prejudices, their uncontrolled passions, their vices, and still more perhaps their savage virtues, consigned them to inevitable destruction. The ruin of these nations began the day Europeans landed on their shores; it has continued ever since, and we are now witnessing its completion. They seem to have been placed by Providence amidst the riches of the New World to enjoy them for a season and then surrender them. Those coasts so admirably suited for commerce and industry; those wide and deep rivers; that inexhaustible valley of the Mississippi—the whole continent, in short—seemed prepared to be the home of a great nation, yet unborn.

In that land the great experiment was to be made by civilized man: the attempt to build society on a new foundation. It was there, for the first time, that theories until then unknown, or deemed impracticable, were to present a spectacle for which the history of the past had not prepared the world.

chapters.title: Chapter II — Origin Of The Anglo-Americans
paragraphs: Origin of the Anglo-Americans, and Its Importance in Relation to Their Future Condition.

After the birth of a human being, his early years are passed obscurely in the toils and pleasures of childhood. As he grows up, the world receives him when his manhood begins, and he comes into contact with his fellows. He is then studied for the first time, and it is imagined that the germ of the vices and the virtues of his mature years is only then formed. This, unless I am mistaken, is a great error. We must begin higher up; we must watch the infant in its mother's arms; we must see the first images the external world casts on the dark mirror of his mind, the first occurrences he witnesses. We must hear the first words that awaken the sleeping powers of thought, and stand by his earliest efforts, if we would understand the prejudices, the habits, and the passions that will rule his life. The entire man is, so to speak, to be seen in the cradle of the child.

The growth of nations presents something analogous to this: they all bear some marks of their origin; and the circumstances that accompanied their birth and contributed to their rise affect the whole course of their existence. If we were able to go back to the elements of states, and to examine the oldest monuments of their history, I have no doubt we should discover the primary cause of the prejudices, the habits, the ruling passions—in short, of all that constitutes what is called the national character. We should then find the explanation of certain customs that now seem at odds with the prevailing manners; of laws that conflict with established principles; and of incoherent opinions here and there to be met with in society, like those fragments of broken chains one sometimes sees hanging from the vault of a building and supporting nothing. This might explain the destinies of certain nations, which seem borne on by an unknown force toward ends of which they themselves are ignorant. But until now, facts have been lacking for research of this kind: the spirit of inquiry has come upon communities only in their later days; and when at last they contemplated their origin, time had already obscured it, or ignorance and pride had adorned it with truth-concealing fables.

America is the only country where it has been possible to witness the natural and tranquil growth of society, and where the influences exerted on the future condition of states by their origin are clearly distinguishable. When the peoples of Europe landed in the New World, their national characteristics were already completely formed; each had a physiognomy of its own; and as they had already reached that stage of civilization at which men are led to study themselves, they have transmitted to us a faithful picture of their opinions, their manners, and their laws. The men of the sixteenth century are almost as well known to us as our contemporaries. America, consequently, exhibits in broad daylight the phenomena that the ignorance or rudeness of earlier ages conceals from our researches. Near enough to the time the states of America were founded to be accurately acquainted with their elements, and sufficiently removed from that period to judge some of their results, the men of our own day seem destined to see further than their predecessors into the chain of human events. Providence has given us a torch our forefathers did not possess, and has allowed us to discern, in the history of the world, fundamental causes that the obscurity of the past concealed from them. If we carefully examine the social and political state of America after studying its history, we shall remain perfectly convinced that not an opinion, not a custom, not a law—I may even say not an event—is on record that the origin of that people will not explain. Readers of this book will find the germ of all that is to follow in this present chapter, and the key to almost the whole work.

The emigrants who came at different times to occupy the territory now covered by the American Union differed from each other in many respects; their aim was not the same, and they governed themselves on different principles. Yet these men had certain features in common, and were all placed in an analogous situation. The tie of language is perhaps the strongest and most durable that can unite mankind. All the emigrants spoke the same tongue; they were all offshoots of the same people. Born in a country that had been agitated for centuries by the struggles of faction, and in which all parties had been obliged in turn to place themselves under the protection of the laws, their political education had been perfected in this rough school, and they were more conversant with the notions of right and the principles of true freedom than the greater part of their European contemporaries. At the time of their first emigrations, the parish system—that fruitful germ of free institutions—was deeply rooted in the habits of the English; and with it the doctrine of the sovereignty of the people had been introduced into the bosom of the monarchy of the House of Tudor.

The religious quarrels that have agitated the Christian world were then at their height. England had plunged into the new order of things with headlong vehemence. The character of its inhabitants, which had always been sedate and reflective, became argumentative and austere. General knowledge had been increased by intellectual debate, and the mind had received a deeper cultivation. While religion was the topic of discussion, the morals of the people were reformed. All these national features are more or less discernible in the physiognomy of the adventurers who came to seek a new home on the opposite shores of the Atlantic.

Another observation, to which we shall have occasion to return, applies not only to the English but to the French, the Spaniards, and all the Europeans who successively established themselves in the New World. All these European colonies contained the elements, if not the full development, of a complete democracy. Two causes led to this result. It may safely be said that on leaving the mother country the emigrants generally had no notion of superiority over one another. The happy and the powerful do not go into exile, and there are no surer guarantees of equality among men than poverty and misfortune. It did happen, however, on several occasions, that persons of rank were driven to America by political and religious quarrels. Laws were made to establish a gradation of ranks; but it was soon found that the soil of America was hostile to a territorial aristocracy. To bring that stubborn land into cultivation, the constant and self-interested exertions of the owner himself were necessary; and when the ground was prepared, its produce proved insufficient to enrich a master and a farmer at the same time. The land was then naturally broken up into small portions that the owner cultivated for himself. Land is the basis of an aristocracy, which clings to the soil that supports it; for an aristocracy is constituted not by privileges alone, nor by birth, but by landed property handed down from generation to generation. A nation may display immense fortunes and extreme wretchedness, but unless those fortunes are territorial there is no aristocracy—only the class of the rich and that of the poor.

All the British colonies had, then, a great degree of similarity at the time of their settlement. All of them, from the first, seemed destined to witness the growth, not of the aristocratic liberty of their mother country, but of that freedom of the middle and lower orders of which the history of the world had as yet furnished no complete example.

Within this general uniformity, however, several striking differences can be observed, which it is necessary to point out. Two branches may be distinguished in the Anglo-American family, which have grown up so far without completely mingling: one in the South, the other in the North.

Virginia received the first English colony; the emigrants took possession of it in 1607. The idea that mines of gold and silver are the sources of national wealth was at that time peculiarly prevalent in Europe—a fatal delusion, which has done more to impoverish the nations that adopted it, and has cost more lives in America, than the combined influence of war and bad laws. The men sent to Virginia *a were seekers of gold, adventurers without resources and without character, whose turbulent and restless spirit endangered the infant colony *b and made its progress uncertain. The artisans and farmers arrived afterwards; and although they were a more moral and orderly group of men, they were in no way above the level of the lower classes in England. *c No lofty conceptions, no intellectual system, guided the foundation of these new settlements. The colony was scarcely established when slavery was introduced, *d and this was the main circumstance that has exercised so prodigious an influence on the character, the laws, and all the future prospects of the South. Slavery, as we shall later show, dishonors labor; it introduces idleness into society, and with idleness, ignorance and pride, luxury and distress. It enervates the powers of the mind and numbs the activity of man. The influence of slavery, combined with the English character, explains the manners and social condition of the Southern States.

a [ The charter granted by the Crown of England in 1609 stipulated, amongst other conditions, that the adventurers should pay to the Crown a fifth of the produce of all gold and silver mines. See Marshall's "Life of Washington," vol. i. pp. 18-66.] [Footnote b: A large portion of the adventurers, says Stith ("History of Virginia"), were unprincipled young men of family, whom their parents were glad to ship off, discharged servants, fraudulent bankrupts, or debauchees; and others of the same class, people more apt to pillage and destroy than to assist the settlement, were the seditious chiefs, who easily led this band into every kind of extravagance and excess. See for the history of Virginia the following works:—
"History of Virginia, from the First Settlements in the year 1624," by Smith.
"History of Virginia," by William Stith.
"History of Virginia, from the Earliest Period," by Beverley.]
c [ It was not till some time later that a certain number of rich English capitalists came to fix themselves in the colony.]
d [ Slavery was introduced about the year 1620 by a Dutch vessel which landed twenty negroes on the banks of the river James. See Chalmer.]

In the North, the same English foundation was modified by the most opposite shades of character; and here I may be allowed to enter into some details. The two or three main ideas that form the basis of the social theory of the United States were first combined in the Northern English colonies, more commonly called the States of New England. *e The principles of New England spread first to the neighboring states; they then passed successively to the more distant ones; and at length they imbued the whole Confederation. They now extend their influence beyond its limits over the whole American world. The civilization of New England has been like a beacon lit upon a hill, which, after diffusing its warmth around, tinges the distant horizon with its glow.
e [ The States of New England are those situated to the east of the Hudson; they are now six in number: 1, Connecticut; 2, Rhode Island; 3, Massachusetts; 4, Vermont; 5, New Hampshire; 6, Maine.]

The founding of New England was a novel spectacle, and all the circumstances attending it were singular and original. The large majority of colonies have been first inhabited either by men without education and without resources, driven by their poverty and their misconduct from the land that gave them birth, or by speculators and adventurers greedy for gain. Some settlements cannot even boast so honorable an origin; St. Domingo was founded by buccaneers, and the criminal courts of England originally supplied the population of Australia.

The settlers who established themselves on the shores of New England all belonged to the more independent classes of their native country. Their union on the soil of America at once presented the singular phenomenon of a society containing neither lords nor common people, neither rich nor poor. These men possessed, in proportion to their number, a greater mass of intelligence than is to be found in any European nation of our own time. All, without a single exception, had received a good education, and many of them were known in Europe for their talents and their attainments. The other colonies had been founded by adventurers without families; the emigrants of New England brought with them the best elements of order and morality—they landed in the wilderness accompanied by their wives and children. But what most especially distinguished them was the aim of their undertaking. They had not been forced by necessity to leave their country; the social position they abandoned was one to be regretted, and their means of subsistence were secure. Nor did they cross the Atlantic to improve their situation or to increase their wealth; the call that summoned them from the comforts of their homes was purely intellectual, and in facing the inevitable sufferings of exile their object was the triumph of an idea.

The emigrants, or, as they deservedly styled themselves, the Pilgrims, belonged to that English sect whose austere principles had earned them the name of Puritans. Puritanism was not merely a religious doctrine; it corresponded in many points with the most absolute democratic and republican theories. It was this tendency that had aroused its most dangerous adversaries. Persecuted by the Government of the mother country, and disgusted by the habits of a society opposed to the rigor of their own principles, the Puritans went forth to seek some rude and unfrequented part of the world where they could live according to their own opinions and worship God in freedom.

A few quotations will throw more light on the spirit of these pious adventurers than all we can say of them. Nathaniel Morton, *f the historian of the first years of the settlement, opens his subject thus:
f [ "New England's Memorial," p. 13; Boston, 1826. See also "Hutchinson's History," vol. ii. p. 440.]

"Gentle Reader,—I have for some length of time looked upon it as a duty incumbent, especially on the immediate successors of those that have had so large experience of those many memorable and signal demonstrations of God's goodness, viz., the first beginners of this Plantation in New England, to commit to writing his gracious dispensations on that behalf; having so many inducements thereunto, not onely otherwise but so plentifully in the Sacred Scriptures: that so, what we have seen, and what our fathers have told us (Psalm lxxviii. 3, 4), we may not hide from our children, showing to the generations to come the praises of the Lord; that especially the seed of Abraham his servant, and the children of Jacob his chosen (Psalm cv. 5, 6), may remember his marvellous works in the beginning and progress of the planting of New England, his wonders and the judgments of his mouth; how that God brought a vine into this wilderness; that he cast out the heathen, and planted it; that he made room for it and caused it to take deep root; and it filled the land (Psalm lxxx. 8, 9). And not onely so, but also that he hath guided his people by his strength to his holy habitation and planted them in the mountain of his inheritance in respect of precious Gospel enjoyments: and that as especially God may have the glory of all unto whom it is most due; so also some rays of glory may reach the names of those blessed Saints that were the main instruments and the beginning of this happy enterprise."

It is impossible to read this opening paragraph without an involuntary feeling of religious awe; it breathes the very savor of Gospel antiquity. The sincerity of the author heightens his power of language. The band that in his eyes was a mere party of adventurers gone forth to seek their fortune beyond the seas appears to the reader as the germ of a great nation borne by Providence to a predestined shore.
The author then continues his narrative of the departure of the first pilgrims:—

"So they left that goodly and pleasant city of Leyden, *g which had been their resting-place for above eleven years; but they knew that they were pilgrims and strangers here below, and looked not much on these things, but lifted up their eyes to Heaven, their dearest country, where God hath prepared for them a city (Heb. xi. 16), and therein quieted their spirits. When they came to Delfs-Haven they found the ship and all things ready; and such of their friends as could not come with them followed after them, and sundry came from Amsterdam to see them shipt, and to take their leaves of them. One night was spent with little sleep with the most, but with friendly entertainment and Christian discourse, and other real expressions of true Christian love. The next day they went on board, and their friends with them, where truly doleful was the sight of that sad and mournful parting, to hear what sighs and sobs and prayers did sound amongst them; what tears did gush from every eye, and pithy speeches pierced each other's heart, that sundry of the Dutch strangers that stood on the Key as spectators could not refrain from tears. But the tide (which stays for no man) calling them away, that were thus loth to depart, their Reverend Pastor falling down on his knees, and they all with him, with watery cheeks commended them with most fervent prayers unto the Lord and his blessing; and then, with mutual embraces and many tears they took their leaves one of another, which proved to be the last leave to many of them."

g [ The emigrants were, for the most part, godly Christians from the North of England, who had quitted their native country because they were "studious of reformation, and entered into covenant to walk with one another according to the primitive pattern of the Word of God." They emigrated to Holland, and settled in the city of Leyden in 1610, where they abode, being lovingly respected by the Dutch, for many years: they left it in 1620 for several reasons, the last of which was, that their posterity would in a few generations become Dutch, and so lose their interest in the English nation; they being desirous rather to enlarge His Majesty's dominions, and to live under their natural prince.—Translator's Note.]

The emigrants numbered about 150, including the women and the children. Their object was to plant a colony on the shores of the Hudson; but after being driven about for some time in the Atlantic Ocean, they were forced to land on that arid coast of New England which is now the site of the town of Plymouth. The rock on which the pilgrims disembarked is still shown. *h

h [ This rock is become an object of veneration in the United States. I have seen bits of it carefully preserved in several towns of the Union. Does not this sufficiently show how entirely all human power and greatness is in the soul of man? Here is a stone which the feet of a few outcasts pressed for an instant, and this stone becomes famous; it is treasured by a great nation, its very dust is shared as a relic: and what is become of the gateways of a thousand palaces?]

"But before we pass on," continues our historian, "let the reader with me make a pause and seriously consider this poor people's present condition, the more to be raised up to admiration of God's goodness towards them in their preservation: for being now passed the vast ocean, and a sea of troubles before them in expectation, they had now no friends to welcome them, no inns to entertain or refresh them, no houses, or much less towns to repair unto to seek for succour: and for the season it was winter, and they that know the winters of the country know them to be sharp and violent, subject to cruel and fierce storms, dangerous to travel to known places, much more to search unknown coasts. Besides, what could they see but a hideous and desolate wilderness, full of wilde beasts, and wilde men? and what multitudes of them there were, they then knew not: for which way soever they turned their eyes (save upward to Heaven) they could have but little solace or content in respect of any outward object; for summer being ended, all things stand in appearance with a weather-beaten face, and the whole country full of woods and thickets, represented a wild and savage hew; if they looked behind them, there was the mighty ocean which they had passed, and was now as a main bar or gulph to separate them from all the civil parts of the world."

It must not be imagined that the piety of the Puritans was merely speculative, or that it took no notice of the course of worldly affairs. Puritanism, as I have already remarked, was scarcely less a political than a religious doctrine. No sooner had the emigrants landed on the barren coast described by Nathaniel Morton than their first care was to constitute a society, by passing the following Act:

"In the name of God. Amen. We, whose names are underwritten, the loyal subjects of our dread Sovereign Lord King James, etc., etc., Having undertaken for the glory of God, and advancement of the Christian Faith, and the honour of our King and country, a voyage to plant the first colony in the northern parts of Virginia; Do by these presents solemnly and mutually, in the presence of God and one another, covenant and combine ourselves together into a civil body politick, for our better ordering and preservation, and furtherance of the ends aforesaid: and by virtue hereof do enact, constitute and frame such just and equal laws, ordinances, acts, constitutions, and officers, from time to time, as shall be thought most meet and convenient for the general good of the Colony: unto which we promise all due submission and obedience," etc. *i

i [ The emigrants who founded the State of Rhode Island in 1638, those who landed at New Haven in 1637, the first settlers in Connecticut in 1639, and the founders of Providence in 1640, began in like manner by drawing up a social contract, which was acceded to by all the interested parties. See "Pitkin's History," pp. 42 and 47.]

This happened in 1620, and from that time onward the emigration continued. The religious and political passions that ravaged the British Empire throughout the reign of Charles I drove fresh crowds of sectarians to the shores of America every year. In England the stronghold of Puritanism was the middle class, and it was from the middle class that most of the emigrants came. The population of New England grew rapidly; and while the hierarchy of rank despotically classed the inhabitants of the mother country, the colony continued to present the novel spectacle of a community homogeneous in all its parts. A democracy more perfect than any antiquity had dreamed of sprang up, full grown and in full armor, from the midst of an ancient feudal society.

The English Government was not displeased with an emigration that removed the elements of fresh discord and further revolutions. On the contrary, everything was done to encourage it, and great efforts were made to ease the hardships of those who sought shelter from the rigor of their country's laws on the soil of America. It seemed as if New England was a region given over to the dreams of fancy and to the unrestrained experiments of innovators.

The English colonies (and this is one of the main causes of their prosperity) have always enjoyed more internal freedom and more political independence than the colonies of other nations; but nowhere was this principle of liberty more extensively applied than in the States of New England.

It was generally held at that time that the territories of the New World belonged to whichever European nation had first discovered them. Nearly the whole coast of North America thus became a British possession toward the end of the sixteenth century. The means used by the English Government to people these new domains were of several kinds. Sometimes the King appointed a governor of his own choice, who ruled a portion of the New World in the name and under the direct orders of the Crown; *j this is the colonial system adopted by other countries of Europe. Sometimes grants of particular tracts were made by the Crown to an individual or to a company, *k in which case all civil and political power fell into the hands of one or more persons, who, under the inspection and control of the Crown, sold the lands and governed the inhabitants. Finally, a third system consisted in allowing a certain number of emigrants to constitute a political society under the protection of the mother country, and to govern themselves in whatever was not contrary to her laws. This mode of colonization, so remarkably favorable to liberty, was only adopted in New England. *l
j [ This was the case in the State of New York.]
k [ Maryland, the Carolinas, Pennsylvania, and New Jersey were in this situation. See "Pitkin's History," vol. i. pp. 11-31.]

l [ See the work entitled "Historical Collection of State Papers and other authentic Documents intended as materials for a History of the United States of America, by Ebenezer Hasard. Philadelphia, 1792," for a great number of documents relating to the commencement of the colonies, which are valuable from their contents and their authenticity: amongst them are the various charters granted by the King of England, and the first acts of the local governments.

See also the analysis of all these charters given by Mr. Story, Judge of the Supreme Court of the United States, in the Introduction to his "Commentary on the Constitution of the United States." It results from these documents that the principles of representative government and the external forms of political liberty were introduced into all the colonies at their origin. These principles were more fully acted upon in the North than in the South, but they existed everywhere.]

In 1628 *m a charter of this kind was granted by Charles I to the emigrants who went to form the colony of Massachusetts. But in general, charters were not given to the colonies of New England until they had acquired a certain existence. Plymouth, Providence, New Haven, the State of Connecticut, and that of Rhode Island *n were founded without the cooperation and almost without the knowledge of the mother country. The new settlers did not derive their incorporation from the seat of the empire, although they did not deny its supremacy; they constituted a society of their own accord, and it was not until thirty or forty years later, under Charles II, that their existence was legally recognized by a royal charter.
m [ See "Pitkin's History," p, 35. See the "History of the Colony of Massachusetts Bay," by Hutchinson, vol. i. p. 9.] [Footnote n: See "Pitkin's History," pp. 42, 47.]

This often makes it difficult to detect the link that connected the emigrants with the land of their forefathers when one studies the earliest historical and legislative records of New England. They exercised the rights of sovereignty; they named their magistrates, concluded peace or declared war, made police regulations, and enacted laws as though their allegiance were due only to God. *o Nothing can be more curious—and at the same time more instructive—than the legislation of that period; it is there that the solution of the great social problem the United States now present to the world is to be found.

o [ The inhabitants of Massachusetts had deviated from the forms which are preserved in the criminal and civil procedure of England; in 1650 the decrees of justice were not yet headed by the royal style. See Hutchinson, vol. i. p. 452.]

Among these documents we shall notice, as especially characteristic, the code of laws promulgated by the little State of Connecticut in 1650. *p The legislators of Connecticut *q begin with the penal laws, and, strange to say, they borrow their provisions from the text of Holy Writ. "Whosoever shall worship any other God than the Lord," says the preamble of the Code, "shall surely be put to death." This is followed by ten or twelve enactments of the same kind, copied verbatim from the books of Exodus, Leviticus, and Deuteronomy. Blasphemy, sorcery, adultery, *r and rape were punished with death; an outrage offered by a son to his parents was to be expiated by the same penalty. The legislation of a rude and half-civilized people was thus applied to an enlightened and moral community. The consequence was that the punishment of death was never more frequently prescribed by the statute, and never more rarely enforced against the guilty.
p [ Code of 1650, p. 28; Hartford, 1830.]

q [ See also in "Hutchinson's History," vol. i. pp. 435, 456, the analysis of the penal code adopted in 1648 by the Colony of Massachusetts: this code is drawn up on the same principles as that of Connecticut.]

r [ Adultery was also punished with death by the law of Massachusetts: and Hutchinson, vol. i. p. 441, says that several persons actually suffered for this crime. He quotes a curious anecdote on this subject, which occurred in the year 1663. A married woman had had criminal intercourse with a young man; her husband died, and she married the lover. Several years had elapsed, when the public began to suspect the previous intercourse of this couple: they were thrown into prison, put upon trial, and very narrowly escaped capital punishment.]
