The consequence is that if all the secondary officers of the administration conform to the law, society in all its branches proceeds with the greatest uniformity: the difficulty is in compelling the secondary officers of the administration to conform to the law. It may be said that, in general, society has only two methods at its disposal for enforcing the execution of the laws: a discretionary power may be entrusted to a superior officer to direct all the others and to dismiss them in case of disobedience; or the courts of justice may be authorized to inflict judicial penalties on the offender. But these two methods are not always available.

The right of directing a civil officer presupposes the right of dismissing him if he does not obey orders, and of rewarding him by promotion if he fulfills his duties properly. But an elected magistrate can neither be dismissed nor promoted. All elective functions are inalienable until their term has expired. In fact, the elected magistrate has nothing to expect or fear from his constituents; and when all public offices are filled by ballot there can be no chain of official rank, because the double right of commanding and of enforcing obedience can never be vested in the same individual, and because the power of issuing an order can never be joined to that of inflicting a punishment or bestowing a reward.

Communities therefore in which the secondary officers of the government are elected are forced to make great use of judicial penalties as a means of administration. This is not obvious at first sight, for those in power tend to regard the institution of elective officers as one concession, and the subjection of the elected magistrate to the judges of the land as another. They are equally averse to both these innovations; and as they are more strongly pressed to grant the former than the latter, they agree to the election of the magistrate and leave him independent of the judicial power. Yet the second of these measures is the only thing that can possibly counterbalance the first; and it will be found that an elective authority not subject to judicial power will, sooner or later, either elude all control or be destroyed. The courts of justice are the only possible medium between the central power and the administrative bodies; they alone can compel the elected officer to obey, without violating the rights of the elector. The extension of judicial power in the political world ought therefore to be in exact ratio to the extension of elective offices: if these two institutions do not go hand in hand, the State must fall into anarchy or into subjection.

It has always been observed that habits of legal business do not fit men for the exercise of administrative authority. The Americans have borrowed from the English, their fathers, the idea of an institution unknown on the continent of Europe: I mean that of the Justices of the Peace. The Justice of the Peace is a sort of mezzo termine between the magistrate and the man of the world, between the civil officer and the judge. A justice of the peace is a well-informed citizen, though not necessarily versed in the knowledge of the laws. His office simply requires him to execute the police regulations of society; a task in which good sense and integrity are of more value than legal science. The justice introduces into the administration a certain taste for established forms and publicity, which makes him a most unserviceable instrument of despotism; and, on the other hand, he is not blinded by those superstitions that render legal officers unfit members of a government. The Americans have adopted the system of the English justices of the peace, but they have stripped it of the aristocratic character discernible in the mother-country. The Governor of Massachusetts *p appoints a certain number of justices of the peace in every county, whose functions last seven years. *q He also designates three individuals from among the whole body of justices who form in each county what is called the Court of Sessions. The justices take a personal share in public business; they are sometimes entrusted with administrative functions alongside elected officers, *r and they sometimes constitute a tribunal before which the magistrates summarily prosecute a refractory citizen, or the citizens inform against the abuses of the magistrate. But it is in the Court of Sessions that they exercise their most important functions. This court meets twice a year in the county town; in Massachusetts it is empowered to enforce the obedience of the greater number *s of public officers. *t It must be noted that in the State of Massachusetts the Court of Sessions is at once an administrative body, properly so called, and a political tribunal. It has been stated that the county is a purely administrative division. The Court of Sessions presides over that small number of affairs which, as they concern several townships, or all the townships of the county in common, cannot be entrusted to any one of them in particular. *u In all that concerns county business, the duties of the Court of Sessions are purely administrative; and if in its investigations it occasionally borrows the forms of judicial procedure, it is only for its own information, *v or as a guarantee to the community over which it presides. But when the administration of the township is brought before it, it always acts as a judicial body, and in some few cases as an official assembly.
p [ We shall learn later what a Governor is: I shall content myself with noting here that he represents the executive power of the whole State.]
q [ See the Constitution of Massachusetts, chap. II. sect. 1. Section 9; chap. III. Section 3.]

r [ Thus, for example, a stranger arrives in a township from a country where a contagious disease prevails, and he falls ill. Two justices of the peace can, with the assent of the selectmen, order the sheriff of the county to remove him and care for him.—Act of June 22, 1797, vol. i. p. 540.

In general the justices intervene in all the important acts of the administration and give them a semi-judicial character.] [Footnote s: I say the greater number, because certain administrative misdemeanors are brought before ordinary tribunals. If, for instance, a township refuses to make the necessary expenditure for its schools or to appoint a school-committee, it is liable to a heavy fine. But this penalty is pronounced by the Supreme Judicial Court or the Court of Common Pleas. See Act of March 10, 1827, Laws of Massachusetts, vol. iii. p. 190. Or when a township neglects to provide the necessary war-stores.—Act of February 21, 1822: Id., vol. ii. p. 570.]

t [ In their individual capacity the justices of the peace take part in the business of the counties and townships.] [Footnote u: These affairs may be grouped under the following heads:—1. The erection of prisons and courts of justice. 2. The county budget, which is afterwards voted by the State. 3. The distribution of the taxes so voted. 4. The granting of certain patents. 5. The laying down and repair of the country roads.]
v [ Thus, when a road is under consideration, almost all difficulties are settled with the help of the jury.]

The first difficulty is to obtain the obedience of an authority as entirely independent of the general laws of the State as the township is. We have noted that assessors are named annually by the town-meetings to levy the taxes. If a township attempts to evade the payment of the taxes by neglecting to name its assessors, the Court of Sessions condemns it to a heavy penalty. *w The fine is levied on each of the inhabitants; and the sheriff of the county, who is the officer of justice, executes the mandate. Thus it is that in the United States the authority of the Government is mysteriously concealed under the forms of a judicial sentence; and its influence is at the same time reinforced by that irresistible power with which men have invested the formalities of law.
w [ See Act of February 20, 1786, Laws of Massachusetts, vol. i. p. 217.]

These proceedings are easy to follow and to understand. The demands made upon a township are in general plain and precisely defined; they consist of a simple fact without any complication, or of a principle without detailed application. *x But the difficulty increases when it is not the obedience of the township, but that of the town officers, which must be enforced. All the blameworthy actions of which a public officer may be guilty can be reduced to the following heads:

x [ There is an indirect method of enforcing the obedience of a township. Suppose the funds that the law requires for the maintenance of the roads have not been voted; the town surveyor is then authorized, ex officio, to levy the supplies. Since he is personally liable to private individuals for the state of the roads, and indictable before the Court of Sessions, he is sure to exercise the extraordinary right the law gives him against the township. Thus by threatening the officer, the Court of Sessions extracts compliance from the town. See Act of March 5, 1787, Id., vol. i. p. 305.]
He may execute the law without energy or zeal;
He may neglect to execute the law;
He may do what the law forbids him to do.

Only the last two violations of duty can come under the cognizance of a tribunal; a positive and measurable fact is the indispensable basis of an action at law. Thus, if the selectmen fail to fulfill the legal formalities usual at town elections, they may be condemned to pay a fine; *y but when the public officer performs his duty without ability, and when he obeys the letter of the law without zeal or energy, he is at least beyond the reach of judicial interference. The Court of Sessions, even when armed with its official powers, is in this case unable to compel him to a more satisfactory obedience. The fear of removal is the only check on these quasi-offences; and as the Court of Sessions does not create the town authorities, it cannot remove officers whom it does not appoint. Moreover, a perpetual investigation would be required to convict the officer of negligence or lukewarmness; and the Court of Sessions sits only twice a year and then only judges such offences as are brought to its notice. The only security for that active and enlightened obedience which a court of justice cannot impose on public officers lies in the possibility of their arbitrary removal. In France this security is sought in powers exercised by the heads of the administration; in America it is sought in the principle of election.
y [ Laws of Massachusetts, vol. ii. p. 45.]

Thus, to sum up in a few words what I have been showing: if a public officer in New England commits a crime in the exercise of his functions, the ordinary courts of justice are always called upon to pass sentence on him. If he commits a fault in his official capacity, a purely administrative tribunal is empowered to punish him; and, if the matter is important or urgent, the judge supplies the omission of the officer. *z Lastly, if the same individual is guilty of one of those intangible offences of which human justice takes no cognizance, he annually appears before a tribunal from which there is no appeal, which can at once reduce him to insignificance and strip him of his office. This system undoubtedly possesses great advantages, but its execution is attended with a practical difficulty that is worth pointing out.

z [ If, for instance, a township persists in refusing to name its assessors, the Court of Sessions appoints them; and the magistrates thus appointed are invested with the same authority as elected officers. See the Act quoted above, February 20, 1787.]

I have already observed that the administrative tribunal, called the Court of Sessions, has no right of inspection over the town officers. It can only intervene when the conduct of a magistrate is specifically brought to its notice; and this is the delicate part of the system. The Americans of New England are unfamiliar with the office of public prosecutor in the Court of Sessions, *a and it may easily be seen that it could not have been established without difficulty. If an accusing magistrate had merely been appointed in the chief town of each county, and if he had been unassisted by agents in the townships, he would have known no more of what was going on in the county than the members of the Court of Sessions. But to appoint agents in each township would have been to concentrate in his person the most formidable of powers, that of a judicial administration. Moreover, laws are the children of habit, and nothing of the kind exists in the legislation of England. The Americans have therefore divided the offices of inspection and of prosecution, as well as all the other functions of the administration. Grand jurors are required by law to notify the court to which they belong of all the misdemeanors committed in their county. *b There are certain great offences that are officially prosecuted by the States; *c but more often the task of punishing offenders falls to the fiscal officer, whose province it is to receive the fine: thus the treasurer of the township is charged with prosecuting such administrative offences as fall under his notice. But a more specific appeal is made by American legislation to the private interest of the citizen; *d and this great principle is constantly encountered in studying the laws of the United States. American legislators are more apt to give men credit for intelligence than for honesty, and they rely not a little on personal self-interest for the execution of the laws. When an individual is genuinely and perceptibly injured by an administrative abuse, it is natural that his personal interest should induce him to prosecute. But if a legal formality is required which, however useful to the community, is of little importance to individuals, plaintiffs may be less easily found; and thus, by a tacit agreement, the laws may fall into disuse. Reduced by their system to this extremity, the Americans are obliged to encourage informers by giving them a portion of the penalty in certain cases, *e and to secure the execution of the laws by the dangerous expedient of degrading the morals of the people. The only administrative authority above the county magistrates is, properly speaking, that of the Government.
a [ I say the Court of Sessions, because in common courts there is a magistrate who exercises some of the functions of a public prosecutor.]
b [ The grand-jurors are, for instance, bound to inform the court of the bad state of the roads.—Laws of Massachusetts, vol. i. p. 308.]

c [ If, for instance, the treasurer of the county holds back his accounts.—Laws of Massachusetts, vol. i. p. 406.] [Footnote d: Thus, if a private individual is thrown from his carriage or wounded because of the bad state of a road, he can sue the township or the county for damages at the sessions.—Laws of Massachusetts, vol. i. p. 309.]

e [ In cases of invasion or insurrection, if the town-officers neglect to furnish the necessary stores and ammunition for the militia, the township may be condemned to a fine of from $200 to $500. One can easily imagine that in such a case no one might care to prosecute; hence the law adds that any citizen may indict offences of this kind, and that half of the fine shall go to the plaintiff. See Act of March 6, 1810, vol. ii. p. 236. The same clause is frequently met with in the law of Massachusetts. Private individuals are not only urged in this way to prosecute public officers; public officers are encouraged in the same way to bring the disobedience of private individuals to justice. If a citizen refuses to perform the work assigned to him on a road, the road surveyor may prosecute him, and he receives half the penalty for himself. See the Laws cited above, vol. i. p. 308.]

General Remarks On The Administration Of The United States Differences among the States of the Union in their system of administration—Activity and perfection of the local authorities decrease towards the South—Power of the magistrate increases; that of the elector diminishes—Administration passes from the township to the county—States of New York, Ohio, Pennsylvania—Principles of administration applicable to the whole Union—Election of public officers, and inalienability of their functions—Absence of gradation of ranks—Introduction of judicial resources into the administration.

I have already suggested that after examining in detail the constitution of the township and the county of New England, I would take a general view of the rest of the Union. Townships and a local activity exist in every State; but in no part of the confederation is a township to be found precisely like those of New England. The farther we descend towards the South, the less active the business of the township or parish becomes; the number of magistrates, of functions, and of rights decreases; the population exercises a less immediate influence over affairs; town meetings are less frequent, and the subjects of debate less numerous. The power of the elected magistrate is enlarged and that of the elector diminished, while the public spirit of the local communities is less awake and less influential. *f These differences can be detected to some extent in the State of New York; they are very noticeable in Pennsylvania; but they become less striking as we advance to the northwest. The majority of the emigrants who settle in the northwestern States are natives of New England, and they carry the habits of their mother country with them into the one they adopt. A township in Ohio is by no means unlike a township in Massachusetts.
f [ For details see the Revised Statutes of the State of New York, part i. chap. xi. vol. i. pp. 336-364, entitled, "Of the Powers, Duties, and Privileges of Towns."

See in the Digest of the Laws of Pennsylvania, the words Assessors, Collector, Constables, Overseer of the Poor, Supervisors of Highways; and in the Acts of a general nature of the State of Ohio, the Act of February 25, 1834, relating to townships, p. 412; besides the peculiar provisions relating to various town-officers, such as Township's Clerk, Trustees, Overseers of the Poor, Fence Viewers, Appraisers of Property, Township's Treasurer, Constables, Supervisors of Highways.]

We have seen that in Massachusetts the mainspring of public administration lies in the township. It forms the common center of the citizens' interests and affections. But this ceases to be the case as we descend to States where knowledge is less widely diffused, and where the township consequently offers fewer guarantees of a wise and active administration. As we leave New England, therefore, we find that the importance of the town is gradually transferred to the county, which becomes the center of administration, and the intermediate power between the Government and the citizen. In Massachusetts the business of the county is conducted by the Court of Sessions, composed of a quorum named by the Governor and his council; but the county has no representative assembly, and its expenditure is voted by the national legislature. In the great State of New York, on the contrary, and in those of Ohio and Pennsylvania, the inhabitants of each county choose a certain number of representatives, who make up the assembly of the county. *g The county assembly has the right to tax the inhabitants to a certain extent; in this respect it enjoys the privileges of a real legislative body. At the same time it exercises an executive power in the county, frequently directs the administration of the townships, and confines their authority within much narrower bounds than in Massachusetts.

g [ See the Revised Statutes of the State of New York, part i. chap. xi. vol. i. p. 340. Id. chap. xii. p. 366; also in the Acts of the State of Ohio, an act relating to county commissioners, February 25, 1824, p. 263. See the Digest of the Laws of Pennsylvania, at the words County-rates and Levies, p. 170. In the State of New York each township elects a representative, who takes part in the administration of the county as well as in that of the township.]

These are the principal differences the systems of county and town administration present in the Federal States. Were I to examine the provisions of American law in minute detail, I would have to point out still further differences in the executive details of the several communities. But what I have already said may suffice to show the general principles on which the administration of the United States rests. These principles are applied differently; their consequences are more or less numerous in various localities; but they are always substantially the same. The laws differ, and their outward features change, but their character does not vary. If the township and the county are not everywhere constituted in the same way, at least it is true that in the United States the county and the township are always based on the same principle: that everyone is the best judge of what concerns himself alone, and the fittest person to supply his private needs. The township and the county are therefore bound to take care of their special interests: the State governs, but it does not interfere with their administration. Exceptions to this rule may be found, but not a contrary principle.

The first consequence of this doctrine has been to have all the magistrates chosen either by, or at least from among, the citizens. As the officers are everywhere elected or appointed for a limited period, it has been impossible to establish the rules of a dependent chain of authorities; there are almost as many independent functionaries as there are functions, and the executive power is dispersed among a multitude of hands. From this arose the indispensable necessity of introducing the control of the courts of justice over the administration, and the system of pecuniary penalties by which the secondary bodies and their representatives are compelled to obey the laws. This system prevails from one end of the Union to the other. The power of punishing the misconduct of public officers, or of performing the part of the executive in urgent cases, has not, however, been bestowed on the same judges in all the States. The Anglo-Americans drew the institution of justices of the peace from a common source; but although it exists in all the States, it is not always put to the same use. The justices of the peace everywhere take part in the administration of the townships and the counties, *h either as public officers or as judges of public misdemeanors, but in most of the States the more important classes of public offences come under the cognizance of the ordinary tribunals.
h [ In some of the Southern States the county courts are charged with all the details of the administration. See the Statutes of the State of Tennessee, arts. Judiciary, Taxes, etc.]

The election of public officers, or the inalienability of their functions, the absence of a gradation of powers, and the introduction of judicial control over the secondary branches of the administration are the universal features of the American system from Maine to the Floridas. In some States (and that of New York has gone furthest in this direction) traces of a centralized administration begin to be discernible. In the State of New York the officers of the central government exercise, in certain cases, a sort of inspection or control over the secondary bodies. *i

i [ For instance, the direction of public instruction is centered in the hands of the Government. The legislature names the members of the University, who are called Regents; the Governor and Lieutenant-Governor of the State are necessarily of the number.—Revised Statutes, vol. i. p. 455. The Regents of the University annually visit the colleges and academies, and make their report to the legislature. Their superintendence is not ineffective, for several reasons: the colleges, in order to become corporations, need a charter, which is only granted on the recommendation of the Regents; every year funds are distributed by the State for the encouragement of learning, and the Regents are the distributors of this money. See chap. xv. "Instruction," Revised Statutes, vol. i. p. 455.
The school-commissioners are required to send an annual report to the Superintendent of the Republic.—Id. p. 488.
A similar report is made annually to the same person on the number and condition of the poor.—Id. p. 631.]

At other times they constitute a court of appeal for the decision of affairs. *j In the State of New York judicial penalties are less used than in other parts as a means of administration, and the right of prosecuting the offences of public officers is vested in fewer hands. *k The same tendency is faintly observable in some other States; *l but in general the prominent feature of the administration in the United States is its excessive local independence.

j [ If anyone considers himself wronged by the school-commissioners (who are town-officers), he can appeal to the superintendent of the primary schools, whose decision is final.—Revised Statutes, vol. i. p. 487.

Provisions similar to those cited above are to be found from time to time in the laws of the State of New York; but in general these attempts at centralization are weak and unproductive. The great authorities of the State have the right to watch and control the subordinate agents, without the right to reward or punish them. The same individual is never empowered both to give an order and to punish disobedience; he has therefore the right to command, without the means of exacting compliance. In 1830 the Superintendent of Schools complained in his Annual Report to the legislature that several school-commissioners had neglected, despite his requests, to furnish him with the accounts that were due. He added that if this omission continued he would be obliged to prosecute them, as the law directs, before the proper tribunals.]

k [ Thus the district-attorney is directed to recover all fines below the sum of fifty dollars, unless such a right has been specifically awarded to another magistrate.—Revised Statutes, vol. i. p. 383.]

l [ Several traces of centralization may be found in Massachusetts; for instance, the committees of the town-schools are directed to make an annual report to the Secretary of State. See Laws of Massachusetts, vol. i. p. 367.]

I have described the townships and the administration; it now remains for me to speak of the State and the Government. I can pass over this ground rapidly, without fear of being misunderstood; for all I have to say is to be found in the written forms of the various constitutions, which are easily to be obtained. These constitutions rest on a simple and rational theory; their forms have been adopted by all constitutional nations and have become familiar to us. Here, therefore, I need only give a short analysis; I shall try afterwards to pass judgment on what I now describe.
Legislative Power Of The State
Division of the Legislative Body into two Houses—Senate—House of Representatives—Different functions of these two Bodies.

The legislative power of the State is vested in two assemblies, the first of which generally bears the name of the Senate. The Senate is commonly a legislative body; but it sometimes becomes an executive and judicial one. It takes part in the government in several ways, according to the constitution of the different States; *m but it is in the nomination of public officers that it most commonly assumes an executive power. It shares in judicial power in the trial of certain political offences, and sometimes also in the decision of certain civil cases. *n The number of its members is always small. The other branch of the legislature, which is usually called the House of Representatives, has no share whatever in the administration, and only takes part in the judicial power insofar as it impeaches public officers before the Senate. The members of the two Houses are almost everywhere subject to the same conditions of election. They are chosen in the same way, and by the same citizens. The only difference between them is that the term for which the Senate is chosen is in general longer than that of the House of Representatives. The latter seldom remain in office longer than a year; the former usually sit two or three years. By granting senators the privilege of being chosen for several years, and of being renewed in rotation, the law takes care to preserve in the legislative body a nucleus of men already accustomed to public business, and capable of exercising a salutary influence on the junior members.
m [ In Massachusetts the Senate is not invested with any administrative functions.]
n [ As in the State of New York.]

The Americans plainly did not intend, by this separation of the legislative body into two branches, to make one house hereditary and the other elective; one aristocratic and the other democratic. It was not their purpose to create in the one a bulwark to power, while the other represented the interests and passions of the people. The only advantages that result from the present constitution of the United States are the division of the legislative power and the consequent check on political assemblies, together with the creation of a tribunal of appeal for the revision of the laws.

Time and experience, however, have convinced the Americans that if these are its only advantages, the division of the legislative power is still a principle of the greatest necessity. Pennsylvania was the only one of the United States that at first attempted to establish a single House of Assembly, and Franklin himself was so far carried away by the natural consequences of the principle of the sovereignty of the people that he concurred in the measure; but the Pennsylvanians were soon obliged to change the law and to create two Houses. Thus the principle of the division of the legislative power was finally established, and its necessity may henceforth be regarded as a demonstrated truth. This theory, which was nearly unknown to the republics of antiquity—which was introduced into the world almost by accident, like so many other great truths—and misunderstood by several modern nations, has at length become an axiom in the political science of the present age.
[See Benjamin Franklin]
The Executive Power Of The State
Office of Governor in an American State—The place he occupies in relation to the Legislature—His rights and his duties—His dependence on the people.

The executive power of the State may truly be said to be represented by the Governor, although he enjoys only a portion of its rights. The supreme magistrate, under the title of Governor, is the official moderator and counsellor of the legislature. He is armed with a veto or suspensive power, which allows him to stop, or at least to delay, its movements at pleasure. He lays the needs of the country before the legislative body and points out the means he thinks may be usefully employed to meet them; he is the natural executor of its decrees in all undertakings that concern the nation at large. *o In the absence of the legislature, the Governor is bound to take all necessary steps to guard the State against violent shocks and unforeseen dangers. The whole military power of the State is at the Governor's disposal. He is the commander of the militia, and head of the armed force. When the authority which is by general consent awarded to the laws is disregarded, the Governor puts himself at the head of the armed force of the State to quell resistance and restore order. Lastly, the Governor takes no share in the administration of townships and counties, except indirectly in the nomination of Justices of the Peace, a nomination he has not the power to cancel. *p The Governor is an elected magistrate, and is generally chosen for one or two years only; so that he always remains strictly dependent on the majority that returned him.

o [ Practically speaking, it is not always the Governor who executes the plans of the Legislature; it often happens that the latter, in voting a measure, names special agents to superintend its execution.]
p [ In some of the States the justices of the peace are not elected by the Governor.]
Political Effects Of The System Of Local Administration In The United States

Necessary distinction between the general centralization of Government and the centralization of the local administration—Local administration not centralized in the United States: great general centralization of the Government—Some bad consequences resulting to the United States from the local administration—Administrative advantages attending this order of things—The power that conducts the Government is less regular, less enlightened, less learned, but much greater than in Europe—Political advantages of this order of things—In the United States the interests of the country are everywhere kept in view—Support given to the Government by the community—Provincial institutions more necessary as the social condition becomes more democratic—Reason for this.

Centralization has become a word in general and daily use, without any precise meaning attached to it. Nevertheless, there are two distinct kinds of centralization, which must be distinguished with care. Certain interests are common to all parts of a nation, such as the enactment of its general laws and the maintenance of its foreign relations. Other interests are peculiar to certain parts of the nation—such, for instance, as the business of different townships. When the power that directs the general interests is centered in one place, or vested in the same persons, it constitutes a central government. Likewise the power of directing partial or local interests, when brought together into one place, constitutes what may be called a central administration.

On some points these two kinds of centralization coincide; but by classifying the objects that fall more particularly within the province of each, they may easily be distinguished. It is clear that a central government acquires immense power when united to administrative centralization. Combined in this way, it accustoms men to set their own will habitually and completely aside; to submit, not only once, or on one point, but in every respect and at all times. Not only, therefore, does this union of power subdue them by force; it affects them in the ordinary habits of life, and influences each individual, first separately and then collectively.

These two kinds of centralization mutually assist and attract each other; but they must not be supposed to be inseparable. It is impossible to imagine a more completely central government than the one that existed in France under Louis XIV; when the same individual was the author and the interpreter of the laws, and the representative of France at home and abroad, he was justified in asserting that the State was identified with his person. Nevertheless, the administration was much less centralized under Louis XIV than it is today.

In England the centralization of the government is carried to great perfection; the State has the compact vigor of a man, and by the sole act of its will it sets immense engines in motion, and wields or gathers the efforts of its authority. Indeed, I cannot conceive that a nation can enjoy a secure or prosperous existence without a powerful centralization of government. But I am of the opinion that a central administration enervates the nations in which it exists by incessantly diminishing their public spirit. If such an administration succeeds in concentrating at a given moment, on a given point, all the disposable resources of a people, it impairs at least the renewal of those resources. It may ensure a victory in the hour of strife, but it gradually relaxes the sinews of strength. It may contribute admirably to the transient greatness of a man, but it cannot ensure the durable prosperity of a nation.

If we pay proper attention, we shall find that whenever it is said that a State cannot act because it has no central point, it is the centralization of the government in which it is deficient. It is frequently asserted, and we are prepared to accept the claim, that the German empire was never able to bring all its powers into action. But the reason was that the State was never able to enforce obedience to its general laws, because the several members of that great body always claimed the right, or found the means, of refusing their cooperation to the representatives of the common authority, even in affairs that concerned the mass of the people; in other words, because there was no centralization of government. The same remark applies to the Middle Ages; the cause of all the confusion of feudal society was that the control, not only of local but of general interests, was divided among a thousand hands, and broken up in a thousand different ways; the absence of a central government prevented the nations of Europe from advancing with energy in any straightforward course.

We have shown that in the United States there is no central administration and no dependent chain of public officers. Local authority has been carried to lengths no European nation could endure without great inconvenience, and which have even produced some disadvantageous consequences in America. But in the United States the centralization of the Government is complete; and it would be easy to prove that the national power is more compact than it has ever been in the old nations of Europe. Not only is there only one legislative body in each State; not only is there only one source of political authority; but district assemblies and county courts have not in general been multiplied, for fear they might be tempted to exceed their administrative duties and interfere with the Government. In America the legislature of each State is supreme; nothing can impede its authority; neither privileges, nor local immunities, nor personal influence, nor even the empire of reason, since it represents that majority which claims to be the sole organ of reason. Its own determination is therefore the only limit to this action. Alongside it, and under its immediate control, is the representative of the executive power, whose duty is to compel the refractory to submit by superior force. The only symptom of weakness lies in certain details of the Government's action. The American republics have no standing armies to intimidate a discontented minority; but as no minority has yet been reduced to declaring open war, the need for an army has not been felt. *q The State usually employs the officers of the township or the county to deal with the citizens. Thus, for instance, in New England, the assessor fixes the rate of taxes; the collector receives them; the town-treasurer transmits the amount to the public treasury; and the disputes that may arise are brought before the ordinary courts of justice. This method of collecting taxes is slow as well as inconvenient, and it would prove a perpetual hindrance to a Government whose financial demands were large. It is desirable that, in whatever materially affects its existence, the Government should be served by officers of its own, appointed by itself, removable at pleasure, and accustomed to rapid methods of proceeding. But it will always be easy for the central government, organized as it is in America, to introduce new and more effective modes of action, proportioned to its needs. [Footnote q: [The Civil War of 1860-65 cruelly belied this statement, and in the course of the struggle the North alone called two and a half million men to arms; but to the honor of the United States it must be added that, with the cessation of the contest, this army disappeared as rapidly as it had been raised.—Translator's Note.]]

The absence of a central government will not, then, as has often been asserted, prove the destruction of the republics of the New World; far from supposing that the American governments are not sufficiently centralized, I shall prove later that they are too much so. The legislative bodies daily encroach on the authority of the Government, and their tendency, like that of the French Convention, is to appropriate it entirely to themselves. In these circumstances the social power is constantly changing hands, because it is subordinate to the power of the people, which is too apt to forget the maxims of wisdom and foresight in the consciousness of its strength: from this arises its danger; and thus its vigor, not its impotence, will probably be the cause of its ultimate destruction.

The system of local administration produces several different effects in America. The Americans seem to me to have overstepped the limits of sound policy in isolating the administration of the Government; for order, even in second-rate affairs, is a matter of national importance. *r As the State has no administrative officers of its own, stationed at different points of its territory, to whom it can give a common impulse, the consequence is that it rarely attempts to issue any general police regulations. The lack of these regulations is keenly felt and is frequently remarked upon by Europeans. The appearance of disorder that prevails on the surface leads him at first to imagine that society is in a state of anarchy; nor does he perceive his mistake until he has gone deeper into the subject. Certain undertakings are of importance to the whole State; but they cannot be carried out, because there is no national administration to direct them. Abandoned to the exertions of the towns or counties, under the care of elected or temporary agents, they lead to no result, or at least to no durable benefit.

r [ The authority that represents the State ought not, I think, to give up the right of inspecting the local administration, even when it does not interfere more actively. Suppose, for instance, that an agent of the Government were stationed at some appointed spot in the country, to prosecute the misdemeanors of the town and county officers: would not a more uniform order result, without in any way compromising the independence of the township? Nothing of the kind, however, exists in America: there is nothing above the county-courts, which have, as it were, only an incidental cognizance of the offences they are meant to repress.]

The partisans of centralization in Europe are accustomed to maintain that the Government directs the affairs of each locality better than the citizens could do it for themselves; this may be true when the central power is enlightened and the local districts are ignorant; when it is as alert as they are slow; when it is accustomed to act, and they to obey. Indeed, it is obvious that this double tendency must grow with the increase of centralization, and that the readiness of the one and the incapacity of the others must become more and more prominent. But I deny that such is the case when the people is as enlightened, as alert to its interests, and as accustomed to reflect on them, as the Americans are. I am persuaded, on the contrary, that in this case the collective strength of the citizens will always promote the public welfare more effectively than the authority of the Government. It is difficult to point out with certainty the means of arousing a sleeping population, and of giving it passions and knowledge it does not possess; it is, I am well aware, an arduous task to persuade men to busy themselves about their own affairs; and it would often be easier to interest them in the niceties of court etiquette than in the repairs of their common dwelling. But whenever a central administration presumes to replace the persons most interested, I am inclined to suppose that it is either misled or wishes to mislead. However enlightened and however skilful a central power may be, it cannot of itself embrace all the details of the existence of a great nation. Such vigilance exceeds the powers of man. And when it attempts to create and set in motion so many complicated springs, it must submit to a very imperfect result, or consume itself in futile efforts.

Centralization succeeds more easily, indeed, in subjecting the external actions of men to a certain uniformity, which at least commands our regard, independently of the objects to which it is applied, like those devotees who worship the statue and forget the deity it represents. Centralization imparts without difficulty an admirable regularity to the routine of business; it provides for the details of the social police with shrewdness; represses the smallest disorder and the most petty misdemeanors; maintains society in a status quo alike secure from improvement and decline; and perpetuates a drowsy precision in the conduct of affairs, which is hailed by the heads of the administration as a sign of perfect order and public tranquillity: *s in short, it excels more in prevention than in action. Its force deserts it when society is to be disturbed or accelerated in its course; and once the cooperation of private citizens is necessary to the furtherance of its measures, the secret of its impotence is revealed. Even while it invokes their assistance, it is on condition that they shall act exactly as much as the Government chooses, and exactly in the manner it appoints. They are to take charge of the details, without aspiring to guide the system; they are to work in a dark and subordinate sphere, and to judge the acts in which they have themselves cooperated only by their results. These, however, are not conditions on which the alliance of the human will is to be obtained; its carriage must be free and its actions responsible, or (such is the constitution of man) the citizen would rather remain a passive spectator than a dependent actor in schemes with which he is unacquainted.

s [ China appears to me to present the most perfect instance of that species of well-being which a completely central administration may furnish to the nations among which it exists. Travellers assure us that the Chinese have peace without happiness, industry without improvement, stability without strength, and public order without public morality. The condition of society is always tolerable, never excellent. I am convinced that, when China is opened to European observation, it will be found to contain the most perfect model of a central administration that exists in the universe.]

It is undeniable that the lack of those uniform regulations which control the conduct of every inhabitant of France is not infrequently felt in the United States. Gross instances of social indifference and neglect are to be met with, and from time to time disgraceful blemishes appear in complete contrast with the surrounding civilization. Useful undertakings that cannot succeed without perpetual attention and rigorous exactitude are very often abandoned in the end; for in America, as in other countries, the people is subject to sudden impulses and momentary exertions. The European, accustomed to finding a functionary always at hand to interfere with all he undertakes, has some difficulty accustoming himself to the complex mechanism of the administration of the townships. In general it may be said that the lesser details of the police, which make life easy and comfortable, are neglected in America; but that the essential guarantees of man in society are as strong there as elsewhere. In America the power that conducts the Government is far less regular, less enlightened, and less learned, but a hundredfold more authoritative than in Europe. In no country in the world do the citizens make such exertions for the common good; and I know of no people that has established schools as numerous and as effective, places of public worship better suited to the needs of the inhabitants, or roads kept in better repair. Uniformity or permanence of design, the minute arrangement of details, *t and the perfection of an ingenious administration, must not be sought in the United States; but it will be easy to find, on the other hand, the signs of a power which, if it is somewhat barbarous, is at least robust; and of an existence which is checkered with accidents indeed, but cheered at the same time by animation and effort.

t [ A writer of talent who, in the comparison he has drawn between the finances of France and those of the United States, has proved that ingenuity cannot always supply the place of a knowledge of facts, very justly reproaches the Americans for the sort of confusion that exists in the accounts of expenditure in the townships; and after giving the model of a departmental budget in France, he adds:—"We are indebted to centralization, that admirable invention of a great man, for the uniform order and method that prevail alike in all the municipal budgets, from the largest town to the humblest commune." Whatever my admiration of this result may be, when I see the communes of France, with their excellent system of accounts, sunk in the grossest ignorance of their true interests, and abandoned to so incorrigible an apathy that they seem to vegetate rather than to live; when, on the other hand, I observe the activity, the information, and the spirit of enterprise that keep society in perpetual labor in those American townships whose budgets are drawn up with little method and with still less uniformity, I am struck by the spectacle; for to my mind the end of a good government is to ensure the welfare of a people, and not to establish order and regularity in the midst of its misery and distress. I am therefore led to suppose that the prosperity of the American townships and the apparent confusion of their accounts, the distress of the French communes and the perfection of their budget, may be attributable to the same cause. At any rate I am suspicious of a benefit that is united to so many evils, and I am not averse to an evil that is compensated by so many benefits.]

Granting for a moment that the villages and counties of the United States would be more usefully governed by a remote authority they had never seen than by officers drawn from their own midst—admitting, for the sake of argument, that the country would be more secure, and the resources of society better employed, if the whole administration were centered in a single arm—still the political advantages the Americans derive from their system would induce me to prefer it to the contrary plan. It profits me little, after all, that a vigilant authority should protect the tranquillity of my pleasures and constantly ward off all dangers from my path, without my care or concern, if that same authority is the absolute mistress of my liberty and of my life, and if it so monopolizes all the energy of existence that when it languishes everything languishes around it, that when it sleeps everything must sleep, that when it dies the State itself must perish.

In certain countries of Europe the natives regard themselves as a kind of settlers, indifferent to the fate of the spot on which they live. The greatest changes are carried out without their participation and (unless chance happens to inform them of the event) without their knowledge; more than that, the citizen is unconcerned about the condition of his village, the policing of his street, the repairs of the church or of the parsonage; for he looks upon all these things as unconnected with himself, and as the property of a powerful stranger whom he calls the Government. He has only a life-interest in these possessions, and he entertains no notion of ownership or of improvement. This lack of interest in his own affairs goes so far that, if his own safety or that of his children is endangered, instead of trying to avert the peril, he will fold his arms and wait for the nation to come to his assistance. This same individual, who has so completely sacrificed his own free will, has no natural propensity to obedience; he cowers, it is true, before the pettiest officer; but he defies the law with the spirit of a conquered foe as soon as its superior force is withdrawn: his oscillations between servitude and license are perpetual. When a nation has reached this state, it must either change its customs and its laws or perish: the source of public virtue is dry, and though it may contain subjects, the race of citizens is extinct. Such communities are a natural prey to foreign conquests, and if they do not disappear from the scene of life, it is because they are surrounded by other nations similar or inferior to themselves; it is because the instinctive feeling of their country's claims still lives in their hearts; and because an involuntary pride in the name it bears, or a vague memory of its bygone fame, is enough to give them the impulse of self-preservation.

Nor can the prodigious exertions made by tribes in the defense of a country to which they did not belong be cited in favor of such a system; for it will be found that in these cases their main incitement was religion. The permanence, the glory, or the prosperity of the nation had become parts of their faith, and in defending the country they inhabited, they defended that Holy City of which they were all citizens. The Turkish tribes never took an active share in the conduct of public affairs, yet they accomplished stupendous enterprises as long as the victories of the Sultan were the triumphs of the Mohammedan faith. In the present age they are in rapid decay, because their religion is departing, and despotism alone remains. Montesquieu, who attributed to absolute power an authority peculiar to itself, did it, as I conceive, an undeserved honor; for despotism, taken by itself, can produce no durable results. On close inspection we shall find that religion, and not fear, has always been the cause of the long-lived prosperity of an absolute government. Whatever exertions may be made, no true power can be founded among men that does not depend on the free union of their inclinations; and patriotism and religion are the only two motives in the world which can permanently direct the whole of a body politic to one end.

Laws cannot succeed in rekindling the ardor of an extinguished faith, but men may be interested in the fate of their country by the laws. Through this influence the vague impulse of patriotism, which never abandons the human heart, may be directed and revived; and if it is connected with the thoughts, the passions, and the daily habits of life, it may be consolidated into a durable and rational sentiment.

Let it not be said that the time for the experiment is already past; for the old age of nations is not like the old age of men, and every fresh generation is a new people ready for the care of the legislator.

It is not the administrative but the political effects of the local system that I most admire in America. In the United States the interests of the country are everywhere kept in view; they are an object of solicitude to the people of the whole Union, and every citizen is as warmly attached to them as if they were his own. He takes pride in the glory of his nation; he boasts of its success, to which he believes he has contributed, and he rejoices in the general prosperity by which he profits. The feeling he entertains towards the State is analogous to the one that unites him to his family, and it is by a kind of egotism that he interests himself in the welfare of his country.

The European generally submits to a public officer because he represents a superior force; but to an American he represents a right. In America it may be said that no one renders obedience to man, but to justice and to law. If the opinion the citizen holds of himself is exaggerated, it is at least salutary; he unhesitatingly trusts his own powers, which appear to him to be all-sufficient. When a private individual plans an undertaking, however directly connected it may be with the welfare of society, he never thinks of requesting the cooperation of the Government, but he publishes his plan, offers to execute it himself, seeks the help of other individuals, and struggles manfully against all obstacles. No doubt he is often less successful than the State might have been in his position; but in the end the sum of these private undertakings far exceeds all that the Government could have done.

As the administrative authority is within the reach of the citizens, whom it in some degree represents, it arouses neither their jealousy nor their hatred; as its resources are limited, every one feels that he must not rely on its assistance alone. Thus, when the administration sees fit to intervene, it is not abandoned to itself as in Europe; the duties of private citizens are not supposed to have lapsed because the State helps in their fulfillment; on the contrary, every one is ready to guide and support it. This action of individual exertions, joined to that of the public authorities, frequently performs what the most energetic central administration would be unable to execute. It would be easy to cite several facts in proof of what I advance, but I had rather give only one, with which I am more thoroughly acquainted. *u In America the means the authorities have at their disposal for the discovery of crimes and the arrest of criminals are few. The State police does not exist, and passports are unknown. The criminal police of the United States cannot be compared to that of France; the magistrates and public prosecutors are not numerous, and the examinations of prisoners are rapid and oral. Nevertheless in no country does crime more rarely elude punishment. The reason is that every one conceives himself to be interested in furnishing evidence of the act committed, and in stopping the offender. During my stay in the United States I witnessed the spontaneous formation of committees for the pursuit and prosecution of a man who had committed a great crime in a certain county. In Europe a criminal is an unhappy being who is struggling for his life against the ministers of justice, while the population is merely a spectator of the conflict; in America he is looked upon as an enemy of the human race, and the whole of mankind is against him.
u [ See Appendix, I.]

I believe that provincial institutions are useful to all nations, but nowhere do they appear to me more indispensable than among a democratic people. In an aristocracy order can always be maintained in the midst of liberty, and as the rulers have a great deal to lose, order is to them a first-rate consideration. In the same way an aristocracy protects the people from the excesses of despotism, because it always possesses an organized power ready to resist a despot. But a democracy without provincial institutions has no security against these evils. How can a populace unaccustomed to freedom in small concerns learn to use it temperately in great affairs? What resistance can be offered to tyranny in a country where every private individual is powerless, and where the citizens are united by no common tie? Those who dread the license of the mob, and those who fear the rule of absolute power, ought alike to desire the progressive growth of provincial liberties.

On the other hand, I am convinced that democratic nations are most exposed to fall beneath the yoke of a central administration, for several reasons, among which is the following. The constant tendency of these nations is to concentrate all the strength of the Government in the hands of the only power that directly represents the people, because beyond the people nothing can be perceived but a mass of equal individuals merged together. But when the same power is already in possession of all the attributes of the Government, it can scarcely refrain from penetrating into the details of the administration, and an opportunity of doing so is sure to present itself in the end, as was the case in France. In the French Revolution there were two impulses in opposite directions, which must never be confused—one was favorable to liberty, the other to despotism. Under the ancient monarchy the King was the sole author of the laws, and beneath the power of the sovereign certain vestiges of provincial institutions, half-destroyed, were still discernible. These provincial institutions were incoherent, ill-compacted, and frequently absurd; in the hands of the aristocracy they had sometimes been turned into instruments of oppression. The Revolution declared itself the enemy of royalty and of provincial institutions at the same time; it confused all that had preceded it—despotic power and the checks on its abuses—in indiscriminate hatred, and its tendency was at once to overthrow and to centralize. This double character of the French Revolution is a fact that has been adroitly handled by the friends of absolute power. Can they be accused of working in the cause of despotism when they are defending that central administration which was one of the great innovations of the Revolution? *v In this way popularity may be reconciled with hostility to the rights of the people, and the secret slave of tyranny may be the professed admirer of freedom.
v [ See Appendix K.]

I have visited the two nations in which the system of provincial liberty has been most perfectly established, and I have listened to the opinions of different parties in those countries. In America I met with men who secretly aspired to destroy the democratic institutions of the Union; in England I found others who attacked the aristocracy openly, but I know of no one who does not regard provincial independence as a great benefit. In both countries I have heard a thousand different causes assigned for the evils of the State, but the local system was never mentioned among them. I have heard citizens attribute the power and prosperity of their country to a multitude of reasons, but they all placed the advantages of local institutions in the foremost rank. Am I to suppose that when men who are naturally so divided on religious opinions and on political theories agree on one point (and that one of which they have daily experience), they are all in error? The only nations that deny the utility of provincial liberties are those that have fewest of them; in other words, those who are unacquainted with the institution are the only persons who pass a censure upon it.

chapters.title: Chapter VI — Judicial Power In The United States
paragraphs: Judicial Power in the United States and Its Influence on Political Society.

I have thought it essential to devote a separate chapter to the judicial authorities of the United States, so that their great political importance will not be diminished in the reader’s eyes by a merely incidental mention. Confederations have existed in countries other than America, and republics have been set up on more than just the shores of the New World. The representative system has been adopted in several European States, but I am not aware of any nation on earth that has organized a judicial power on the principle the Americans have now adopted. The judicial organization of the United States is the institution a foreigner finds hardest to understand. He hears the authority of a judge invoked in the political events of every day, and he naturally concludes that in the United States the judges are important political officials. Yet when he examines the nature of the courts, they offer nothing contrary to the usual habits and privileges of such bodies, and the magistrates seem to him to intervene in public affairs by chance — but by a chance that recurs daily.

When the Parliament of Paris protested, refused to register an edict, or summoned an official accused of corruption to its bar, its political influence as a judicial body was clearly visible. Nothing of the kind is to be seen in the United States. The Americans have kept all the ordinary characteristics of judicial authority and have carefully restricted its action to the ordinary range of its functions.

The first characteristic of judicial power in all nations is the duty of arbitration. But rights must be contested for a court to intervene, and an action must be brought before a judge can rule. So long as the law is uncontested, the judicial authority is not called on to discuss it, and it may exist without being noticed. When a judge, in a particular case, challenges a law bearing on that case, he expands the circle of his ordinary duties without stepping outside it, since he is in some measure obliged to rule on the law in order to rule on the case. But if he pronounces on a law without resting on a case, he plainly steps beyond his own sphere and invades that of the legislature.

The second characteristic of judicial power is that it rules on particular cases, not on general principles. If a judge, in deciding a specific point, destroys a general principle by issuing a judgment that tends to reject all the inferences from that principle — and thus annul it — he still remains within the ordinary limits of his office. But if he directly attacks a general principle without having a particular case in view, he steps outside the circle in which all nations have agreed to confine his authority. He takes on a more important, and perhaps more useful, role than that of a magistrate, but he ceases to be a representative of the judicial power.

The third characteristic of the judicial power is that it cannot act unless it is appealed to, or until a matter has been brought before it. This characteristic is less universal than the other two, but despite the exceptions, I think it can be regarded as essential. The judicial power is by its nature inert; it must be set in motion to produce a result. When it is called on to repress a crime, it punishes the criminal; when a wrong must be redressed, it is ready to redress it; when an act requires interpretation, it is prepared to interpret it. But it does not pursue criminals, hunt out wrongs, or examine evidence on its own initiative. A judicial officer who opened proceedings on his own and usurped the role of censor of the laws would in some measure do violence to the passive nature of his authority.

The Americans have kept these three distinguishing characteristics of judicial power. An American judge can only render a decision when litigation has arisen; he deals only with particular cases; and he cannot act until the case has been duly brought before the court. His position is therefore exactly like that of the magistrate in other nations — and yet he is vested with immense political power. If the scope of his authority and his means of action are the same as those of other judges, one must ask where he derives a power they do not possess. The cause of this difference lies in a simple fact: the Americans have recognized the right of judges to base their decisions on the constitution rather than on statutes. In other words, they have left judges free not to apply laws that appear to them to be unconstitutional.

I am aware that a similar right has been claimed — but claimed in vain — by courts in other countries. In America, however, it is recognized by all authorities, and not a party, not even an individual, is found to contest it. This fact can only be explained by the principles of the American constitution. In France the constitution is (or at least is presumed to be) immutable, and the received doctrine is that no power has the right to change any part of it. In England, Parliament has an acknowledged right to modify the constitution; since the constitution can therefore undergo continual change, it does not in reality exist. Parliament is at once a legislative and a constituent assembly. The political theories of America are simpler and more rational. An American constitution is not assumed to be immutable as in France, nor is it open to modification by the ordinary powers of society as in England. It forms a distinct whole which, as it represents the determination of the whole people, is no less binding on the legislator than on the private citizen; but it may be altered by the will of the people, in predetermined cases, according to established rules. In America the constitution may therefore change, but as long as it exists it is the source of all authority and the sole vehicle of the dominant force. *a

a [ [The fifth article of the original Constitution of the United States provides the mode in which amendments of the Constitution may be made. Amendments must be proposed by two-thirds of both Houses of Congress, and ratified by the Legislatures of three-fourths of the several States. Fifteen amendments of the Constitution have been made at different times since 1789, the most important of which are the Thirteenth, Fourteenth, and Fifteenth, framed and ratified after the Civil War. The original Constitution of the United States, followed by these fifteen amendments, is printed at the end of this edition. —Translator’s Note, 1874.]]

It is easy to see how these differences must affect the position and rights of the judicial bodies in the three countries I have cited. If the courts in France were authorized to disobey laws on the grounds that they conflicted with the constitution, the supreme power would effectively fall into their hands, since they alone would have the right to interpret a constitution whose clauses no authority can modify. They would therefore take the place of the nation and exercise as absolute a sway over society as the inherent weakness of judicial power would allow. It is true that, since French judges are not competent to declare a law unconstitutional, the power of changing the constitution is indirectly granted to the legislature, because no legal barrier would obstruct the alterations it might prescribe. But it is better to grant the power of changing the people’s constitution to men who represent (however imperfectly) the will of the people than to men who represent no one but themselves.

It would be still more unreasonable to give English judges the right to resist the decisions of the legislature, since the Parliament that makes the laws also makes the constitution. Consequently, a law that emanates from the three powers of the State can in no case be unconstitutional. But neither of these observations applies to America.

In the United States the constitution governs the legislator as much as the private citizen. Since it is the first of laws, it cannot be modified by an ordinary law, and it is therefore right that the courts should obey the constitution in preference to any statute. This condition is essential to the power of the judiciary, for it is every magistrate’s natural right to choose the legal obligation that most strictly binds him.

In France the constitution is also the first of laws, and judges have the same right to base their decisions on it. But if they were to exercise that right, they would necessarily encroach on rights more sacred than their own — those of society, in whose name they act. In that case the interest of the State clearly prevails over the motives of an individual. In America, where the nation can always bring its magistrates back into line by changing its constitution, no such danger is to be feared. On this point, then, the political and the logical reasons agree, and the people and the judges alike retain their privileges.

Whenever a law the judge considers unconstitutional is argued before a court in the United States, he may refuse to accept it as a rule. This power is the only one unique to the American magistrate, but it gives rise to immense political influence. Few laws can escape the searching analysis of the judicial power for long, because few are not prejudicial to some private interest, and none cannot be brought before a court by the choice of the parties or by the necessity of the case. But from the moment a judge has refused to apply a given law in a case, that law loses part of its moral force. Those whose interests it harms learn that there are ways to evade its authority; similar suits multiply, until it becomes powerless. At that point one of two alternatives must be chosen: the people must change the constitution, or the legislature must repeal the law. The political power the Americans have entrusted to their courts is therefore immense, but its dangers are considerably reduced by the obligation to attack laws only through the courts. If the judge had been empowered to contest laws on grounds of theoretical generalities — if he could open an attack on the legislator or issue a censure — he would have played a prominent part in the political arena. As the champion or adversary of a party, he would have marshaled the hostile passions of the nation into the conflict. But when a judge contests a law applied to a particular case, in an obscure proceeding, the importance of his attack is hidden from public view. His decision bears on an individual’s interest, and if the law is slighted, it is only incidentally. What is more, though the law is censured, it is not abolished; its moral force may be weakened, but its force as law is not suspended. Its final destruction can only be achieved by the repeated attacks of judicial officers. It is easy to see how, by linking the censorship of laws to the private interests of citizens and by intimately joining the prosecution of the law to the prosecution of an individual, legislation is protected from reckless attackers and from the daily aggressions of party spirit. The legislator’s errors are exposed at the very moments when their bad consequences are most felt, and it is always a concrete, demonstrable fact that serves as the basis of the prosecution.

I am inclined to believe that this practice of the American courts is at once the most favorable to liberty and to public order. If the judge could only attack the legislator openly and directly, he would sometimes be afraid to offer any resistance to his will, while at other moments party spirit might encourage him to defy it at every turn. The laws would then be attacked when the power they came from was weak, and obeyed when it was strong. In other words, they would be contested when it would be useful to respect them, and respected when they would be easy to turn into instruments of oppression. The American judge, however, is brought into the political arena independently of his own will. He rules on the law only because he is obliged to rule on a case. The political question he is called on to resolve is tied to the interests of the litigants, and he cannot refuse to decide it without abdicating the duties of his office. He performs his public role as a citizen by fulfilling the precise duties of his profession as a magistrate. It is true that under this system the judicial censorship exercised by the courts over legislation cannot extend to all laws indiscriminately, since some of them can never give rise to the specific kind of dispute called a lawsuit. And even when such a dispute is possible, it may happen that no one cares to bring it before a court. The Americans have often felt this disadvantage, but they have left the remedy incomplete, for fear of giving it an efficacy that might in some cases prove dangerous. Within these limits, the power vested in the American courts to declare a statute unconstitutional is one of the most powerful barriers ever devised against the tyranny of political assemblies.
Other Powers Granted to American Judges

In the United States all citizens have the right to indict public officials before the ordinary courts — How they use this right — Article 75 of the French Constitution of the Year VIII — The Americans and the English cannot understand the purport of this clause.

It is perfectly natural that in a free country like America, all citizens should have the right to indict public officials before the ordinary courts, and that all judges should have the power to punish public offenses. The right granted to the courts to try the agents of the executive when they have broken the laws is so natural that it cannot be considered an extraordinary privilege. Nor does it seem to me that the springs of government are weakened in the United States by the custom of making all public officers answerable to the judges of the land. On the contrary, the Americans seem to me to have increased by this means the respect due to the authorities, and at the same time to have made those in power more careful about offending public opinion. I was struck by the small number of political trials that take place in the United States, but I had no difficulty accounting for it. A lawsuit, of whatever kind, is always a difficult and expensive undertaking. It is easy to attack a public man in a newspaper, but the grounds required to warrant a legal action must be serious. A solid basis for complaint is therefore needed to induce someone to prosecute a public officer, and public officers are careful not to provide such grounds when they fear being prosecuted.

This does not depend on the republican form of American institutions, for the same facts appear in England. These two nations do not regard the impeachment of the chief officers of State as a sufficient guarantee of their independence. They hold that the right of minor prosecutions, within reach of the whole community, is a better pledge of freedom than those great judicial actions which are rarely employed until it is too late.

In the Middle Ages, when it was very hard to catch offenders, the judges inflicted the most dreadful tortures on the few who were arrested — which did nothing to reduce the number of crimes. It has since been discovered that when justice is more certain and more mild, it is at the same time more effective. The English and the Americans hold that tyranny and oppression should be treated like any other crime: by reducing the penalty and making conviction easier.

In the Year VIII of the French Republic a constitution was drawn up in which the following clause was introduced: “Art. 75. All the agents of the government below the rank of ministers can only be prosecuted for offences relating to their several functions by virtue of a decree of the Conseil d’Etat; in which case the prosecution takes place before the ordinary tribunals.” This clause survived the “Constitution de l’An VIII” and is still maintained, in spite of the just complaints of the nation. I have always found the greatest difficulty in explaining its meaning to Englishmen or Americans. They were immediately led to conclude that the Conseil d’Etat in France was a great court, set up at the center of the kingdom, which exercised a preliminary and somewhat tyrannical jurisdiction over all political cases. But when I told them that the Conseil d’Etat was not a judicial body in the ordinary sense, but an administrative council made up of men dependent on the Crown — so that the king, after ordering one of his servants (called a Prefect) to commit an injustice, has the power to order another of his servants (called a Councillor of State) to prevent the first from being punished; when I demonstrated to them that the citizen injured by the sovereign’s order is obliged to ask the sovereign for permission to seek redress — they refused to believe so flagrant an abuse, and were tempted to accuse me of falsehood or ignorance. It often happened before the Revolution that a Parliament issued a warrant against a public officer who had committed an offense, and sometimes the proceedings were stopped by the authority of the Crown, which enforced compliance with its absolute and despotic will.
