The geographical position of the country contributed to increase the advantages the American legislators drew from the manners and customs of the inhabitants, and it is to this circumstance that the adoption and the maintenance of the Federal system are mainly attributable.

The most important event that can mark the annals of a people is the breaking out of a war. In war, a people struggles with the energy of a single man against foreign nations in defense of its very existence. The skill of a government, the good sense of the community, and the natural fondness men feel for their country may suffice to maintain peace within a district and to favor its internal prosperity; but a nation can only carry on a great war at the cost of more numerous and more painful sacrifices, and to suppose that a great number of men will of their own accord comply with these demands of the State is to betray an ignorance of mankind. All the peoples obliged to sustain a long and serious war have consequently been led to augment the power of their government. Those that have not succeeded in this attempt have been subjugated. A long war almost always places nations in the wretched alternative of being abandoned to ruin by defeat or to despotism by success. War therefore makes the symptoms of the weakness of a government most palpable and most alarming; and I have shown that the inherent defect of federal governments is that of being weak.

The Federal system is not only deficient in every kind of centralized administration, but the central government itself is imperfectly organized, which is invariably a powerful cause of inferiority when the nation is opposed to other countries governed by a single authority. In the Federal Constitution of the United States, by which the central government possesses more real force, this evil is still extremely perceptible. An example will make the case clear to the reader.

The Constitution confers on Congress the right to call forth the militia to execute the laws of the Union, suppress insurrections, and repel invasions; and another article declares that the President of the United States is the commander-in-chief of the militia. In the war of 1812 the President ordered the militia of the Northern States to march to the frontiers; but Connecticut and Massachusetts, whose interests were damaged by the war, refused to obey the command. They argued that the Constitution authorizes the Federal Government to call forth the militia in case of insurrection or invasion, but that in the present instance there was neither invasion nor insurrection. They added that the same Constitution that conferred on the Union the right of calling forth the militia reserved to the States the naming of the officers, and that consequently (as they understood the clause) no officer of the Union had any right to command the militia, even in wartime, except the President in person — and in this case they were ordered to join an army commanded by another individual. These absurd and pernicious doctrines received the sanction not only of the governors and the legislative bodies but also of the courts of justice in both States, and the Federal Government was obliged to raise elsewhere the troops it required. *v

v [ Kent’s “Commentaries,” vol. i. p. 244. I have selected an example which relates to a time posterior to the promulgation of the present Constitution. If I had gone back to the days of the Confederation, I might have given still more striking instances. The whole nation was at that time in a state of enthusiastic excitement; the Revolution was represented by a man who was the idol of the people; but at that very period Congress had, to say the truth, no resources at all at its disposal. Troops and supplies were perpetually wanting. The best-devised projects failed in the execution, and the Union, which was constantly on the verge of destruction, was saved by the weakness of its enemies far more than by its own strength. [All doubt as to the powers of the Federal Executive was, however, removed by its efforts in the Civil War, and those powers were largely extended.]]

The only safeguard the American Union possesses, with all the relative perfection of its laws, against the dissolution that would be produced by a great war lies in its probable exemption from that calamity. Placed in the center of an immense continent that offers a boundless field for human industry, the Union is almost as much insulated from the world as if its frontiers were girt by the ocean. Canada contains only a million inhabitants, and its population is divided into two hostile nations. The rigor of the climate limits the extension of its territory and closes its ports for the six months of winter. From Canada to the Gulf of Mexico, only a few savage tribes are to be met with, which retire, perishing in their retreat, before six thousand soldiers. To the south, the Union has a point of contact with the empire of Mexico, and it is from there that serious hostilities may one day be expected to arise. But for a long time to come the uncivilized state of the Mexican community, the depravity of its morals, and its extreme poverty will prevent that country from ranking high among nations. *w As for the Powers of Europe, they are too distant to be formidable.
w [ [War broke out between the United States and Mexico in 1846, and ended in the conquest of an immense territory, including California.]]

The great advantage of the United States does not, then, consist in a Federal Constitution that allows them to carry on great wars, but in a geographical position that makes such enterprises extremely improbable.

No one can be more inclined than I am to appreciate the advantages of the federal system, which I hold to be one of the combinations most favorable to the prosperity and freedom of man. I envy the lot of those nations that have been enabled to adopt it; but I cannot believe that any confederate peoples could sustain a long or an equal contest with a nation of similar strength in which the government was centralized. A people that should divide its sovereignty into fractional powers, in the presence of the great military monarchies of Europe, would, in my opinion, by that very act abdicate its power, and perhaps its existence and its name. But such is the admirable position of the New World that man has no other enemy than himself; and that, in order to be happy and to be free, it suffices to seek the gifts of prosperity and the knowledge of freedom.

chapters.title: Chapter IX — Why The People May Strictly Be Said To Govern In The United States
paragraphs: Up to this point I have examined the institutions of the United States. I have reviewed their legislation, and I have described the current features of political society in that country. But above these institutions and beyond these defining features, a sovereign power exists that can destroy or reshape them at will — I mean the power of the people. It remains to be shown how this power, which regulates the laws, actually operates: what its tendencies and passions are, what the hidden springs are that slow, speed up, or guide its irresistible course, and what effects its unlimited authority produces, along with the destiny probably reserved for it.

In America the people appoints both the legislative and the executive power, and it provides the jurors who punish every offense against the laws. American institutions are democratic not only in principle but in all their consequences. The people elects its representatives directly, and for the most part annually, to ensure their dependence on it. The people is therefore the real governing power. Although the form of government is representative, it is clear that the opinions, prejudices, interests, and even passions of the community face no lasting obstacles and exert a perpetual influence on society. In the United States the majority governs in the name of the people, as happens in every country where the people is supreme. That majority is made up mainly of peaceful citizens who, whether by inclination or by interest, sincerely want the welfare of their country. But they are surrounded by the constant agitation of parties, which try to draw them in and make use of their support.

chapters.title: Chapter X — Parties In The United States
paragraphs: A great distinction must be drawn between parties. Some countries are so large that the different populations within them have contradictory interests, even though they are subjects of the same government, and they may therefore be in a perpetual state of opposition. In such a case the different fractions of the people should more properly be regarded as distinct nations than as mere parties. If a civil war breaks out, the struggle is carried on by rival peoples rather than by factions within a single state.

But when the citizens hold different opinions on subjects that affect the whole country alike — such as the principles on which the government is to be run — then distinctions arise that may correctly be called parties. Parties are a necessary evil in free governments, but they do not always have the same character and the same tendencies.

At certain times a nation may be oppressed by such unbearable evils that it conceives the idea of a total change in its political constitution. At other times the mischief lies still deeper, and the existence of society itself is endangered. These are the times of great revolutions and of great parties. But between these epochs of misery and confusion there are periods during which human society seems to rest and humanity seems to take a pause. This pause is really only apparent, for time does not stop its course for nations any more than for men. They are all moving toward a goal they do not know, and we only imagine them to be motionless when their progress escapes our observation — just as men walking at a slow pace seem to be standing still to those who are running.

However that may be, there are certain periods in which the changes that take place in the social and political constitution of nations are so slow and so imperceptible that men imagine their present state to be final. The human mind, believing itself firmly based on certain foundations, does not push its investigations beyond the horizon it can see. These are the times of small parties and of intrigue.

The political parties I call great are those that cling to principles more than to consequences, to general rather than particular cases, to ideas rather than men. These parties are usually marked by a nobler character, by more generous passions, by more genuine convictions, and by a bolder and more open conduct than the others. In them, private interest — which always plays the chief part in political passions — is more carefully veiled under the pretext of the public good, and it may sometimes be hidden even from the eyes of those whom it excites and drives.

Minor parties, on the other hand, are generally deficient in political faith. As they are not sustained or ennobled by any lofty purpose, they openly display the selfishness of their character in their actions. They burn with a manufactured zeal; their language is vehement, but their conduct is timid and irresolute. The means they use are as wretched as the ends they aim at. That is why, when a calm state of affairs follows a violent revolution, the leaders of society seem suddenly to disappear and the powers of the human mind to lie hidden. Society is convulsed by great parties; it is agitated by minor ones. It is torn by the former and degraded by the latter. If the great parties sometimes save it by a salutary shock, the minor ones invariably disturb it to no good end.

America has already lost the great parties that once divided the nation. Though her happiness has been considerably increased, her morality has suffered by their extinction. When the War of Independence ended and the foundations of the new government were to be laid, the nation was divided between two opinions — two opinions as old as the world, which are perpetually to be met with under all the forms and names that have ever existed in free communities. One of them tended to limit, the other to extend indefinitely, the power of the people. The conflict of these two opinions never took on, in America, the degree of violence it has frequently shown elsewhere. Both American parties were, in fact, agreed on the most essential points, and neither had to destroy a traditional constitution or overthrow the structure of society in order to guarantee its own triumph. In neither of them, consequently, were a great many private interests affected by success or failure. But moral principles of a high order — such as the love of equality and independence — were at stake in the struggle, and they were enough to kindle violent passions.

The party that wanted to limit the power of the people tried to apply its doctrines above all to the Constitution of the Union, from which it took the name Federal. The other party, which claimed to be more exclusively attached to the cause of liberty, took the name Republican. America is a land of democracy, and the Federalists were always in a minority. But they counted on their side almost all the great men brought forward by the War of Independence, and their moral influence was very considerable. Their cause was also favored by circumstances. The ruin of the Confederation had filled the people with a dread of anarchy, and the Federalists did not fail to make use of this temporary disposition of the multitude. For ten or twelve years they were at the head of affairs and were able to apply some, though not all, of their principles; for the hostile current was growing daily too violent to be checked or resisted. In 1801 the Republicans took control of the government. Thomas Jefferson was chosen President, and he strengthened the influence of their party by the weight of his celebrity, the greatness of his talents, and the immense extent of his popularity.

The means by which the Federalists had kept their position were artificial, and their resources were temporary. It was by the virtues or the talents of their leaders that they had risen to power. When the Republicans reached that lofty station, their opponents were overwhelmed by utter defeat. An immense majority declared itself against the outgoing party, and the Federalists found themselves in so small a minority that they at once despaired of ever succeeding again. From that moment the Republican, or Democratic, party*a has gone from conquest to conquest, until it has acquired absolute supremacy in the country. The Federalists, seeing that they were beaten beyond recovery and isolated in the midst of the nation, split into two groups. One joined the victorious Republicans; the other abandoned its rallying point and its name. Many years have now passed since they ceased to exist as a party.

a [[It is hardly necessary to remark that in more recent times the meaning of these terms has changed. The Republicans are the representatives of the old Federalists, and the Democrats of the old Republicans. — Trans. Note (1861).]] The accession of the Federalists to power was, in my opinion, one of the most fortunate incidents that accompanied the formation of the great American Union. They resisted the inevitable tendencies of their age and of their country. But whether their theories were good or bad, they had the defect of being inapplicable, as a system, to the society they claimed to govern, and what occurred under Jefferson's auspices was therefore bound to happen sooner or later. But their government gave the new republic time to acquire a certain stability, and afterwards to support the rapid growth of the very doctrines they had combated. A considerable number of their principles were in fact embodied in the political creed of their opponents, and the Federal Constitution that still exists today is a lasting monument to their patriotism and their wisdom.

Great political parties, then, are not to be met with in the United States at the present time. Parties do exist that threaten the future tranquility of the Union, but there are none that seem to contest the present form of government or the present course of society. The parties that menace the Union do not rest on abstract principles, but on material interests. These interests, spread across the provinces of so vast an empire, may be said to form rival nations rather than rival parties. Thus, on a recent occasion, the North argued for a system of commercial prohibition and the South took up arms in favor of free trade, simply because the North is a manufacturing district and the South an agricultural one, and the restrictive system that benefited the one was harmful to the other.*b

b [[The divisions of North and South have since gained a far greater intensity, and the South, though conquered, still presents a formidable spirit of opposition to Northern government. — Translator's Note, 1875.]]

In the absence of great parties, the United States abounds with lesser controversies, and public opinion is divided into a thousand minute shades of difference on questions of very little importance. The pains taken to create parties are inconceivable, and at present it is no easy task. In the United States there is no religious animosity, because all religion is respected and no sect is predominant. There is no jealousy of rank, because the people is everything and no one can contest its authority. And lastly, there is no public destitution to provide the fuel for agitation, because the physical situation of the country opens so wide a field to industry that a man can accomplish the most surprising undertakings with his own native resources. Nevertheless, ambitious men have an interest in the creation of parties, since it is hard to remove a person from office on the mere ground that his place is coveted by others. The skill of the actors in the political world therefore consists in the art of creating parties. A political aspirant in the United States begins by identifying his own interest and calculating what interests can be gathered around it and joined with it. He then contrives to find some doctrine or principle that will suit the purposes of this new association, and which he adopts in order to put forward his party and secure his popularity. In much the same way, a king's imprimatur was formerly bound into the volume it authorized, though it did not really belong to the book at all. When these preliminaries are complete, the new party is ushered into the political world.

All the domestic controversies of the Americans at first appear to a stranger so incomprehensible and so childish that he is at a loss whether to pity a people that takes such trifles seriously or to envy the happiness that allows it to discuss them. But when he comes to study the secret tendencies that govern the factions of America, he easily sees that most of them are more or less connected with one or the other of those two divisions that have always existed in free communities. The deeper we look into the workings of these parties, the more clearly we see that the object of the one is to limit the popular authority, and that of the other to extend it. I do not claim that the declared aim, or even the secret aim, of American parties is to promote the rule of aristocracy or democracy in the country. But I do affirm that aristocratic or democratic passions may easily be detected at the bottom of every party, and that although they escape a superficial observation, they are the main point and the very soul of every faction in the United States.

To give a recent example: when the President attacked the Bank, the country was stirred up and parties formed. The well-informed classes rallied to the Bank, the common people to the President. But it must not be imagined that the people had formed a rational opinion on a question that presents so many difficulties even to the most experienced statesmen. The Bank is a great institution with an independent existence of its own, and the people, accustomed to making and unmaking whatever it pleases, is startled to meet such an obstacle to its authority. In the midst of the constant flux of society, the community is irritated by so permanent an institution and is led to attack it, to see whether it can be shaken and controlled like all the other institutions of the country.
Remains Of The Aristocratic Party In The United States

Secret opposition of wealthy individuals to democracy — Their retirement — Their taste for exclusive pleasures and for luxury at home — Their simplicity in public — Their affected condescension toward the people.

It sometimes happens among a people in which various opinions prevail that the balance between the several parties is lost, and one of them gains an irresistible preponderance, overcomes all obstacles, harasses its opponents, and appropriates all the resources of society to its own purposes. The defeated citizens despair of success and conceal their dissatisfaction in silence and general apathy. The nation seems to be governed by a single principle, and the ruling party takes credit for restoring peace and unanimity to the country. But this apparent unanimity is merely a cloak for alarming dissensions and perpetual opposition.

This is exactly what happened in America. When the democratic party gained the upper hand, it took exclusive possession of the conduct of affairs, and from that time on the laws and customs of society have been shaped to fit its whims. Today the more prosperous classes of society are so entirely removed from the direction of political affairs in the United States that wealth, far from conferring a right to exercise power, is more an obstacle than a means to it. The wealthy members of the community leave the field, unwilling to contend, and often to contend in vain, against the poorest classes of their fellow citizens. They concentrate all their enjoyments in the privacy of their homes, where they occupy a rank that cannot be claimed in public. They form a private society within the state, with its own tastes and its own pleasures. They submit to this situation as an irremediable evil, but they are careful not to show that they chafe under it. It is even not uncommon to hear them extolling, in public, the charms of republican government and the advantages of democratic institutions. Next to hating their enemies, men are most inclined to flatter them.

Notice, for example, that wealthy citizen who is as anxious to hide his wealth as a Jew of the Middle Ages. His dress is plain, his manner unassuming. But the interior of his home glitters with luxury, and only a few chosen guests — whom he haughtily calls his equals — are allowed into this sanctuary. No European noble is more exclusive in his pleasures or more jealous of the smallest privileges his station confers. But the very same man crosses the city to reach a dark counting-house in the center of the business district, where anyone who pleases may come up and speak to him. If he meets his cobbler on the way, they stop and talk. The two citizens discuss the affairs of the state, in which they have an equal stake, and they shake hands before parting.

But beneath this manufactured enthusiasm and these obsequious attentions to the dominant power, it is easy to see that the wealthy members of the community harbor a hearty distaste for the democratic institutions of their country. The populace is at once the object of their scorn and of their fears. If the mismanagement of the democracy ever brings about a revolutionary crisis, and if monarchical institutions ever become practicable in the United States, the truth of what I am saying will become obvious.
The two main weapons parties use to secure success are the public press and the formation of associations.

chapters.title: Chapter XI — Liberty Of The Press In The United States
paragraphs: The influence of the liberty of the press does not affect political opinions alone; it extends to all of men's opinions and modifies customs as well as laws. In another part of this work I shall try to determine the degree of influence that the liberty of the press has exercised on civil society in the United States, and to indicate the direction it has given to the ideas, as well as the tone it has imparted to the character and feelings, of the Anglo-Americans. For now, I propose simply to examine the effects produced by the liberty of the press in the political world.

I confess that I do not feel toward the liberty of the press the firm and complete attachment that things supremely good in their very nature tend to excite in the mind. I approve of it more from a recollection of the evils it prevents than from consideration of the advantages it ensures.

If anyone could point out an intermediate yet tenable position between the complete independence and the entire subjection of public opinion, I should perhaps be inclined to adopt it. But the difficulty is to find that position. If your intention is to correct the abuses of an unlicensed press and to restore the use of orderly language, you may at first try the offender before a jury; but if the jury acquits him, the opinion that was that of a single individual becomes the opinion of the country at large. Too much and too little has therefore been done. If you press on, you must bring the offender before a court of permanent judges. But even here the case must be heard before it can be decided; and the very principles no book would have ventured to avow are now blazoned forth in the pleadings. What was obscurely hinted at in a single composition is then repeated in a multitude of other publications. The language in which a thought is expressed is the mere carcass of the thought, not the idea itself; tribunals may condemn the form, but the sense and spirit of the work are too subtle for their authority. Too much has still been done to retreat, too little to reach your end; so you must press on. If you establish a censorship of the press, the public speaker's tongue will still make itself heard, and you have only increased the mischief. The powers of thought do not depend, like those of physical strength, on the number of their mechanical agents, nor can a host of authors be counted like the troops that compose an army. On the contrary, the authority of a principle is often increased by the smallness of the number of men who express it. The words of a strong-minded man, penetrating the passions of a listening assembly, have more power than the shouts of a thousand orators; and if free speech is allowed in any one public place, the consequence is the same as if it were allowed in every village. The liberty of discourse must therefore be destroyed as well as the liberty of the press; this is the necessary end of your efforts. But if your object was to repress the abuses of liberty, they have brought you to the feet of a despot. You have been led from the extreme of independence to the extreme of subjection without meeting a single tenable position for shelter or repose.

Certain nations have special reasons for cherishing the liberty of the press, apart from the general motives I have just pointed out. For in certain countries that profess to enjoy the privileges of freedom, every individual agent of the Government may violate the laws with impunity, since those whom he oppresses cannot prosecute him before the courts of justice. In this case the liberty of the press is not merely a guarantee, but the only guarantee, of the liberty and security the citizens possess. If the rulers of these nations propose to abolish the independence of the press, the people would be justified in saying: give us the right to prosecute your offenses before the ordinary tribunals, and perhaps we may then waive our right of appeal to the tribunal of public opinion.

But in countries where the doctrine of the sovereignty of the people ostensibly prevails, the censorship of the press is not only dangerous but absurd. When the right of every citizen to take part in the government of society is acknowledged, every citizen must be presumed capable of distinguishing between the different opinions of his contemporaries, and of weighing the different facts from which inferences may be drawn. The sovereignty of the people and the liberty of the press may therefore be regarded as correlative institutions, just as the censorship of the press and universal suffrage are two things irreconcilably opposed, which cannot long be kept together among the institutions of the same people. Not a single individual of the twelve millions who inhabit the territory of the United States has yet dared to propose any restriction on the liberty of the press. The first newspaper I laid eyes on upon my arrival in America contained the following article:

In all this affair the language of Jackson has been that of a heartless despot, concerned only with the preservation of his own authority. Ambition is his crime, and it will be his punishment too: intrigue is his native element, and intrigue will confound his tricks and deprive him of his power. He governs by means of corruption, and his immoral practices will redound to his shame and confusion. His conduct in the political arena has been that of a shameless and lawless gamester. He succeeded at the time, but the hour of reckoning approaches, and he will be forced to disgorge his winnings, throw aside his false dice, and end his days in some retirement where he may curse his madness at leisure—for repentance is a virtue his heart is likely never to know.

In France it is not uncommonly imagined that the virulence of the press comes from the uncertain social condition, the political excitement, and the general sense of consequent evil that prevail in that country; and it is therefore supposed that once society regains a certain degree of composure, the press will give up its present vehemence. I am inclined to think that these causes explain the extraordinary ascendancy it has gained over the nation, but that they have little influence on the tone of its language. The periodical press seems to me to be driven by passions and tendencies independent of the circumstances in which it is placed, and the present condition of America bears this out.

America is perhaps at this moment the country in the whole world that contains the fewest germs of revolution; yet the press is no less destructive in its principles than in France, and it shows the same violence without the same grounds for indignation. In America, as in France, it constitutes a singular power, so strangely composed of mingled good and evil that it is at once indispensable to the existence of freedom and nearly incompatible with the maintenance of public order. Its power is certainly much greater in France than in the United States, though nothing is rarer in the latter country than to hear of a prosecution having been brought against it. The reason is perfectly simple: the Americans, having once admitted the doctrine of the sovereignty of the people, apply it with perfect consistency. It was never their intention to found a permanent state of things with elements that undergo daily modification; and so there is nothing criminal in attacking the existing laws, provided the attack is not accompanied by a violent breach of them. They are of the opinion, moreover, that courts of justice are unable to check the abuses of the press, and that since the subtlety of human language perpetually eludes the severity of judicial analysis, offenses of this kind tend to escape the hand that tries to seize them. They hold that to act effectively on the press it would be necessary to find a tribunal not only devoted to the existing order of things, but capable of surmounting the influence of public opinion—a tribunal that would conduct its proceedings without publicity, pronounce its decrees without stating its reasons, and punish the intentions even more than the language of an author. Whoever had the power of creating and maintaining such a tribunal would waste his time in prosecuting the liberty of the press, for he would be the supreme master of the whole community, and he would be as free to rid himself of the authors as of their writings. On this question, then, there is no middle ground between servitude and extreme license; to enjoy the priceless benefits the liberty of the press ensures, one must submit to the inevitable evils it engenders. To expect to gain the former and escape the latter is to cherish one of those illusions that commonly mislead nations in their times of sickness—when, tired with faction and exhausted by effort, they try to combine hostile opinions and opposing principles on the same soil.
The small influence of the American journals is attributable to several reasons, among them the following:

The liberty of writing, like every other liberty, is most formidable when it is a novelty; for a people that has never been accustomed to take part in the conduct of State affairs places implicit confidence in the first tribune who arouses its attention. The Anglo-Americans have enjoyed this liberty ever since the founding of the settlements; besides, the press cannot of its own power create human passions, however skillfully it may kindle them where they exist. In America politics are discussed with animation and a varied activity, but they rarely touch those deep passions that are stirred whenever the positive interest of a part of the community is damaged. And in the United States the interests of the community are in a most prosperous condition. A single glance at a French and an American newspaper is enough to show the difference between the two nations on this point. In France the space given to commercial advertisements is very limited, and the news items are not extensive; the most essential part of the journal is that which contains the discussion of the politics of the day. In America three-quarters of the enormous sheet set before the reader are filled with advertisements, and the rest is frequently occupied by political news or trivial anecdotes; only from time to time does one find a corner devoted to passionate discussions like those with which the journalists of France are accustomed to indulge their readers.

Observation has shown, and the innate shrewdness of the pettiest as well as the greatest of despots has discovered, that the influence of a power is increased in proportion as its direction is made more central. In France the press combines a twofold centralization: almost all its power is concentrated in the same spot and vested in the same hands, for its organs are far from numerous. The influence of a public press so constituted upon a skeptical nation must be unbounded. It is an enemy with which a Government may sign an occasional truce, but which it is difficult to resist for any length of time.

Neither kind of centralization exists in America. The United States has no metropolis; the intelligence as well as the power of the country are dispersed abroad, and instead of radiating from a single point, they cross each other in every direction. The Americans have established no central control over the expression of opinion, any more than over the conduct of business. These are circumstances that do not depend on human foresight; but it is owing to the laws of the Union that there are no licenses to be granted to printers, no securities demanded from editors as in France, and no stamp duty as in France and formerly in England. As a result, nothing is easier than to set up a newspaper, and a small number of readers is enough to cover the editor's expenses.

The number of periodical and occasional publications that appear in the United States actually surpasses belief. The most enlightened Americans attribute the subordinate influence of the press to this excessive dissemination; and it is adopted as an axiom of political science in that country that the only way to neutralize the effect of public journals is to multiply them indefinitely. I cannot conceive why a truth so self-evident has not already been more generally admitted in Europe. It is understandable that those who hope to bring about revolutions by means of the press should want to confine its action to a few powerful organs; but it is perfectly incredible that the partisans of the existing state of things, and the natural supporters of the law, should try to diminish the influence of the press by concentrating its authority. The Governments of Europe seem to treat the press with the courtesy of the knights of old; they are eager to furnish it with that same central power they have found to be so trusty a weapon, so as to enhance the glory of their resistance to its attacks.

In America there is scarcely a hamlet that does not have its own newspaper. It is easy to imagine that neither discipline nor unity of design can be imposed on so scattered a host, and each one is consequently led to fight under his own standard. All the political journals of the United States are indeed arrayed on the side of the administration or against it; but they attack and defend in a thousand different ways. They cannot succeed in forming those great currents of opinion that overwhelm the most solid obstacles. This division of the influence of the press produces a variety of other consequences scarcely less remarkable. The ease with which journals can be established draws a multitude of individuals into them; but since the extent of competition rules out the possibility of considerable profit, the most distinguished classes of society are rarely led to take up these undertakings. Yet such is the number of public prints that, even if they were a source of wealth, writers of ability could not be found to direct them all. The journalists of the United States are usually placed in a very humble position, with scanty education and a vulgar turn of mind. The will of the majority is the most general of laws, and it establishes certain habits that become the marks of each particular class of society; thus it dictates the etiquette practiced at courts and the etiquette of the bar. The characteristic of the French journalist consists in a violent, but frequently eloquent and lofty, manner of discussing the politics of the day; the exceptions to this habitual practice are only occasional. The characteristic of the American journalist consists in an open and coarse appeal to the passions of the populace; he habitually abandons the principles of political science to assail the characters of individuals, to pursue them into private life, and to disclose all their weaknesses and errors.

Nothing can be more deplorable than this abuse of the powers of thought. I shall have occasion later to point out the influence of the newspapers on the taste and the morality of the American people, but my present subject concerns only the political world. It cannot be denied that the effects of this extreme license of the press tend indirectly to the maintenance of public order. Individuals who already stand high in the esteem of their fellow citizens are afraid to write in the newspapers, and are thus deprived of the most powerful instrument they could use to excite the passions of the multitude to their own advantage. *a

a [ They only write in the papers when they choose to address the people in their own name; as, for instance, when they are called upon to repel calumnious imputations, and to correct a misstatement of facts.]

The personal opinions of the editors carry no weight whatever in the eyes of the public. The only use of a journal is that it conveys the knowledge of certain facts, and it is only by altering or distorting those facts that a journalist can contribute to the support of his own views.

But although the press is limited to these resources, its influence in America is immense. It is the power that drives the circulation of political life through all the districts of that vast territory. Its eye is constantly open to detect the secret springs of political designs and to summon the leaders of all parties to the bar of public opinion. It rallies the interests of the community around certain principles and draws up the creed that factions adopt; for it provides a means of communication between parties that hear one another and address one another without ever being in direct contact. When a great number of the organs of the press adopt the same line of conduct, their influence becomes irresistible; and public opinion, when perpetually assailed from the same side, eventually yields to the attack. In the United States each individual journal exercises but little authority, but the power of the periodical press is second only to that of the people. *b
b [ See Appendix, P.]
The opinions established in the United States under the empire of the liberty of the press are often more firmly rooted than those formed elsewhere under the sanction of a censor.

In the United States democracy perpetually raises fresh individuals to the conduct of public affairs, and so the measures of the administration are seldom regulated by strict rules of consistency or of order. But the general principles of the Government are more stable, and the opinions most prevalent in society are generally more durable than in many other countries. Once the Americans have taken up an idea, whether well or ill founded, nothing is harder than to root it out of their minds. The same tenacity of opinion has been observed in England, where, for the last century, greater freedom of conscience and more invincible prejudices have existed than in all the other countries of Europe. I attribute this to a cause that may at first sight seem to have an opposite tendency: to the liberty of the press. Nations among which this liberty exists are apt to cling to their opinions out of pride as much as out of conviction. They cherish them because they hold them to be just, and because they exercised their own free will in choosing them; they maintain them not only because they are true, but because they are their own. Several other reasons lead to the same end.

A man of genius once remarked that "ignorance lies at the two ends of knowledge." It would perhaps have been more accurate to say that absolute convictions are to be found at the two extremes, and that doubt lies in the middle. For the human intellect may be considered in three distinct states, which frequently succeed one another. A man believes implicitly, because he adopts a proposition without inquiry. He doubts as soon as he is assailed by the objections his inquiries may have aroused. But he often succeeds in satisfying these doubts, and then he begins to believe afresh: he no longer grasps a truth in its most shadowy and uncertain form, but sees it clearly before him, and advances by the light it gives him. *c
c [ It may, however, be doubted whether this rational and self-guiding conviction arouses as much fervor or enthusiastic devotedness in men as their first dogmatical belief.]

When the liberty of the press acts upon men who are in the first of these three states, it does not immediately disturb their habit of believing implicitly, without investigation; but it constantly modifies the objects of their intuitive convictions. The human mind continues to make out only one point in the whole intellectual horizon, and that point is in continual motion. Such are the symptoms of sudden revolutions, and of the misfortunes sure to befall those generations which abruptly adopt the unconditional freedom of the press.

The circle of novel ideas, however, is soon exhausted; the touch of experience is upon them, and the doubt and mistrust their uncertainty produces become universal. We may be sure that the majority of mankind will either believe without knowing why, or will not know what to believe. Few are the beings who can ever hope to reach that state of rational and independent conviction which true knowledge can beget in defiance of the attacks of doubt.

It has been remarked that in times of great religious fervor, men sometimes change their religious opinions, whereas in times of general skepticism everyone clings to his own persuasion. The same thing happens in politics under the liberty of the press. In countries where all the theories of social science have in turn been contested, the citizens who have adopted one of them stick to it, not so much because they are convinced of its excellence, as because they are not convinced of the superiority of any other. In the present age, men are not very ready to die in defense of their opinions, but they are rarely inclined to change them; and there are fewer martyrs as well as fewer apostates.

Another, still more compelling reason may be added: when no abstract opinions are regarded as certain, men cling to the mere inclinations and external interests of their position, which are naturally more tangible and more permanent than any opinions in the world.

It is no easy question whether aristocracy or democracy is more fit to govern a country. But it is certain that democracy annoys one part of the community, and that aristocracy oppresses another part. When the question is reduced to the simple expression of the struggle between poverty and wealth, the tendency of each side of the dispute becomes perfectly clear without further debate.

chapters.title: Chapter XII — Political Associations In The United States
paragraphs: In no country in the world has the principle of association been more successfully used, or more unsparingly applied to a multitude of different objects, than in America. Besides the permanent associations established by law under the names of townships, cities, and counties, a vast number of others are formed and maintained through the agency of private individuals.

The citizen of the United States is taught from his earliest infancy to rely on his own exertions in order to resist the evils and the difficulties of life; he looks upon social authority with an eye of mistrust and anxiety, and he only claims its assistance when he is quite unable to manage without it. This habit may even be traced in the schools of the rising generation, where the children in their games habitually submit to rules they have themselves established, and punish misdemeanors they have themselves defined. The same spirit pervades every act of social life. If a stoppage occurs in a thoroughfare and the circulation of the public is hindered, the neighbors immediately constitute a deliberative body; and this extemporaneous assembly gives rise to an executive power which remedies the inconvenience before anyone has thought of resorting to an authority superior to that of the persons immediately concerned. If public pleasures are concerned, an association is formed to provide for the splendor and regularity of the entertainment. Societies are formed to resist enemies that are exclusively of a moral nature, and to diminish the vice of intemperance; in the United States associations are established to promote public order, commerce, industry, morality, and religion; for there is no end which the human will, seconded by the collective exertions of individuals, despairs of attaining.

I shall have occasion later to show the effects of association on the course of society, and I must confine myself for the present to the political world. Once the right of association is recognized, the citizens may employ it in several different ways.

An association consists simply in the public assent which a number of individuals give to certain doctrines, and in the engagement they contract to promote the spread of those doctrines by their exertions. The right of association with these views is very analogous to the liberty of unlicensed writing; but societies thus formed possess more authority than the press. When an opinion is represented by a society, it necessarily assumes a more exact and explicit form. It counts its partisans, and commits their welfare to its cause; they, on the other hand, become acquainted with each other, and their zeal is increased by their number. An association unites the efforts of minds which tend to diverge in one single channel, and urges them vigorously toward one single end which it points out.

The second degree in the right of association is the power of meeting. When an association is allowed to establish centers of action at certain important points in the country, its activity is increased and its influence extended. Men have the opportunity of seeing each other; means of execution are more readily combined, and opinions are maintained with a warmth and energy that written language cannot approach.

Lastly, in the exercise of the right of political association, there is a third degree: the partisans of an opinion may unite in electoral bodies, and choose delegates to represent them in a central assembly. This is, properly speaking, the application of the representative system to a party.

Thus, in the first instance, a society is formed between individuals professing the same opinion, and the tie that keeps it together is of a purely intellectual nature. In the second case, small assemblies are formed that represent only a fraction of the party. Lastly, in the third case, they constitute a separate nation within the nation, a government within the Government. Their delegates, like the real delegates of the majority, represent the entire collective force of their party; and they enjoy a certain degree of that national dignity and great influence which belong to the chosen representatives of the people. It is true they do not have the right of making the laws, but they have the power of attacking those in being, and of drawing up beforehand those which they may afterwards cause to be adopted.

If, in a people imperfectly accustomed to the exercise of freedom, or exposed to violent political passions, a deliberating minority, confining itself to the contemplation of future laws, is placed in juxtaposition to the legislative majority, I cannot but believe that public tranquility incurs very great risks in that nation. There is doubtless a very wide difference between proving that one law is in itself better than another, and proving that the former ought to be substituted for the latter. But the imagination of the populace is very apt to overlook this difference, which is so apparent to the minds of thinking men. It sometimes happens that a nation is divided into two nearly equal parties, each affecting to represent the majority. If, in immediate contiguity to the directing power, another power is established which exercises almost as much moral authority as the former, it is not to be believed that it will long be content to speak without acting, or that it will always be restrained by the abstract consideration of the nature of associations meant to direct but not to enforce opinions, to suggest but not to make the laws.

The more we consider the independence of the press in its principal consequences, the more we are convinced that it is the chief and, so to speak, the constitutive element of freedom in the modern world. A nation determined to remain free is therefore right in demanding the unrestrained exercise of this independence. But the unrestrained liberty of political association cannot be entirely assimilated to the liberty of the press. The one is at once less necessary and more dangerous than the other. A nation may confine it within certain limits without forfeiting any part of its self-control; and it may sometimes be obliged to do so in order to maintain its own authority.
In America the liberty of association for political purposes is unbounded. An example will show in the clearest light the extent to which this privilege is tolerated.

The question of the tariff, or of free trade, produced a great manifestation of party feeling in America; the tariff was not only a subject of debate as a matter of opinion, but it exercised a favorable or a prejudicial influence on several very powerful interests of the States. The North attributed a great portion of its prosperity, and the South all its sufferings, to this system, so that for a long time the tariff was the sole source of the political animosities which agitated the Union.

In 1831, when the dispute was raging with the utmost virulence, a private citizen of Massachusetts proposed, in the public prints, to all the enemies of the tariff that they send delegates to Philadelphia to consult together on the means most fitted to promote freedom of trade. This proposal circulated in a few days from Maine to New Orleans through the power of the printing-press; the opponents of the tariff adopted it with enthusiasm; meetings were formed on all sides, and delegates were named. The majority of these individuals were well known, and some of them had earned a considerable degree of celebrity. South Carolina alone, which afterwards took up arms in the same cause, sent sixty-three delegates. On October 1, 1831, this assembly, which according to American custom had taken the name of a Convention, met at Philadelphia; it consisted of more than two hundred members. Its debates were public, and they at once assumed a legislative character; the extent of the powers of Congress, the theories of free trade, and the different clauses of the tariff were discussed in turn. At the end of ten days' deliberation the Convention broke up, after having published an address to the American people, in which it declared:
I. That Congress had not the right of making a tariff, and that the existing tariff was unconstitutional;
II. That the prohibition of free trade was prejudicial to the interests of all nations, and to that of the American people in particular.

It must be acknowledged that the unrestrained liberty of political association has not so far produced, in the United States, those fatal consequences that might perhaps be expected from it elsewhere. The right of association was imported from England, and it has always existed in America, so that the exercise of this privilege is now amalgamated with the manners and customs of the people. At the present time the liberty of association has become a necessary guarantee against the tyranny of the majority. In the United States, as soon as a party has become preponderant, all public authority passes under its control; its private supporters occupy all the places, and have all the force of the administration at their disposal. As the most distinguished partisans of the other side of the question are unable to surmount the obstacles excluding them from power, they require some means of establishing themselves on their own basis, and of opposing the moral authority of the minority to the physical power that domineers over it. Thus a dangerous expedient is used to obviate a still more formidable danger.

The omnipotence of the majority appears to me to present such extreme perils to the American Republics that the dangerous measure used to repress it seems more advantageous than prejudicial. And here I am about to advance a proposition which may remind the reader of what I said before in speaking of municipal freedom: there are no countries in which associations are more needed — to prevent the despotism of faction or the arbitrary power of a prince — than those which are democratically constituted. In aristocratic nations the body of the nobles and the more opulent part of the community are in themselves natural associations, which act as checks on the abuses of power. In countries in which these associations do not exist, if private individuals are unable to create an artificial and temporary substitute for them, I can imagine no permanent protection against the most galling tyranny; and a great people may be oppressed by a small faction, or by a single individual, with impunity.

The meeting of a great political Convention (for there are Conventions of all kinds), which may frequently become a necessary measure, is always a serious event, even in America, and one that judicious friends of the country never look forward to without alarm. This was very perceptible in the Convention of 1831, where the exertions of all the most distinguished members of the Assembly tended to moderate its language, and to restrain the subjects it treated within certain limits. It is probable, in fact, that the Convention of 1831 exercised a very great influence on the minds of the malcontents, and prepared them for the open revolt against the commercial laws of the Union which took place in 1832.

It cannot be denied that the unrestrained liberty of association for political purposes is the privilege a people is longest in learning how to exercise. If it does not throw the nation into anarchy, it perpetually augments the chances of that calamity. On one point, however, this perilous liberty offers a security against dangers of another kind: in countries where associations are free, secret societies are unknown. In America there are numerous factions, but no conspiracies.
Different ways in which the right of association is understood in Europe and in the United States — Different use which is made of it.

The most natural privilege of man, next to the right of acting for himself, is that of combining his exertions with those of his fellow creatures, and of acting in common with them. I am therefore led to conclude that the right of association is almost as inalienable as the right of personal liberty. No legislator can attack it without impairing the very foundations of society. Nevertheless, if the liberty of association is a fruitful source of advantages and prosperity to some nations, it may be perverted or carried to excess by others, and the element of life may be changed into an element of destruction. A comparison of the different methods associations pursue in those countries where they are managed with discretion, as well as in those where liberty degenerates into license, may perhaps be thought useful both to governments and to parties.

The greater part of Europeans look upon an association as a weapon to be hastily fashioned, and immediately tried in the conflict. A society is formed for discussion, but the idea of impending action prevails in the minds of those who compose it; it is, in fact, an army, and the time given to parley serves to reckon up the strength and animate the courage of the host, after which they direct their march against the enemy. Resources that lie within the bounds of the law may suggest themselves to those who compose it as means, but never as the only means, of success.

Such, however, is not the manner in which the right of association is understood in the United States. In America the citizens who form the minority associate, in the first place, to show their numerical strength, and so to diminish the moral authority of the majority; and, in the second place, to stimulate competition, and to discover those arguments most fitted to act upon the majority; for they always entertain hopes of drawing over their opponents to their own side, and of afterwards disposing of the supreme power in their name. Political associations in the United States are therefore peaceable in their intentions, and strictly legal in the means they employ; and they assert with perfect truth that they only aim at success by lawful expedients.

The difference between the Americans and ourselves depends on several causes. In Europe there are numerous parties so diametrically opposed to the majority that they can never hope to acquire its support, and at the same time they think they are sufficiently strong in themselves to struggle and defend their cause. When a party of this kind forms an association, its object is not to conquer, but to fight. In America the individuals who hold opinions very much opposed to those of the majority are no sort of impediment to its power, and all other parties hope to win it over to their own principles in the end. The exercise of the right of association becomes dangerous in proportion to the impossibility that excludes great parties from acquiring the majority. In a country like the United States, where differences of opinion are mere differences of hue, the right of association may remain unrestrained without evil consequences. The inexperience of many European nations in the enjoyment of liberty leads them only to look on the liberty of association as a right of attacking the Government. The first notion that presents itself to a party, as well as to an individual, when it has acquired a consciousness of its own strength, is that of violence; the notion of persuasion arises at a later period, and is only derived from experience. The English, who are divided into parties that differ most essentially from each other, rarely abuse the right of association, because they have long been accustomed to exercise it. In France the passion for war is so intense that there is no undertaking so mad, or so injurious to the welfare of the State, that a man does not consider himself honored in defending it, at the risk of his life.

But perhaps the most powerful of the causes that tend to mitigate the excesses of political association in the United States is Universal Suffrage. In countries where universal suffrage exists, the majority is never doubtful, because neither party can pretend to represent that portion of the community which has not voted. The associations formed are aware, as well as the nation at large, that they do not represent the majority; this is, indeed, a condition inseparable from their existence, for if they did represent the preponderating power, they would change the law instead of soliciting its reform. The consequence of this is that the moral influence of the Government they attack is very much increased, and their own power very much enfeebled.

In Europe there are few associations which do not affect to represent the majority, or which do not believe that they represent it. This conviction or this pretension tends to augment their force amazingly, and contributes no less to legalize their measures. Violence may seem excusable in defence of the cause of oppressed right. Thus it is, in the vast labyrinth of human laws, that extreme liberty sometimes corrects the abuses of license, and that extreme democracy obviates the dangers of democratic government. In Europe, associations consider themselves, in some degree, as the legislative and executive councils of the people, which is unable to speak for itself. In America, where they only represent a minority of the nation, they argue and they petition.

The means which the associations of Europe employ are in accordance with the end they propose to obtain. Since the principal aim of these bodies is to act, and not to debate, to fight rather than to persuade, they are naturally led to adopt a form of organization which differs from the ordinary customs of civil bodies, and which assumes the habits and maxims of military life. They centralize the direction of their resources as much as possible, and they entrust the power of the whole party to a very small number of leaders.

The members of these associations respond to a watchword, like soldiers on duty; they profess the doctrine of passive obedience — say rather, that in uniting together they at once abjure the exercise of their own judgment and free will. The tyrannical control these societies exercise is often far more insupportable than the authority possessed over society by the Government they attack. Their moral force is much diminished by these excesses, and they lose the powerful interest always excited by a struggle between oppressors and the oppressed. The man who in given cases consents to obey his fellows with servility, and submits his activity and even his opinions to their control, can have no claim to rank as a free citizen.

The Americans have also established certain forms of government that are applied to their associations, but these are invariably borrowed from the forms of civil administration. The independence of each individual is formally recognized; the tendency of the members of the association points, as it does in the body of the community, toward the same end, but they are not obliged to follow the same track. No one abjures the exercise of his reason and his free will; but every one exerts that reason and that will for the benefit of a common undertaking.

chapters.title: Chapter XIII — Government Of The Democracy In America
paragraphs: I am well aware of the difficulties that attend this part of my subject; but although every expression I am about to use may clash, on some one point, with the feelings of the different parties that divide my country, I shall speak my opinion with the most perfect openness.

In Europe we are at a loss how to judge the true character and the more permanent propensities of democracy, because in Europe two conflicting principles exist, and we do not know what to attribute to the principles themselves, and what to refer to the passions they bring into collision. Such, however, is not the case in America; there the people reigns without any obstacle, and has no perils to dread and no injuries to avenge. In America, democracy is swayed by its own free propensities; its course is natural and its activity is unrestrained; the United States consequently afford the most favorable opportunity of studying its real character. And to no people can this inquiry be more vitally interesting than to the French nation, which is blindly driven onward by a daily and irresistible impulse toward a state of things that may prove either despotic or republican, but which will assuredly be democratic.

I have already observed that universal suffrage has been adopted in all the States of the Union; it consequently operates among different populations which occupy very different positions on the scale of society. I have had opportunities of observing its effects in different localities, and among races of men who are nearly strangers to each other in their language, religion, and manner of life — in Louisiana as well as in New England, in Georgia and in Canada. I have remarked that universal suffrage is far from producing in America either all the good or all the evil consequences attributed to it in Europe, and that its effects differ very widely from those usually ascribed to it.
Choice Of The People, And Instinctive Preferences Of The American Democracy

In the United States the most able men are rarely placed at the head of affairs — Reason of this peculiarity — The envy which prevails in the lower orders of France against the higher classes is not a French, but a purely democratic sentiment — For what reason the most distinguished men in America frequently seclude themselves from public affairs.

Many people in Europe are apt to believe without saying it, or to say without believing it, that one of the great advantages of universal suffrage is that it entrusts the direction of public affairs to men worthy of the public confidence. They admit that the people is unable to govern for itself, but they aver that it is always sincerely disposed to promote the welfare of the State, and that it instinctively designates those persons who are animated by the same good wishes, and who are most fit to wield the supreme authority. I confess that the observations I made in America by no means coincide with these opinions. On my arrival in the United States I was surprised to find so much distinguished talent among the subjects, and so little among the heads of the Government. It is a well-authenticated fact that today the most able men in the United States are very rarely placed at the head of affairs; and it must be acknowledged that such has been the result in proportion as democracy has overstepped all its former limits. The race of American statesmen has evidently dwindled most remarkably in the course of the last fifty years.

Several causes may be assigned to this phenomenon. It is impossible, notwithstanding the most strenuous exertions, to raise the intelligence of the people above a certain level. Whatever the facilities for acquiring information, whatever the profusion of easy methods and cheap science, the human mind can never be instructed and educated without devoting a considerable amount of time to those objects.

The greater or the lesser possibility of subsisting without labor is therefore the necessary boundary of intellectual improvement. This boundary is more remote in some countries and more restricted in others; but it must exist somewhere as long as the people is constrained to work in order to procure the means of physical subsistence — that is to say, as long as it retains its popular character. It is therefore quite as difficult to imagine a State in which all the citizens should be very well informed, as a State in which they should all be wealthy; these two difficulties may be looked upon as correlative. It may very readily be admitted that the mass of the citizens are sincerely disposed to promote the welfare of their country; nay more, it may even be allowed that the lower classes are less apt to be swayed by considerations of personal interest than the higher orders. But it is always more or less impossible for them to discern the best means of attaining the end they desire with sincerity. Long and patient observation, joined to a multitude of different notions, is required to form a just estimate of the character of a single individual; and can it be supposed that the vulgar have the power of succeeding in an inquiry that misleads the penetration of genius itself? The people has neither the time nor the means essential to the prosecution of an investigation of this kind; its conclusions are hastily formed from a superficial inspection of the more prominent features of a question. Hence it often assents to the clamor of a mountebank who knows the secret of stimulating its tastes, while its truest friends frequently fail in their exertions.

Moreover, democracy is not only deficient in the soundness of judgment necessary to select men really deserving of its confidence; it has neither the desire nor the inclination to find them out. It cannot be denied that democratic institutions have a very strong tendency to promote the feeling of envy in the human heart — not so much because they afford to every one the means of rising to the level of any of his fellow citizens, as because those means perpetually disappoint the persons who employ them. Democratic institutions awaken and foster a passion for equality which they can never entirely satisfy. This complete equality eludes the grasp of the people at the very moment at which it thinks to hold it fast, and "flies," as Pascal says, "with eternal flight"; the people is excited in the pursuit of an advantage which is the more precious because it is not sufficiently remote to be unknown, nor sufficiently near to be enjoyed. The lower orders are agitated by the chance of success, and irritated by its uncertainty; they pass from the enthusiasm of pursuit to the exhaustion of ill-success, and lastly to the acrimony of disappointment. Whatever transcends their own limits appears to be an obstacle to their desires, and there is no kind of superiority, however legitimate, that is not irksome in their sight.

It has been supposed that the secret instinct which leads the lower orders to remove their superiors as much as possible from the direction of public affairs is peculiar to France. This, however, is an error; the propensity to which I allude is not inherent in any particular nation, but in democratic institutions in general; and although it may have been heightened by peculiar political circumstances, it owes its origin to a higher cause.

In the United States the people is not disposed to hate the superior classes of society, but it is not very favorably inclined toward them, and carefully excludes them from the exercise of authority. It does not entertain any dread of distinguished talents, but it is rarely captivated by them; and it awards its approbation very sparingly to such as have risen without popular support.

While the natural propensities of democracy lead the people to reject the most distinguished citizens as its rulers, these individuals are no less apt to retire from a political career in which it is almost impossible to retain their independence, or to advance without degrading themselves. This opinion has been very candidly set forth by Chancellor Kent, who says, in speaking with great eulogiums of that part of the Constitution which empowers the Executive to nominate the judges: "It is indeed probable that the men who are best fitted to discharge the duties of this high office would have too much reserve in their manners, and too much austerity in their principles, for them to be returned by the majority at an election where universal suffrage is adopted." Such were the opinions printed without contradiction in America in the year 1830!
I hold it to be sufficiently demonstrated that universal suffrage is by no means a guarantee of the wisdom of the popular choice, and that, whatever its advantages may be, this is not one of them.

Causes Which May Partly Correct These Tendencies Of The Democracy — Contrary effects produced on peoples as well as on individuals by great dangers — Why so many distinguished men stood at the head of affairs in America fifty years ago — Influence which the intelligence and the manners of the people exercise upon its choice — Example of New England — States of the Southwest — Influence of certain laws upon the choice of the people — Election by an elected body — Its effects upon the composition of the Senate.

When a State is threatened by serious dangers, the people frequently succeeds in selecting the citizens most able to save it. It has been observed that man rarely retains his customary level in the presence of very critical circumstances; he rises above or he sinks below his usual condition, and the same thing occurs in nations at large. Extreme perils sometimes quench the energy of a people instead of stimulating it; they excite without directing its passions, and instead of clearing they confuse its powers of perception. The Jews deluged the smoking ruins of their temple with the carnage of the remnant of their host. But it is more common, both in the case of nations and of individuals, to find extraordinary virtues arising from the very imminence of the danger. Great characters are then thrown into relief, as buildings concealed by the gloom of night are illuminated by the glare of a conflagration. At those dangerous times genius no longer abstains from presenting itself in the arena; and the people, alarmed by the perils of its situation, buries its envious passions in a short oblivion. Great names may then be drawn from the ballot-box.

I have already observed that the American statesmen of the present day are very inferior to those who stood at the head of affairs fifty years ago. This is as much a consequence of the circumstances as of the laws of the country. When America was struggling in the high cause of independence to throw off the yoke of another country, and when it was about to usher a new nation into the world, the spirits of its inhabitants were roused to the height their great efforts required. In this general excitement the most distinguished men were ready to forestall the wants of the community, and the people clung to them for support, and placed them at its head. But events of this magnitude are rare, and it is from an inspection of the ordinary course of affairs that our judgment must be formed.

If passing events sometimes act as checks upon the passions of democracy, the intelligence and the manners of the community exercise an influence which is no less powerful and far more permanent. This is extremely perceptible in the United States.

In New England the education and the liberties of the communities were engendered by the moral and religious principles of their founders. Where society has acquired a sufficient degree of stability to enable it to hold certain maxims and retain fixed habits, the lower orders are accustomed to respect intellectual superiority and to submit to it without complaint, although they set at naught all those privileges which wealth and birth have introduced among mankind. The democracy in New England consequently makes a more judicious choice than it does elsewhere.

But as we descend toward the South, to those States in which the constitution of society is more modern and less strong, where instruction is less general, and where the principles of morality, of religion, and of liberty are less happily combined, we perceive that the talents and virtues of those in authority become more and more rare.

Lastly, when we arrive at the new Southwestern States, in which the constitution of society dates only from yesterday, and presents an agglomeration of adventurers and speculators, we are amazed at the persons invested with public authority, and are led to ask by what force, independent of legislation and of the men who direct it, the State can be protected, and society be made to flourish.

There are certain laws of a democratic nature which contribute, nevertheless, to correct, in some measure, the dangerous tendencies of democracy. On entering the House of Representatives in Washington one is struck by the vulgar demeanor of that great assembly. The eye frequently does not discover a man of celebrity within its walls. Its members are almost all obscure individuals whose names present no associations to the mind; they are mostly village lawyers, men in trade, or even persons belonging to the lower classes of society. In a country in which education is very general, it is said that the representatives of the people do not always know how to write correctly.

At a few yards' distance from this spot is the door of the Senate, which contains within a small space a large proportion of the celebrated men of America. Scarcely an individual is to be seen in it who does not recall the idea of an active and illustrious career; the Senate is composed of eloquent advocates, distinguished generals, wise magistrates, and statesmen of note, whose language would at all times do honor to the most remarkable parliamentary debates of Europe.

What, then, is the cause of this strange contrast, and why are the most able citizens to be found in one assembly rather than in the other? Why is the former body remarkable for its vulgarity and its poverty of talent, while the latter seems to enjoy a monopoly of intelligence and of sound judgment? Both of these assemblies emanate from the people; both of them are chosen by universal suffrage; and no voice has yet been heard in America to assert that the Senate is hostile to the interests of the people. From what cause, then, does so startling a difference arise? The only reason that appears to me adequately to account for it is that the House of Representatives is elected by the populace directly, and that the Senate is elected by elected bodies. The whole body of the citizens names the legislature of each State, and the Federal Constitution converts these legislatures into so many electoral bodies, which return the members of the Senate.
