If, then, the Catholic citizens of the United States are not forcibly led by the nature of their beliefs to adopt democratic and republican principles, at least they are not necessarily opposed to them; and their social position, as well as their small numbers, compels them to adopt these opinions. Most of the Catholics are poor, and they have no chance of taking part in government unless it is open to all citizens. They are a minority, and all rights must be respected in order to secure them the free exercise of their own. These two causes lead them, unconsciously, to adopt political doctrines that they would perhaps support with less zeal if they were rich and dominant.

The Catholic clergy of the United States has never attempted to oppose this political tendency; it seeks rather to justify its results. The priests in America have divided the intellectual world into two parts: in the one they place the doctrines of revealed religion, which command their assent; in the other they leave the truths they believe have been freely left open to political inquiry. Thus the Catholics of the United States are at once the most faithful believers and the most zealous citizens.

It may be said that in the United States no religious doctrine shows the slightest hostility to democratic and republican institutions. The clergy of all the different sects speak the same language; their opinions are in tune with the laws; and the human intellect flows onward in a single current.

I happened to be staying in one of the largest towns in the Union when I was invited to attend a public meeting called for the purpose of helping the Poles, and of sending them supplies of arms and money. I found two or three thousand people gathered in a vast hall prepared to receive them. After a short time a priest in his ecclesiastical robes stepped to the front of the platform: the spectators rose and stood bareheaded while he spoke in the following terms:—

"Almighty God! God of Armies! Thou who didst strengthen the hearts and guide the arms of our fathers when they fought for the sacred rights of national independence; Thou who didst make them triumph over a hateful oppression, and hast granted our people the benefits of liberty and peace: turn, O Lord, a favorable eye upon the other hemisphere; look down with pity upon that heroic nation which is even now struggling as we did in former times, and for the same rights we defended with our blood. Thou who didst create Man in the likeness of the same image, let not tyranny mar Thy work and establish inequality upon the earth. Almighty God! watch over the destiny of the Poles, and make them worthy to be free. May Thy wisdom direct their councils, and may Thy strength sustain their arms! Shed forth Thy terror upon their enemies, scatter the powers that take counsel against them, and grant that the injustice the world has witnessed for fifty years may not be consummated in our time. O Lord, who holdest alike the hearts of nations and of men in Thy powerful hand: raise up allies to the sacred cause of right; rouse the French nation from the apathy in which its rulers hold it, so that it may go forth again to fight for the liberties of the world.

"Lord, turn not Thy face from us, and grant that we may always be the most religious as well as the freest people of the earth. Almighty God, hear our supplications this day. Save the Poles, we beseech Thee, in the name of Thy well-beloved Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, who died upon the cross for the salvation of men. Amen."
The whole meeting responded "Amen!" with devotion.
Indirect Influence of Religious Opinions on Political Society in the United States

Christian morality common to all sects—Influence of religion on the manners of the Americans—Respect for the marriage tie—How religion confines the imagination of the Americans within certain limits and checks the passion for innovation—Opinion of the Americans on the political usefulness of religion—Their efforts to extend and secure its predominance.

I have just shown what the direct influence of religion on politics is in the United States, but its indirect influence appears to me to be even greater, and it never instructs the Americans more fully in the art of being free than when it says nothing about freedom.

The sects in the United States are innumerable. They all differ as to the worship due from man to his Creator, but they all agree as to the duties man owes to man. Each sect worships the Deity in its own particular way, but every sect preaches the same moral law in the name of God. If it is of the highest importance to man as an individual that his religion should be true, it is not the same with society. Society has no future life to hope for or to fear; and provided the citizens profess a religion, the particular tenets of that religion are of very little importance to its interests. Moreover, almost all the sects of the United States fall within the great unity of Christianity, and Christian morality is everywhere the same.

It may reasonably be believed that a certain number of Americans follow a particular form of worship from habit more than from conviction. In the United States the sovereign authority is religious, and so hypocrisy must be common; but there is no country in the whole world in which the Christian religion retains a greater influence over the souls of men than in America; and there can be no greater proof of its usefulness, and of its fit with human nature, than that its influence is most powerfully felt in the most enlightened and free nation on earth.

I have noted that the members of the American clergy in general, without even excepting those who do not admit religious liberty, are all in favor of civil freedom; but they do not support any particular political system. They keep aloof from parties and from public affairs. In the United States, religion exerts little influence on the laws or on the details of public opinion, but it directs the manners of the community, and by regulating domestic life it regulates the State.

I do not doubt that the great austerity of manners noticeable in the United States arises, in the first instance, from religious faith. Religion is often unable to restrain man from the countless temptations of fortune, nor can it check the passion for gain that every incident of his life contributes to arouse; but its influence on the mind of woman is supreme, and women are the protectors of morals. There is certainly no country in the world where the marriage tie is so much respected as in America, or where conjugal happiness is more highly or worthily valued. In Europe, almost all the disturbances of society arise from the irregularities of domestic life. To despise the natural bonds and legitimate pleasures of home is to contract a taste for excess, a restlessness of heart, and the evil of shifting desires. Stirred by the tumultuous passions that often disturb his home, the European is galled by the obedience the legislative powers of the State demand. But when the American retires from the turmoil of public life to the bosom of his family, he finds there the image of order and of peace. There his pleasures are simple and natural, his joys innocent and calm; and since he finds that an orderly life is the surest path to happiness, he accustoms himself without difficulty to moderating his opinions as well as his tastes. While the European tries to forget his domestic troubles by agitating society, the American draws from his own home that love of order which he afterwards carries with him into public affairs.

In the United States the influence of religion is not limited to manners—it extends to the intelligence of the people. Among the Anglo-Americans there are some who profess the doctrines of Christianity from sincere belief, and others who do so because they are afraid of being suspected of unbelief. Christianity therefore reigns without obstacle, by universal consent; and the consequence is, as I have already observed, that every principle of the moral world is fixed and determinate, even though the political world is left to the debates and experiments of men. Thus the human mind is never left to wander across a boundless field; and whatever its pretensions, it is checked from time to time by barriers it cannot cross. Before it can innovate, certain primal and unchanging principles are laid down, and the boldest conceptions of human design are subjected to certain forms that slow and halt their completion.

The imagination of the Americans, even in its greatest flights, is cautious and hesitant; its impulses are checked, its works unfinished. These habits of restraint recur in political society and are remarkably favorable both to the tranquility of the people and to the durability of the institutions it has established. Nature and circumstances combined to make the inhabitants of the United States bold men, as is sufficiently attested by the enterprising spirit with which they pursue fortune. If the American mind were free of all restraints, they would very shortly become the most daring innovators and the most implacable disputants in the world. But the revolutionaries of America are obliged to profess an outward respect for Christian morality and equity, which does not easily allow them to violate the laws that stand in the way of their designs; nor would they find it easy to overcome the scruples of their supporters, even if they were able to overcome their own. So far, no one in the United States has dared to advance the maxim that everything is permitted in the interest of society—an impious adage that seems to have been invented in an age of freedom to shelter all the tyrants of future ages. Thus, while the law permits the Americans to do what they please, religion prevents them from conceiving, and forbids them to commit, what is rash or unjust.

Religion in America takes no direct part in the government of society, but it must nevertheless be regarded as the foremost of the political institutions of that country; for if it does not give a taste for freedom, it makes the use of free institutions easier. Indeed, it is from this very point of view that the inhabitants of the United States themselves look upon religious belief. I do not know whether all Americans have a sincere faith in their religion—for who can search the human heart?—but I am certain that they hold it to be indispensable to the maintenance of republican institutions. This opinion does not belong to one class of citizens or to one party; it belongs to the whole nation, to every rank of society.

In the United States, if a political figure attacks a sect, this may not prevent even the supporters of that same sect from backing him; but if he attacks all the sects together, everyone abandons him, and he is left alone.

While I was in America, a witness who happened to be called at the assizes of the county of Chester (State of New York) declared that he did not believe in the existence of God or in the immortality of the soul. The judge refused to admit his testimony, on the ground that the witness had already destroyed all the Court's confidence in what he was about to say. *e The newspapers reported the fact without any further comment.

e [ The New York Spectator of August 23, 1831, relates the fact in the following terms:—"The Court of Common Pleas of Chester county (New York) a few days since rejected a witness who declared his disbelief in the existence of God. The presiding judge remarked that he had not before been aware that there was a man living who did not believe in the existence of God; that this belief constituted the sanction of all testimony in a court of justice, and that he knew of no cause in a Christian country where a witness had been permitted to testify without such belief."]

The Americans combine the notions of Christianity and of liberty so intimately in their minds that it is impossible to make them conceive one without the other; and with them this conviction does not spring from that barren traditionary faith that seems to vegetate in the soul rather than to live.

I have known of societies formed by the Americans to send ministers of the Gospel out into the new Western States to found schools and churches there, lest religion be allowed to die away in those remote settlements and the rising States be less fit to enjoy free institutions than the people from which they had come. I met wealthy New Englanders who abandoned the country in which they were born in order to lay the foundations of Christianity and of freedom on the banks of the Missouri, or in the prairies of Illinois. Thus religious zeal is perpetually stimulated in the United States by the duties of patriotism. These men do not act from an exclusive consideration of the promises of a future life; eternity is only one motive of their devotion to the cause; and if you converse with these missionaries of Christian civilization, you will be surprised to find how much value they set on the goods of this world—you meet a politician where you expected to find a priest. They will tell you that "all the American republics are collectively bound up with each other; if the republics of the West were to fall into anarchy, or to be mastered by a despot, the republican institutions that now flourish on the shores of the Atlantic Ocean would be in great peril. It is therefore in our interest that the new States should be religious, in order to maintain our liberties."

Such are the opinions of the Americans; and if anyone holds that the religious spirit I admire is the very thing most amiss in America, and that all that is missing for the freedom and happiness of the human race is to believe in some blind cosmogony, or to assert with Cabanis that thought is a secretion of the brain, I can only reply that those who speak this way have never been in America, and that they have never seen a religious or a free nation. When they return from their expedition, we shall hear what they have to say.

There are people in France who regard republican institutions as a temporary means to power, wealth, and distinction—men who are the condottieri of liberty, and who fight for their own advantage whatever the colors they wear. It is not to them that I am speaking. But there are others who look forward to the republican form of government as a calm and lasting state, toward which modern society is daily pushed by the ideas and manners of the time, and who sincerely wish to prepare men to be free. When these men attack religious opinions, they obey the dictates of their passions to the prejudice of their interests. Despotism may govern without faith, but liberty cannot. Religion is far more necessary in the republic they paint in glowing colors than in the monarchy they attack; and it is more needed in democratic republics than in any others. How is it possible that society should escape destruction if the moral tie is not tightened in proportion as the political tie is loosened? And what can be done with a people that is its own master, if it is not submissive to the Divinity?

Principal Causes That Make Religion Powerful in America: Care taken by the Americans to separate Church and State—The laws, public opinion, and even the efforts of the clergy combine to promote this end—Influence of religion on the mind in the United States attributable to this cause—Reason for this—What is the natural state of men with regard to religion at the present time—What are the peculiar and incidental causes that prevent men, in certain countries, from reaching this state.

The philosophers of the eighteenth century explained the gradual decay of religious faith in a very simple way. Religious zeal, they said, must necessarily fall as liberty is more widely established and knowledge more widely spread. Unfortunately, the facts are by no means in agreement with their theory. There are certain populations in Europe whose unbelief is matched only by their ignorance and debasement, while in America one of the freest and most enlightened nations in the world fulfills all the outward duties of religious fervor.

On my arrival in the United States, the religious aspect of the country was the first thing that struck my attention; and the longer I stayed there, the more I perceived the great political consequences flowing from this state of things, to which I was unaccustomed. In France I had almost always seen the spirit of religion and the spirit of freedom following courses diametrically opposed to each other; but in America I found them intimately united, reigning together over the same country. My desire to discover the causes of this phenomenon increased from day to day. To satisfy it, I questioned the members of all the different sects, and I more especially sought the company of the clergy, who are the depositaries of the different persuasions and who are most concerned for their endurance. As a member of the Roman Catholic Church, I was brought particularly into contact with several of its priests, with whom I became intimately acquainted. To each of these men I expressed my astonishment and explained my doubts; I found that they differed only on matters of detail, and that they attributed the peaceful dominion of religion in their country chiefly to the separation of Church and State. I do not hesitate to affirm that during my stay in America I did not meet a single individual, of the clergy or of the laity, who was not of the same opinion on this point.

This led me to examine more attentively than I had before the place the American clergy occupies in political society. I learned with surprise that they fill no public appointments; *f not one of them is to be met with in the administration, and they are not even represented in the legislative assemblies. In several States *g the law excludes them from political life, public opinion in all. And when I came to inquire into the prevailing spirit of the clergy, I found that most of its members seem to retire of their own accord from the exercise of power, and that they make it a point of professional pride to abstain from politics.
f [ Unless this term be applied to the functions which many of them fill in the schools. Almost all education is entrusted to the clergy.]

g [ See the Constitution of New York, art. 7, Section 4:—"And whereas the ministers of the gospel are, by their profession, dedicated to the service of God and the care of souls, and ought not to be diverted from the great duties of their functions: therefore no minister of the gospel, or priest of any denomination whatsoever, shall at any time hereafter, under any pretence or description whatever, be eligible to, or capable of holding, any civil or military office or place within this State."
See also the constitutions of North Carolina, art. 31; Virginia; South Carolina, art. I, Section 23; Kentucky, art. 2, Section 26; Tennessee, art. 8, Section I; Louisiana, art. 2, Section 22.]

I heard them inveigh against ambition and deceit, under whatever political opinions these vices might lurk; but I learned from their discourses that in the eye of God men are not guilty for any opinions concerning political government they may profess sincerely, any more than they are for their mistakes in building a house or driving a furrow. I saw that these ministers of the gospel shunned all parties with the care that attends personal interest. These facts convinced me that what I had been told was true; and it then became my aim to investigate their causes, and to inquire how it happened that the real authority of religion was increased by a state of things that diminished its apparent force. These causes did not long escape my inquiry.

The short span of threescore years can never content the imagination of man, nor can the imperfect joys of this world satisfy his heart. Man alone, of all created beings, shows a natural contempt of existence and yet a boundless desire to exist; he scorns life, but he dreads annihilation. These different feelings ceaselessly drive his soul toward the contemplation of a future state, and religion directs his musings there. Religion, then, is simply another form of hope, and it is no less natural to the human heart than hope itself. Men cannot abandon their religious faith without a kind of mental aberration and a sort of violent distortion of their true natures; but they are inevitably brought back to more pious sentiments—for unbelief is an accident, and faith is the only permanent state of mankind. If we consider religious institutions only from a purely human point of view, they may be said to draw an inexhaustible element of strength from man himself, since they belong to one of the constituent principles of human nature.

I am aware that at certain times religion may reinforce this influence, which originates in itself, by the artificial power of the laws and the support of the temporal institutions that direct society. Religions closely united to the governments of the earth have been known to exercise a sovereign authority drawn from the twofold source of terror and faith; but when a religion enters into an alliance of this kind, I do not hesitate to affirm that it commits the same error as a man who would sacrifice his future to his present welfare. In obtaining a power to which it has no claim, it risks the authority that is rightfully its own. When a religion founds its empire on the desire for immortality that lives in every human heart, it may aspire to universal dominion; but when it links itself with a government, it must necessarily adopt maxims that apply only to certain nations. Thus, by forming an alliance with a political power, religion increases its authority over a few and forfeits the hope of reigning over all.

As long as a religion rests on those sentiments that are the consolation of all affliction, it may win the affections of mankind. But if it is mixed up with the bitter passions of the world, it may be forced to defend allies whom its interests, and not the principle of love, have given to it; or to push away as opponents men who are still attached to its own spirit, however opposed they may be to the powers with which it is allied. The Church cannot share the temporal power of the State without also becoming the object of a portion of the hostility that the latter provokes.

The political powers that seem most firmly established often have no better guarantee of their duration than the opinions of a generation, the interests of the time, or the life of an individual. A law can modify the social condition that seems most fixed and determinate; and with the social condition, everything else must change. The powers of society are more or less fleeting, like the years we spend on earth; they succeed one another rapidly, like the passing cares of life; and no government has ever yet been founded on an unchanging disposition of the human heart or on an imperishable interest.

As long as a religion is sustained by those feelings, tendencies, and passions that recur in the same forms at every period of history, it may defy the efforts of time; at the very least, it can be destroyed only by another religion. But when religion clings to the interests of the world, it becomes almost as fragile a thing as the powers of the earth. It is the only one of them all that can hope for immortality; but if it is bound to their ephemeral authority, it shares their fortunes and may fall with the transient passions that supported them for a day. The alliance a religion contracts with political powers is bound to be a burden to it, since it does not need their help to live, and by giving them its own help it exposes itself to decay.

The danger I have just pointed out always exists, but it is not always equally visible. In some ages governments seem imperishable; in others, the existence of society appears more precarious than the life of a man. Some constitutions plunge the citizens into a lethargic drowsiness, others rouse them to feverish excitement. When governments appear so strong and laws so stable, men do not perceive the dangers that may come from a union of Church and State. When governments display so much weakness and laws so much inconstancy, the danger is self-evident, but it is no longer possible to avoid it; to be effective, measures must be taken to detect its approach.

In proportion as a nation takes on a democratic social condition, and as communities show democratic tendencies, it becomes more and more dangerous to connect religion with political institutions. For the time is coming when authority will be passed from hand to hand, when political theories will follow one another, and when men, laws, and constitutions will disappear or be modified from day to day—and this, not for a season only, but unceasingly. Agitation and changefulness are inherent in the nature of democratic republics, just as stagnation and inertness are the law of absolute monarchies.

If the Americans—who change the head of the Government once in four years, who elect new legislators every two years, and renew the provincial officers every twelvemonth—if the Americans, who have abandoned the political world to the attempts of innovators, had not placed religion beyond their reach, where could it abide in the ebb and flow of human opinions? Where would the respect that is its due be paid, amid the struggles of faction? And what would become of its immortality, in the midst of perpetual decay? The American clergy were the first to perceive this truth, and to act accordingly. They saw that they must give up their religious influence if they were to strive for political power; and they chose to give up the support of the State rather than share its vicissitudes.

In America, religion is perhaps less powerful than it has been at certain periods in the history of certain peoples; but its influence is more lasting. It confines itself to its own resources, but of those none can deprive it: its circle is limited to certain principles, but those principles are entirely its own, and under its undisputed control.

On every side in Europe we hear voices complaining of the absence of religious faith, and asking the means of restoring to religion some remnant of its original authority. It seems to me that we must first consider carefully what the natural state of men with regard to religion ought to be at the present time; and when we know what we have to hope and to fear, we may discern the end toward which our efforts should be directed.

The two great dangers that threaten the existence of religions are schism and indifference. In ages of fervent devotion, men sometimes abandon their religion, but they only cast it off in order to adopt another. Their faith changes the objects to which it is directed, but it suffers no decline. The old religion then excites enthusiastic attachment in one party and bitter enmity in the other; some leave it with anger, others cling to it with increased devotedness; and although persuasions differ, irreligion is unknown. Such, however, is not the case when a religious belief is secretly undermined by doctrines that may be called negative, since they deny the truth of one religion without affirming that of any other. Prodigious revolutions then take place in the human mind, without the apparent cooperation of human passions, and almost without man's knowledge. Men lose the objects of their fondest hopes, as if by forgetfulness. They are carried away by an imperceptible current that they have not the courage to stem, but which they follow with regret, since it bears them from a faith they love to a skepticism that plunges them into despair.

In ages that match this description, men desert their religious opinions from lukewarmness rather than from dislike; they do not reject them, but the sentiments that once nourished them disappear. But even if the unbeliever does not admit religion to be true, he still considers it useful. Looking at religious institutions from a human point of view, he acknowledges their influence on manners and on legislation. He admits that they may serve to make men live in peace with one another, and to prepare them gently for the hour of death. He regrets the faith he has lost; and since he is deprived of a treasure whose full value he has come to appreciate, he scruples to take it from those who still possess it.

On the other hand, those who continue to believe are not afraid to avow their faith openly. They look upon those who do not share their conviction as more deserving of pity than of opposition; and they are aware that to gain the esteem of unbelievers they are not obliged to follow their example. They are hostile to no one in the world; and since they do not regard the society in which they live as an arena in which religion is bound to face its thousand deadly foes, they love their contemporaries even as they condemn their weaknesses and lament their errors.

Since those who do not believe conceal their incredulity, and those who believe display their faith, public opinion declares itself in favor of religion: love, support, and honor are bestowed upon it, and only by searching the human soul can one detect the wounds it has received. The mass of mankind, which is never without religious feeling, sees nothing at variance with the established faith. The instinctive desire for a future life brings the crowd around the altar, and opens the hearts of men to the precepts and consolations of religion.

But this picture does not apply to us. Among us there are men who have stopped believing in Christianity without adopting any other religion; others who are in the perplexities of doubt, and who already make a show of not believing; and others still who are afraid to avow the Christian faith that they still cherish in secret.

Amid these lukewarm partisans and ardent antagonists a small number of believers exist, ready to brave all obstacles and to scorn all dangers in defense of their faith. They have done violence to human weakness in order to rise above public opinion. Stirred up by the effort they have made, they hardly know where to stop; and since they know that the first use the French made of independence was to attack religion, they look upon their contemporaries with dread, and they recoil in alarm from the liberty their fellow-citizens are trying to obtain. Because unbelief seems to them a novelty, they lump together everything new in one indiscriminate animosity. They are at war with their age and country, and they look upon every opinion put forward there as the necessary enemy of the faith.

This is not the natural state of men with regard to religion at the present day; some extraordinary or incidental cause must be at work in France to prevent the human mind from following its original tendencies and to drive it beyond the limits at which it ought naturally to stop. I am deeply convinced that this extraordinary and incidental cause is the close connection between politics and religion. The unbelievers of Europe attack the Christians as their political opponents rather than as their religious adversaries; they hate the Christian religion as the opinion of a party far more than as an error of belief; and they reject the clergy less because they are the representatives of the Divinity than because they are the allies of authority.

In Europe, Christianity has been intimately united to the powers of the earth. Those powers are now in decay, and religion is, as it were, buried under their ruins. The living body of religion has been bound to the dead corpse of a superannuated polity: cut but the bonds that hold it, and that which is alive will rise once more. I do not know what could restore the Christian Church of Europe to the energy of its earlier days; that power belongs to God alone. But it may be the effect of human policy to leave the faith in the full exercise of the strength that still remains to it.
How the Instruction, the Habits, and the Practical Experience of the Americans Promote the Success of Their Democratic Institutions

What is to be understood by the instruction of the American people—The human mind more superficially instructed in the United States than in Europe—No one completely uninstructed—Reason for this—Rapidity with which opinions are diffused even in the uncultivated States of the West—Practical experience more useful to the Americans than book-learning.
I have very little to add to what I have already said about the influence that the instruction and habits of the Americans exert on the maintenance of their political institutions.

America has so far produced very few writers of distinction; it has no great historians, and not a single eminent poet. The inhabitants of that country regard what are properly called literary pursuits with a kind of disapproval; and there are second-rate towns in Europe in which more literary works are published each year than in the twenty-four States of the Union put together. The spirit of the Americans is averse to general ideas, and does not seek theoretical discoveries. Neither politics nor manufactures direct them to such occupations; and although new laws are continually being enacted in the United States, no great writers have yet inquired into the general principles of their legislation. The Americans have lawyers and commentators, but no jurists; *h and they furnish examples rather than lessons to the world. The same remark applies to the mechanical arts. In America, the inventions of Europe are adopted with sagacity; they are perfected, and adapted with admirable skill to the needs of the country. Manufactures exist, but the science of manufacture is not cultivated; they have good workmen, but very few inventors. Fulton was obliged to offer his services to foreign nations for a long time before he was able to devote them to his own country.
h [ [This cannot be said with truth of the country of Kent, Story, and Wheaton.]]

The observer who wishes to form an opinion on the state of instruction among the Anglo-Americans must consider the same object from two different points of view. If he singles out only the learned, he will be astonished to find how rare they are; but if he counts the ignorant, the American people will appear to be the most enlightened community in the world. The whole population, as I observed elsewhere, stands between these two extremes. In New England, every citizen receives the elementary notions of human knowledge; he is also taught the doctrines and the evidences of his religion, the history of his country, and the leading features of its Constitution. In Connecticut and Massachusetts, it is extremely rare to find a man imperfectly acquainted with all these things, and a person wholly ignorant of them is a sort of phenomenon.

When I compare the Greek and Roman republics with these American States—the manuscript libraries of the former and their rude population with the innumerable journals and the enlightened people of the latter; when I remember all the attempts that are made to judge the modern republics by the help of those of antiquity, and to infer what will happen in our time from what took place two thousand years ago—I am tempted to burn my books, in order to bring nothing but new ideas to bear on so new a condition of society.

What I have said of New England must not, however, be applied without distinction to the whole Union; as we move westward or southward, the instruction of the people declines. In the States bordering the Gulf of Mexico, a certain number of individuals may be found, as in our own countries, who lack the rudiments of instruction. But there is not a single district in the United States sunk in complete ignorance, and for a very simple reason: the peoples of Europe started from the darkness of a barbarous condition to advance toward the light of civilization; their progress has been unequal; some of them have improved rapidly, while others have loitered on their way, and some have stopped and are still sleeping beside it. *i

i [ [In the Northern States the number of persons destitute of instruction is inconsiderable, the largest number being 241,152 in the State of New York (according to Spaulding's Handbook of American Statistics for 1874); but in the South no less than 1,516,339 whites and 2,671,396 colored persons are returned as "illiterate."]]

This has not been the case in the United States. The Anglo-Americans settled in a state of civilization on the territory their descendants now occupy; they did not have to begin to learn, and it was enough for them not to forget. Now the children of these same Americans are the people who, year by year, carry their dwellings into the wilds—and with their dwellings, the knowledge they have acquired and their esteem for knowledge. Education has taught them the usefulness of instruction, and has enabled them to pass that instruction on to their posterity. In the United States, society has no infancy; it is born fully grown.

The Americans never use the word "peasant," because they have no idea of the particular class that term denotes; the ignorance of more remote ages, the simplicity of rural life, and the rusticity of the villager have not been preserved among them, and they are equally unacquainted with the virtues, the vices, the coarse habits, and the simple graces of an early stage of civilization. At the extreme borders of the Confederate States, on the edge of society and the wilderness, a population of bold adventurers has settled, who pierce the solitudes of the American woods and seek a country there in order to escape the poverty that awaited them in their native provinces. As soon as the pioneer reaches the spot that is to serve him as a refuge, he fells a few trees and builds a log house. Nothing could offer a more miserable aspect than these isolated dwellings. The traveler who approaches one of them toward nightfall sees the flicker of the hearth-flame through the chinks in the walls; and at night, if the wind rises, he hears the roof of boughs swaying to and fro amid the great forest trees. Who would not suppose that this poor hut is the asylum of rudeness and ignorance? Yet no sort of comparison can be drawn between the pioneer and the dwelling that shelters him. Everything about him is primitive and unformed, but he himself is the result of the labor and experience of eighteen centuries. He wears the dress and speaks the language of cities; he is acquainted with the past, curious about the future, and ready to argue about the present. He is, in short, a highly civilized being who consents, for a time, to inhabit the backwoods, and who penetrates the wilds of the New World with a Bible, an axe, and a file of newspapers.

It is difficult to imagine the incredible speed with which public opinion circulates in the midst of these deserts. *j I do not think that so much intellectual intercourse takes place in the most enlightened and populous districts of France. *k It cannot be doubted that, in the United States, the instruction of the people powerfully contributes to the support of a democratic republic; and such must always be the case, I believe, where instruction that awakens the understanding is not separated from moral education that amends the heart. But I by no means exaggerate this benefit, and I am still further from thinking, as so many people in Europe do, that men can be instantly made into citizens by teaching them to read and write. True information is mainly drawn from experience; and if the Americans had not been gradually accustomed to govern themselves, their book-learning would not help them much today.

j [ I travelled along a portion of the frontier of the United States in a sort of cart that was called the mail. We passed, day and night, at great speed, along the roads that were scarcely marked out, through immense forests; when the gloom of the woods became impenetrable, the coachman lighted branches of fir, and we journeyed along by the light they cast. From time to time we came to a hut in the midst of the forest, which was a post-office. The mail dropped an enormous bundle of letters at the door of this isolated dwelling, and we pursued our way at full gallop, leaving the inhabitants of the neighboring log houses to send for their share of the treasure.

[When the author visited America the locomotive and the railroad were scarcely invented, and not yet introduced in the United States. It is superfluous to point out the immense effect of those inventions in extending civilization and developing the resources of that vast continent. In 1831 there were 51 miles of railway in the United States; in 1872 there were 60,000 miles of railway.]]

k [ In 1832 each inhabitant of Michigan paid a sum equivalent to 1 fr. 22 cent. (French money) to the post-office revenue, and each inhabitant of the Floridas paid 1 fr. 5 cent. (See National Calendar, 1833, p. 244.) In the same year each inhabitant of the Département du Nord paid 1 fr. 4 cent. to the revenue of the French post-office. (See the Compte rendu de l'administration des Finances, 1833, p. 623.) Now the State of Michigan only contained at that time 7 inhabitants per square league, and Florida only 5; the public instruction and the commercial activity of these districts are inferior to those of most of the States in the Union, whilst the Département du Nord, which contains 3,400 inhabitants per square league, is one of the most enlightened and manufacturing parts of France.]

I have lived a great deal among the people in the United States, and I cannot express how much I admire their experience and good sense. An American should never be allowed to speak of Europe; for he will then probably display a great deal of presumption and very foolish pride. He will fall back on those crude and vague notions that are so useful to the ignorant all over the world. But if you question him about his own country, the cloud that dimmed his intelligence will immediately lift; his language will become as clear and precise as his thoughts. He will tell you what his rights are, and by what means he exercises them; he will be able to point out the customs that prevail in the political world. You will find that he is well acquainted with the rules of the administration, and that he is familiar with the mechanism of the laws. The citizen of the United States does not acquire his practical knowledge and his definite notions from books; the instruction he has acquired may have prepared him to receive those ideas, but it did not furnish them. The American learns the laws by taking part in the act of legislation, and he takes a lesson in the forms of government by governing. The great work of society is constantly going on before his eyes, and, as it were, under his hands.

In the United States, politics is the end and aim of education; in Europe its principal object is to fit men for private life. The participation of citizens in public affairs is too rare an occurrence to be anticipated in advance. A glance over society in the two hemispheres shows these differences even in its outward appearance.

In Europe we frequently introduce the ideas and habits of private life into public affairs; and since we pass at once from the domestic circle to the government of the State, we may often be heard discussing the great interests of society in the same manner in which we converse with our friends. The Americans, on the other hand, carry the habits of public life over into their manners in private; and in their country the jury is introduced into the games of schoolboys, and parliamentary forms are observed at the order of a feast.
The Laws Contribute More to the Maintenance of the Democratic Republic in the United States Than the Physical Circumstances of the Country, and the Manners More Than the Laws

All the nations of America have a democratic state of society—Yet democratic institutions subsist only among the Anglo-Americans—The Spaniards of South America, equally favored by physical causes as the Anglo-Americans, unable to maintain a democratic republic—Mexico, which has adopted the Constitution of the United States, in the same predicament—The Anglo-Americans of the West less able to maintain it than those of the East—Reason for these different results.

I have remarked that the maintenance of democratic institutions in the United States is due to the circumstances, the laws, and the manners of that country. *l Most Europeans know only the first of these three causes, and they are apt to give it a preponderating importance it does not really possess.
l [ I remind the reader of the general sense I give to the word "manners," namely, the moral and intellectual characteristics of social man taken collectively.]

It is true that the Anglo-Saxons settled in the New World in a state of social equality; the low-born and the noble were not to be found among them, and professional prejudices were always as entirely unknown as the prejudices of birth. Thus, since the condition of society was democratic, the empire of democracy was established without difficulty. But this circumstance is by no means peculiar to the United States; almost all the trans-Atlantic colonies were founded by men equal among themselves, or who became so by settling them. In no part of the New World have Europeans been able to create an aristocracy. Nevertheless, democratic institutions prosper nowhere but in the United States.

The American Union has no enemies to contend with; it stands in the wilds like an island in the ocean. But the Spaniards of South America were no less isolated by nature; yet their position has not spared them the burden of standing armies. They make war on each other when they have no foreign enemies to fight; and the Anglo-American democracy is the only one that has so far been able to maintain itself in peace. *m
m [ [A remark which, since the great Civil War of 1861-65, ceases to be applicable.]]

The territory of the Union offers a boundless field to human activity, and inexhaustible materials for industry and labor. The passion for wealth takes the place of ambition, and the heat of faction is tempered by a sense of prosperity. But in what part of the globe shall we find more fertile plains, mightier rivers, or more unexplored and inexhaustible riches than in South America?

Nevertheless, South America has been unable to maintain democratic institutions. If the welfare of nations depended on being placed in a remote position, with an unbounded stretch of habitable territory before them, the Spaniards of South America would have no reason to complain of their lot. And although they might enjoy less prosperity than the inhabitants of the United States, their condition might still be such as to excite the envy of some nations in Europe. Yet there are no nations on the face of the earth more miserable than those of South America.

Thus, not only are physical causes unable to produce results similar to those that occur in North America—they cannot even raise the population of South America above the level of European States, where they act in the opposite direction. Physical causes do not, therefore, affect the destiny of nations as much as has been supposed.

I have met men in New England who were on the point of leaving a country where they could have stayed in comfortable circumstances, in order to go seek their fortune in the wilds. Not far from that district I found a French population in Canada, crowded into a narrow territory although the same wilds were close at hand; and while the emigrant from the United States bought an extensive estate with the earnings of a short spell of labor, the Canadian paid as much for land as he would have paid in France. Nature offers the solitudes of the New World to Europeans, but they do not always know how to turn her gifts to account. Other peoples of America have the same physical conditions of prosperity as the Anglo-Americans, but without their laws and their manners; and these peoples are wretched. The laws and manners of the Anglo-Americans are therefore the effective cause of their greatness—the object of my inquiry.

I am far from supposing that the American laws are pre-eminently good in themselves; I do not hold them to be applicable to all democratic peoples, and several of them seem to me dangerous, even in the United States. Nevertheless, it cannot be denied that American legislation, taken as a whole, is extremely well suited to the genius of the people and the nature of the country it is meant to govern. The American laws are therefore good, and to them must be attributed a large share of the success that attends the government of democracy in America; but I do not believe them to be the principal cause of that success. And if they seem to me to have more influence on the social happiness of the Americans than the nature of the country, there is, on the other hand, reason to believe that their effect is still less than that produced by the manners of the people.

The Federal laws are undoubtedly the most important part of the legislation of the United States. Mexico, which is no less fortunately situated than the Anglo-American Union, has adopted the same laws, yet is unable to accustom itself to the government of democracy. Some other cause is therefore at work, independently of the physical circumstances and the particular laws that enable democracy to rule in the United States.

Another still more striking proof may be offered. Almost all the inhabitants of the territory of the Union are descendants of a common stock; they speak the same language, they worship God in the same manner, they are affected by the same physical causes, and they obey the same laws. Where, then, do their characteristic differences come from? Why, in the Eastern States of the Union, does the republican government display vigor and regularity, and proceed with mature deliberation? Whence does it draw the wisdom and the durability that mark its acts, while in the Western States, on the contrary, society seems to be ruled by the powers of chance? There, public business is conducted with an irregularity and a passionate, feverish excitement that does not promise a long or sure duration.

I am no longer comparing the Anglo-American States to foreign nations; I am contrasting them with each other, and trying to discover why they are so unlike. The arguments drawn from the nature of the country and from differences in legislation are here all set aside. Recourse must be had to some other cause; and what other cause can there be, except the manners of the people?

It is in the Eastern States that the Anglo-Americans have been longest accustomed to the government of democracy, and that they have formed the habits and conceived the notions most favorable to its maintenance. Democracy has gradually penetrated their customs, their opinions, and the forms of social intercourse; it is found in all the details of daily life as much as in the laws. In the Eastern States, the instruction and practical education of the people have been most fully developed, and religion has been most thoroughly amalgamated with liberty. Now these habits, opinions, customs, and convictions are precisely the constituent elements of what I have called manners.

In the Western States, by contrast, a portion of these same advantages is still lacking. Many of the Americans of the West were born in the woods, and they mix the ideas and customs of savage life with the civilization of their parents. Their passions are more intense, their religious morality less authoritative, their convictions less secure. The inhabitants exercise no sort of control over their fellow-citizens, for they are scarcely acquainted with each other. The nations of the West show, to a certain extent, the inexperience and rude habits of a people in its infancy; for although they are made up of old elements, their assemblage is of recent date.

The manners of the Americans of the United States are, then, the real cause that makes that people the only one of the American nations able to sustain a democratic government; and it is the influence of manners that produces the different degrees of order and prosperity that may be distinguished in the several Anglo-American democracies. Thus the effect that the geographical position of a country may have on the duration of democratic institutions is exaggerated in Europe. Too much importance is attributed to legislation, too little to manners. These three great causes serve, no doubt, to regulate and direct the American democracy; but if they were to be ranked in their proper order, I should say that physical circumstances are less effective than the laws, and the laws very subordinate to the manners of the people. I am convinced that the most advantageous situation and the best possible laws cannot maintain a constitution in spite of the manners of a country; while the latter may turn the most unfavorable positions and the worst laws to some advantage. The importance of manners is a common truth to which study and experience incessantly direct our attention. It may be regarded as a central point in the range of human observation, and the common end of all inquiry. So seriously do I insist on this point that, if I have so far failed to make the reader feel the important influence which I attribute to the practical experience, the habits, the opinions—in short, to the manners of the Americans—on the maintenance of their institutions, I have failed in the principal object of my work.
Whether Laws and Manners Are Sufficient to Maintain Democratic Institutions in Other Countries Besides America

The Anglo-Americans, if transported into Europe, would be obliged to modify their laws—Distinction to be made between democratic institutions and American institutions—Democratic laws may be conceived better than, or at least different from, those the American democracy has adopted—The example of America only proves that it is possible to regulate democracy by the help of manners and legislation.

I have asserted that the success of democratic institutions in the United States is more intimately connected with the laws themselves and the manners of the people than with the nature of the country. But does it follow that the same causes would of themselves produce the same results if they were put into operation elsewhere? And if the country cannot adequately substitute for laws and manners, can laws and manners in turn substitute for the country? It will readily be understood that the elements necessary to answer this question are lacking: other peoples besides the Anglo-Americans are to be found in the New World, and as these peoples are affected by the same physical circumstances as the latter, they may fairly be compared with them. But there are no nations outside America that have adopted the same laws and manners while being destitute of the physical advantages peculiar to the Anglo-Americans. No standard of comparison therefore exists, and we can only venture an opinion on this subject.

It appears to me, in the first place, that a careful distinction must be made between the institutions of the United States and democratic institutions in general. When I reflect on the state of Europe, its mighty nations, its populous cities, its formidable armies, and the complex nature of its politics, I cannot suppose that even the Anglo-Americans, if they were transported to our hemisphere with their ideas, their religion, and their manners, could exist without considerably altering their laws. But a democratic nation may be imagined, organized differently from the American people. It is not impossible to conceive a government truly founded on the will of the majority—but one in which the majority, suppressing its natural leaning toward equality, should consent, for the sake of the order and stability of the State, to invest a family or an individual with all the prerogatives of the executive. A democratic society might exist in which the forces of the nation would be more centralized than they are in the United States; the people would exert a less direct and less irresistible influence on public affairs, and yet every citizen invested with certain rights would participate, within his sphere, in the conduct of the government. The observations I made among the Anglo-Americans lead me to believe that democratic institutions of this kind, prudently introduced into society so as gradually to mix with the habits and be interfused with the opinions of the people, might subsist in other countries besides America. If the laws of the United States were the only imaginable democratic laws, or the most perfect it is possible to conceive, I should admit that the success of those institutions affords no proof of the success of democratic institutions in general in a country less favored by natural circumstances. But since the laws of America appear to me to be defective in several respects, and since I can readily imagine others of the same general nature, the peculiar advantages of that country do not prove that democratic institutions cannot succeed in a nation less favored by circumstances, if it is ruled by better laws.

If human nature were different in America from what it is elsewhere, or if the social condition of the Americans generated among them habits and opinions different from those that arise from the same social condition in the Old World, the American democracies would offer no means of predicting what may happen in other democracies. If the Americans displayed the same propensities as all other democratic nations, and if their legislators had relied on the nature of the country and the favor of circumstances to hold those propensities within proper limits, the prosperity of the United States would be attributable exclusively to physical causes, and it would offer no encouragement to a people inclined to imitate their example without sharing their natural advantages. But neither of these suppositions is borne out by the facts.

In America the same passions are to be found as in Europe—some arising from human nature, others from the democratic condition of society. Thus in the United States I found that restlessness of heart which is natural to men when all ranks are nearly equal and the chances of advancement are the same for all. I found the democratic feeling of envy expressed in a thousand different forms. I observed that the people frequently displayed, in the conduct of affairs, a consummate mixture of ignorance and presumption, and I concluded that in America men are liable to the same failings and the same absurdities as among ourselves. But on examining the state of society more attentively, I soon discovered that the Americans had made great and successful efforts to counteract these imperfections of human nature, and to correct the natural defects of democracy. Their various municipal laws seemed to me a means of restraining the ambition of the citizens within a narrow sphere, and of turning those same passions which might have worked havoc in the State to the good of the township or the parish. The American legislators have succeeded to a certain extent in setting the notion of rights against the feelings of envy; the permanence of the religious world against the continual shifting of politics; the experience of the people against its theoretical ignorance; and its practical knowledge of business against the impatience of its desires.

The Americans, then, have not relied on the nature of their country to counterbalance the dangers arising from their Constitution and their political laws. To evils common to all democratic peoples they have applied remedies which none but themselves had ever thought of before; and although they were the first to make the experiment, they have succeeded in it.

The manners and laws of the Americans are not the only ones that may suit a democratic people; but the Americans have shown that it would be wrong to despair of regulating democracy by the help of manners and laws. If other nations should borrow this general and pregnant idea from the Americans, without, however, intending to imitate them in the particular application they have given it; if they should attempt to fit themselves for the social condition that it seems to be the will of Providence to impose upon the generations of this age, and so to escape from the despotism or the anarchy that threatens them—what reason is there to suppose that their efforts would not be crowned with success? The organization and establishment of democracy in Christendom is the great political problem of the time. The Americans, unquestionably, have not solved this problem, but they furnish useful data to those who undertake the task.
Importance of What Precedes with Respect to the State of Europe

It may readily be seen with what intention I undertook the foregoing inquiries. The question discussed here is interesting not only to the United States but to the whole world; it concerns not a nation but all mankind. If those nations whose social condition is democratic could remain free only so long as they inhabited the wilds, we could not but despair of the future destiny of the human race; for democracy is rapidly gaining a wider sway, and the wilds are gradually being peopled with men. If it were true that laws and manners are insufficient to maintain democratic institutions, what refuge would remain open to the nations but the despotism of a single individual? I am aware that there are many worthy people at the present time who are not alarmed at this latter alternative, and who are so tired of liberty as to be glad of repose, far from the storms that attend it. But these individuals are ill acquainted with the haven toward which they are bound. They are so deluded by their memories that they judge the tendency of absolute power by what it was in former times, and not by what it might become today.

If absolute power were re-established among the democratic nations of Europe, I am persuaded that it would take on a new form, and appear with features unknown to our forefathers. There was a time in Europe when the laws and the consent of the people had invested princes with almost unlimited authority; but they scarcely ever made use of it. I do not speak of the prerogatives of the nobility, of the authority of supreme courts of justice, of corporations and their chartered rights, or of provincial privileges, all of which served to break the blows of the sovereign authority and to keep a spirit of resistance alive in the nation. Apart from these political institutions—which, however opposed they may have been to personal liberty, served to keep the love of freedom alive in the public mind, and may be reckoned useful in this respect—the manners and opinions of the nation confined royal authority within barriers that were no less powerful for being less conspicuous. Religion, the affections of the people, the benevolence of the prince, the sense of honor, family pride, provincial prejudices, custom, and public opinion all limited the power of kings and restrained their authority within an invisible circle. The constitution of nations was despotic at that time, but their manners were free. Princes had the right, but they had neither the means nor the desire, of doing whatever they pleased.

But what now remains of the barriers that once arrested the aggressions of tyranny? Since religion has lost its empire over the souls of men, the most prominent boundary that divided good from evil has been overthrown; the very elements of the moral world are uncertain; the princes and the peoples of the earth are guided by chance, and none can define the natural limits of despotism or the bounds of license. Long revolutions have forever destroyed the respect that once surrounded the rulers of the State; and now that they have been relieved of the burden of public esteem, princes may henceforward surrender themselves without fear to the seductions of arbitrary power.

When kings find that the hearts of their subjects are turned toward them, they are clement, because they are conscious of their strength; and they are careful of their people's affection, because that affection is the bulwark of the throne. A mutual exchange of goodwill then takes place between the prince and the people, like the gracious intercourse of domestic society. The subjects may murmur at the sovereign's decree, but they are grieved to displease him; and the sovereign chastises his subjects with the light hand of parental affection.

But once the spell of royalty is broken in the tumult of revolution; when successive monarchs have passed across the throne, so as alternately to display to the people the weakness of their right and the harshness of their power—the sovereign is no longer regarded by any as the Father of the State, and is feared by all as its master. If he is weak, he is despised; if he is strong, he is detested. He himself is full of animosity and alarm; he finds himself a stranger in his own country, and he treats his subjects like conquered enemies.

When the provinces and the towns formed so many different nations within their common country, each of them had a will of its own, opposed to the general spirit of subjection; but now that all the parts of the same empire, after having lost their immunities, their customs, their prejudices, their traditions, and their names, are subjected and accustomed to the same laws, it is no more difficult to oppress them collectively than it was formerly to oppress them one by one.

While the nobles enjoyed their power, and indeed long after that power was lost, the honor of aristocracy conferred an extraordinary degree of force on their personal opposition. They provide instances of men who, despite their weakness, still held a high opinion of their personal worth, and dared to stand alone against the efforts of the public authority. But at the present day, when all ranks are more and more blurred together, when the individual disappears into the throng and is easily lost in a common obscurity, when the honor of monarchy has almost lost its empire without being succeeded by public virtue, and when nothing enables a man to rise above himself, who shall say at what point the demands of power and the servility of weakness will stop?

As long as family feeling was kept alive, the opponent of oppression was never alone; he looked around him and found his clients, his hereditary friends, and his kinsfolk. If this support was lacking, he was sustained by his ancestors and animated by his posterity. But when patrimonial estates are divided, and when a few years suffice to confound the distinctions of a race, where can family feeling be found? What force can there be in the customs of a country that has changed and is still perpetually changing its aspect—a country in which every act of tyranny has a precedent, and every crime an example; in which there is nothing so old that its antiquity can save it from destruction, and nothing so unparalleled that its novelty can prevent it from being done? What resistance can be offered by manners of so pliant a make that they have already often yielded? What strength can even public opinion retain when no twenty persons are connected by a common tie; when not a man, nor a family, nor a chartered corporation, nor a class, nor a free institution, has the power of representing or asserting that opinion; and when every citizen—being equally weak, equally poor, and equally dependent—has only his personal impotence to oppose to the organized force of the government?

The annals of France furnish nothing analogous to the condition into which that country might then be thrown. But it may more aptly be likened to the times of old, and to those hideous eras of Roman oppression, when the manners of the people were corrupted, their traditions obliterated, their habits destroyed, their opinions shaken, and freedom, expelled from the laws, could find no refuge in the land; when nothing protected the citizens, and the citizens no longer protected themselves; when human nature was the sport of man, and princes wearied out the clemency of Heaven before they exhausted the patience of their subjects. Those who hope to revive the monarchy of Henry IV or of Louis XIV appear to me to be afflicted with mental blindness; and when I consider the present condition of several European nations—a condition toward which all the others tend—I am led to believe that they will soon be left with no other alternative than democratic liberty or the tyranny of the Caesars. *n
n [ [This prediction of the return of France to imperial despotism, and of the true character of that despotic power, was written in 1832, and realized to the letter in 1852.]]

And indeed it is worth considering whether men are to be entirely emancipated or entirely enslaved; whether their rights are to be made equal, or wholly taken away from them. If the rulers of society were reduced either to raise the crowd gradually to their own level, or to sink the citizens below that of humanity, would not the doubts of many be resolved, the consciences of many be healed, and the community prepared to make great sacrifices with little difficulty? In that case, the gradual growth of democratic manners and institutions should be regarded, not as the best, but as the only means of preserving freedom; and without liking the government of democracy, it might be adopted as the most applicable and the fairest remedy for the present ills of society.

It is difficult to associate a people in the work of government; but it is still more difficult to supply it with experience and to inspire in it the feelings it needs in order to govern well. I grant that the caprices of democracy are perpetual; its instruments are rough; its laws imperfect. But if it were true that soon no middle ground would exist between the empire of democracy and the dominion of a single arm, should we not rather incline toward the former than submit voluntarily to the latter? And if complete equality is to be our fate, is it not better to be leveled by free institutions than by despotic power?

Those who, after reading this book, should imagine that my intention in writing it has been to propose the laws and manners of the Anglo-Americans for the imitation of all democratic peoples, would be making a very great mistake; they must have paid more attention to the form than to the substance of my ideas. My aim has been to show, by the example of America, that there may exist laws, and especially manners, that will allow a democratic people to remain free. But I am very far from thinking that we ought to follow the example of the American democracy, and copy the means it has used to attain its ends; for I am well aware of the influence that the nature of a country and its political precedents exert on a constitution, and I should regard it as a great misfortune for mankind if liberty were to exist all over the world under the same forms.

But I am of the opinion that if we do not succeed in gradually introducing democratic institutions into France, and if we despair of imparting to the citizens those ideas and sentiments that first prepare them for freedom and afterward allow them to enjoy it, there will be no independence at all—neither for the middling classes nor the nobility, for the poor nor the rich—but an equal tyranny over all; and I foresee that if the peaceable empire of the majority is not founded among us in time, we shall sooner or later arrive at the unlimited authority of a single despot.

chapters.title: Chapter XVIII — Future Condition Of Three Races In The United States
paragraphs: The Present and Probable Future Condition of the Three Races Which Inhabit the Territory of the United States

The principal part of the task I set for myself is now complete. I have shown, as best I could, the laws and manners of American democracy. I might stop here; but the reader would perhaps feel I had not met his expectations.

The absolute supremacy of democracy is not all that we find in America; the inhabitants of the New World can be considered from more than one point of view. In the course of this work my subject has often led me to speak of the Indians and the Negroes, but I have never been able to pause in order to show what place these two races occupy in the midst of the democratic people I was engaged in describing. I have mentioned in what spirit, and according to what laws, the Anglo-American Union was formed; but I could only glance at the dangers that threaten that confederation, and it was equally impossible for me to give a detailed account of its chances of endurance, apart from its laws and manners. When speaking of the united republican States, I hazarded no conjectures on the permanence of republican forms in the New World; and while I frequently alluded to the commercial activity that reigns in the Union, I was unable to inquire into the future condition of the Americans as a commercial people.

These topics are collaterally connected with my subject without forming a part of it; they are American without being democratic; and to portray democracy has been my principal aim. It was therefore necessary to postpone these questions, which I now take up as the proper conclusion of my work.

The territory now occupied or claimed by the American Union spreads from the shores of the Atlantic to those of the Pacific. To the east and west its limits are those of the continent itself. To the south it advances nearly to the tropic, and it extends upward to the icy regions of the North. The human beings scattered over this space do not form, as in Europe, so many branches of the same stock. Three races, naturally distinct and, I might almost say, hostile to each other, are discernible among them at first glance. Almost insurmountable barriers had been raised between them by education and by law, as well as by their origin and outward characteristics; but fortune has brought them together on the same soil, where, though mixed together, they do not amalgamate, and each race fulfills its destiny apart.

Among these widely differing families of men, the first that attracts attention — superior in intelligence, in power, and in enjoyment — is the white or European, the man preeminent; and in subordinate grades, the Negro and the Indian. These two unhappy races have nothing in common: neither birth, nor features, nor language, nor habits. Their only resemblance lies in their misfortunes. Both occupy an inferior rank in the country they inhabit; both suffer from tyranny; and if their wrongs are not the same, they originate, at any rate, with the same authors.

If we reasoned from what passes in the world, we should almost say that the European is to the other races of mankind what man is to the lower animals — he makes them subservient to his use, and when he cannot subdue, he destroys them. Oppression has, at one stroke, deprived the descendants of the Africans of almost all the privileges of humanity. The Negro of the United States has lost all remembrance of his country; the language his forefathers spoke is never heard around him; he abjured their religion and forgot their customs when he ceased to belong to Africa, without acquiring any claim to European privileges. But he remains halfway between the two communities — sold by the one, repulsed by the other, finding not a spot in the universe to call by the name of country, except the faint image of a home which the shelter of his master's roof affords.

The Negro has no family; woman is merely the temporary companion of his pleasures, and his children are on an equality with himself from the moment of their birth. Am I to call it a proof of God's mercy or a visitation of his wrath, that man in certain conditions appears insensible to his extreme wretchedness, and almost affects, with a depraved taste, the cause of his misfortunes? The Negro, plunged in this abyss of evils, scarcely feels his own calamitous situation. Violence made him a slave, and the habit of servitude gives him the thoughts and desires of a slave; he admires his tyrants more than he hates them, and finds his joy and his pride in the servile imitation of those who oppress him: his understanding is degraded to the level of his soul.

The Negro enters upon slavery as soon as he is born — nay, he may have been purchased in the womb, and have begun his slavery before he began his existence. Equally devoid of wants and of enjoyment, and useless to himself, he learns, with his first notions of existence, that he is the property of another, who has an interest in preserving his life, and that the care of it does not fall upon himself; even the power of thought appears to him a useless gift of Providence, and he quietly enjoys the privileges of his debasement. If he becomes free, independence is often felt by him to be a heavier burden than slavery; for having learned, in the course of his life, to submit to everything except reason, he is too unacquainted with her dictates to obey them. A thousand new desires beset him, and he is destitute of the knowledge and energy necessary to resist them: these are masters he must contend with, and he has learned only to submit and obey. In short, he sinks to such a depth of wretchedness that while servitude brutalizes him, liberty destroys him.

Oppression has been no less fatal to the Indian than to the Negro race, but its effects are different. Before the arrival of white men in the New World, the inhabitants of North America lived quietly in their woods, enduring the vicissitudes and practicing the virtues and vices common to savage nations. The Europeans, having dispersed the Indian tribes and driven them into the deserts, condemned them to a wandering life full of inexpressible sufferings.

Savage nations are controlled only by opinion and by custom. When the North American Indians had lost the sentiment of attachment to their country; when their families were dispersed, their traditions obscured, and the chain of their recollections broken; when all their habits were changed, and their wants increased beyond measure — European tyranny rendered them more disorderly and less civilized than they had been before. The moral and physical condition of these tribes continually grew worse, and they became more barbarous as they became more wretched. Nevertheless, the Europeans have not been able to transform the character of the Indians; and though they have had power to destroy them, they have never been able to make them submit to the rules of civilized society.

The lot of the Negro lies at the extreme limit of servitude, while that of the Indian lies at the uttermost verge of liberty; and slavery does not produce more fatal effects upon the first than independence does upon the second. The Negro has lost all property in his own person, and he cannot dispose of his existence without committing a sort of fraud. But the savage is his own master as soon as he is able to act: parental authority is scarcely known to him; he has never bent his will to that of any of his kind, nor learned the difference between voluntary obedience and a shameful subjection; and the very name of law is unknown to him. To be free, for him, means to escape from all the shackles of society. As he delights in this barbarous independence, and would rather perish than sacrifice the least part of it, civilization has little power over him.
