Among such nations, then, literature will not easily be subjected to strict rules, and it is impossible that any such rules should ever be permanent.

In democracies, it is by no means the case that all the men who cultivate literature have received a literary education. And most of those who have some tinge of belles-lettres are either engaged in politics or in a profession that only allows them to taste the pleasures of the mind occasionally and by stealth. These pleasures, therefore, do not form the principal charm of their lives; they are considered as a transient and necessary recreation amid the serious labors of life. Such a man can never acquire a sufficiently intimate knowledge of the art of literature to appreciate its more delicate beauties, and the minor shades of expression must escape him. Since the time he can devote to letters is very short, he seeks to make the best use of all of it. He prefers books that can be easily procured, quickly read, and that require no learned research to be understood. He asks for beauties that are self-proffered and easily enjoyed. Above all, he must have what is unexpected and new. Accustomed to the struggle, the setbacks, and the monotony of practical life, he requires rapid emotions, startling passages — truths or errors brilliant enough to rouse him up and plunge him at once, as if by violence, into the midst of a subject.

Why should I say more? Who does not understand what is about to follow before I have expressed it? Taken as a whole, literature in democratic ages can never present, as it does in periods of aristocracy, an aspect of order, regularity, science, and art. Its form will, on the contrary, ordinarily be slighted, sometimes despised. Style will frequently be fantastic, incorrect, overburdened, and loose — almost always vehement and bold. Authors will aim at rapidity of execution more than at perfection of detail. Small productions will be more common than bulky books; there will be more wit than erudition, more imagination than depth; and literary performances will bear marks of an untutored and rude vigor of thought, frequently of great variety and singular fertility. The object of authors will be to astonish rather than to please, and to stir the passions more than to charm the taste. Here and there, doubtless, writers will appear who choose a different track, and who, if they are gifted with superior abilities, will succeed in finding readers in spite of their defects or their better qualities. But these exceptions will be rare, and even the authors who so depart from received practice in the main subject of their works will always relapse into it in some lesser details.

I have just depicted two extreme conditions. The transition by which a nation passes from the former to the latter is not sudden but gradual, and marked with shades of very various intensity. In the passage that carries a lettered people from the one to the other, there is almost always a moment when the literary genius of democratic nations has its confluence with that of aristocracies, and both seek to establish their joint sway over the human mind. Such epochs are transient but very brilliant — fertile without exuberance, and animated without confusion. The French literature of the eighteenth century may serve as an example.

I should say more than I mean if I were to assert that the literature of a nation is always subordinate to its social condition and its political constitution. I am aware that, apart from these causes, there are several others that confer certain characteristics on literary productions. But these appear to me to be the chief. The relations that exist between the social and political condition of a people and the genius of its authors are always very numerous: whoever knows the one is never completely ignorant of the other.

chapters.title: Chapter XIV — The Trade Of Literature
paragraphs: Democracy not only instills a taste for letters among the trading classes, but introduces a trading spirit into literature itself. In aristocracies, readers are fastidious and few; in democracies, they are far more numerous and far less difficult to please. The consequence is that among aristocratic nations, no one can hope to succeed without immense exertions — exertions that may bestow a great deal of fame but can never earn much money. Among democratic nations, by contrast, a writer may flatter himself that he will obtain at little cost a modest reputation and a large fortune. For this purpose he need not be admired; it is enough that he be liked. The ever-growing crowd of readers, and their continual craving for something new, ensures the sale of books that nobody much esteems.

In democratic periods the public frequently treats authors as kings treat their courtiers: they enrich them, and they despise them. What more do the venal souls born in courts, or worthy to live there, require? Democratic literature is always infested with a tribe of writers who look upon letters as a mere trade; and for every few great authors who adorn it, you may count thousands of idea-mongers.

chapters.title: Chapter XV — The Study Of Greek And Latin Literature Peculiarly Useful In Democratic Communities
paragraphs: Democratic Communities

What was called the People in the most democratic republics of antiquity was very different from what we mean by that term. In Athens all the citizens took part in public affairs, but there were only 20,000 citizens out of more than 350,000 inhabitants. All the rest were slaves and performed most of the duties that today belong to the lower or even the middle classes. Athens, then, with her universal suffrage, was after all nothing more than an aristocratic republic in which all the nobles had an equal right to govern. The struggle between patricians and plebeians in Rome must be seen in the same light: it was simply an internal quarrel between the elder and younger branches of the same family. All the citizens belonged, in fact, to the aristocracy and shared its character.

It should also be noted that among the ancients books were always scarce and expensive, and that great difficulties stood in the way of their publication and circulation. These conditions concentrated literary tastes and habits in a small number of men, who formed a small literary aristocracy out of the choicer spirits of the great political aristocracy. Accordingly, there is nothing to suggest that literature was ever treated as a trade among the Greeks and Romans.

These peoples, which were not only aristocracies but also highly polished and free nations, naturally imparted to their literary productions the defects and the merits that characterize the literature of aristocratic ages. Indeed, a very superficial survey of the literary remains of the ancients is enough to convince us that if those writers were sometimes lacking in variety, or in fertility of subject matter, or in boldness, vivacity, or power of generalization in their thoughts, they always showed exquisite care and skill in their details. Nothing in their works seems done hastily or at random: every line is written for the eye of the connoisseur, and every line is shaped after some conception of ideal beauty. No literature sets in bolder relief the fine qualities in which the writers of democracies are naturally deficient than does that of the ancients. No literature, therefore, ought to be more studied in democratic ages. This study is better suited than any other to counter the literary defects inherent in those ages. As for their more praiseworthy literary qualities, those will spring up on their own, without anyone needing to learn how to acquire them.

This point must be clearly understood. A particular course of study may be useful to the literature of a people without being appropriate to its social and political needs. If people insisted on teaching nothing but the literature of the dead languages in a community where everyone is habitually driven to make strenuous efforts to increase or maintain his fortune, the result would be a very polished but very dangerous race of citizens. Since their social and political condition would daily give them a sense of needs their education would never teach them to meet, they would trouble the State in the name of the Greeks and Romans, instead of enriching it by their productive work.

It is clear that in democratic communities the interest of individuals, as well as the security of the commonwealth, demands that the education of the majority be scientific, commercial, and industrial, rather than literary. Greek and Latin should not be taught in every school, but it is important that those who by natural disposition or by fortune are destined to cultivate literature, or are prepared to enjoy it, should find schools where a complete knowledge of ancient literature can be acquired and where the true scholar can be formed. A few excellent universities would do more toward this end than a vast number of poor grammar schools, where superfluous subjects, badly learned, stand in the way of sound instruction in necessary studies.

All who aspire to literary excellence in democratic nations should often refresh themselves at the springs of ancient literature: there is no more wholesome course for the mind. Not that I consider the literary productions of the ancients beyond reproach. But I believe they have certain special merits, admirably suited to counterbalance our particular defects. They are a prop on the side where we are most in danger of falling.

chapters.title: Chapter XVI — The Effect Of Democracy On Language
paragraphs: If the reader has rightly grasped what I have already said about literature in general, he will have no difficulty in understanding the kind of influence a democratic social condition and democratic institutions can exercise over language itself, which is the chief instrument of thought.

American authors can truly be said to live more in England than in their own country, since they constantly study the English writers and take them every day as their models. But this is not the case with the bulk of the population, which is more directly subject to the particular causes at work in the United States. It is therefore not to the written but to the spoken language that attention must be paid, if we wish to detect the changes the idiom of an aristocratic people undergoes when it becomes the language of a democracy.

Educated Englishmen — more competent judges than I can be of the finer shades of expression — have often assured me that the language of the educated classes in the United States is noticeably different from that of the educated classes in Great Britain. They complain not only that the Americans have brought into use a number of new words — the difference and the distance between the two countries might be enough to explain that much — but that these new words are especially drawn from the jargon of parties, the mechanical arts, or the language of trade. They add that old English words are often used by the Americans in new senses. And lastly, that the inhabitants of the United States frequently mix their phrasing in the strangest way, sometimes placing together words that are always kept apart in the language of the mother country. These remarks, made to me at various times by persons who seemed worthy of credit, led me to reflect on the subject; and my reflections brought me, by theoretical reasoning, to the same point my informants had reached through practical observation.

In aristocracies, language naturally shares in that state of repose in which everything stays put. Few new words are coined because few new things are made; and even if new things were made, they would be called by known words whose meanings have been fixed by tradition. If the human mind does at last stir itself, or is roused by light breaking in from outside, the new expressions introduced bear a stamp of learning, intelligence, and philosophy that shows they do not originate in a democracy. After the fall of Constantinople turned the tide of science and literature toward the west, the French language was almost immediately invaded by a multitude of new words, all with Greek or Latin roots. An erudite neologism then sprang up in France, confined to the educated classes and producing no noticeable effect on the people, or at most a very gradual one. All the nations of Europe in turn exhibited the same change. Milton alone introduced more than six hundred words into the English language, almost all drawn from Latin, Greek, or Hebrew. The constant agitation that prevails in a democratic community tends, by contrast, ceaselessly to change the character of the language, just as it changes the look of affairs. Amid this general stir and competition of minds, a great number of new ideas are formed, and old ideas are lost, or reappear, or are subdivided into an infinite variety of minor shades. The result is that many words must fall out of use and others must be brought into it.

Democratic nations love change for its own sake, and this is as visible in their language as in their politics. Even when they have no need to change words, they sometimes feel a wish to transform them. The genius of a democratic people shows itself not only in the great number of words it puts into circulation, but in the nature of the ideas those new words represent. Among such a people the majority makes the law in language, as it does in everything else, and its prevailing spirit is as evident in that as in other respects. But the majority is more occupied with business than with study, with political and commercial interests than with philosophical speculation or literary pursuits. Most of the words coined or adopted for its use will therefore bear the mark of these habits; they will mostly serve to express the needs of business, the passions of party, or the details of public administration. In these areas the language will constantly spread, while on the other hand it will gradually lose ground in metaphysics and theology.

As to the source from which democratic nations usually draw their new expressions, and the way they go about coining them, both can easily be described. Men living in democratic countries know little of the language spoken at Athens or Rome, and they do not care to dive into the lore of antiquity to find the expression they happen to want. If they sometimes resort to learned etymologies, vanity will lead them to search at the roots of the dead languages, but erudition does not naturally supply them with its resources. It sometimes happens that the most ignorant make the most use of them. The eminently democratic desire to rise above one's own sphere will often lead men to dignify a common profession with a Greek or Latin name. The lower the calling, and the further from learning, the more pompous and erudite its name. Thus French rope-dancers have transformed themselves into acrobates and funambules.

In the absence of knowledge of the dead languages, democratic nations are apt to borrow words from living tongues; for their mutual dealings become perpetual, and the inhabitants of different countries imitate each other the more readily as they grow more alike every day.

But it is chiefly on their own languages that democratic nations attempt innovations. From time to time they revive forgotten expressions from their vocabulary and bring them back into use, or they borrow from some particular class of the community a term peculiar to it and introduce it with a figurative meaning into the language of daily life. Many expressions that originally belonged to the technical language of a profession or a party are drawn in this way into general circulation.

The most common expedient by which democratic nations introduce innovations into language is to give an unusual meaning to an expression already in use. This method is very simple, quick, and convenient. No learning is required to use it correctly, and ignorance itself rather helps the practice. But that practice is most dangerous to the language. When a democratic people doubles the meaning of a word in this way, it sometimes leaves the meaning it keeps as ambiguous as the one it acquires. An author begins with a slight deflection of a known expression from its original meaning and adapts it, thus modified, as best he can to his subject. A second writer twists the sense of the expression in another way; a third takes possession of it for another purpose. Since there is no common appeal to the verdict of a permanent tribunal that could definitively settle the meaning of the word, it remains in an ambiguous state. The result is that writers hardly ever seem to dwell on a single thought; they always seem to aim at a cluster of ideas, leaving the reader to judge which of them has been hit. This is a deplorable consequence of democracy. I would rather that the language should be made hideous with words imported from the Chinese, the Tartars, or the Hurons than that the meaning of a word in our own language should become indeterminate. Harmony and uniformity are only secondary beauties in composition; many of these things are conventional, and strictly speaking they can be done without. But without clear phrasing there is no good language.

The principle of equality necessarily introduces several other changes into language. In aristocratic ages, when each nation tends to stand apart from all others and likes to have distinct characteristics of its own, it often happens that several peoples with a common origin nevertheless become estranged from one another, so that, without ceasing to understand the same language, they no longer all speak it in the same way. In these ages each nation is divided into a certain number of classes that see little of each other and do not mingle. Each of these classes contracts, and invariably keeps, habits of mind peculiar to itself, and chooses certain words and terms that are afterwards handed down from generation to generation, like their estates. The same idiom then includes a language of the poor and a language of the rich — a language of the citizen and a language of the nobility, a learned language and a vulgar one. The deeper the divisions and the more impassable the barriers of society become, the more this must be the case. I would lay a wager that among the castes of India there are astonishing variations of language, and that there is almost as much difference between the language of the pariah and that of the Brahmin as there is in their dress. By contrast, when men, no longer restrained by ranks, meet in constant contact — when castes are destroyed and the classes of society recruit and blend with each other — all the words of a language are mingled. Those unsuitable to the greater number die out; the rest form a common store from which everyone draws almost at random. Nearly all the different dialects that once divided the idioms of European nations are visibly declining; there is no patois in the New World, and it is disappearing every day from the old countries.

The influence of this revolution in social conditions is felt in style as much as in phrasing. Not only does everyone use the same words, but a habit springs up of using them without discrimination. The rules style had set up are almost abolished. The line ceases to be drawn between expressions that seem by their very nature common and others that appear refined. People coming from different ranks of society carry the terms and expressions they are used to with them into whatever circles they move in. The origin of words is thus lost, like the origin of individuals, and there is as much confusion in language as there is in society.

I am aware that in the classification of words there are rules that do not belong to one form of society more than to another, but are drawn from the nature of things. Some expressions and phrases are vulgar because the ideas they are meant to express are low in themselves; others are of a higher character because the objects they are meant to designate are naturally elevated. No intermixture of ranks will ever erase these differences. But the principle of equality cannot fail to root out whatever is merely conventional and arbitrary in the forms of thought. Perhaps the necessary classification I have just pointed out will always be less respected by a democratic people than by any other, because among such a people there are no men permanently disposed by education, culture, and leisure to study the natural laws of language and to cause those laws to be respected by observing them themselves.

I will not leave this topic without touching on a feature of democratic languages that is perhaps more characteristic of them than any other. It has already been shown that democratic nations have a taste, and sometimes a passion, for general ideas, and that this arises from their peculiar merits and defects. This liking for general ideas shows itself in democratic languages in the continual use of generic terms and abstract expressions, and in the way they are used. This is the great merit and the great defect of these languages. Democratic nations are passionately addicted to generic terms and abstract expressions because such modes of speech enlarge thought and assist the operations of the mind by enabling it to include several objects in a small compass. A French democratic writer will be apt to say capacités in the abstract for men of capacity, without specifying the objects to which their capacity is applied. He will speak of actualités to designate in a single word the things happening before his eyes at that moment, and he will take in under the term éventualités whatever may happen in the universe from the moment he is speaking. Democratic writers are perpetually coining words of this kind, in which they sublimate into further abstraction the already abstract terms of the language. More than that, to make their mode of speech more concise, they personify the subject of these abstract terms and make it act as a real entity. Thus they will say in French: "La force des choses veut que les capacités gouvernent."

I cannot better illustrate what I mean than by my own example. I have often used the word "equality" in an absolute sense; indeed I have personified equality in several places. Thus I have said that equality does such and such things, or refrains from doing others. It may be said that the writers of the age of Louis XIV would not have used such expressions. They would never have thought of using the word "equality" without applying it to some particular object, and they would rather have given up the term altogether than consent to turn it into a living personage.

These abstract terms, which abound in democratic languages and are used on every occasion without being attached to any particular fact, enlarge and obscure the thoughts they are meant to convey. They make the mode of speech more concise and the idea in it less clear. But where language is concerned, democratic nations prefer obscurity to labor. I do not know whether this loose style has some secret charm for those who speak and write among these nations. Since the men who live there are often thrown back on the efforts of their individual minds, they are almost always prey to doubt. And since their situation in life is forever changing, they are never held fast to any of their opinions by the secure tenure of their fortunes. Men living in democratic countries are therefore apt to have unsettled ideas, and they need loose expressions to convey them. Since they never know whether the idea they express today will be appropriate to the new position they may occupy tomorrow, they naturally develop a liking for abstract terms. An abstract term is like a box with a false bottom: you can put in it whatever ideas you please and take them out again without being observed.

Among all nations, generic and abstract terms form the basis of language. I do not, then, pretend to banish these terms from democratic languages. I simply note that men have a special tendency, in the ages of democracy, to multiply words of this kind — to take them always by themselves in their most abstract sense, and to use them on every occasion, even when the nature of the discourse does not call for them.

chapters.title: Chapter XVII — Of Some Of The Sources Of Poetry Amongst Democratic Nations
paragraphs: The word "poetry" has been given various different meanings. It would weary my readers if I led them into a discussion of which of these definitions ought to be chosen. I prefer to tell them at once the one I have chosen. In my opinion, poetry is the search for and the delineation of the ideal. The poet is the one who, by suppressing part of what exists, adding some imaginary touches to the picture, and combining certain real circumstances that do not in fact occur together, completes and extends the work of nature. So the object of poetry is not to represent what is true, but to adorn it, and to present to the mind some loftier imagery. Verse, regarded as the ideal beauty of language, may be eminently poetical — but verse by itself does not constitute poetry.

I now proceed to ask whether, among the actions, sentiments, and opinions of democratic nations, there are any that lead to a conception of ideal beauty, and may for this reason be considered natural sources of poetry. It must first be acknowledged that the taste for ideal beauty, and the pleasure derived from expressing it, are never so intense or so widespread among a democratic people as among an aristocratic one. In aristocratic nations it sometimes happens that the body goes on acting, as it were, spontaneously, while the higher faculties are bound and burdened by repose. Among these nations the people will very often display poetic tastes, and sometimes allow their fancy to range beyond and above what surrounds them. But in democracies the love of physical gratification, the idea of bettering one's condition, the excitement of competition, and the charm of anticipated success are so many spurs driving men forward in the active professions they have embraced, without letting them deviate for a moment from the track. The main stress of the faculties is pressed to this point. The imagination is not extinct — but its chief function is to devise what may be useful and to represent what is real.

The principle of equality not only diverts men from the description of ideal beauty — it also reduces the number of objects to be described. Aristocracy, by holding society in a fixed position, is favorable to the solidity and duration of positive religions, as well as to the stability of political institutions. It not only keeps the human mind within a certain sphere of belief, but it predisposes the mind to adopt one faith rather than another. An aristocratic people will always be inclined to place intermediate powers between God and man. In this respect it may be said that the aristocratic element is favorable to poetry. When the universe is peopled with supernatural creatures — not palpable to the senses but discovered by the mind — the imagination ranges freely, and poets, finding a thousand subjects to depict, also find a countless audience to take an interest in their productions. In democratic ages, on the contrary, it sometimes happens that men are as much adrift in matters of belief as they are in their laws. Skepticism then draws the imagination of poets back to earth and confines them to the real and visible world. Even when the principle of equality does not disturb religious belief, it tends to simplify it and to divert attention from secondary agents, fixing it principally on the Supreme Power. Aristocracy naturally leads the human mind to the contemplation of the past and fixes it there. Democracy, on the contrary, gives men a sort of instinctive distaste for what is ancient. In this respect aristocracy is far more favorable to poetry, for things commonly grow larger and more obscure as they are more remote — and for this twofold reason they are better suited to the delineation of the ideal.

After having deprived poetry of the past, the principle of equality robs it in part of the present. Among aristocratic nations there are a certain number of privileged figures whose situation is, as it were, outside of and above the condition of man. Power, wealth, fame, wit, refinement, and distinction in all things appear peculiarly to belong to them. The crowd never sees them very closely, or does not watch them in minute detail — and little is needed to make the description of such men poetical. On the other hand, among the same people you will meet with classes so ignorant, low, and enslaved that they are no less fit objects for poetry — from the excess of their rudeness and wretchedness — than the former are from their greatness and refinement. Besides, since the different classes of which an aristocratic community is composed are widely separated and imperfectly acquainted with each other, the imagination may always represent them with some addition to, or subtraction from, what they really are. In democratic communities, where men are all insignificant and very much alike, each man immediately sees all his fellows when he surveys himself. The poets of democratic ages can therefore never take any particular man as the subject of a piece; for an object of slender importance, clearly seen on all sides, will never lend itself to an ideal conception. Thus the principle of equality, as it has established itself in the world, has dried up most of the old springs of poetry. Let us now try to show what new ones it may open.

When skepticism had depopulated heaven, and the progress of equality had reduced each individual to smaller and better-known proportions, the poets — not yet aware of what they could substitute for the great themes departing along with the aristocracy — turned their eyes to inanimate nature. As they lost sight of gods and heroes, they set themselves to describe streams and mountains. From this came, in the last century, that kind of poetry which has been called, by way of distinction, the descriptive. Some have thought that this sort of delineation, adorned with all the physical and inanimate objects that cover the earth, was the kind of poetry peculiar to democratic ages. But I believe this to be a mistake, and that it belongs only to a period of transition.

I am convinced that in the end democracy diverts the imagination from all that is external to man, and fixes it on man alone. Democratic nations may amuse themselves for a while by considering the productions of nature; but they are only truly excited by a survey of themselves. Here, and here alone, are the true sources of poetry among such nations to be found. And it may be believed that the poets who neglect to draw their inspiration from this source will lose all sway over the minds they wish to enchant, and will be left in the end with none but unmoved spectators of their transports. I have shown how the ideas of progress and of the indefinite perfectibility of the human race belong to democratic ages. Democratic nations care little for what has been, but they are haunted by visions of what will be. In this direction their unbounded imagination grows and expands beyond all measure. Here, then, is the widest range open to the genius of poets — one that allows them to place their works at a sufficient distance from the eye. Democracy shuts the past against the poet but opens the future before him. Since all the citizens who make up a democratic community are nearly equal and alike, the poet cannot dwell upon any one of them. But the nation itself invites the exercise of his powers. The general similarity of individuals, which makes any one of them taken separately an improper subject of poetry, allows poets to include them all in the same imagery, and to take a general view of the people itself. Democratic nations have a clearer perception than any others of their own aspect — and an aspect so imposing is admirably suited to the delineation of the ideal.

I readily admit that the Americans have no poets; I cannot allow that they have no poetic ideas. In Europe people talk a great deal about the wilds of America, but the Americans themselves never think about them. They are insensible to the wonders of inanimate nature, and it may be said that they do not perceive the mighty forests surrounding them until they fall beneath the hatchet. Their eyes are fixed on another sight: the American people views its own march across these wilds — draining swamps, turning the course of rivers, populating the solitudes, and subduing nature. This magnificent image of themselves does not meet the gaze of the Americans only at intervals; it may be said to haunt every one of them in his least as well as in his most important actions, and to be always flitting before his mind. Nothing conceivable is as petty, as insipid, as crowded with paltry interests — in a word, as anti-poetic — as the life of a man in the United States. But among the thoughts it suggests, there is always one that is full of poetry, and that is the hidden nerve which gives vigor to the frame.

In aristocratic ages, each people, as well as each individual, is inclined to stand separate and aloof from all others. In democratic ages, the extreme fluctuations of men and the impatience of their desires keep them perpetually on the move. So the inhabitants of different countries mingle, see, listen to, and borrow from each other's stores. It is not only the members of the same community who grow more alike; communities themselves are assimilated to one another, and the whole assemblage presents to the spectator's eye one vast democracy, each citizen of which is a people. This displays the aspect of mankind, for the first time, in the broadest light. All that belongs to the existence of the human race taken as a whole — to its vicissitudes and to its future — becomes an abundant mine of poetry. The poets who lived in aristocratic ages were eminently successful in their delineations of certain incidents in the life of a people or a man. But none of them ever ventured to include within his works the destinies of mankind — a task that poets writing in democratic ages may attempt. At the same time at which every man, raising his eyes above his country, begins at last to discern mankind at large, the Divinity is more and more manifest to the human mind in full and entire majesty. If in democratic ages faith in positive religions is often shaken, and belief in intermediate agents — by whatever name they are called — is clouded, on the other hand men are inclined to form a far broader idea of Providence itself, and its interference in human affairs takes on a new and more imposing appearance in their eyes. Looking at the human race as one great whole, they easily conceive that its destinies are regulated by the same design; and in the actions of every individual they are led to recognize a trace of that universal and eternal plan by which God rules our race. This consideration may be taken as another rich source of poetry opened up in democratic ages. Democratic poets will always appear trivial and frigid if they try to invest gods, demons, or angels with bodily forms, or attempt to draw them down from heaven to dispute the supremacy of earth. But if they strive to connect the great events they commemorate with the general providential designs that govern the universe, and, without showing the finger of the Supreme Governor, reveal the thoughts of the Supreme Mind, their works will be admired and understood — for the imagination of their contemporaries takes this direction of its own accord.

It may be foreseen in the same way that poets living in democratic ages will prefer the delineation of passions and ideas to that of persons and achievements. The language, the dress, and the daily actions of men in democracies are repugnant to ideal conceptions. These things are not poetic in themselves; and even if they were, they would cease to be so, because they are too familiar to all those to whom the poet would speak of them. This forces the poet constantly to search below the external surface, which is palpable to the senses, in order to read the inner soul. And nothing lends itself more to the delineation of the ideal than the scrutiny of the hidden depths in the immaterial nature of man. I do not need to roam over earth and sky to discover a wondrous object woven of contrasts — of infinite greatness and littleness, of intense gloom and amazing brightness — capable at once of exciting pity, admiration, terror, contempt. I find that object in myself. Man springs out of nothing, crosses time, and disappears forever into the bosom of God. He is seen only for a moment, staggering on the verge of the two abysses, and there he is lost. If man were wholly ignorant of himself, he would have no poetry in him; for it is impossible to describe what the mind does not conceive. If man clearly discerned his own nature, his imagination would remain idle, and would have nothing to add to the picture. But the nature of man is sufficiently disclosed for him to apprehend something of himself — and sufficiently obscure for all the rest to be plunged in thick darkness, in which he gropes forever, and forever in vain, to lay hold of some fuller notion of his being.

Among a democratic people, poetry will not be fed with legendary lays or the memorials of old traditions. The poet will not attempt to populate the universe with supernatural beings in whom his readers, and his own fancy, have ceased to believe. Nor will he present virtues and vices in the mask of frigid personification, which are better received under their own features. All these resources fail him — but Man remains, and the poet needs no more. The destinies of mankind — man himself, taken apart from his age and country, standing in the presence of Nature and of God, with his passions, his doubts, his rare prosperities and inconceivable wretchedness — will become the chief, if not the sole theme of poetry among these nations. Experience may confirm this assertion if we consider the productions of the greatest poets who have appeared since the world has been turned to democracy. The authors of our age who have so admirably delineated the features of Faust, Childe Harold, René, and Jocelyn did not seek to record the actions of an individual, but to enlarge and throw light on some of the obscurer recesses of the human heart. Such are the poems of democracy. The principle of equality, then, does not destroy all the subjects of poetry. It makes them less numerous, but more vast.

chapters.title: Chapter XVIII — Of The Inflated Style Of American Writers And Orators
paragraphs: I have often noticed that the Americans, who generally treat business in clear, plain language, devoid of any ornament, and so extremely simple as to be often coarse, are apt to become inflated as soon as they attempt a more poetic diction. They then vent their pomposity from one end of a speech to the other. To hear them lavish imagery on every occasion, one might imagine they never spoke of anything with simplicity. The English are more rarely given to a similar failing. The cause of this can be pointed out without much difficulty. In democratic communities, each citizen is habitually occupied with the contemplation of a very puny object — namely, himself. If he ever raises his eyes higher, he then sees nothing but the immense form of society at large, or the still more imposing aspect of mankind. His ideas are either extremely small and clear, or extremely general and vague. What lies between is an open void. So when he has been drawn out of his own sphere, he always expects some amazing object to be offered to his attention. And it is only on these terms that he consents to tear himself for a moment from the petty complicated cares that form the charm and the excitement of his life. This seems to me enough to explain why people in democracies, whose concerns are in general so paltry, call upon their poets for conceptions so vast and descriptions so unlimited.

The authors, for their part, do not fail to obey an inclination they themselves share. They continually inflate their imaginations and, expanding them beyond all bounds, they not infrequently abandon the great in order to reach the gigantic. By these means they hope to attract the attention of the multitude and to fix it easily upon themselves. Nor are their hopes disappointed. For since the multitude looks for nothing in poetry but subjects of very vast dimensions, it has neither the time to measure accurately the proportions of all the subjects set before it, nor a taste correct enough to perceive at once in what respect they are out of proportion. The author and the public corrupt one another.

We have just seen that among democratic nations the sources of poetry are grand but not abundant. They are soon exhausted. And poets, not finding the elements of the ideal in what is real and true, abandon them entirely and create monsters. I do not fear that the poetry of democratic nations will prove too insipid, or that it will fly too close to the ground. I rather fear that it will forever lose itself in the clouds, and will at last range into purely imaginary regions. I fear that the productions of democratic poets may often be overloaded with immense and incoherent imagery, with exaggerated descriptions and strange creations — and that the fantastic beings of their brain may sometimes make us regret the world of reality.

chapters.title: Chapter XIX — Some Observations On The Drama Amongst Democratic Nations
paragraphs: When the revolution that overturns the social and political state of an aristocratic people begins to reach literature, it generally shows itself first in the drama, and it always remains most conspicuous there. The spectator of a dramatic piece is, to some degree, caught off guard by the impression it produces. He has no time to consult his memory or to ask those better able to judge than he is. It does not occur to him to resist the new literary tendencies he begins to feel; he yields to them before he knows what they are. Authors are very quick to detect which way the public's taste is thus secretly leaning. They shape their productions accordingly, and the literature of the stage, after serving as an indicator of the coming literary revolution, quickly completes it. If you want to judge in advance the literature of a people sliding into democracy, study its dramatic productions.

The literature of the stage, moreover, even among aristocratic nations, is the most democratic part of their literature. No kind of literary enjoyment is so accessible to the multitude as that drawn from theatrical performances. Neither preparation nor study is required to enjoy them; they seize you in the midst of your prejudices and your ignorance. When the still untutored love of the pleasures of the mind begins to touch a class of the community, it draws that class instantly toward the stage. The theaters of aristocratic nations have always been filled with spectators who do not belong to the aristocracy. In the theater alone do the upper ranks mix with the middle and lower classes; there alone do they consent to listen to the opinion of those below them, or at least allow them to give an opinion at all. At the theater, men of cultivation and literary accomplishment have always had more difficulty than elsewhere in making their taste prevail over that of the people, or in keeping themselves from being carried along by it. The pit has often made laws for the boxes.

If it is difficult for an aristocracy to keep the people from gaining the upper hand in the theater, it will easily be understood that the people will be supreme there once democratic principles have crept into the laws and customs — when ranks are mingled, when minds as well as fortunes are brought closer together, and when the upper class has lost, along with its hereditary wealth, its power, its precedents, and its leisure. The tastes and tendencies natural to democratic nations in literature will therefore appear first in the drama, and it can be foreseen that they will break out there with force. In written works, the literary canons of aristocracy will be gently, gradually, and, so to speak, legally modified; in the theater they will be riotously overthrown. The drama brings out most of the good qualities, and almost all the defects, inherent in democratic literature. Democratic peoples hold erudition very cheap and care little for what happened in Rome and Athens; they want to hear something that concerns themselves, and the portrayal of the present age is what they demand.

When the heroes and manners of antiquity are frequently brought upon the stage, and dramatic authors faithfully observe the rules of old precedent, that alone is enough to conclude that the democratic classes have not yet gained the upper hand over the theaters. Racine makes a very humble apology in the preface to Britannicus for having placed Junia among the Vestals, who, according to Aulus Gellius, he says, "admitted no one below the age of six or above ten." We may be sure he would neither have accused himself of the offense nor defended himself against censure if he had been writing for our contemporaries. A fact of this kind illustrates not only the state of literature at the time it occurred, but also the state of society itself. A democratic stage does not prove that the nation is in a state of democracy; for, as we have just seen, even in aristocracies democratic tastes may affect the drama. But when the spirit of aristocracy reigns exclusively on the stage, the fact irrefutably shows that society as a whole is aristocratic, and one may boldly conclude that the same lettered and learned class that sways the dramatic writers also commands the people and governs the country.

The refined tastes and the arrogant bearing of an aristocracy will rarely fail to lead it, when it controls the stage, to make a kind of selection within human nature. Some conditions of society claim its chief interest, and the scenes that depict their manners are preferred on the stage. Certain virtues, and even certain vices, are thought more especially to deserve a place there, and they are applauded while all the others are excluded. On the stage, as elsewhere, an aristocratic audience will meet only persons of quality and share the emotions of kings. The same applies to style: an aristocracy is apt to impose on dramatic authors certain modes of expression that set the key in which everything must be delivered. By these means the stage often comes to depict only one side of man, or sometimes even to represent what is not to be found in human nature at all — to rise above nature and go beyond it.

In democratic communities the spectators have no such preferences, and they rarely show any such antipathies. They like to see upon the stage that mixture of conditions, feelings, and opinions which occurs before their eyes. The drama becomes more striking, more common, and more true. Sometimes, however, those who write for the stage in democracies also overstep the bounds of human nature — but on a different side from their predecessors. By trying to depict in minute detail the small peculiarities of the moment and the particular features of certain characters, they forget to portray the general features of the race.

When the democratic classes rule the stage, they introduce as much license in the way subjects are treated as in the choice of them. Since the love of drama is, of all literary tastes, the most natural to democratic nations, the number of authors, spectators, and theatrical performances constantly increases among these communities. A multitude made up of such different elements, scattered in so many different places, cannot acknowledge the same rules or submit to the same laws. No agreement is possible among so many judges, who do not know when they may meet again, so each pronounces his own verdict on the piece. If the general effect of democracy is to question the authority of all literary rules and conventions, on the stage it abolishes them altogether and puts in their place nothing but the whim of each author and each public.

The drama also displays in a particular way the truth of what I have said earlier about style and art in democratic literature more generally. Reading the criticisms provoked by the dramatic productions of the age of Louis XIV, one is surprised to notice the great stress the public laid on the probability of the plot, and the importance attached to the perfect consistency of the characters and to their doing nothing that could not be easily explained and understood. The value placed on the forms of language in that period, and the petty quarrels about words with which dramatic authors were assailed, are no less surprising. It seems the men of the age of Louis XIV attached exaggerated importance to details that may be noticed in the study but escape attention on the stage. For after all, the chief purpose of a dramatic piece is to be performed, and its chief merit is to move the audience. But audience and readers in that age were the same people: on leaving the theater they summoned the author to judgment at their own firesides. In democracies dramatic pieces are listened to, but not read. Most of those who frequent the amusements of the stage do not go there to seek the pleasures of the mind, but the keen emotions of the heart. They do not expect to hear a fine literary work, but to see a play. As long as the author writes his country's language correctly enough to be understood, and his characters stir curiosity and awaken sympathy, the audience is satisfied. They ask no more of fiction and return immediately to real life. Accuracy of style is therefore less required, because a careful observance of its rules is less noticeable on the stage. As for probability of plot, it is incompatible with perpetual novelty, surprise, and rapidity of invention. It is therefore neglected, and the public excuses the neglect. You may be sure that if you succeed in bringing your audience into the presence of something that moves them, they will not care by what road you brought them there, and they will never reproach you for having stirred their emotions in spite of dramatic rules.

The Americans display very broadly all the different tendencies I have just described when they go to the theater. But it must be admitted that as yet very few of them go to theaters at all. Although playgoers and plays have increased prodigiously in the United States over the last forty years, the population indulges this kind of amusement with the greatest reserve. This is due to special causes the reader already knows, of which a few words will suffice as a reminder. The Puritans who founded the American republics were not only enemies of amusements; they professed a special abhorrence of the stage. They regarded it as an abominable pastime, and as long as their principles held undivided sway, theatrical performances were wholly unknown among them. These opinions of the first fathers of the colony have left very deep marks on the minds of their descendants. The extreme regularity of habits and the great strictness of manners in the United States have so far raised further obstacles to the growth of dramatic art. There are no dramatic subjects in a country that has witnessed no great political catastrophes, and in which love invariably leads by a straight and easy road to matrimony. People who spend every day of the week making money, and Sunday going to church, offer nothing to invite the muse of Comedy.

A single fact is enough to show that the stage is not very popular in the United States. The Americans, whose laws allow the utmost freedom and even license of language in every other respect, have nonetheless subjected their dramatic authors to a kind of censorship. Theatrical performances can only take place with the permission of the municipal authorities. This helps show how much communities resemble individuals: they surrender without scruple to their ruling passions, and afterwards take the greatest care not to yield too much to the force of tastes they do not possess.

No branch of literature is tied by closer or more numerous bonds to the present state of society than the drama. The drama of one period can never suit the next, if in the meantime an important revolution has changed the manners and the laws of the nation. The great authors of an earlier age may still be read, but pieces written for a different public will not be followed. The dramatic authors of the past survive only in books. The traditional taste of certain individuals, together with vanity, fashion, or the genius of an actor, may sustain or revive for a time the aristocratic drama in a democracy. But it will quickly fade away on its own — not overthrown, but abandoned.

chapters.title: Chapter XX — Characteristics Of Historians In Democratic Ages
paragraphs: Historians who write in aristocratic ages tend to trace all events back to the particular will or temper of certain individuals, and they are apt to attribute the most important revolutions to very slight accidents. They trace the smallest causes with shrewdness, and frequently miss the greatest ones. Historians who live in democratic ages show exactly the opposite tendencies. Most of them attribute almost no influence to the individual over the destiny of the race, nor to citizens over the fate of a people. On the other hand, they assign great general causes to the smallest incidents. These contrary tendencies explain each other.

When the historian of aristocratic ages surveys the theater of the world, he sees at once a very small number of prominent actors who manage the whole performance. These great figures, who occupy the front of the stage, arrest his attention and fix it on themselves. While the historian is intent on penetrating the secret motives that make them speak and act, the rest escape his memory. The importance of the things some men are seen to do gives him an exaggerated estimate of the influence one man may have, and this naturally leads him to think that in order to explain the impulses of the multitude, one must refer them to the particular influence of some single individual.

When, on the contrary, all the citizens are independent of one another, and each of them is individually weak, no one is seen to exert a great—let alone a lasting—power over the community. At first sight, individuals appear to have no influence over it at all, and society seems to advance on its own, through the free and voluntary cooperation of all the men who compose it. This naturally leads the mind to search for that general reason which operates on so many men's faculties at the same time, turning them all simultaneously in the same direction.

I am quite convinced that even among democratic nations, the genius, the vices, or the virtues of certain individuals slow down or speed up the natural current of a people's history. But causes of this secondary and incidental nature are infinitely more varied, more concealed, more complex, less powerful, and consequently less easy to trace in periods of equality than in ages of aristocracy, when the historian's task is simply to pick out from the mass of general events the particular influence of one man or of a few men. In the first case the historian is soon worn out by the effort; his mind loses itself in the labyrinth. Unable to see clearly or point out conspicuously the influence of individuals, he denies their existence. He prefers to talk about the characteristics of race, the physical features of the country, or the genius of civilization, which shortens his own labor and satisfies his reader far better at less cost.

Lafayette says somewhere in his Memoirs that the exaggerated system of general causes offers surprising consolation to second-rate statesmen. I will add that its effects are no less consoling to second-rate historians. It can always supply a few mighty reasons to extricate them from the most difficult part of their work, and it indulges the laziness or incapacity of their minds, while conferring on them the honors of deep thinking.

For my part, I believe that at all times one great portion of the events of this world is attributable to general facts, and another to special influences. These two kinds of cause are always at work: only their proportion varies. General facts serve to explain more things in democratic than in aristocratic ages, and fewer things can then be assigned to special influences. In periods of aristocracy the reverse is true: special influences are stronger, general causes weaker—unless, of course, we consider the very fact of the inequality of conditions as a general cause, since it allows some individuals to thwart the natural tendencies of all the rest. The historians who try to describe what happens in democratic societies are right, therefore, to assign much to general causes, and to devote their chief attention to discovering them. But they are wrong to deny altogether the special influence of individuals, simply because they cannot easily trace or follow it.

Historians who live in democratic ages are prone not only to assign a great cause to every incident, but also to connect incidents together in order to deduce a system from them. In aristocratic ages, since the attention of historians is constantly drawn to individuals, the connection of events escapes them—or rather, they do not believe in any such connection. To them, the thread of history seems at every moment crossed and broken by the footstep of man. In democratic ages, on the contrary, since the historian sees much more of actions than of actors, he can easily establish some kind of sequence and methodical order among them. Ancient literature, which is so rich in fine historical works, does not contain a single great historical system, while even the poorest of modern literatures are full of them. It seems that the ancient historians did not make sufficient use of those general theories that our own historical writers are always ready to carry to excess.

Those who write in democratic ages have another, more dangerous tendency. When the traces of individual action upon nations are lost, it often happens that the world continues to move, though the moving agent can no longer be discovered. Since it becomes extremely difficult to identify and analyze the reasons that, acting separately on the will of each member of the community, ultimately combine to produce movement in the whole mass, men are led to believe that this movement is involuntary, and that societies unconsciously obey some superior force ruling over them. But even when the general fact that governs the private will of all individuals is supposedly discovered on earth, the principle of human free will is not secure. A cause extensive enough to affect millions of men at once, and strong enough to bend them all together in the same direction, may well seem irresistible. Having seen that mankind yields to it, the mind is close to the inference that mankind cannot resist it.

Historians who live in democratic ages, then, not only deny that the few have any power of acting upon the destiny of a people, but they also deprive the people themselves of the power of changing their own condition, and they subject them either to an inflexible Providence or to some blind necessity. According to them, each nation is indissolubly bound by its position, its origin, its precedents, and its character, to a certain fate that no efforts can ever alter. They bind one generation to the next, and so, going back from age to age and from necessity to necessity all the way to the origin of the world, they forge a close and enormous chain that girds and binds the human race. To their minds it is not enough to show what events have occurred: they must also show that events could not have occurred otherwise. They take a nation at a certain stage of its history, and they affirm that it could do nothing but follow the path that brought it there. It is easier to make such an assertion than to show by what means the nation might have taken a better course.

Reading the historians of aristocratic ages, and especially those of antiquity, one is led to believe that in order to be master of his fate and govern his fellow creatures, man only needs to be master of himself. Reading the historical volumes our age has produced, one is led to believe that man is utterly powerless over himself and over everything around him. The historians of antiquity taught how to command; those of our time teach only how to obey. In their writings the author often appears great, but humanity is always diminished. If this doctrine of necessity, which is so attractive to those who write history in democratic ages, passes from authors to readers until it infects the whole mass of the community and takes possession of the public mind, it will soon paralyze the activity of modern society and reduce Christians to the level of the Turks. I would add that such principles are especially dangerous at the point we have reached. Our contemporaries are all too prone to doubt the human free will, because each of them feels himself hemmed in on every side by his own weakness. But they are still willing to acknowledge the strength and independence of men united in society. Let this principle not be lost sight of, for the great object in our time is to raise the faculties of men, not to complete their prostration.

chapters.title: Chapter XXI — Of Parliamentary Eloquence In The United States
paragraphs: Among aristocratic nations all the members of the community are connected with and dependent on each other; the graduated scale of different ranks acts as a tie that keeps everyone in his proper place and the whole body in subordination. Something of the same kind always happens in the political assemblies of these nations. Parties naturally range themselves under certain leaders, whom they obey by a sort of instinct, which is only the result of habits contracted elsewhere. They carry the manners of general society into the lesser assemblage.

In democratic countries it often happens that a great number of citizens are tending toward the same point, but each moves there, or at least flatters himself that he moves, of his own accord. Accustomed to regulate his doings by personal impulse alone, he does not willingly submit to dictation from without. This taste and habit of independence accompany him into the councils of the nation. If he consents to connect himself with other men in the pursuit of the same purpose, at least he insists on remaining free to contribute to the common success in his own way. Hence, in democratic countries, parties are so impatient of control, and are never manageable except in moments of great public danger. Even then, the authority of leaders, which in such circumstances may be able to make men act or speak, hardly ever reaches the point of making them keep silent.

Among aristocratic nations, the members of political assemblies are also members of the aristocracy. Each of them enjoys an established rank in his own right, and the position he occupies in the assembly is often less important in his eyes than the one he fills in the country. This consoles him for playing no part in the discussion of public affairs, and restrains him from too eagerly attempting to play an insignificant one.

In America, it generally happens that a Representative only becomes somebody through his position in the Assembly. He is therefore perpetually haunted by a craving to acquire importance there, and he feels a petulant desire to be constantly obtruding his opinions on the House. His own vanity is not the only stimulant driving him on in this course — there is also the vanity of his constituents, and the continual necessity of propitiating them. Among aristocratic nations, a member of the legislature is rarely in strict dependence on his constituents. He is often a sort of unavoidable representative for them; sometimes they are themselves strictly dependent on him; and if in the end they reject him, he may easily get elected elsewhere, or, retiring from public life, he may still enjoy the pleasures of splendid idleness. In a democratic country like the United States, a Representative hardly ever has a lasting hold on the minds of his constituents. However small an electoral body may be, the fluctuations of democracy are constantly changing its aspect; it must therefore be courted unceasingly. He is never sure of his supporters, and if they forsake him he is left without a resource, for his natural position is not elevated enough for him to be easily known to those outside his immediate circle; and with the complete state of independence prevailing among the people, he cannot hope that his friends or the government will send him down to be returned by an electoral body unacquainted with him. The seeds of his fortune are therefore sown in his own neighborhood; from that nook of earth he must start, to raise himself to the command of a people and to influence the destinies of the world. Thus it is natural that in democratic countries the members of political assemblies think more of their constituents than of their party, while in aristocracies they think more of their party than of their constituents.

But what ought to be said to gratify constituents is not always what ought to be said to serve the party to which Representatives profess to belong. The general interest of a party frequently demands that its members should not speak on great questions they understand imperfectly; that they should speak only a little on those minor questions that impede the great ones; and lastly, and for the most part, that they should not speak at all. To keep silent is the most useful service an indifferent spokesman can render to the commonwealth. Constituents, however, do not think so. The population of a district sends a representative to take part in the government of a country because they entertain a very lofty notion of his merits. Since men appear greater in proportion to the littleness of the objects surrounding them, the opinion held of the delegate will be so much the higher as talents are more rare among his constituents. It will therefore frequently happen that the less constituents have to expect from their representative, the more they will anticipate from him; and however incompetent he may be, they will not fail to call upon him for signal exertions, corresponding to the rank they have conferred on him.

Besides regarding him as a legislator of the State, the electors also see their Representative as the natural patron of the constituency in the Legislature. They almost consider him the proxy of each of his supporters, and they flatter themselves that he will be no less zealous in defense of their private interests than of those of the country. Thus the electors are well assured beforehand that the Representative of their choice will be an orator, that he will speak often if he can, and that, if he is forced to refrain, he will at least strive to compress into his less frequent orations an inquiry into all the great questions of state, combined with a statement of all the petty grievances they have to complain of. So even if he is not able to come forward frequently, he should on each occasion prove what he is capable of; and instead of perpetually lavishing his powers, he should occasionally condense them in a small compass, so as to furnish a sort of complete and brilliant epitome of his constituents and of himself. On these terms they will vote for him at the next election. These conditions drive worthy men of humble abilities to despair, men who, knowing their own powers, would never voluntarily have come forward. But thus urged on, the Representative begins to speak, to the great alarm of his friends; and rushing imprudently into the midst of the most celebrated orators, he perplexes the debate and wearies the House.

All laws that tend to make the Representative more dependent on the elector not only affect the conduct of the legislators, as I have remarked elsewhere, but also their language. They exercise a simultaneous influence on affairs themselves and on the manner in which affairs are discussed.

There is hardly a member of Congress who can make up his mind to go home without having dispatched at least one speech to his constituents, or who will endure any interruption until he has introduced into his harangue whatever useful suggestions can be made touching the twenty-four States of which the Union is composed — and especially the district he represents. He therefore presents to the minds of his auditors a succession of great general truths (which he himself only understands and expresses confusedly), and of petty minutiae, which he is only too able to discover and point out. The consequence is that the debates of that great assembly are frequently vague and perplexed, and they seem to drag their slow length along rather than to advance toward any distinct object. Some such state of things will, I believe, always arise in the public assemblies of democracies.

Propitious circumstances and good laws might succeed in drawing to the legislature of a democratic people men far superior to those the Americans return to Congress; but nothing will ever prevent the men of slender abilities who sit there from obtruding themselves with complacency, and in every way, upon the public. The evil does not appear to me susceptible of entire cure, because it originates not only in the tactics of that assembly but in its constitution and in that of the country. The inhabitants of the United States seem themselves to consider the matter in this light, and they show their long experience of parliamentary life not by abstaining from making bad speeches, but by courageously submitting to hear them. They are resigned to it, as to an evil they know to be inevitable.

We have shown the petty side of political debates in democratic assemblies — let us now exhibit the more imposing one. The proceedings within the Parliament of England for the last one hundred and fifty years have never caused any great sensation outside that country; the opinions and feelings expressed by the speakers have never awakened much sympathy, even among the nations placed nearest to the great arena of British liberty. Europe, on the other hand, was stirred by the very first debates that took place in the small colonial assemblies of America at the time of the Revolution. This was attributable not only to particular and fortuitous circumstances, but to general and lasting causes. I can conceive of nothing more admirable or more powerful than a great orator debating on great questions of state in a democratic assembly. Since no particular class is ever represented there by men commissioned to defend its own interests, it is always to the whole nation, and in the name of the whole nation, that the orator speaks. This expands his thoughts and heightens his power of language. Since precedents have little weight there — since there are no longer any privileges attached to certain kinds of property, nor any rights inherent in certain bodies or certain individuals — the mind must have recourse to general truths drawn from human nature to resolve the particular question under discussion. Hence the political debates of a democratic people, however small it may be, have a degree of breadth that frequently makes them attractive to all mankind. All men are interested in them, because they treat of man, who is everywhere the same. Among the greatest aristocratic nations, by contrast, the most general questions are almost always argued on some particular grounds drawn from the practice of a particular time, or from the rights of a particular class — grounds that interest that class alone, or at most the people among whom that class happens to exist. It is to this, as much as to the greatness of the French people and the favorable disposition of the nations who listen to them, that we must attribute the great effect French political debates sometimes produce in the world. The orators of France frequently speak to mankind, even when they are addressing their countrymen alone.
Section 2: Influence of Democracy on the Feelings of Americans

chapters.title: Chapter I — Why Democratic Nations Show A More Ardent And Enduring Love Of Equality Than Of Liberty
paragraphs: Of Equality Than of Liberty

The first and most intense passion engendered by the equality of conditions is, I hardly need say, the love of that same equality. My readers will therefore not be surprised that I speak of it before all others. Everyone has remarked that in our time, and especially in France, this passion for equality is every day gaining ground in the human heart. It has been said a hundred times that our contemporaries are far more ardently and tenaciously attached to equality than to freedom; but since I do not find that the causes of this fact have been sufficiently analyzed, I shall try to point them out.

It is possible to imagine an extreme point at which freedom and equality would meet and be confounded together. Let us suppose that all the members of the community take part in the government, and that each of them has an equal right to take part in it. Since none is different from his fellows, none can exercise a tyrannical power: men will be perfectly free because they will all be entirely equal, and they will all be perfectly equal because they will be entirely free. Democratic nations tend toward this ideal state. Such is the completest form equality can assume on earth, but there are a thousand others which, without being equally perfect, are not less cherished by those nations.

The principle of equality may be established in civil society without prevailing in the political world. Equal rights may exist to indulge in the same pleasures, to enter the same professions, to frequent the same places — in a word, to live in the same manner and to seek wealth by the same means — although all men do not take an equal share in the government. A kind of equality may even be established in the political world, though there is no political freedom there. A man may be the equal of all his countrymen save one, who is the master of all without distinction, and who selects equally from among them all the agents of his power. Several other combinations might easily be imagined, by which very great equality would be united with institutions more or less free, or even with institutions wholly without freedom. Although men cannot become absolutely equal unless they are entirely free, and consequently equality, pushed to its furthest extent, may be confounded with freedom, there is nonetheless good reason for distinguishing the one from the other. The taste men have for liberty and the one they feel for equality are in fact two different things; and I am not afraid to add that among democratic nations they are two unequal things.

Upon close inspection, it will be seen that in every age there is some peculiar and preponderating fact with which all others are connected. This fact almost always gives birth to some pregnant idea or some ruling passion, which attracts to itself and bears away in its course all the feelings and opinions of the time: it is like a great stream toward which each of the surrounding rivulets seems to flow. Freedom has appeared in the world at different times and under various forms; it has not been exclusively bound to any social condition, and it is not confined to democracies. Freedom cannot therefore form the distinguishing characteristic of democratic ages. The peculiar and preponderating fact that marks those ages as its own is the equality of conditions; the ruling passion of men in those periods is the love of this equality. Ask not what singular charm the men of democratic ages find in being equal, or what special reasons they may have for clinging so tenaciously to equality rather than to the other advantages society holds out to them: equality is the distinguishing characteristic of the age they live in; that of itself is enough to explain that they prefer it to all the rest.

But independently of this reason, several others will at all times habitually lead men to prefer equality to freedom. If a people could ever succeed in destroying, or even in diminishing, the equality that prevails within it, it could only be accomplished by long and laborious efforts. Its social condition must be modified, its laws abolished, its opinions superseded, its habits changed, its manners corrupted. Political liberty, on the other hand, is more easily lost: to neglect to hold it fast is to allow it to escape. Men therefore not only cling to equality because it is dear to them; they also adhere to it because they think it will last forever.

That political freedom, in its excesses, may compromise the tranquillity, the property, and the lives of individuals is obvious to the narrowest and most unthinking minds. But only attentive and clear-sighted men perceive the perils with which equality threatens us, and they commonly avoid pointing them out. They know that the calamities they apprehend are remote, and they flatter themselves that these calamities will only fall on future generations, for which the present generation takes little thought. The evils that freedom sometimes brings are immediate; they are apparent to all, and all are more or less affected by them. The evils that extreme equality may produce are slowly disclosed; they creep gradually into the social frame; they are only seen at intervals, and at the moment when they become most violent, habit already makes them no longer felt. The advantages freedom brings are only shown by length of time, and it is always easy to mistake the cause in which they originate. The advantages of equality are instantaneous, and they can constantly be traced back to their source. Political liberty bestows exalted pleasures, from time to time, on a certain number of citizens. Equality every day confers a number of small enjoyments on every man. The charms of equality are every instant felt, and are within the reach of all; the noblest hearts are not insensible to them, and the most vulgar souls exult in them. The passion that equality engenders must therefore be at once strong and general. Men cannot enjoy political liberty without purchasing it by some sacrifices, and they never obtain it without great exertions. But the pleasures of equality are self-proffered: each of the petty incidents of life seems to occasion them, and in order to taste them nothing is required but to live.

Democratic nations are at all times fond of equality, but there are certain epochs at which the passion they entertain for it swells to the height of fury. This occurs at the moment when the old social system, long menaced, completes its own destruction after a last internal struggle, and when the barriers of rank are at last thrown down. At such times men pounce upon equality as their booty, and they cling to it as to some precious treasure they fear to lose. The passion for equality penetrates on every side into men’s hearts, expands there, and fills them entirely. Tell them not that by this blind surrender of themselves to an exclusive passion they risk their dearest interests: they are deaf.
