Show them not freedom escaping from their grasp while they are looking the other way: they are blind — or rather, they can discern but one sole object to be desired in the universe.

What I have said is applicable to all democratic nations; what I am about to say concerns the French alone. Among most modern nations, and especially among all those on the Continent of Europe, the taste and the idea of freedom only began to exist and to spread at the time when social conditions were tending toward equality, and as a consequence of that very equality. Absolute kings were the most efficient levelers of ranks among their subjects. Among these nations equality preceded freedom: equality was therefore a fact of some standing when freedom was still a novelty. The former had already created customs, opinions, and laws belonging to it, when the latter, alone and for the first time, came into actual existence. Thus freedom was still only an affair of opinion and of taste, while equality had already crept into the habits of the people, possessed itself of their manners, and given a particular turn to the smallest actions of their lives. Can it be wondered that the men of our own time prefer the one to the other?

I think that democratic communities have a natural taste for freedom: left to themselves, they will seek it, cherish it, and view any privation of it with regret. But for equality their passion is ardent, insatiable, incessant, invincible. They call for equality in freedom; and if they cannot obtain that, they still call for equality in slavery. They will endure poverty, servitude, barbarism — but they will not endure aristocracy. This is true at all times, and especially in our own. All men and all powers that seek to cope with this irresistible passion will be overthrown and destroyed by it. In our age, freedom cannot be established without it, and despotism itself cannot reign without its support.

chapters.title: Chapter II — Of Individualism In Democratic Countries
paragraphs: I have shown how, in ages of equality, every person looks for his opinions within himself. I am now going to show how, in those same ages, all his feelings turn toward himself alone. Individualism*a is a new expression, born from a new idea. Our forefathers knew only selfishness. Selfishness is a passionate and exaggerated love of self that leads a man to connect everything to his own person and to prefer himself to everything else in the world. Individualism is a mature and calm feeling that disposes each member of the community to cut himself off from the mass of his fellow creatures and to withdraw with his family and friends. Having formed this little circle of his own, he willingly leaves society at large to take care of itself. Selfishness comes from blind instinct. Individualism springs from mistaken judgment more than from corrupt feelings; it arises as much from deficiencies of the mind as from the perversity of the heart. Selfishness blights the seed of every virtue. Individualism at first only undermines the virtues of public life, but in the long run it attacks and destroys all the others, and is finally absorbed into outright selfishness. Selfishness is a vice as old as the world and belongs to no one form of society more than another. Individualism is of democratic origin, and it threatens to spread in the same proportion as equality of conditions.

[Footnote a: [I retain the expression used in the original, however strange it may sound to English ears, partly because it illustrates the remark made in an earlier chapter about the introduction of general terms into democratic language, and partly because I know of no English word that exactly corresponds to it. The chapter itself defines the meaning the author gives it. — Translator's Note.]]

Among aristocratic nations, since families remain for centuries in the same condition and often on the same piece of ground, all generations become, as it were, contemporaries. A man almost always knows his ancestors and respects them. He feels he can already see his remote descendants, and he loves them. He willingly takes on duties toward both, and he will often sacrifice his own pleasures for those who came before him and those who will come after him. Aristocratic institutions also have the effect of binding each man closely to several of his fellow citizens. Because the classes of an aristocratic people are sharply marked and permanent, each class is regarded by its own members as a kind of lesser country, more tangible and more cherished than the country at large. Since in aristocratic communities all citizens occupy fixed positions, one above the other, each of them always sees a man above him whose patronage he needs, and another below him whose cooperation he can claim. Men living in aristocratic ages are therefore almost always closely attached to something outside their own sphere, and they are often ready to forget themselves. It is true that in such ages the idea of human fellowship is faint, and men seldom think of sacrificing themselves for humanity as a whole; but they often sacrifice themselves for particular other men. In democratic ages, by contrast, when each person's duties toward the human race are much more clearly understood, devoted service to any single individual becomes rarer. The bond of human affection is stretched wider, but it is also loosened.

Among democratic nations new families are constantly springing up, others are constantly falling away, and all those that remain are changing their condition. The fabric of time is broken every instant, and the track of the generations is erased. Those who went before are soon forgotten; of those who will come after, no one has any idea. A man's interest is confined to those in close proximity to himself. As each class draws nearer to the others and blends with them, its members become indifferent and as strangers to one another. Aristocracy had made a chain of all the members of the community, from the peasant to the king. Democracy breaks that chain and severs every link. As social conditions become more equal, the number increases of those who, though neither rich enough nor powerful enough to exert great influence over their fellow creatures, have still acquired or kept enough education and property to meet their own needs. They owe nothing to anyone and expect nothing from anyone. They form the habit of always thinking of themselves as standing alone, and are apt to imagine that their whole destiny lies in their own hands. Thus democracy not only makes every man forget his ancestors; it hides his descendants from him and separates him from his contemporaries. It throws him back forever upon himself alone, and threatens in the end to confine him entirely within the solitude of his own heart.

chapters.title: Chapter III — Individualism Stronger At The Close Of A Democratic Revolution Than At Other Periods
paragraphs: Revolution Than At Other Periods

The period right after the construction of a democratic society on the ruins of an aristocracy has just been completed is the one in which this separation of men from one another, and the selfishness that results from it, most forcibly strike the observer. Democratic communities not only contain a large number of independent citizens; they are also constantly filled with men who, having entered their independent condition only yesterday, are intoxicated with their new power. They have a presumptuous confidence in their own strength. Since they do not imagine they will ever need to call on the help of their fellow creatures again, they make no effort to hide the fact that they care for nobody but themselves.

An aristocracy seldom yields without a long struggle, in the course of which implacable animosities are kindled between the different classes of society. These passions survive the victory, and traces of them can be seen amid the democratic confusion that follows. Those members of the community who were at the top of the old gradations of rank cannot immediately forget their former greatness; they will long regard themselves as strangers in the midst of the newly formed society. They look upon all those whom this state of society has made their equals as oppressors whose fate can inspire no sympathy. They have lost sight of their former peers and no longer feel bound by any common interest to their fate. Each of them, standing apart, thinks he is reduced to caring for himself alone. Those, on the contrary, who were formerly at the foot of the social scale, and who have been raised to the common level by a sudden revolution, cannot enjoy their newly acquired independence without secret uneasiness. If they meet any of their former superiors on the same footing as themselves, they stand apart from them with an expression of triumph mixed with fear. It is, then, usually at the outset of democratic society that citizens are most inclined to live apart. Democracy does not lead men to draw closer to their fellow creatures; but democratic revolutions lead them to avoid each other, and perpetuate in a state of equality the animosities that the state of inequality produced. The great advantage of the Americans is that they have arrived at a state of democracy without having to endure a democratic revolution, and that they are born equal instead of becoming so.

chapters.title: Chapter IV — That The Americans Combat The Effects Of Individualism By Free Institutions
paragraphs: Despotism, which is of a very timorous nature, is never more secure of continuance than when it can keep men apart; and all its influence is commonly exerted for that purpose. No vice of the human heart is so acceptable to it as egoism; a despot readily forgives his subjects for not loving him, provided they do not love each other. He does not ask them to help him govern the State; it is enough that they do not aspire to govern it themselves. He stigmatizes as turbulent and unruly spirits those who would combine their exertions to promote the prosperity of the community, and, perverting the natural meaning of words, he applauds as good citizens those who have no sympathy for anyone but themselves. So the vices that despotism engenders are precisely those which equality fosters. These two things mutually and perniciously complete and assist each other. Equality places men side by side, unconnected by any common tie; despotism raises barriers to keep them apart; the former predisposes them not to consider their fellow creatures, the latter makes general indifference a kind of public virtue.

Despotism, then, which is at all times dangerous, is especially to be feared in democratic ages. It is easy to see that in those same ages men stand most in need of freedom. When the members of a community are forced to attend to public affairs, they are necessarily drawn from the circle of their own interests, and at times snatched from self-observation. As soon as a man begins to treat of public affairs in public, he begins to perceive that he is not so independent of his fellow men as he had at first imagined, and that, in order to obtain their support, he must often lend them his cooperation.

When the public is supreme, there is no man who does not feel the value of public goodwill, or who does not endeavor to court it by drawing to himself the esteem and affection of those among whom he is to live. Many of the passions that congeal and keep human hearts apart are then obliged to retire and hide below the surface. Pride must be dissembled; disdain dares not break out; egoism fears its own self. Under a free government, as most public offices are elective, the men whose elevated minds or aspiring hopes are too closely circumscribed in private life constantly feel that they cannot do without the population that surrounds them. Men learn at such times to think of their fellow men from ambitious motives, and they frequently find it, in a manner, their interest to forget themselves.

I may here be met by an objection drawn from electioneering intrigues, the meannesses of candidates, and the calumnies of their opponents. These are opportunities for animosity that occur the more often the more frequent elections become. Such evils are doubtless great, but they are transient; whereas the benefits that attend them remain. The desire of being elected may lead some men for a time to violent hostility; but this same desire leads all men in the long run to support each other mutually; and if it happens that an election accidentally severs two friends, the electoral system brings a multitude of citizens permanently together who would otherwise always have remained unknown to each other. Freedom begets private animosities, but despotism gives birth to general indifference.

The Americans have combated by free institutions the tendency of equality to keep men apart, and they have subdued it. The legislators of America did not suppose that a general representation of the whole nation would suffice to ward off a disorder at once so natural to the frame of democratic society and so fatal; they also thought that it would be well to infuse political life into each portion of the territory, in order to multiply to an infinite extent opportunities for all members of the community to act in concert, and to make them constantly feel their mutual dependence on each other. The plan was a wise one. The general affairs of a country only engage the attention of leading politicians, who assemble from time to time in the same places; and since they often lose sight of each other afterward, no lasting ties are established between them. But if the object is to have the local affairs of a district conducted by the men who reside there, the same persons are always in contact, and they are, in a manner, forced to be acquainted, and to adapt themselves to one another.

It is difficult to draw a man out of his own circle to interest him in the destiny of the State, because he does not clearly understand what influence the destiny of the State can have upon his own lot. But if it is proposed to lay a road across the end of his estate, he will see at a glance that there is a connection between this small public affair and his greatest private affairs; and he will discover, without its being shown to him, the close tie that unites private to general interest. Thus, far more may be done toward interesting citizens in the public welfare, and convincing them that they constantly need one another in order to provide for it, by entrusting to them the administration of minor affairs than by surrendering to them the control of important ones. A brilliant achievement may win for you the favor of a people at one stroke; but to earn the love and respect of the population around you, a long succession of little services rendered and obscure good deeds — a constant habit of kindness and an established reputation for disinterestedness — will be required. Local freedom, then, which leads a great number of citizens to value the affection of their neighbors and their kindred, perpetually brings men together, and forces them to help one another, in spite of the tendencies that separate them.

In the United States the more prosperous citizens take great care not to stand aloof from the people; on the contrary, they constantly keep on easy terms with the lower classes; they listen to them, they speak to them every day. They know that the rich in democracies always stand in need of the poor; and that in democratic ages you attach a poor man to you more by your manner than by benefits conferred. The magnitude of such benefits, which sets off the difference of conditions, causes a secret irritation to those who reap advantage from them; but the charm of simplicity of manners is almost irresistible; their affability carries men away, and even their lack of polish is not always displeasing. This truth does not take root at once in the minds of the rich. They generally resist it as long as the democratic revolution lasts, and they do not acknowledge it immediately after that revolution is accomplished. They are very ready to do good to the people, but they still choose to keep them at arm's length; they think this is sufficient, but they are mistaken. They might spend fortunes this way without warming the hearts of the population around them; that population does not ask them for the sacrifice of their money, but of their pride.

It would seem as if every imagination in the United States were stretched to invent means of increasing the wealth and satisfying the wants of the public. The best-informed inhabitants of each district constantly use their information to discover new truths that may augment the general prosperity; and if they have made any such discoveries, they eagerly surrender them to the mass of the people.

When the vices and weaknesses frequently shown by those who govern in America are closely examined, the prosperity of the people occasions — but improperly occasions — surprise. Elected magistrates do not make American democracy flourish; it flourishes because the magistrates are elective.

It would be unjust to suppose that the patriotism and the zeal every American displays for the welfare of his fellow citizens are wholly insincere. Although private interest directs the greater part of human actions in the United States as elsewhere, it does not regulate them all. I must say that I have often seen Americans make great and real sacrifices to the public welfare; and I have noted a hundred instances in which they hardly ever failed to lend faithful support to each other. The free institutions that the inhabitants of the United States possess, and the political rights of which they make so much use, remind every citizen, and in a thousand ways, that he lives in society. They every instant impress on his mind the notion that it is the duty, as well as the interest, of men to make themselves useful to their fellow creatures; and since he sees no particular ground for animosity toward them, being never either their master or their slave, his heart readily leans to the side of kindness. Men attend to the interests of the public, first by necessity, afterwards by choice; what was intentional becomes an instinct; and by dint of working for the good of one's fellow citizens, the habit and the taste for serving them is at length acquired.

Many people in France consider equality of conditions as one evil, and political freedom as a second. When they are obliged to yield to the former, they strive at least to escape from the latter. But I contend that in order to combat the evils that equality may produce, there is only one effectual remedy — namely, political freedom.

chapters.title: Chapter V — Of The Use Which The Americans Make Of Public Associations In Civil Life
paragraphs: I do not propose to speak of those political associations — by which men try to defend themselves against the despotic influence of a majority, or against the aggressions of regal power. I have already treated that subject. If each citizen did not learn, as he individually becomes more feeble and consequently less capable of preserving his freedom single-handed, to combine with his fellow citizens for the purpose of defending it, it is clear that tyranny would inevitably grow alongside equality.

Only those associations formed in civil life, without reference to political objects, are under discussion here. The political associations that exist in the United States are only a single feature in the immense assemblage of associations in that country. Americans of all ages, all conditions, and all dispositions are constantly forming associations. They have not only commercial and manufacturing companies, in which all take part, but associations of a thousand other kinds — religious, moral, serious, trivial, broad or restricted, enormous or tiny. The Americans form associations to give entertainments, to found educational establishments, to build inns, to construct churches, to distribute books, to send missionaries to the antipodes. In this manner they found hospitals, prisons, and schools. If it is proposed to advance some truth, or to foster some feeling by the encouragement of a great example, they form a society. Wherever, at the head of some new undertaking, you see the government in France, or a man of rank in England, in the United States you will be sure to find an association. I met with several kinds of associations in America of which I confess I had no previous notion. I have often admired the extreme skill with which the inhabitants of the United States propose a common object to the exertions of a great many men, and get them to pursue it voluntarily. I have since traveled through England, from which the Americans have taken some of their laws and many of their customs; and it seemed to me that the principle of association was by no means so constantly or so adroitly used in that country. The English often perform great things alone, whereas the Americans form associations for the smallest undertakings. It is clear that the former people consider association as a powerful means of action, while the latter seem to regard it as the only means they have of acting.

Thus the most democratic country on the face of the earth is the one in which, in our time, men have carried to the highest perfection the art of pursuing in common the object of their common desires, and have applied this new science to the greatest number of purposes. Is this the result of accident? Or is there in reality a necessary connection between the principle of association and that of equality? Aristocratic communities always contain, among a multitude of people who by themselves are powerless, a small number of powerful and wealthy citizens, each of whom can accomplish great undertakings single-handed. In aristocratic societies, men do not need to combine in order to act, because they are strongly held together. Every wealthy and powerful citizen is the head of a permanent and compulsory association, composed of all those who depend on him, or whom he makes subservient to the execution of his designs. Among democratic nations, on the contrary, all citizens are independent and feeble. They can do hardly anything by themselves, and none of them can compel his fellow men to lend him their assistance. They all, therefore, fall into a state of incapacity if they do not learn voluntarily to help each other. If men living in democratic countries had no right and no inclination to associate for political purposes, their independence would be in great jeopardy; but they might long preserve their wealth and their cultivation. Whereas if they never acquired the habit of forming associations in ordinary life, civilization itself would be endangered. A people among which individuals lost the power of achieving great things single-handed, without acquiring the means of producing them by united effort, would soon relapse into barbarism.

Unhappily, the same social condition that makes associations so necessary to democratic nations makes their formation more difficult among those nations than among all others. When several members of an aristocracy agree to combine, they easily succeed. Since each of them brings great strength to the partnership, the number of its members can be very limited; and when the members of an association are few, they can easily become mutually acquainted, understand one another, and establish fixed regulations. The same opportunities do not arise among democratic nations, where the associated members must always be very numerous for their association to have any power.

I am aware that many of my countrymen are not in the least troubled by this difficulty. They argue that the more enfeebled and incompetent the citizens become, the more able and active the government ought to be made, so that society at large may execute what individuals can no longer accomplish. They believe this answers the whole difficulty, but I think they are mistaken. A government might perform the part of some of the largest American companies; and several States of the Union have already attempted it. But what political power could ever carry on the vast multitude of smaller undertakings that American citizens perform every day with the aid of the principle of association? It is easy to foresee that the time is drawing near when man will be less and less able to produce, by himself alone, the commonest necessities of life. The task of the governing power will therefore continually increase, and its very efforts will extend it every day. The more it stands in the place of associations, the more will individuals, losing the notion of combining, require its assistance. These are causes and effects that unceasingly engender one another. Will the administration of the country ultimately assume the management of all the manufactures that no single citizen is able to carry on? And if at last a time arrives when, as a result of the extreme subdivision of landed property, the soil is split into an infinite number of parcels so that it can only be cultivated by companies of farmers, will it be necessary for the head of the government to leave the helm of state to follow the plow? The morals and the intelligence of a democratic people would be as much endangered as its business and manufactures if the government ever wholly usurped the place of private companies.

Feelings and opinions are recruited, the heart is enlarged, and the human mind is developed by no other means than by the reciprocal influence of men upon one another. I have shown that these influences are almost null in democratic countries. They must therefore be artificially created, and this can only be accomplished by associations.

When the members of an aristocratic community adopt a new opinion, or conceive a new sentiment, they give it a place, as it were, beside themselves, on the lofty platform where they stand. And opinions or sentiments so conspicuous to the eyes of the multitude are easily introduced into the minds or hearts of all around. In democratic countries the governing power alone is naturally in a position to act in this manner. But it is easy to see that its action is always inadequate and often dangerous. A government can no more be competent to keep alive and to renew the circulation of opinions and feelings among a great people than to manage all the speculations of productive industry. As soon as a government attempts to go beyond its political sphere and to enter upon this new track, it exercises, even unintentionally, an insupportable tyranny. For a government can only dictate strict rules; the opinions it favors are rigidly enforced, and it is never easy to distinguish between its advice and its commands. Worse still will be the case if the government really believes itself interested in preventing all circulation of ideas. It will then stand motionless, oppressed by the heaviness of voluntary torpor. Governments, therefore, should not be the only active powers. In democratic nations, associations ought to stand in place of those powerful private individuals whom equality of conditions has swept away.

As soon as several inhabitants of the United States have taken up an opinion or a feeling they want to promote in the world, they look for mutual assistance. And as soon as they have found each other, they combine. From that moment they are no longer isolated individuals but a power seen from afar, whose actions serve as an example and whose language is listened to. The first time I heard in the United States that 100,000 men had bound themselves publicly to abstain from spirituous liquors, it appeared to me more like a joke than a serious engagement. I did not at once see why these temperate citizens could not content themselves with drinking water by their own firesides. At last I understood that 300,000 Americans, alarmed by the progress of drunkenness around them, had made up their minds to patronize temperance. They acted just like a man of high rank who dresses very plainly in order to inspire the humbler orders with a contempt for luxury. It is probable that if these 100,000 men had lived in France, each of them would individually have petitioned the government to watch the public houses all over the kingdom.

Nothing, in my opinion, is more deserving of our attention than the intellectual and moral associations of America. The political and industrial associations of that country strike us forcibly; but the others elude our observation, or if we discover them, we understand them imperfectly, because we have hardly ever seen anything of the kind. It must, however, be acknowledged that they are as necessary to the American people as the former, and perhaps more so. In democratic countries, the science of association is the mother of science; the progress of all the rest depends on the progress it has made. Among the laws that rule human societies there is one that seems more precise and clearer than all others. If men are to remain civilized, or to become so, the art of associating together must grow and improve in the same proportion in which the equality of conditions is increased.

chapters.title: Chapter VI — Of The Relation Between Public Associations And Newspapers
paragraphs: When men are no longer bound to each other by firm and lasting ties, it is impossible to get the cooperation of any great number of them unless you can convince every man whose participation you need that his own private interest obliges him voluntarily to join his efforts to everyone else's. This can only be done regularly and conveniently by means of a newspaper. Nothing but a newspaper can drop the same thought into a thousand minds at the same moment. A newspaper is an adviser who does not need to be sought out but comes of his own accord and talks to you briefly, every day, about the common good, without pulling you away from your private affairs.

Newspapers therefore become more necessary as men become more equal and individualism grows more to be feared. To suppose they only serve to protect freedom would be to understate their importance: they sustain civilization. I will not deny that in democratic countries newspapers often lead citizens into badly thought-out schemes; but without newspapers there would be no common activity at all. The harm they do is therefore much less than the harm they cure.

The effect of a newspaper is not only to suggest the same purpose to a great many people; it also supplies the means for them to carry out together plans they may each have conceived singly. The leading citizens of an aristocratic country can see each other from far off, and if they wish to combine their forces, they move toward each other, drawing a crowd after them. In democratic countries, by contrast, it often happens that a great many men who would like or need to combine cannot, because being very minor and lost in the crowd, they cannot see one another and do not know where to find one another. A newspaper then takes up the idea or the feeling that had occurred to each of them at the same time but separately. All are at once drawn toward this beacon, and these wandering minds, which had long sought each other in the dark, at last meet and unite.

The newspaper brought them together, and the newspaper is still needed to keep them united. For an association among a democratic people to have any real power, it must be a numerous body. The people who make it up are therefore scattered over a wide area, and each of them is kept at home by the narrowness of his income or by the small unceasing efforts by which he earns it. A way must then be found for them to converse every day without seeing each other, and to act in common without having met. Hardly any democratic association can do without newspapers. There is therefore a necessary connection between public associations and newspapers: newspapers make associations, and associations make newspapers. And if it has been correctly said that associations will grow in number as the conditions of men become more equal, it is no less certain that the number of newspapers grows in proportion to the number of associations. That is why in America we find at the same time the greatest number of associations and of newspapers.

This connection between the number of newspapers and the number of associations leads us to another connection between the state of the periodical press and the form of administration in a country. It shows that the number of newspapers must diminish or increase in a democratic people in proportion as its administration is more or less centralized. For among democratic nations the exercise of local powers cannot be entrusted to the leading members of the community, as it is in aristocracies. Those powers must either be abolished or placed in the hands of very large numbers of men, who in fact then form an association permanently established by law to administer the affairs of a certain stretch of territory; and they need a journal to bring them each day, in the middle of their own minor concerns, some news of the state of their public affairs. The more local powers there are, the greater the number of men in whom they are vested by law; and since this need is felt constantly, the more abundantly newspapers multiply.

The extraordinary subdivision of administrative power has much more to do with the enormous number of American newspapers than does the country's great political freedom or the absolute liberty of its press. If all the inhabitants of the Union had the vote — but a vote only for the choice of their legislators in Congress — they would need only a few newspapers, because they would have to act together only on a few very important but very rare occasions. But within the large association of the nation, smaller associations have been established by law in every county, every city, and even every village, for the purposes of local administration. The laws of the country thus compel every American to cooperate every day of his life with some of his fellow citizens for a common purpose, and each of them needs a newspaper to tell him what all the others are doing.

I am of the opinion that a democratic people*a without any national representative assemblies but with a great number of small local powers would in the end have more newspapers than a people governed by a centralized administration and an elective legislature. What best explains to me the enormous circulation of the daily press in the United States is that I find among the Americans the greatest national freedom combined with local freedom of every kind. There is a prevailing opinion in France and England that the circulation of newspapers could be indefinitely increased by removing the taxes laid on the press. This is a very exaggerated estimate of the effects of such a reform. Newspapers multiply not in proportion to their cheapness, but in proportion to the more or less frequent need a great many people may feel to communicate with each other and to combine.

[Footnote a: I say a democratic people: the administration of an aristocratic people may be anything but centralized, and yet the need for newspapers may be little felt, because local powers are then held by a very small number of men who either act on their own or know one another and can easily meet and come to an understanding.]

In the same way I would attribute the growing influence of the daily press to causes more general than those usually cited. A newspaper can only survive on the condition that it publishes sentiments or principles held by a great many people. A newspaper therefore always represents an association made up of its regular readers. That association may be more or less defined, more or less narrow, more or less numerous; but the fact that the newspaper keeps going is proof that at least the germ of such an association exists in its readers' minds.

This leads me to one last reflection, with which I will close this chapter. The more equal the conditions of men become, and the less strong men are as individuals, the more easily they give way to the current of the multitude, and the harder it is for them to stand alone in holding an opinion that the multitude rejects. A newspaper represents an association. It may be said to address each of its readers in the name of all the others, and to exert its influence over them in proportion to their individual weakness. The power of the newspaper press must therefore grow as the social conditions of men become more equal.

chapters.title: Chapter VII — Connection Of Civil And Political Associations
paragraphs: There is only one country on the face of the earth where citizens enjoy unlimited freedom of association for political purposes. This same country is the only one in the world where the continual exercise of the right of association has been brought into civil life as well, and where all the advantages civilization can confer are obtained through it. In every country where political associations are prohibited, civil associations are rare. It is hardly likely that this is the result of chance. The inference should rather be that there is a natural, and perhaps a necessary, connection between these two kinds of associations. Some men happen to share a common interest in some concern — a commercial venture to be managed, some manufacturing speculation to be tried; they meet, they combine, and in this way they gradually become familiar with the principle of association. The greater the variety of small affairs, the more men acquire, even without knowing it, the facility for carrying on great undertakings together. Civil associations, then, make political association easier. But conversely, political association remarkably strengthens and improves associations for civil purposes. In civil life every man may, strictly speaking, imagine he can provide for his own needs; in politics he can imagine no such thing. When a people, then, has any knowledge of public life, the idea of association and the wish to unite present themselves every day to the whole community. Whatever natural reluctance may restrain men from acting in concert, they will always be ready to combine for the sake of a party. So political life makes the love and practice of association more general; it arouses a desire for union and teaches the means of combination to numbers of men who would otherwise have always lived apart.

Politics gives rise not only to numerous associations but to associations on a large scale. In civil life it seldom happens that any single interest brings a very large number of men to act together; much skill is required to bring such an interest into being. But in politics, opportunities arise every day. It is only in large associations, however, that the full value of the principle of association is displayed. Citizens who are individually powerless do not clearly see the strength they can acquire by uniting; it has to be shown to them before they understand. It is often easier, therefore, to gather a multitude for a public purpose than to gather a few people for a private one. A thousand citizens do not see what interest they have in combining; ten thousand will see it perfectly clearly. In politics men combine for great undertakings, and the use they make of the principle of association in important affairs teaches them, in practice, that it is their interest to help each other in lesser ones. A political association at once draws a number of individuals out of their own circle. However they may naturally be kept apart by age, temperament, or fortune, it brings them closer together and into contact. Once they have met, they can always meet again.

Men can enter few civil partnerships without putting a share of their possessions at risk; this is so with all manufacturing and trading companies. When men are still little versed in the art of association and unfamiliar with its main rules, they are afraid, the first time they combine in this way, of paying dearly for their experience. They therefore prefer to deprive themselves of a powerful instrument of success rather than run the risks it involves. They are, however, less reluctant to join political associations, which appear to them to be without danger because they stake no money in them. But they cannot belong to such associations for any length of time without discovering how order is maintained among a large number of men, and by what contrivance they are brought to move, harmoniously and methodically, toward the same object. So they learn to surrender their own will to that of all the rest, and to make their own efforts subordinate to the common impulse — things no less necessary to know in civil than in political associations. Political associations can therefore be regarded as large free schools where all the members of the community go to learn the general theory of association.

But even if political association did not directly contribute to the progress of civil association, to destroy the former would be to weaken the latter. When citizens can only meet in public for certain purposes, they regard such meetings as a strange, rare event, and they hardly think about them at all. When they are allowed to meet freely for any purpose, they come to see public association as the universal, and in a way the only, means men can use to accomplish the various purposes they have in mind. Every new need instantly revives the notion. The art of association then becomes, as I have said before, the mother of action — studied and applied by all.

When some kinds of associations are prohibited and others permitted, it is difficult to tell the former from the latter in advance. In this state of uncertainty, men abstain from associations altogether, and a kind of public opinion takes hold that tends to regard any association whatsoever as a bold and almost illicit enterprise.*a

[Footnote a: This is especially true when the executive government has discretionary power to allow or prohibit associations. When certain associations are simply prohibited by law, and the courts of justice have to punish violations of that law, the evil is far less serious. Every citizen then knows beforehand roughly what to expect. He judges himself before he is judged by the law, and, abstaining from prohibited associations, he enters those that are legally sanctioned. It is by such restrictions that all free nations have always admitted the right of association may be limited. But if the legislature were to give a man the power of deciding in advance which associations are dangerous and which are useful, and to authorize him either to destroy all associations in the bud or to let them be formed, then, since no one could foresee in what cases associations might be established and in what cases they would be suppressed, the spirit of association would be entirely paralyzed. The first kind of law would only strike at certain associations; the second would strike at society itself and injure it. I can conceive of a regular government resorting to the first; I do not grant that any government has the right to enact the second.]

It is therefore a fantasy to suppose that the spirit of association, when repressed on one point, will nevertheless display the same vigor on all others, and that if men are allowed to carry on certain undertakings in common, that will be enough to make them eager to do so. When the members of a community are allowed and accustomed to combine for every purpose, they will combine as readily for small purposes as for great ones. But if they are only allowed to combine for small matters, they will be neither inclined nor able to do so. It is in vain to leave them entirely free to carry on their business as joint-stock companies. They will hardly bother to take advantage of the rights you have granted them. And after exhausting your strength in vain efforts to suppress the prohibited associations, you will be surprised that you cannot persuade men to form the associations you encourage.

I do not say that there can be no civil associations in a country where political association is prohibited, for men can never live in society without entering into some common undertakings. But I maintain that in such a country civil associations will always be few in number, feebly conceived, clumsily managed; they will never form any vast designs, or they will fail in carrying them out.

This naturally leads me to think that freedom of association in political matters is not as dangerous to public tranquility as is supposed, and that possibly, after having stirred society up for a time, it may in the end strengthen the state. In democratic countries political associations are, so to speak, the only powerful persons who aspire to rule the state. Accordingly, the governments of our time regard such associations just as sovereigns in the Middle Ages regarded the great vassals of the crown: they feel a kind of instinctive abhorrence of them and combat them on every occasion. They bear, by contrast, a natural goodwill toward civil associations, because they readily notice that, instead of directing the minds of the community to public affairs, such institutions divert them from such reflections. By engaging men more and more in the pursuit of objects that cannot be attained without public tranquility, civil associations deter them from revolutions. But these governments fail to notice that political associations amazingly multiply and facilitate those of a civil character, and that in avoiding a dangerous evil they deprive themselves of an effective remedy.

When you see the Americans freely and constantly forming associations to promote some political principle, to raise one man to the head of affairs or wrest power from another, you have some difficulty understanding how men so independent do not constantly fall into the abuse of freedom. If, on the other hand, you survey the countless trading companies in operation in the United States, and see that the Americans are everywhere ceaselessly engaged in carrying out important and difficult plans which the slightest revolution would throw into confusion, you readily understand why people so well occupied are in no way tempted to disturb the state or to destroy the public tranquility from which they all benefit.

Is it enough to observe these things separately, or should we not look for the hidden tie that connects them? In their political associations, Americans of all conditions, minds, and ages daily acquire a general taste for association and grow accustomed to using it. There they meet in large numbers, they converse, they listen to each other, and they stimulate one another to all kinds of undertakings. Then they carry the notions they have thus acquired over into civil life and put them to a thousand uses. Thus it is by enjoying a dangerous freedom that the Americans learn the art of making the dangers of freedom less formidable.

If a particular moment in the life of a nation is selected, it is easy to show that political associations disturb the state and paralyze productive industry. But take the whole life of a people, and it may perhaps be easy to demonstrate that freedom of association in political matters is favorable to the prosperity and even the tranquility of the community.

I said in the earlier part of this work: "The unrestrained liberty of political association cannot be entirely equated with the liberty of the press. The first is at once less necessary and more dangerous than the second. A nation may confine it within certain limits without ceasing to be its own master, and it may sometimes be obliged to do so in order to maintain its own authority." And further on I added: "It cannot be denied that the unrestrained liberty of association for political purposes is the last degree of liberty a people is fit for. If it does not throw them into anarchy, it perpetually brings them, as it were, to the brink of it." So I do not think a nation is always free to grant its citizens an absolute right of association for political purposes, and I doubt that in any country, in any age, it is wise to set no limits to freedom of association. A certain nation, it is said, could not maintain tranquility in the community, get its laws respected, or establish a lasting government if the right of association were not confined within narrow limits. These blessings are undoubtedly invaluable, and I can imagine that, to acquire or preserve them, a nation may impose on itself severe temporary restrictions. But it is still well for the nation to know at what price these blessings are bought. I can understand that it may be wise to cut off a man's arm to save his life, but it would be ridiculous to claim that he will be as dexterous afterward as he was before he lost it.

chapters.title: Chapter VIII — The Americans Combat Individualism By The Principle Of Interest Rightly Understood
paragraphs: Interest Rightly Understood

When the world was managed by a few rich and powerful individuals, those people liked to hold a lofty idea of man's duties. They were fond of declaring that it is praiseworthy to forget oneself, and that good should be done without hope of reward, as the Deity himself does it. Such were the standard moral opinions of that age. I doubt that men were more virtuous in aristocratic ages than in others, but they were incessantly talking about the beauty of virtue — its usefulness was studied only in secret. Now that the imagination takes less lofty flights and every man's thoughts are centered on himself, moralists are alarmed by the idea of self-sacrifice and no longer dare to hold it up to the human mind. So they content themselves with asking whether the personal advantage of each member of the community does not consist in working for the good of all. When they hit on some point where private interest and public interest meet and merge, they are quick to point it out. Observations of this kind are gradually multiplied: what was only a single remark becomes a general principle, and it is held as a truth that a man serves himself in serving his fellow creatures, and that his private interest is to do good.

I have already shown, in several parts of this work, by what means the inhabitants of the United States almost always manage to combine their own advantage with that of their fellow citizens. My present purpose is to point out the general rule that allows them to do so. In the United States hardly anyone talks about the beauty of virtue, but they maintain that virtue is useful, and they prove it every day. American moralists do not claim that men ought to sacrifice themselves for their fellow creatures because such sacrifices are noble; they boldly declare that such sacrifices are as necessary to the one who makes them as to the one for whose sake they are made. They have discovered that in their country and their age, man is drawn back to himself by an irresistible force. Giving up all hope of stopping that force, they turn all their thought to directing it. They therefore do not deny that every man may pursue his own interest; rather, they try to prove that it is in every man's interest to be virtuous. I will not go into the reasons they give, which would take me from my subject. It is enough to say that they have convinced their fellow countrymen.

Montaigne said long ago: "If I did not follow the straight road for its straightness, I would follow it for having found by experience that in the end it is usually the happiest and most useful path." The doctrine of interest rightly understood is therefore not new. But among the Americans of our time it meets with universal acceptance. It has become popular there. You can trace it at the bottom of all their actions; you will notice it in everything they say. It is as often found on the lips of the poor man as of the rich. In Europe the principle of interest is much cruder than it is in America, but at the same time it is less common, and especially less openly avowed. Among us, men still constantly pretend to a great self-denial they no longer feel. The Americans, by contrast, are fond of explaining almost every action of their lives by the principle of interest rightly understood. They show with satisfaction how an enlightened concern for themselves constantly prompts them to help each other, and disposes them willingly to sacrifice a share of their time and property to the welfare of the state. In this respect I think they often fail to do themselves justice. For in the United States, as elsewhere, people are sometimes seen giving way to those disinterested and spontaneous impulses that are natural to man. But the Americans rarely admit that they yield to such emotions — they are more anxious to do honor to their philosophy than to themselves.

I might stop here without attempting to pass judgment on what I have described. The extreme difficulty of the subject would excuse me, but I shall not use that excuse. I would rather have my readers, clearly seeing my aim, refuse to follow me, than leave them in suspense. The principle of interest rightly understood is not a lofty one, but it is clear and sure. It does not aim at great objects, but it reaches, without excessive effort, all those it does aim at. Since it lies within the reach of every intelligence, everyone can easily grasp and retain it. Thanks to its admirable fit with human weaknesses, it easily gains great dominion; and that dominion is not precarious, since the principle checks one personal interest by another, using to direct the passions the very instrument that excites them. The principle of interest rightly understood produces no great acts of self-sacrifice, but it suggests daily small acts of self-denial. By itself it cannot make a man virtuous, but it disciplines a great many citizens in habits of regularity, temperance, moderation, foresight, and self-command. If it does not lead men straight to virtue by an act of will, it gradually draws them in that direction through their habits. If the principle of interest rightly understood were to govern the whole moral world, extraordinary virtues would no doubt be rarer; but I think gross depravity would also be less common. The principle perhaps prevents some men from rising far above the level of mankind, but a great many other men, who were falling far below it, are caught and restrained by it. Look at some few individuals — they are lowered by it. Look at mankind as a whole — it is raised. I am not afraid to say that the principle of interest rightly understood seems to me the best suited of all philosophical theories to the needs of the men of our time, and that I regard it as their chief remaining safeguard against themselves. The minds of moralists in our age should therefore turn toward it. Even if they judge it incomplete, it must still be adopted as necessary.

On the whole I do not think there is more selfishness among us than in America. The only difference is that there it is enlightened, and here it is not. Every American will sacrifice a share of his private interests to preserve the rest; we would like to preserve the whole, and often end up losing it all. Everyone around me seems bent on teaching his contemporaries, by precept and example, that what is useful is never wrong. Will no one take on the task of making them understand how what is right may be useful? No power on earth can prevent the growing equality of conditions from inclining the human mind to seek out what is useful, or from leading every member of the community to become wrapped up in himself. We must therefore expect personal interest to become more than ever the chief, if not the only, spring of men's actions. But it remains to be seen how each man will understand his personal interest. If the members of a community, as they grow more equal, also grow more ignorant and coarse, it is hard to foresee to what pitch of stupid excess their selfishness may lead them; and no one can predict into what disgrace and wretchedness they would plunge themselves rather than sacrifice any of their own well-being to the prosperity of their fellow creatures. I do not think that the system of interest as it is professed in America is, in all its parts, self-evident; but it contains a great many truths so evident that men, provided they are educated, cannot fail to see them. Educate, then, at all costs — for the age of implicit self-sacrifice and instinctive virtues is already receding far from us, and the time is fast approaching when freedom, public peace, and social order itself will not be able to exist without education.

chapters.title: Chapter IX — That The Americans Apply The Principle Of Interest Rightly Understood To Religious Matters
paragraphs: Understood To Religious Matters

If the principle of interest rightly understood had only this world in view, it would be very inadequate. For there are many sacrifices that can only find their recompense in another. And however much ingenuity may be applied to demonstrating the utility of virtue, it will never be an easy task to make a man live rightly who has no thoughts of dying. So it is necessary to determine whether the principle of interest rightly understood is easily compatible with religious belief. The philosophers who teach this system of morals tell men that, to be happy in this life, they must watch their own passions and steadily control their excess; that lasting happiness can only be secured by renouncing a thousand transient gratifications; and that a man must perpetually triumph over himself in order to secure his own advantage. The founders of almost all religions have used the same language. The path they point out to man is the same — only the goal is more remote. Instead of placing in this world the reward of the sacrifices they impose, they transfer it to another. Nevertheless, I cannot believe that all who practice virtue from religious motives are driven only by the hope of a reward. I have known zealous Christians who constantly forgot themselves in order to work with greater ardor for the happiness of their fellow human beings, and I have heard them declare that everything they did was only to earn the blessings of a future state. I cannot help thinking they deceive themselves. I respect them too much to believe them.

Christianity does teach that a man must prefer his neighbor to himself in order to gain eternal life. But Christianity also teaches that men ought to benefit their fellow creatures for the love of God. A sublime expression! Man, searching with his intellect into the divine conception and seeing that order is the purpose of God, freely joins in carrying out the great design. And while he sacrifices his personal interests to this consummate order of all created things, he expects no other recompense than the pleasure of contemplating it. I do not believe that interest is the sole motive of religious men. But I believe that interest is the principal means religions themselves employ to govern men, and I do not doubt that in this way they reach the multitude and become popular. It is not easy to see clearly why the principle of interest rightly understood should keep aloof from religious opinions, and it seems to me easier to show why it should draw men to them. Suppose that, in order to obtain happiness in this world, a man combats his instinct on every occasion and deliberately calculates every action of his life; that, instead of yielding blindly to the impetuosity of first desires, he has learned the art of resisting them; and that he has accustomed himself to sacrifice without effort the pleasure of a moment to the lasting interest of his whole life. If such a man believes in the religion he professes, it will cost him little to submit to the restrictions it may impose. Reason herself counsels him to obey, and habit has prepared him to endure them. If he has conceived any doubts as to the object of his hopes, he will still not easily allow himself to be stopped by them. He will decide that it is wise to risk some of the advantages of this world in order to preserve his rights to the great inheritance promised him in another. "To be mistaken in believing that the Christian religion is true," says Pascal, "is no great loss to anyone; but how dreadful to be mistaken in believing it to be false!"

The Americans do not affect a brutal indifference to a future state. They affect no childish pride in despising perils they hope to escape. They therefore profess their religion without shame and without weakness. But there is generally, even in their zeal, something so indescribably tranquil, methodical, and deliberate about it that it would seem the head, far more than the heart, brings them to the foot of the altar. The Americans not only follow their religion out of interest, but they often place in this world the interest that makes them follow it. In the Middle Ages the clergy spoke of nothing but a future state; they hardly bothered to prove that a sincere Christian can be a happy man here below. But the American preachers are constantly referring to the earth, and it is only with great difficulty that they can turn their attention from it. To move their congregations, they always show them how favorable religious opinions are to freedom and public tranquility. And it is often difficult to tell from their sermons whether the principal object of religion is to procure eternal happiness in the other world, or prosperity in this one.

chapters.title: Chapter X — Of The Taste For Physical Well-Being In America
paragraphs: In America the passion for physical well-being is not always exclusive, but it is general; and if all do not feel it in the same way, it is felt by all. To satisfy carefully all, even the smallest wants of the body, and to provide the little conveniences of life, is uppermost in every mind. Something of the same character is more and more apparent in Europe. Among the causes that produce these similar consequences in both hemispheres, several are so closely connected with my subject that they deserve notice.

When wealth is fixed in families by inheritance, there are a great number of men who enjoy the comforts of life without feeling an exclusive taste for them. The human heart is not so much caught by the undisturbed possession of anything valuable as by the desire—still imperfectly satisfied—of possessing it, and by the constant fear of losing it. In aristocratic communities, the wealthy, never having known any condition different from their own, have no fear of changing it. The existence of such conditions hardly occurs to them. The comforts of life are not for them the end of life, but simply a way of living; they regard them as existence itself—enjoyed, but scarcely thought about. Since the natural and instinctive taste all men feel for being well off is thus satisfied without trouble and without anxiety, their faculties are turned elsewhere, and fasten onto more arduous and lofty undertakings that excite and engross their minds. That is why, in the midst of physical gratifications, the members of an aristocracy often display a haughty contempt for these very enjoyments, and show singular powers of endurance when deprived of them. All the revolutions that have ever shaken or destroyed aristocracies have shown how easily men accustomed to superfluous luxuries can do without the necessities of life; whereas men who have toiled to acquire a competence can hardly live once they have lost it.

If I shift my observation from the upper to the lower classes, I find similar effects produced by opposite causes. In a nation where aristocracy predominates in society and keeps it stationary, the people in the end grow as accustomed to poverty as the rich to their opulence. The rich spend no anxiety on their physical comforts because they enjoy them without effort; the poor do not think of things they despair of obtaining, and which they hardly know well enough even to desire. In communities of this kind, the imagination of the poor is driven to seek another world. The miseries of real life surround it, but it escapes their control and flies off to seek its pleasures far beyond. When, on the contrary, the distinctions of rank are blurred and privileges destroyed—when hereditary property is subdivided, and education and freedom are widely diffused—the desire to acquire the comforts of the world haunts the imagination of the poor, and the fear of losing them haunts that of the rich. Many small fortunes spring up; those who possess them have a sufficient share of physical gratifications to develop a taste for these pleasures, but not enough to satisfy it. They never get them without effort, and they never indulge in them without anxiety. They are therefore always straining to pursue or to retain gratifications so delightful, so imperfect, so fleeting.

If I were to ask what passion is most natural to men who are both stimulated and restricted by the obscurity of their birth or the mediocrity of their fortune, I could find none more peculiarly suited to their condition than this love of physical prosperity. The passion for physical comforts is essentially a passion of the middle classes: with those classes it grows and spreads, with them it predominates. From them it rises into the higher orders of society and descends into the mass of the people. I never met a citizen in America so poor that he did not cast a glance of hope and envy on the enjoyments of the rich, nor whose imagination did not seize in anticipation on the good things that fate still obstinately withheld from him. On the other hand, I never noticed among the wealthier inhabitants of the United States that proud contempt for physical gratifications that is sometimes found even in the most opulent and dissolute aristocracies. Most of these wealthy men were once poor; they have felt the sting of want; they were long at the mercy of adverse fortune. Now that the victory is won, the passions that accompanied the struggle have survived it: their minds are, as it were, intoxicated by the small enjoyments they have pursued for forty years. Not that in the United States, as elsewhere, there is not a certain number of wealthy people who, having come into their property by inheritance, possess without effort an opulence they have not earned. But even these men are no less devotedly attached to the pleasures of material life. The love of well-being has now become the predominant taste of the nation. The great current of men's passions runs in that channel, and sweeps everything along with it.

chapters.title: Chapter XI — Peculiar Effects Of The Love Of Physical Gratifications In Democratic Ages
paragraphs: One might suppose, from what has just been said, that the love of physical gratification must constantly drive the Americans into moral irregularities, disturb the peace of families, and threaten the security of society at large. That is not the case. The passion for physical gratification produces very different effects in democracies from those it produces in aristocratic nations. Sometimes an aristocracy — worn out by public affairs and glutted with wealth, amid the ruin of religious belief and the decline of the state — is gradually seduced into pursuing only sensual enjoyment. At other times the power of the monarch or the weakness of the people, without stripping the nobility of its fortune, forces it to stand apart from the administration of affairs. With the road to great undertakings closed, the aristocracy is left to the restlessness of its own desires. It then falls heavily back upon itself and seeks in bodily pleasures the forgetfulness of its former greatness. When the members of an aristocratic body are thus exclusively devoted to the pursuit of physical gratification, they usually concentrate in that direction all the energy they draw from their long experience of power. Such men are not content with the pursuit of comfort. They demand sumptuous depravity and splendid corruption. The worship they offer the senses is a gorgeous one, and they seem to compete in the art of degrading their own natures. The stronger, the more famous, and the freer an aristocracy has been, the more depraved it will then become. However brilliant its virtues may once have shone, I dare predict that they will always be outdone by the splendor of its vices.

The taste for physical gratification leads a democratic people into no such excesses. There, the love of well-being shows itself as a tenacious, exclusive, universal passion, but its range is limited. No one thinks of building vast palaces, of conquering or imitating nature, of ransacking the world to gratify one man's passions. Instead, people think of adding a few acres to their land, of planting an orchard, of enlarging a house, of always making life more comfortable and convenient, of avoiding trouble, and of satisfying the smallest needs without effort and almost without cost. These are small objects, but the soul clings to them. It dwells on them closely, day after day, until in the end they shut out the rest of the world, and sometimes even come between the soul and heaven.

It may be objected that this can only apply to members of the community in humble circumstances, and that wealthier people will display tastes like those they had in aristocratic ages. I dispute the claim. When it comes to physical gratification, the richest members of a democracy show tastes not very different from those of the people — whether because, having risen from the people, they actually share those tastes, or because they feel it is their duty to conform. In democratic society the public appetite has taken a moderate and quiet course to which everyone is bound to conform. It is as hard to depart from the common rule by one's vices as by one's virtues. Rich men living in democratic nations are therefore more intent on providing for their smallest wants than on extraordinary enjoyments. They gratify a host of petty desires without indulging in any great outbursts of passion. They are thus more likely to become enervated than debauched. The particular taste men of democratic ages have for physical enjoyments is not by nature opposed to the principles of public order. On the contrary, it often needs order in order to be satisfied. Nor is it hostile to regularity of morals, for good morals contribute to public tranquility and favor industry. It may even often be combined with a kind of religious morality. Men wish to be as well off as they can in this world without forgoing their chance of another. Some physical gratifications cannot be indulged in without committing a crime, and from these they strictly abstain. Others are sanctioned by religion and morality, and to these the heart, the imagination, and life itself are given up without reserve — until, in snatching at these lesser goods, men lose sight of those more precious possessions that constitute the glory and greatness of mankind. The reproach I direct at the principle of equality is not that it leads men astray in pursuit of forbidden enjoyments, but that it absorbs them entirely in the pursuit of allowed ones. By this means a kind of virtuous materialism may ultimately establish itself in the world — one that would not corrupt but enervate the soul, and silently slacken its springs of action.

chapters.title: Chapter XII — Causes Of Fanatical Enthusiasm In Some Americans
paragraphs: Although the desire of acquiring the good things of this world is the prevailing passion of the American people, certain momentary outbreaks occur when their souls seem suddenly to burst the bonds of matter by which they are restrained, and to soar impetuously toward heaven. In all the States of the Union, but especially in the half-peopled country of the Far West, wandering preachers may be met with who hawk about the word of God from place to place. Whole families — old men, women, and children — cross rough passes and untrodden wilds, coming from a great distance to join a camp meeting, where for several days and nights they totally forget, in listening to these discourses, the cares of business and even the most urgent wants of the body. Here and there, in the midst of American society, you meet with men full of a fanatical and almost wild enthusiasm, which hardly exists in Europe. From time to time strange sects arise, which endeavor to strike out extraordinary paths to eternal happiness. Religious insanity is very common in the United States.

Nor should these facts surprise us. It was not man who implanted in himself the taste for what is infinite and the love of what is immortal: those lofty instincts are not the offspring of his capricious will; their steadfast foundation is fixed in human nature, and they exist in spite of his efforts. He may cross and distort them — destroy them he cannot. The soul has wants that must be satisfied, and whatever pains be taken to divert it from itself, it soon grows weary, restless, and disquieted amid the enjoyments of sense. If ever the faculties of the great majority of mankind were exclusively bent on the pursuit of material objects, it might be anticipated that an amazing reaction would take place in the souls of some men. They would drift at large in the world of spirits, for fear of remaining shackled by the close bondage of the body.

It is not then surprising if, in the midst of a community whose thoughts tend earthward, a small number of individuals are found who turn their looks to heaven. I should be surprised if mysticism did not soon make some advance among a people solely engaged in promoting its own worldly welfare. It is said that the deserts of the Thebaid were peopled by the persecutions of the emperors and the massacres of the Circus; I should rather say that it was by the luxuries of Rome and the Epicurean philosophy of Greece. If their social condition, their present circumstances, and their laws did not confine the minds of the Americans so closely to the pursuit of worldly welfare, it is likely that they would display more reserve and more experience whenever their attention is turned to things immaterial, and that they would check themselves without difficulty. But they feel imprisoned within bounds which, apparently, they will never be allowed to pass. As soon as they have passed these bounds, their minds know not where to fix themselves, and they often rush unrestrained beyond the range of common sense.

chapters.title: Chapter XIII — Causes Of The Restless Spirit Of Americans In The Midst Of Their Prosperity
paragraphs: In certain remote corners of the Old World you may still sometimes stumble upon a small district that seems to have been forgotten amid the general tumult, and to have remained stationary while everything around it was in motion. The inhabitants are for the most part extremely ignorant and poor; they take no part in the business of the country, and they are frequently oppressed by the government; yet their countenances are generally placid, and their spirits light. In America I saw the freest and most enlightened men, placed in the happiest circumstances the world affords: it seemed to me as if a cloud habitually hung upon their brow, and I thought them serious and almost sad even in their pleasures. The chief reason for this contrast is that the former do not think of the ills they endure — the latter are forever brooding over advantages they do not possess. It is strange to see with what feverish ardor the Americans pursue their own welfare, and to watch the vague dread that constantly torments them that they may not have chosen the shortest path that leads to it. A native of the United States clings to this world’s goods as if he were certain never to die, and he is so hasty in grasping at all within his reach that one would suppose he was constantly afraid of not living long enough to enjoy them. He clutches everything, he holds nothing fast, but soon loosens his grasp to pursue fresh gratifications.

In the United States a man builds a house to spend his latter years in it, and sells it before the roof is on. He plants a garden, and lets it just as the trees are coming into bearing. He brings a field into tillage, and leaves other men to gather the crops. He embraces a profession, and gives it up. He settles in a place that he soon afterward leaves to carry his changeable longings elsewhere. If his private affairs leave him any leisure, he instantly plunges into the vortex of politics; and if at the end of a year of unremitting labor he finds he has a few days’ vacation, his eager curiosity whirls him over the vast extent of the United States, and he will travel fifteen hundred miles in a few days, to shake off his happiness. Death at length overtakes him, but it is before he is weary of his bootless chase of that complete felicity which is forever on the wing.

At first sight there is something surprising in this strange unrest of so many happy men, restless in the midst of abundance. The spectacle itself, however, is as old as the world; the novelty is to see a whole people furnish an example of it. Their taste for physical gratifications must be regarded as the original source of that secret inquietude the actions of the Americans betray, and of that inconstancy of which they afford fresh examples every day. He who has set his heart exclusively on the pursuit of worldly welfare is always in a hurry, for he has but a limited time at his disposal to reach it, to grasp it, and to enjoy it. The recollection of the brevity of life is a constant spur to him. Besides the good things he possesses, he every instant fancies a thousand others that death will prevent him from trying if he does not try them soon. This thought fills him with anxiety, fear, and regret, and keeps his mind in ceaseless trepidation, which leads him perpetually to change his plans and his abode. If to the taste for physical well-being a social condition is added in which the laws and customs make no condition permanent, there is a great additional stimulant to this restlessness of temper. Men will then be seen continually to change their track, for fear of missing the shortest cut to happiness. It is easy to see that if men passionately bent on physical gratifications desire eagerly, they are also easily discouraged: since their ultimate object is to enjoy, the means to reach that object must be prompt and easy, or the trouble of acquiring the gratification would be greater than the gratification itself. Their prevailing frame of mind is at once ardent and relaxed, violent and enervated. Death is often less dreaded than perseverance in continuous efforts toward one end.

The equality of conditions leads by a still straighter road to several of the effects I have here described. When all the privileges of birth and fortune are abolished, when all professions are accessible to all, and a man’s own energies may place him at the top of any of them, an easy and unbounded career seems open to his ambition, and he will readily persuade himself that he is born to no vulgar destinies. But this is an erroneous notion, corrected by daily experience. The same equality that allows every citizen to conceive these lofty hopes renders all the citizens less able to realize them; it circumscribes their powers on every side while giving freer scope to their desires. Not only are they themselves powerless, but they are met at every step by immense obstacles, which they did not at first perceive.
