They have swept away the privileges of some of their fellow creatures that stood in their way, but they have opened the door to universal competition. The barrier has changed its shape rather than its position. When men are nearly alike and all follow the same track, it is very difficult for any one individual to walk quickly and cleave a way through the dense throng that surrounds and presses him. This constant strife between the propensities springing from the equality of conditions and the means it supplies to satisfy them harasses and wearies the mind.

It is possible to conceive of men arrived at a degree of freedom that should completely content them; they would then enjoy their independence without anxiety and without impatience. But men will never establish any equality with which they can be contented. Whatever efforts a people may make, they will never succeed in reducing all the conditions of society to a perfect level; and even if they unhappily attained that absolute and complete depression, the inequality of minds would still remain, which, coming directly from the hand of God, will forever escape the laws of man. However democratic, then, the social state and the political constitution of a people may be, it is certain that every member of the community will always find several points about him that command his own position; and we may foresee that his eyes will be doggedly fixed in that direction. When inequality of conditions is the common law of society, the most marked inequalities do not strike the eye. When everything is nearly on the same level, the slightest are marked enough to hurt it. Hence the desire of equality always becomes more insatiable in proportion as equality is more complete.

Among democratic nations men easily attain a certain equality of conditions: they can never attain the equality they desire. It perpetually retires from before them, yet without hiding itself from their sight, and in retiring draws them on. At every moment they think they are about to grasp it; at every moment it escapes from their hold. They are near enough to see its charms, but too far off to enjoy them; and before they have fully tasted its delights they die. To these causes must be attributed that strange melancholy that often haunts the inhabitants of democratic countries in the midst of their abundance, and that disgust at life that sometimes seizes them in the midst of calm and easy circumstances. Complaints are made in France that the number of suicides is increasing; in America suicide is rare, but insanity is said to be more common than anywhere else. These are all different symptoms of the same disease. The Americans do not put an end to their lives, however disquieted they may be, because their religion forbids it; and among them materialism may be said hardly to exist, notwithstanding the general passion for physical gratification. The will resists — reason frequently gives way. In democratic ages enjoyments are more intense than in the ages of aristocracy, and especially the number of those who partake in them is larger. But on the other hand it must be admitted that man’s hopes and desires are oftener blasted, the soul is more stricken and perturbed, and care itself more keen.

chapters.title: Chapter XIV — Taste For Physical Gratifications United In America To Love Of Freedom And Attention To Public Affairs
paragraphs: Of Freedom And Attention To Public Affairs

When a democratic state turns into an absolute monarchy, the activity that was previously directed toward public as well as private affairs is suddenly concentrated on private affairs alone. The immediate consequence, for a time, is great physical prosperity. But the impulse soon slackens, and the level of productive industry begins to stall. I do not know whether a single trading or manufacturing people can be named — from the Tyrians down to the Florentines and the English — that was not also a free people. There is therefore a close bond and a necessary relation between these two elements: freedom and productive industry. This is generally true of all nations, but especially of democratic nations. I have already shown that men who live in ages of equality continually need to form associations in order to obtain the things they want. And I have also shown how greatly political freedom improves and spreads the art of association. In such ages freedom is therefore especially favorable to the production of wealth. It is not hard to see that despotism is especially hostile to that result. The nature of despotic power in democratic ages is not to be fierce or cruel, but minute and meddling. Despotism of this kind, though it does not trample on humanity, stands directly opposed to the spirit of commerce and the pursuits of industry.

So men of democratic ages need to be free in order to obtain more readily those physical enjoyments they are always longing for. It sometimes happens, however, that the excessive taste they develop for those same enjoyments hands them over to the first master who appears. The passion for worldly welfare then defeats itself and, without their noticing, pushes the very object of their desires further away.

There is, indeed, a most dangerous passage in the history of a democratic people. When the taste for physical gratification among such a people has grown faster than its education and its experience of free institutions, a time comes when men are carried away and lose all self-restraint at the sight of the new possessions they are about to seize. In their intense and exclusive anxiety to make a fortune, they lose sight of the close connection between the private fortune of each and the prosperity of all. It is not necessary to use violence against such a people in order to strip them of the rights they enjoy; they themselves willingly let go. The performance of political duties seems to them a troublesome annoyance that diverts them from their occupations and business. If they are required to elect representatives, to support the government by personal service, to gather for public business, they have no time — they cannot waste their precious time on useless engagements. Such idle pursuits are unsuited to serious men engaged in the more important interests of life. These people think they are following the principle of self-interest, but the idea they have of that principle is a very crude one. In order to look after what they call their business, they neglect their chief business, which is to remain their own masters.

Since the citizens who work do not care to attend to public business, and since the class that might devote its leisure to these duties has ceased to exist, the place of government is, as it were, left vacant. If at that critical moment some able and ambitious man seizes supreme power, he will find the road to every kind of usurpation open before him. If he attends for a while to the material prosperity of the country, nothing more will be required of him. Above all, he must guarantee public tranquility. Men possessed by the passion for physical gratification generally discover that the turmoil of freedom disturbs their well-being before they discover how freedom itself actually promotes it. If the slightest rumor of public commotion intrudes on the petty pleasures of their private lives, they are stirred and alarmed by it. The fear of anarchy perpetually haunts them, and they are always ready to throw away their freedom at the first disturbance.

I readily admit that public tranquility is a great good. But at the same time I cannot forget that all nations have been enslaved by being kept in good order. Certainly this is not to suggest that nations should despise public tranquility. But that state of affairs should not be enough for them. A nation that asks nothing of its government except the maintenance of order is already a slave at heart — the slave of its own well-being, waiting only for the hand that will bind it. By such a nation the despotism of a faction is no less to be feared than the despotism of an individual. When the bulk of the community is absorbed by private concerns, the smallest parties need not despair of gaining the upper hand in public affairs. At such times it is not rare to see, upon the great stage of the world, what we see at our theaters — a multitude represented by a few actors, who alone speak in the name of an absent or inattentive crowd. They alone are in motion while all the rest are still; they regulate everything by their own whim; they change the laws and tyrannize at will over the customs of the country. Then men are astonished to see into how small a number of weak and worthless hands a great people can fall.

Up to now the Americans have fortunately escaped all the dangers I have just described, and in this respect they truly deserve admiration. Perhaps there is no country in the world where fewer idle men are to be found than in America, or where those who work are more eager to promote their own welfare. But if the Americans' passion for physical gratifications is intense, at least it is not undiscriminating; and reason, though unable to restrain it, still guides its course. An American attends to his private concerns as if he were alone in the world, and the next minute he gives himself up to the common good as if he had forgotten them. At one moment he seems driven by the most selfish greed, at another by the most lively patriotism. The human heart cannot really be split in two. The inhabitants of the United States display so strong and so similar a passion for their own welfare and for their freedom, by turns, that one must suppose these passions are united and blended somewhere in their character. And indeed the Americans believe their freedom to be the best instrument and the surest safeguard of their welfare. They are attached to the one through the other. They by no means think they are not called to take part in the public good. On the contrary, they believe their chief business is to secure for themselves a government that will allow them to obtain the things they want and will not bar them from the peaceful enjoyment of the possessions they have acquired.

chapters.title: Chapter XV — That Religious Belief Sometimes Turns The Thoughts Of The Americans To Immaterial Pleasures
paragraphs: Americans to Immaterial Pleasures

In the United States, on the seventh day of every week, the trading and working life of the nation seems suspended; all noises cease; a deep tranquillity — say rather the solemn calm of meditation — succeeds the turmoil of the week, and the soul resumes possession and contemplation of itself. On this day the marts of traffic are deserted; every member of the community, accompanied by his children, goes to church, where he listens to strange language that would seem unsuited to his ear. He is told of the countless evils caused by pride and covetousness; he is reminded of the necessity of checking his desires, of the finer pleasures that belong to virtue alone, and of the true happiness that attends it. On his return home, he does not turn to the ledgers of his trade, but opens the book of Holy Scripture. There he meets with sublime or affecting descriptions of the greatness and goodness of the Creator, of the infinite magnificence of the handiwork of God, of the lofty destinies of man, of his duties, and of his immortal privileges. Thus it is that the American at times steals an hour from himself; and laying aside for a while the petty passions that agitate his life and the ephemeral interests that engross it, he strays at once into an ideal world, where all is great, eternal, and pure.

I have endeavored to point out in another part of this work the causes to which the maintenance of the political institutions of the Americans is attributable, and religion appeared to be one of the most prominent among them. I am now treating of the Americans in an individual capacity, and I again observe that religion is no less useful to each citizen than to the whole State. The Americans show, by their practice, that they feel the high necessity of imparting morality to democratic communities by means of religion. What they think of themselves in this respect is a truth of which every democratic nation ought to be thoroughly persuaded.

I do not doubt that the social and political constitution of a people predisposes them to adopt a certain belief and certain tastes, which afterward flourish without difficulty among them; while the same causes may divert a people from certain opinions and propensities, without any voluntary effort and, as it were, without any distinct consciousness on their part. The whole art of the legislator is to discern these natural inclinations of communities of men correctly in advance, in order to know whether they should be assisted, or whether it may not be necessary to check them. For the duties incumbent on the legislator differ at different times; the goal toward which the human race ought ever to be tending is alone stationary; the means of reaching it are perpetually to be varied.

If I had been born in an aristocratic age, in the midst of a nation where the hereditary wealth of some and the irremediable penury of others equally divert men from the idea of bettering their condition, and hold the soul, as it were, in a state of torpor fixed on the contemplation of another world, I should then wish it were possible for me to rouse that people to a sense of their wants. I should seek to discover more rapid and easier means of satisfying the fresh desires I had awakened, and, directing the most strenuous efforts of the human mind to physical pursuits, I should endeavor to stimulate it to promote the well-being of man. If it happened that some men were immoderately incited to the pursuit of riches and displayed an excessive liking for physical gratifications, I should not be alarmed; these peculiar symptoms would soon be absorbed in the general aspect of the people.

The attention of the legislators of democracies is called to other cares. Give democratic nations education and freedom, and leave them alone. They will soon learn to draw from this world all the benefits it can afford; they will improve each of the useful arts, and will day by day render life more comfortable, more convenient, and easier. Their social condition naturally urges them in this direction; I do not fear that they will slacken their course.

But while man takes delight in this honest and lawful pursuit of his well-being, it is to be feared that he may in the end lose the use of his sublimest faculties, and that while he is busied in improving all around him, he may at length degrade himself. Here, and here only, does the peril lie. It should therefore be the unceasing object of the legislators of democracies, and of all the virtuous and enlightened men who live there, to raise the souls of their fellow citizens and keep them lifted up toward heaven. All who feel an interest in the future destinies of democratic society must unite, and all must make joint and continual efforts to diffuse the love of the infinite, a sense of greatness, and a love of pleasures not of earth. If among the opinions of a democratic people any of those pernicious theories exist which tend to inculcate that all perishes with the body, let the men by whom such theories are professed be marked as the natural foes of such a people.

The materialists are offensive to me in many respects; their doctrines I hold to be pernicious, and I am disgusted at their arrogance. If their system could be of any utility to man, it would seem to be by giving him a modest opinion of himself. But these reasoners show that it is not so; and when they think they have said enough to establish that they are brutes, they show themselves as proud as if they had demonstrated that they are gods. Materialism is, among all nations, a dangerous disease of the human mind; but it is more especially to be dreaded among a democratic people, because it readily amalgamates with that vice which is most familiar to the heart under such circumstances. Democracy encourages a taste for physical gratification: this taste, if it becomes excessive, soon disposes men to believe that all is matter only; and materialism in turn hurries them back with mad impatience to these same delights. Such is the fatal circle within which democratic nations are driven round. It would be well that they should see the danger and hold back.

Most religions are only general, simple, and practical means of teaching men the doctrine of the immortality of the soul. That is the greatest benefit a democratic people derives from its belief, and hence belief is more necessary to such a people than to any other. When therefore any religion has struck its roots deep into a democracy, beware lest you disturb them; rather watch it carefully, as the most precious bequest of aristocratic ages. Seek not to supersede the old religious opinions of men by new ones, lest in the passage from one faith to another, the soul being left for a while stripped of all belief, the love of physical gratifications should grow upon it and fill it wholly.

The doctrine of metempsychosis is assuredly no more rational than that of materialism; nevertheless, if it were absolutely necessary that a democracy should choose one of the two, I should not hesitate to decide that the community would run less risk of being brutalized by believing that the soul of man will pass into the carcass of a hog, than by believing that the soul of man is nothing at all. The belief in a supersensual and immortal principle, united for a time to matter, is so indispensable to man’s greatness that its effects are striking even when it is not united to the doctrine of future reward and punishment, and when it holds no more than that after death the divine principle contained in man is absorbed in the Deity, or transferred to animate the frame of some other creature. Men holding so imperfect a belief will still consider the body as the secondary and inferior portion of their nature, and they will despise it even while they yield to its influence; whereas they have a natural esteem and secret admiration for the immaterial part of man, even though they sometimes refuse to submit to its dominion. That is enough to give a lofty cast to their opinions and their tastes, and to bid them tend, with no interested motive, and as it were by impulse, to pure feelings and elevated thoughts.

It is not certain that Socrates and his followers had very fixed opinions as to what would befall man hereafter; but the sole point of belief on which they were determined — that the soul has nothing in common with the body, and survives it — was enough to give the Platonic philosophy that sublime aspiration by which it is distinguished. It is clear from the works of Plato that many philosophical writers, his predecessors or contemporaries, professed materialism. These writers have not reached us, or have reached us only in fragments. The same thing has happened in almost all ages: most of the most famous minds in literature adhere to the doctrines of a supersensual philosophy. The instinct and the taste of the human race maintain those doctrines; they save them oftentimes in spite of men themselves, and raise the names of their defenders above the tide of time. It must not then be supposed that at any period, or under any political condition, the passion for physical gratifications, and the opinions such a passion gives rise to, can ever content a whole people. The heart of man is of a larger mold: it can at once comprise a taste for the possessions of earth and the love of those of heaven. At times it may seem to cling devotedly to the one, but it will never be long without thinking of the other.

If it is easy to see that it is particularly important in democratic ages that spiritual opinions should prevail, it is not easy to say by what means those who govern democratic nations may make them predominate. I am no believer in the prosperity, any more than in the durability, of official philosophies; and as to state religions, I have always held that if they are sometimes of momentary service to the interests of political power, they always, sooner or later, become fatal to the Church. Nor do I think with those who assert that, in order to raise religion in the eyes of the people and to make them do honor to her spiritual doctrines, it is desirable indirectly to give her ministers a political influence the laws deny them. I am so much alive to the almost inevitable dangers that beset religious belief whenever the clergy take part in public affairs, and I am so convinced that Christianity must be maintained at any cost in the bosom of modern democracies, that I would rather shut up the priesthood within the sanctuary than allow them to step beyond it.

What means, then, remain in the hands of constituted authorities to bring men back to spiritual opinions, or to hold them fast to the religion by which those opinions are suggested? My answer will do me harm in the eyes of politicians. I believe that the only effective means governments can employ to have the doctrine of the immortality of the soul duly respected is to act ever as if they believed in it themselves; and I think it is only by scrupulous conformity to religious morality in great affairs that they can hope to teach the community at large to know, to love, and to observe it in the lesser concerns of life.

chapters.title: Chapter XVI — That Excessive Care Of Worldly Welfare May Impair That Welfare
paragraphs: There is a closer tie than is commonly supposed between the improvement of the soul and the improvement of what belongs to the body. A man may hold the two apart and consider each in turn, but he cannot separate them completely without finally losing sight of both. The beasts have the same senses we do, and very nearly the same appetites. We have no sensual passions that are not shared with our species and theirs, and that are not found, at least in germ, in a dog as well as in a man. Why then can the animals provide only for their first and lowest needs, while we can endlessly vary and endlessly expand our enjoyments?

We are superior to the beasts in this: we use our souls to discover those material goods toward which they are drawn only by instinct. In man, the angel teaches the brute the art of satisfying its desires. It is because man is capable of rising above the things of the body, and of despising life itself — of which the beasts have not the least notion — that he can multiply those very bodily goods to a degree inferior species are equally incapable of conceiving. Whatever raises, enlarges, and expands the soul makes it more capable of succeeding even in undertakings that do not concern it. Whatever, on the other hand, weakens or debases it makes it weaker for all purposes, the greatest as well as the least, and threatens to render it almost equally powerless in both. That is why the soul must remain great and strong, even if only to devote that strength and greatness from time to time to the service of the body. If men were ever to content themselves with material objects, they would probably lose by degrees the art of producing them, and would end up enjoying them like the brutes — without discernment and without improvement.

chapters.title: Chapter XVII — That In Times Marked By Equality Of Conditions And Sceptical Opinions, It Is Important To Remove To A Distance The Objects Of Human Actions
paragraphs: Sceptical Opinions, It Is Important To Remove To A Distance The Objects Of Human Actions

In ages of faith the final end of life is placed beyond life itself. People of those ages therefore naturally, and almost involuntarily, grow accustomed to fixing their gaze for a long course of years on some unmovable object toward which they are constantly tending; and they learn by imperceptible degrees to suppress a multitude of small passing desires in order to be better able to satisfy that great and lasting desire which possesses them. When these same men turn to the affairs of this world, the same habits can be traced in their conduct. They tend to set up some general and definite aim for their actions here below, toward which all their efforts are directed; they do not turn from day to day to chase some new object of desire, but have settled designs they never tire of pursuing. This explains why religious nations have so often achieved such lasting results: while they were thinking only of the other world, they had discovered the great secret of success in this one. Religions give men a general habit of conducting themselves with an eye to the future; in that respect they are no less useful to happiness in this life than to felicity in the next — and this is one of their chief political characteristics.

But as the light of faith grows dim, the range of man's sight narrows, as though the end and aim of human actions were drawing daily closer within his reach. Once men have let themselves stop thinking about what is to come after life, they readily lapse into that complete and brutal indifference to the future which is only too conformable to certain tendencies of mankind. As soon as they have lost the habit of placing their chief hopes on remote events, they naturally seek to gratify their smallest desires without delay; and no sooner do they despair of living forever than they are disposed to act as if they were to exist only for a single day. In sceptical ages it is therefore always to be feared that men may give themselves up perpetually to their daily passing desires, and, wholly renouncing whatever cannot be acquired without sustained effort, may establish nothing great, permanent, and calm.

If the social condition of a people, under these circumstances, becomes democratic, the danger I have pointed out is thereby increased. When everyone is constantly striving to change his position — when an immense field for competition is thrown open to all — when wealth is amassed or dissipated in the shortest possible span of time amid the turmoil of democracy, visions of sudden and easy fortunes, of great possessions quickly won and lost, of chance in all its forms, haunt the mind. The instability of society itself fosters the natural instability of man's desires. Amid these perpetual fluctuations of his lot, the present grows on his mind until it hides the future from his sight, and his looks go no further than tomorrow.

In those countries where, unhappily, irreligion and democracy coexist, the most important duty of philosophers and of those in power is to strive constantly to set the objects of human action far beyond man's immediate reach. Constrained by the character of his country and his age, the moralist must learn to vindicate his principles from within that position. He must constantly endeavor to show his contemporaries that, even amid the perpetual commotion around them, it is easier than they think to conceive and execute sustained undertakings. He must teach them that although the look of mankind may have changed, the methods by which men may provide for their prosperity in this world are still the same; and that among democratic nations, as elsewhere, only by resisting a thousand petty selfish passions of the hour can the general and unquenchable passion for happiness be satisfied.

The task of those in power is no less clearly marked out. At all times it matters that those who govern nations act with a view to the future; but this is even more necessary in democratic and sceptical ages than in any others. By acting this way, the leading men of democracies not only make public affairs prosperous, but they also teach private individuals, by their example, the art of managing private concerns. Above all they must strive as much as possible to banish chance from the sphere of politics. The sudden and undeserved promotion of a courtier makes only a fleeting impression in an aristocratic country, because the aggregate institutions and opinions of the nation habitually compel men to advance slowly along tracks they cannot step off. But nothing is more pernicious than similar instances of favor displayed before a democratic people; they give a final impulse to the public mind in a direction in which everything already drives it. In times of scepticism and equality especially, the favor of the people or of the prince, which chance may bestow or chance withhold, ought never to stand in place of attainments or services. It is desirable that every advancement there should appear to be the result of some effort, so that no greatness may be too easily acquired, and that ambition should be obliged to fix its gaze long upon an object before it is satisfied. Governments must apply themselves to restoring to men that love of the future which religion and the state of society no longer inspire in them; and, without saying so, they must practically teach the community day by day that wealth, fame, and power are the rewards of labor — that great success stands at the furthest reach of long desires, and that nothing lasting is obtained except by toil. When men have grown accustomed to foresee from afar what is likely to happen in the world, and to feed on hopes, they can hardly confine their minds within the precise circumference of life, and are ready to break the boundary and cast their looks beyond it. I have no doubt that by training the members of a community to think of their future condition in this world, they would gradually and unconsciously be brought nearer to religious convictions. So the means that allow men, up to a certain point, to go without religion, are perhaps after all the only means we still possess for bringing mankind back, by a long and roundabout path, to a state of faith.

chapters.title: Chapter XVIII — That Amongst The Americans All Honest Callings Are Honorable
paragraphs: Among a democratic people, where there is no inherited wealth, every man either works for a living, has worked, or is born of parents who have worked. The idea of labor is therefore presented to the mind on every side as the necessary, natural, and honest condition of human existence. Not only is labor not dishonorable among such a people; it is held in honor. The prejudice is not against it, but in its favor. In the United States a wealthy man thinks he owes it to public opinion to devote his leisure to some kind of industrial or commercial pursuit, or to public affairs. He would think himself in bad standing if he spent his life solely on living. It is to escape this obligation to work that so many rich Americans come to Europe, where they find scattered remains of aristocratic society among which idleness is still honored.

Equality of conditions not only ennobles the idea of labor in men's eyes; it raises the idea of labor undertaken for profit. In aristocracies it is not exactly labor that is scorned, but labor pursued for gain. Labor is honorable in itself when undertaken at the sole command of ambition or virtue. Yet in aristocratic society it constantly happens that a man who works for honor is not indifferent to the attractions of profit. These two desires mingle only in the innermost depths of his soul. He carefully hides from every eye the point at which they meet; he would like to hide it even from himself. In aristocratic countries there are few public officials who do not claim to serve their country without self-interested motives. Their salary is a detail they think little about, and always pretend not to think about at all. In this way the notion of profit is kept separate from the notion of labor. However closely the two may be joined in fact, they are not thought of together.

In democratic communities, by contrast, these two notions are always openly united. Since the desire for well-being is universal, since fortunes are modest or fluctuating, since everyone wants either to increase his own resources or to provide new ones for his children, men see clearly that it is profit which — if not entirely, at least partly — leads them to work. Even those chiefly driven by the love of fame are necessarily brought to the thought that fame is not their only motive. They discover that the desire to earn a living is mixed in their minds with the desire to make life distinguished.

As soon as, on the one hand, labor is regarded by the whole community as an honorable necessity of man's condition, and, on the other, as soon as labor is always openly performed wholly or in part for the sake of earning remuneration, the immense gap that once separated the various callings in aristocratic societies disappears. If all are not alike, all at least have one feature in common. No profession exists in which men do not work for money, and the remuneration common to all gives them all a kind of family resemblance. This helps explain the opinions Americans hold about different callings. In America no one is degraded because he works, for everyone around him also works; nor is anyone humiliated by the thought of receiving pay, for the President of the United States also works for pay. He is paid for commanding, other men for obeying orders. In the United States professions are more or less laborious, more or less profitable, but they are never high or low: every honest calling is honorable.

chapters.title: Chapter XIX — That Almost All The Americans Follow Industrial Callings
paragraphs: Of all the useful arts, agriculture is perhaps the one that improves most slowly among democratic nations. Often, indeed, it would seem to be stationary, because other arts are making rapid strides toward perfection. On the other hand, almost all the tastes and habits produced by equality of conditions naturally lead men to commercial and industrial occupations.

Suppose an active, enlightened, and free man, enjoying a competence but full of desires. He is too poor to live in idleness; he is rich enough to feel safe from the immediate fear of want, and he thinks about how he can better his condition. This man has acquired a taste for physical gratifications, in which thousands of his fellow men indulge around him. He has himself begun to enjoy these pleasures, and he is eager to increase his means of satisfying these tastes more completely. But life is slipping away, time is urgent—what is he to turn to? The cultivation of the ground promises an almost certain result from his efforts, but a slow one. Men are not enriched by it without patience and toil. Agriculture is therefore only suited to those who already have large, superfluous wealth, or to those whose poverty bids them only seek a bare subsistence. A man like the one we have imagined soon makes his choice: he sells his plot of ground, leaves his dwelling, and embarks on some hazardous but lucrative calling. Democratic communities abound in men of this kind, and in proportion as equality of conditions grows, their numbers increase. Thus democracy not only swells the number of working men, but it also leads men to prefer one kind of labor to another. While it diverts them from agriculture, it encourages their taste for commerce and manufactures. *a

[Footnote a: It has often been observed that manufacturers and merchants are inordinately given to physical gratifications, and this has been attributed to commerce and manufactures. But this, I think, is to take the effect for the cause. The taste for physical gratifications is not imparted to men by commerce or manufactures; rather, it is this taste that leads men to take up commerce and manufactures, as a means by which they hope to satisfy themselves more quickly and more completely. If commerce and manufactures increase the desire for well-being, it is because every passion gathers strength the more it is cultivated, and is increased by all the efforts made to satisfy it. All the causes that make the love of worldly welfare predominate in the human heart are favorable to the growth of commerce and manufactures. Equality of conditions is one of those causes; it encourages trade, not directly by giving men a taste for business, but indirectly by strengthening and expanding in their minds a taste for prosperity.]

This spirit can be seen even among the richest members of the community. In democratic countries, however opulent a man is supposed to be, he is almost always dissatisfied with his fortune, because he finds himself less rich than his father was, and he fears that his sons will be less rich than he is. Most rich men in democracies are therefore constantly haunted by the desire to acquire more wealth, and they naturally turn their attention to trade and manufactures, which seem to offer the readiest and most powerful means of success. In this respect they share the instincts of the poor, without feeling the same necessities. Or rather, they feel the most imperious necessity of all: that of not sinking in the world.

In aristocracies the rich are also those who govern. The attention they constantly devote to important public affairs diverts them from the smaller concerns that trade and manufactures demand. If the will of an individual should nevertheless turn his attention to business, the will of the body to which he belongs will immediately prevent him from pursuing it. For however much men may rail against the rule of numbers, they cannot wholly escape its sway. Even among those aristocratic bodies that most obstinately refuse to acknowledge the rights of the majority of the nation, a private majority is formed that governs the rest. *b

[Footnote b: Some aristocracies, however, have devoted themselves eagerly to commerce, and have cultivated manufactures with success. The history of the world could furnish several conspicuous examples. But generally speaking, it can be said that the aristocratic principle is not favorable to the growth of trade and manufactures. Moneyed aristocracies are the only exception to the rule. Among such aristocracies there are hardly any desires that do not require wealth to satisfy them; the love of riches becomes, so to speak, the main road of human passions, which is crossed by or connected with all lesser paths. The love of money and the thirst for that distinction which attaches to power are then so closely intermingled in the same souls that it becomes difficult to tell whether men grow greedy from ambition, or ambitious from greed. This is the case in England, where men seek to get rich in order to attain distinction, and seek distinctions as a manifestation of their wealth. The mind is then seized by both ends, and hurried into trade and manufactures, which are the shortest roads that lead to opulence.

This, however, strikes me as an exceptional and transitory state of affairs. When wealth has become the only symbol of aristocracy, it is very difficult for the wealthy to keep sole possession of political power, to the exclusion of all other men. The aristocracy of birth and pure democracy are at the two extremes of the social and political state of nations: between them the moneyed aristocracy finds its place. It approaches the aristocracy of birth by conferring great privileges on a small number of persons; it belongs to the democratic element insofar as these privileges may in turn be acquired by all. It often forms a natural transition between these two conditions of society, and it is hard to say whether it closes the reign of aristocratic institutions or already opens the new era of democracy.]

In democratic countries, where money does not bring those who possess it political power, but often removes them from it, the rich do not know how to spend their leisure. They are driven into active life by the restlessness and greatness of their desires, by the extent of their resources, and by the taste for what is extraordinary that is almost always felt by those who rise, by whatever means, above the crowd. Trade is the only road open to them. In democracies nothing is greater or more brilliant than commerce: it attracts the attention of the public and fills the imagination of the multitude; all the energetic passions are directed toward it. Neither their own prejudices nor those of anyone else can prevent the rich from devoting themselves to it. The wealthy members of democracies never form a body that has manners and regulations of its own; the opinions peculiar to their class do not hold them back, and the common opinions of their country urge them on. Moreover, since all the large fortunes to be found in a democratic community have come from commerce, many generations must pass before those who possess them can have entirely laid aside their habits of business.

Confined within the narrow space that politics leaves them, rich men in democracies eagerly throw themselves into commercial enterprise. There they can extend and employ their natural advantages. Indeed, it is even by the boldness and scale of their industrial speculations that we can measure how little esteem they would have shown for productive industry had they been born into an aristocracy.

A similar observation also applies to all men living in democracies, whether poor or rich. Those who live in the midst of democratic fluctuations always have before their eyes the phantom of chance, and they end by liking all undertakings in which chance plays a part. They are therefore all led to engage in commerce, not only for the sake of the profit it holds out to them, but for the love of the constant excitement that pursuit produces.

The United States of America have only been free for half a century [in 1840] from the state of colonial dependence in which they stood toward Great Britain. The number of large fortunes there is small, and capital is still scarce. Yet no people in the world has made such rapid progress in trade and manufactures as the Americans. They are today the second maritime nation in the world, and although their manufactures have to struggle with almost insurmountable natural obstacles, they are not prevented from making great and daily advances. In the United States the greatest undertakings and speculations are carried out without difficulty, because the whole population is engaged in productive industry, and because the poorest as well as the most opulent members of the commonwealth are ready to combine their efforts for these purposes. The result is that a stranger is constantly amazed by the immense public works carried out by a nation that contains, so to speak, no rich men. The Americans arrived only yesterday on the territory they inhabit, and they have already changed the whole order of nature to their own advantage. They have joined the Hudson to the Mississippi, and made the Atlantic Ocean communicate with the Gulf of Mexico, across a continent more than five hundred leagues wide that separates the two seas. The longest railroads built up to the present time are in America. But what most astonishes me in the United States is not so much the marvelous grandeur of some undertakings as the countless multitude of small ones. Almost all the farmers of the United States combine some trade with agriculture; most of them make agriculture itself a trade. It seldom happens that an American farmer settles for good on the land he occupies. Especially in the districts of the Far West, he brings land into cultivation in order to sell it again, not to farm it. He builds a farmhouse on the speculation that, since the state of the country will soon be changed by the increase of population, a good price will be obtained for it. Every year a swarm of inhabitants from the North arrive in the Southern States and settle in the areas where the cotton plant and the sugar cane grow. These men cultivate the soil in order to make it produce in a few years enough to enrich them; and they already look forward to the time when they may return home to enjoy the competence thus acquired. Thus the Americans carry their business-like qualities into agriculture, and their trading passions are displayed there as in their other pursuits.

The Americans make immense progress in productive industry, because they all devote themselves to it at once; and for this same reason they are exposed to very unexpected and formidable troubles. Since they are all engaged in commerce, their commercial affairs are affected by such various and complex causes that it is impossible to foresee what difficulties may arise. Since they are all more or less engaged in productive industry, at the slightest shock given to business all private fortunes are put in jeopardy at the same time, and the State is shaken. I believe that the recurrence of these commercial panics is an endemic disease of the democratic nations of our age. It can be made less dangerous, but it cannot be cured, because it does not come from accidental circumstances, but from the temperament of these nations.

chapters.title: Chapter XX — That Aristocracy May Be Engendered By Manufactures
paragraphs: I have shown that democracy is favorable to the growth of manufactures and that it increases the numbers of the manufacturing classes without limit. We shall now see by what side road manufacturers may, in their turn, possibly bring men back to aristocracy. It is acknowledged that when a workman is engaged every day on the same detail, the whole commodity is produced with greater ease, speed, and economy. It is also acknowledged that the cost of producing manufactured goods is reduced by the size of the establishment in which they are made, and by the amount of capital employed or of credit. These truths had long been imperfectly understood, but in our time they have been demonstrated. They have already been applied to many very important kinds of manufacture, and the humblest will gradually be governed by them. I know of nothing in politics that deserves to fix the attention of the legislator more closely than these two new axioms of the science of manufactures.

When a workman is unceasingly and exclusively engaged in the making of one thing, he ultimately does his work with singular dexterity; but at the same time he loses the general faculty of applying his mind to the direction of the work. Each day he becomes more skillful and less industrious, so that it may be said of him that in proportion as the workman improves, the man is degraded. What can be expected of a man who has spent twenty years of his life making heads for pins? And to what can that mighty human intelligence, which has so often stirred the world, be applied in him, except to investigate the best method of making pinheads? When a workman has spent a considerable portion of his existence in this way, his thoughts are forever fixed on the object of his daily toil; his body has contracted certain fixed habits that it can never shake off. In a word, he no longer belongs to himself, but to the calling he has chosen. It is in vain that laws and manners have taken pains to level all barriers around such a man and to open to him on every side a thousand different paths to fortune; a theory of manufactures more powerful than manners and laws binds him to a craft, and often to a spot, which he cannot leave. It assigns him a certain place in society, beyond which he cannot go. In the midst of universal movement, it has made him stationary.

In proportion as the principle of the division of labor is more widely applied, the workman becomes weaker, more narrow-minded, and more dependent. The art advances, the artisan recedes. On the other hand, in proportion as it becomes clearer that manufactured products are cheaper and better the larger the manufacture and the more considerable the amount of capital employed, wealthy and educated men come forward to embark in manufactures previously abandoned to poor or ignorant craftsmen. The magnitude of the efforts required, and the importance of the results to be obtained, attract them. Thus at the very moment when the science of manufactures lowers the class of workmen, it raises the class of masters.

While the workman concentrates his faculties more and more on the study of a single detail, the master surveys a larger whole, and the mind of the latter is enlarged in proportion as that of the former is narrowed. Before long, the one will need nothing but physical strength without intelligence; the other will need science, and almost genius, to ensure success. This man resembles more and more the administrator of a vast empire—that man, a brute. Master and workman then have no similarity here, and their differences increase every day. They are only connected as the two rings at the ends of a long chain. Each of them fills the station made for him, and out of which he cannot climb: the one is continually, closely, and necessarily dependent on the other, and seems as much born to obey as the other is to command. What is this but aristocracy?

As the conditions of men composing the nation become more and more equal, the demand for manufactured commodities becomes more general and more extensive; and the cheapness that places these objects within the reach of slender fortunes becomes a great element of success. Hence every day there are more men of great wealth and education who devote their riches and knowledge to manufactures, and who seek, by opening large establishments and applying a strict division of labor, to meet the fresh demands coming in from all sides. Thus, in proportion as the mass of the nation turns to democracy, that particular class engaged in manufactures becomes more aristocratic. Men grow more alike in the one, more different in the other; inequality increases within the less numerous class in the same ratio in which it decreases in the community. Hence it would appear, on searching to the bottom, that aristocracy should naturally spring from the bosom of democracy.

But this kind of aristocracy in no way resembles those that preceded it. It will be noticed at once that since it applies exclusively to manufactures and to some manufacturing callings, it is a monstrous exception in the general aspect of society. The small aristocratic societies formed by some manufacturers in the midst of the immense democracy of our age contain, like the great aristocratic societies of former ages, some men who are very opulent and a multitude who are wretchedly poor. The poor have few means of escaping from their condition and becoming rich; but the rich are constantly becoming poor, or they give up business once they have made a fortune. Thus the elements of which the class of the poor is composed are fixed; but the elements of which the class of the rich is composed are not. To tell the truth, though there are rich men, the class of rich men does not exist. These rich individuals have no feelings or purposes in common, no shared traditions, no shared hopes. There are therefore members, but no body.

Not only are the rich not tightly united among themselves, but there is no real bond between them and the poor. Their relative position is not a permanent one; they are constantly drawn together or separated by their interests. The workman is generally dependent on the master, but not on any particular master. These two men meet in the factory, but do not know each other elsewhere; and while they come into contact on one point, they stand very wide apart on all others. The manufacturer asks nothing of the workman but his labor; the workman expects nothing from him but his wages. The one takes on no obligation to protect, nor the other to defend; they are not permanently connected by habit or by duty. The aristocracy created by business rarely settles in the midst of the manufacturing population it directs; the object is not to govern that population, but to use it. An aristocracy constituted in this way can have no great hold on those it employs, and even if it manages to keep them at one moment, they escape the next. It does not know how to will, and it cannot act. The territorial aristocracy of former ages was either bound by law, or thought itself bound by custom, to come to the relief of its serving men, and to help them in their distresses. But the manufacturing aristocracy of our age first impoverishes and debases the men who serve it, and then abandons them to be supported by the charity of the public. This is a natural consequence of what has been said before. Between the workmen and the master there are frequent relations, but no real partnership.

I am of the opinion, on the whole, that the manufacturing aristocracy now growing up under our eyes is one of the harshest that ever existed in the world; but at the same time it is one of the most confined and least dangerous. Nevertheless, the friends of democracy should keep their eyes anxiously fixed in this direction. For if ever a permanent inequality of conditions and aristocracy again penetrate the world, it can be predicted that this is the channel by which they will enter.
Book Three: Influence Of Democracy On Manners, Properly So Called

chapters.title: Chapter I — That Manners Are Softened As Social Conditions Become More Equal
paragraphs: We perceive that for several ages social conditions have tended toward equality, and we discover that over the same period the manners of society have been softened. Are these two things merely contemporaneous, or does some secret link exist between them, so that the one cannot advance without making the other advance? Several causes may combine to make the manners of a people less rude, but of all these causes, the most powerful appears to me to be the equality of conditions. Equality of conditions and growing civility of manners are, then, in my eyes, not only contemporaneous occurrences but correlative facts. When the fabulists want to interest us in the actions of beasts, they invest them with human notions and passions; the poets who sing of spirits and angels do the same. There is no wretchedness so deep, and no happiness so pure, as to fill the human mind and touch the heart, unless we are ourselves held up to our own eyes under other features.

This applies strictly to the subject we are now engaged with. When all men are irrevocably marshaled in an aristocratic community according to their professions, their property, and their birth, the members of each class, considering themselves as children of the same family, cherish a constant and lively sympathy toward one another, which can never be felt to the same degree by the citizens of a democracy. But the same feeling does not exist between the several classes toward one another. Among an aristocratic people, each caste has its own opinions, feelings, rights, manners, and modes of living. Thus the men of whom each caste is composed do not resemble the mass of their fellow citizens. They do not think or feel in the same way, and they scarcely believe that they belong to the same human race. They cannot, therefore, fully understand what others feel, nor judge of others by themselves. Yet they are sometimes eager to lend each other mutual aid — but this is not contrary to my previous observation. These aristocratic institutions, which made the beings of one and the same race so different, nevertheless bound them to each other by close political ties. Although the serf had no natural interest in the fate of nobles, he still thought himself obliged to devote his person to the service of whichever noble happened to be his lord. And although the noble held himself to be of a different nature from that of his serfs, he nevertheless held that his duty and his honor compelled him to defend, at the risk of his own life, those who lived on his domains.

It is clear that these mutual obligations did not originate in the law of nature, but in the law of society; and that the claim of social duty was more stringent than that of mere humanity. These services were not supposed to be due from man to man, but to the vassal or to the lord. Feudal institutions awakened a lively sympathy for the sufferings of certain men, but none at all for the miseries of mankind. They infused generosity rather than mildness into the manners of the time. And although they prompted men to great acts of self-devotion, they engendered no real sympathies. For real sympathies can only exist between those who are alike, and in aristocratic ages men acknowledge none but the members of their own caste to be like themselves.

When the chroniclers of the Middle Ages — who all belonged to the aristocracy by birth or education — relate the tragic end of a noble, their grief flows freely. Whereas they tell you in a single breath, and without wincing, of massacres and tortures inflicted on the common sort of people. Not that these writers felt habitual hatred or systematic disdain for the people; war between the several classes of the community was not yet declared. They were driven by instinct rather than by passion. Since they had formed no clear notion of a poor man's sufferings, they cared little for his fate. The same feelings animated the lower orders whenever the feudal tie was broken. The same ages which witnessed so many heroic acts of self-devotion on the part of vassals for their lords were stained with atrocious barbarities, committed from time to time by the lower classes on the higher. It must not be supposed that this mutual insensibility arose solely from the absence of public order and education; traces of it are to be found in the following centuries, which became tranquil and enlightened while they remained aristocratic. In 1675 the lower classes in Brittany revolted against the imposition of a new tax. These disturbances were put down with unexampled atrocity. Observe the language in which Madame de Sévigné, a witness of these horrors, relates them to her daughter: —
"Aux Rochers, 30 Octobre, 1675.

"Mon Dieu, ma fille, que votre lettre d'Aix est plaisante! Au moins relisez vos lettres avant que de les envoyer; laissez-vous surpendre à leur agrément, et consolez-vous par ce plaisir de la peine que vous avez d'en tant écrire. Vous avez donc baisé toute la Provence? il n'y aurait pas satisfaction à baiser toute la Bretagne, à moins qu'on n'aimât à sentir le vin. . . . Voulez-vous savoir des nouvelles de Rennes? On a fait une taxe de cent mille écus sur le bourgeois; et si on ne trouve point cette somme dans vingt-quatre heures, elle sera doublée et exigible par les soldats. On a chassé et banni toute une grand rue, et défendu de les recueillir sous peine de la vie; de sorte qu'on voyait tous ces misérables, vieillards, femmes accouchées, enfans, errer en pleurs au sortir de cette ville sans savoir où aller. On roua avant-hier un violon, qui avait commencé la danse et la pillerie du papier timbré; il a été écartelé après sa mort, et ses quatre quartiers exposés aux quatre coins de la ville. On a pris soixante bourgeois, et on commence demain les punitions. Cette province est un bel exemple pour les autres, et surtout de respecter les gouverneurs et les gouvernantes, et de ne point jeter de pierres dans leur jardin." *a

[Footnote a: To feel the point of this joke the reader should recollect that Madame de Grignan was Gouvernante de Provence.] "Madame de Tarente était hier dans ces bois par un temps enchanté: il n'est question ni de chambre ni de collation; elle entre par la barrière et s'en retourne de même. . . ."
In another letter she adds: —

"Vous me parlez bien plaisamment de nos misères; nous ne sommes plus si roués; un en huit jours, pour entretenir la justice. Il est vrai que la penderie me paraît maintenant un rafraîchissement. J'ai une tout autre idée de la justice, depuis que je suis en ce pays. Vos galériens me paraissent une société d'honnêtes gens qui se sont retirés du monde pour mener une vie douce."

It would be a mistake to suppose that Madame de Sévigné, who wrote these lines, was a selfish or cruel person. She was passionately attached to her children, and very ready to sympathize with the sorrows of her friends; indeed, her letters show that she treated her vassals and servants with kindness and indulgence. But Madame de Sévigné had no clear notion of suffering in anyone who was not a person of quality.

In our time the harshest man writing to the most insensible person of his acquaintance would not dare wantonly to indulge in the cruel jocularity I have quoted. And even if his own manners allowed him to do so, the manners of society at large would forbid it. Where does this come from? Have we more sensibility than our forefathers? I do not know that we have. But I am sure that our insensibility is extended to a far greater range of objects. When all the ranks of a community are nearly equal, and when all men think and feel in nearly the same way, each of them can in a moment judge of the sensations of all the others. He casts a rapid glance upon himself, and that is enough. There is no wretchedness into which he cannot readily enter, and a secret instinct reveals to him its extent. It does not matter that the sufferers are strangers or foes; imagination puts him in their place. Something like a personal feeling is mingled with his pity, and makes him suffer while the body of his fellow creature is in torture. In democratic ages men rarely sacrifice themselves for one another, but they display a general compassion for the members of the human race. They inflict no useless harm, and they are happy to relieve the griefs of others when they can do so without much hurting themselves. They are not disinterested, but they are humane.

Although the Americans have, in a manner, reduced egotism to a social and philosophical theory, they are nevertheless extremely open to compassion. In no country is criminal justice administered with more mildness than in the United States. While the English seem disposed carefully to retain the bloody traces of the dark ages in their penal legislation, the Americans have almost expunged capital punishment from their codes. North America is, I think, the only country on earth in which the life of no single citizen has been taken for a political offense in the last fifty years. The circumstance that conclusively shows that this singular mildness of the Americans arises chiefly from their social condition is the manner in which they treat their slaves. Perhaps there is not, on the whole, a single European colony in the New World in which the physical condition of the blacks is less severe than in the United States. Yet the slaves still endure horrid sufferings there, and are constantly exposed to barbarous punishments. It is easy to see that the lot of these unhappy beings inspires their masters with but little compassion, and that they look upon slavery not only as an institution profitable to them, but as an evil that does not affect them. Thus the same man who is full of humanity toward his fellow creatures when they are at the same time his equals becomes insensible to their afflictions as soon as that equality ceases. His mildness should therefore be attributed to the equality of conditions, rather than to civilization and education.

What I have here observed of individuals is, to a certain extent, applicable to nations. When each nation has its distinct opinions, beliefs, laws, and customs, it looks upon itself as the whole of mankind, and is moved by no sorrows but its own. Should war break out between two nations animated by this feeling, it is sure to be waged with great cruelty. At the time of their highest culture, the Romans slaughtered the generals of their enemies, after having dragged them in triumph behind a chariot; and they threw their prisoners to the beasts of the Circus for the amusement of the people. Cicero, who declaimed so vehemently at the notion of crucifying a Roman citizen, had not a word to say against these horrible abuses of victory. It is clear that in his eyes a barbarian did not belong to the same human race as a Roman. On the contrary, as nations become more alike, they become reciprocally more compassionate, and the law of nations is mitigated.

chapters.title: Chapter II — That Democracy Renders The Habitual Intercourse Of The Americans Simple And Easy
paragraphs: Americans Simple And Easy

Democracy does not bind men strongly to one another, but it places their habitual interactions on an easier footing. If two Englishmen happen to meet at the Antipodes, surrounded by strangers whose language and manners are almost unknown to them, they will first stare at each other with great curiosity and a kind of secret uneasiness; they will then turn away, or, if one addresses the other, they will take care to converse only with a constrained and absent air on very unimportant subjects. Yet there is no enmity between these men; they have never seen each other before, and each believes the other to be a respectable person. Why then do they stand so cautiously apart? We must go back to England to learn the reason.

When birth alone, independent of wealth, classes men in society, everyone knows exactly where he stands on the social scale; he does not seek to rise, and he does not fear to fall. In a community so organized, men of different castes communicate very little with each other; but if chance brings them together, they are ready to converse without hoping or fearing to lose their own position. Their intercourse is not on a footing of equality, but it is not constrained. When an aristocracy of money succeeds an aristocracy of birth, the case is altered. The privileges of some are still extremely great, but the possibility of acquiring those privileges is open to all; from which it follows that those who possess them are constantly haunted by the fear of losing them, or of other men sharing them. Those who do not yet enjoy them long to possess them at any cost, or at least to appear to possess them — which is not impossible. Since the social importance of men is no longer ostensibly and permanently fixed by blood, and is infinitely varied by wealth, ranks still exist, but it is not easy to distinguish at a glance who belongs to which. Secret hostilities then arise in the community: one set of men strive by countless artifices to penetrate, or appear to penetrate, among those above them; another set are constantly on guard against these usurpers of their rights; or rather the same individual does both at once, and while he tries to raise himself into a higher circle, he is always on the defensive against the intrusion of those below him.

Such is the condition of England at the present time; and I am of the opinion that the peculiarity mentioned above is principally attributable to this cause. Since aristocratic pride is still extremely strong among the English, and since the limits of aristocracy are ill-defined, everyone lives in constant fear of someone taking advantage of his familiarity. Unable to judge at once the social position of those he meets, an Englishman prudently avoids all contact with them. Men are afraid that some slight service rendered may draw them into an unsuitable acquaintance; they dread civilities, and they avoid a stranger's obtrusive gratitude as much as his hatred. Many people attribute these singular anti-social tendencies, and the reserved and taciturn bearing of the English, to purely physical causes. I may admit that there is something of this in their race, but much more of it is attributable to their social condition, as is proved by the contrast of the Americans.

In America, where the privileges of birth never existed, and where wealth confers no special rights on those who possess it, men who do not know each other are very willing to frequent the same places, and find neither peril nor advantage in the free exchange of their thoughts. If they meet by chance, they neither seek nor avoid interaction; their manner is therefore natural, frank, and open. It is easy to see that they hardly expect or apprehend anything from each other, and that they do not care either to display or to conceal their position in the world. If their demeanor is often cold and serious, it is never haughty or constrained; and if they do not converse, it is because they are not in the mood to talk, not because they think it in their interest to be silent. In a foreign country, two Americans are instantly friends, simply because they are Americans. They are repelled by no prejudice; they are drawn together by their common country. For two Englishmen, shared blood is not enough; they must be brought together by shared rank. The Americans notice this unsociable mood of the English as much as the French do, and they are no less astonished by it. Yet the Americans are connected with England by their origin, their religion, their language, and in part by their manners; they differ only in their social condition. It may therefore be inferred that the reserve of the English proceeds from the constitution of their country much more than from that of its inhabitants.

chapters.title: Chapter III — Why The Americans Show So Little Sensitiveness In Their Own Country, And Are So Sensitive In Europe
paragraphs: Country, and Are So Sensitive in Europe

The temper of the Americans is vindictive, like that of all serious and reflecting nations. They hardly ever forget an offense, but it is not easy to offend them; and their resentment is as slow to kindle as it is to abate. In aristocratic communities, where a small number of persons manage everything, the outward intercourse of men is subject to settled conventional rules. Everyone then thinks he knows exactly what marks of respect or of condescension he ought to display, and none are presumed to be ignorant of the science of etiquette. These usages of the first class in society afterward serve as a model to all the others; besides which, each of the latter lays down a code of its own, to which all its members are bound to conform. Thus the rules of politeness form a complex system of legislation that is difficult to be perfectly master of, but from which it is dangerous for anyone to deviate. Men are therefore constantly exposed, involuntarily, to inflict or to receive bitter affronts. But as the distinctions of rank are obliterated, as men differing in education and birth meet and mingle in the same places of resort, it is almost impossible to agree on the rules of good breeding. Since its laws are uncertain, to disobey them is not a crime, even in the eyes of those who know what they are. Men attach more importance to intentions than to forms, and they grow less civil, but at the same time less quarrelsome. There are many little attentions that an American does not care about; he thinks they are not due to him, or he presumes that they are not known to be due: he therefore either does not perceive a rudeness or forgives it. His manners become less courteous, and his character more plain and masculine.

The mutual indulgence the Americans display, and the manly confidence with which they treat each other, also result from another, deeper, more general cause, which I have already touched on in the preceding chapter. In the United States the distinctions of rank in civil society are slight; in political society they are null. An American, therefore, does not think himself bound to pay particular attentions to any of his fellow citizens, nor does he require such attentions from them toward himself. As he does not see that it is his interest eagerly to seek the company of any of his countrymen, he is slow to fancy that his own company is declined. Despising no one on account of his station, he does not imagine that anyone can despise him for that reason; and until he has clearly perceived an insult, he does not suppose that an affront was intended. The social condition of the Americans naturally accustoms them not to take offense in small matters; and, on the other hand, the democratic freedom they enjoy transfuses this same mildness of temper into the character of the nation. The political institutions of the United States constantly bring citizens of all ranks into contact and compel them to pursue great undertakings in concert. People thus engaged have scarcely time to attend to the details of etiquette, and they are besides too strongly interested in living harmoniously to stick at such things. They therefore soon acquire a habit of considering the feelings and opinions of those they meet more than their manners, and they do not allow themselves to be annoyed by trifles.

I have often noticed in the United States that it is not easy to make a man understand that his presence may be dispensed with; hints will not always suffice to shake him off. I contradict an American at every word he says, to show him that his conversation bores me; he instantly labors with fresh pertinacity to convince me. I preserve a dogged silence, and he thinks I am meditating deeply on the truths he is uttering. At last I rush from his company, and he supposes that some urgent business hurries me elsewhere. This man will never understand that he wearies me to extinction unless I tell him so; and the only way to get rid of him is to make him my enemy for life.

It appears surprising at first sight that the same man transported to Europe suddenly becomes so sensitive and captious that I often find it as difficult to avoid offending him here as it was to put him out of countenance there. These two opposite effects proceed from the same cause. Democratic institutions generally give men a lofty notion of their country and of themselves. An American leaves his country with a heart swollen with pride; on arriving in Europe he at once finds out that we are not so engrossed by the United States and the great people who inhabit them as he had supposed, and this begins to annoy him. He has been informed that the conditions of society are not equal in our part of the globe, and he observes that among the nations of Europe the traces of rank are not wholly obliterated; that wealth and birth still retain some indeterminate privileges, which force themselves on his notice while eluding definition. He is therefore profoundly ignorant of the place he ought to occupy in this half-ruined scale of classes, which are sufficiently distinct to hate and despise each other, yet sufficiently alike for him to be always confounding them. He is afraid of ranging himself too high — still more is he afraid of being ranged too low. This twofold peril keeps his mind constantly on the stretch and embarrasses all he says and does. He learns from tradition that in Europe ceremonial observances were infinitely varied according to different ranks; this recollection of former times completes his perplexity, and he is the more afraid of not obtaining the marks of respect due to him, since he does not exactly know in what they consist. He is like a man surrounded by traps: society is not a recreation for him but a serious toil. He weighs your least actions, interrogates your looks, and scrutinizes all you say, lest there should be some hidden allusion to affront him. I doubt whether there was ever a provincial man of quality so punctilious in breeding as he is. He endeavors to attend to the slightest rules of etiquette and does not allow one of them to be waived toward himself. He is full of scruples and at the same time of pretensions. He wishes to do enough, but fears to do too much; and as he does not very well know the limits of the one or of the other, he keeps up a haughty and embarrassed air of reserve.

But this is not all: here is yet another double of the human heart. An American is forever talking of the admirable equality that prevails in the United States; aloud he makes it the boast of his country, but in secret he deplores it for himself, and he aspires to show that, for his part, he is an exception to the general state of things he vaunts. There is hardly an American to be met with who does not claim some remote kindred with the first founders of the colonies; and as for the scions of the noble families of England, America seemed to me to be covered with them. When an opulent American arrives in Europe, his first care is to surround himself with all the luxuries of wealth. He is so afraid of being taken for the plain citizen of a democracy that he adopts a hundred distorted ways of bringing some new instance of his wealth before you every day. His house will be in the most fashionable part of the town; he will always be surrounded by a host of servants. I have heard an American complain that in the best houses of Paris the society was rather mixed; the taste that prevailed there was not pure enough for him; and he ventured to hint that, in his opinion, there was a want of elegance of manner; he could not accustom himself to see wit concealed under such unpretending forms.

These contrasts ought not to surprise us. If the vestiges of former aristocratic distinctions were not so completely effaced in the United States, the Americans would be less simple and less tolerant in their own country — they would require less, and be less fond of, borrowed manners in ours.

chapters.title: Chapter IV — Consequences Of The Three Preceding Chapters
paragraphs: When men feel a natural compassion for each other’s sufferings — when they are brought together by easy and frequent intercourse, and no sensitive feelings keep them apart — it may readily be supposed that they will lend assistance to one another whenever it is needed. When an American asks for the cooperation of his fellow citizens, it is seldom refused, and I have often seen it afforded spontaneously and with great goodwill. If an accident happens on the highway, everybody hastens to help the sufferer; if some great and sudden calamity befalls a family, the purses of a thousand strangers are at once willingly opened, and small but numerous donations pour in to relieve their distress. It often happens among the most civilized nations of the globe that a poor wretch is as friendless in the midst of a crowd as the savage in his wilds: this is hardly ever the case in the United States. The Americans, who are always cold and often coarse in their manners, seldom show insensibility; and if they do not proffer services eagerly, yet they do not refuse to render them.

All this is not in contradiction to what I have said before about individualism. The two things are so far from conflicting that I can see how they agree. Equality of conditions, while it makes men feel their independence, shows them their own weakness. They are free, but exposed to a thousand accidents, and experience soon teaches them that, although they do not habitually require the assistance of others, a time almost always comes when they cannot do without it. We constantly see in Europe that men of the same profession are ever ready to assist each other; they are all exposed to the same ills, and that is enough to teach them to seek mutual preservatives, however hard-hearted and selfish they may otherwise be. When one of them falls into danger from which the others may save him by a slight transient sacrifice or a sudden effort, they do not fail to make the attempt. Not that they are deeply interested in his fate; for if by chance their exertions are unavailing, they immediately forget the object of them and return to their own business. But a sort of tacit and almost involuntary agreement has been made between them, by which each owes to the others a temporary support that he may in turn claim for himself. Extend to a people the remark here applied to a class, and you will understand my meaning.
