They will one day discover that they have hazarded their own power by making it so necessary, and that the safer and more honest course would have been to teach their subjects the art of providing for themselves. *a

[Footnote a: As a matter of fact, more recent experience has shown that place-hunting is quite as intense in the United States as in any country in Europe. It is regarded by the Americans themselves as one of the great evils of their social condition, and it powerfully affects their political institutions. But the American who seeks a place seeks not so much a means of subsistence as the distinction which office and public employment confer. In the absence of any true aristocracy, the public service creates a spurious one, which is as much an object of ambition as the distinctions of rank in aristocratic countries.--Translator's Note.]

chapters.title: Chapter XXI — Why Great Revolutions Will Become More Rare
paragraphs: A people that has existed for centuries under a system of castes and classes can only arrive at a democratic state of society by passing through a long series of more or less critical transformations, accomplished by violent efforts, and after numerous vicissitudes, in the course of which property, opinions, and power are rapidly transferred from one hand to another. Even after this great revolution is completed, the revolutionary habits it has produced can long be traced, and it will be followed by deep commotion. Since all this takes place at the very time when social conditions are becoming more equal, it is inferred that some concealed relation and secret tie exist between the principle of equality itself and revolution, so much so that the one cannot exist without giving rise to the other.

On this point reasoning may seem to lead to the same result as experience. Among a people whose ranks are nearly equal, no visible bond connects men together, or keeps them settled in their station. None of them has either a permanent right or power to command; none are forced by their condition to obey. Every man, finding himself possessed of some education and some resources, may choose his own path and go apart from all his fellow men. The same causes that make the members of the community independent of each other continually drive them to new and restless desires, and constantly spur them onward. It therefore seems natural that in a democratic community, men, things, and opinions should be forever changing their form and place, and that democratic ages should be times of rapid and incessant transformation.

But is this really the case? Does the equality of social conditions habitually and permanently lead men to revolution? Does that state of society contain some disturbing principle that prevents the community from ever settling into calm, and disposes the citizens to alter their laws, their principles, and their manners without pause? I do not believe so; and since the subject is important, I beg the reader's close attention. Almost all the revolutions that have changed the face of nations have been made to consolidate or to destroy social inequality. Remove the secondary causes that have produced the great convulsions of the world, and you will almost always find the principle of inequality at the bottom. Either the poor have tried to plunder the rich, or the rich to enslave the poor. If, then, a state of society can ever be founded in which every man has something to keep, and little to take from others, much will have been done for the peace of the world. I am aware that among a great democratic people there will always be some members of the community in great poverty and others in great opulence. But the poor, instead of forming the immense majority of the nation, as is always the case in aristocratic communities, are comparatively few in number, and the laws do not bind them together by ties of irremediable and hereditary penury. The wealthy, on their side, are scarce and powerless. They have no privileges that attract public attention; even their wealth, since it is no longer incorporated and bound up with the soil, is impalpable and, as it were, invisible. Just as there is no longer a race of poor men, so there is no longer a race of rich men; the latter spring up daily from the multitude, and relapse into it again. Hence they do not form a distinct class, which can be easily marked out and plundered; and moreover, since they are connected with the mass of their fellow citizens by a thousand secret ties, the people cannot attack them without inflicting an injury on itself. Between these two extremes of democratic communities stand an innumerable multitude of men, almost alike, who, without being exactly either rich or poor, possess enough property to desire the maintenance of order, yet not enough to excite envy. Such men are the natural enemies of violent commotions: their stillness keeps all beneath them and above them still, and secures the balance of the fabric of society. Not that even these men are content with what they have, or that they feel a natural abhorrence for a revolution in which they might share the spoil without sharing the calamity. On the contrary, they desire, with unexampled ardor, to get rich; but the difficulty is to know from whom riches can be taken. The same state of society that constantly prompts desires restrains these desires within necessary limits. It gives men more liberty of changing and less interest in change.

Not only are the men of democracies not naturally desirous of revolutions—they are afraid of them. All revolutions more or less threaten the tenure of property; but most of those who live in democratic countries possess property, and not only do they possess property, they live in the condition of men who set the greatest store by it. If we consider each of the classes of which society is composed, it is easy to see that the passions produced by property are keenest and most tenacious among the middle classes. The poor often care little for what they possess, because they suffer much more from the want of what they do not have than they enjoy the little they do have. The rich have many other passions besides that of riches to satisfy; and besides, the long and arduous enjoyment of a great fortune sometimes makes them, in the end, insensible to its charms. But the men who have a competence, alike removed from opulence and from penury, attach an enormous value to their possessions. Since they are still almost within reach of poverty, they see its privations near at hand, and dread them. Between poverty and themselves there is nothing but a scanty fortune, on which they immediately fix their anxieties and their hopes. Every day increases the interest they take in it, through the constant cares it requires; and they are the more attached to it by their continual efforts to increase it. The idea of surrendering the smallest part of it is unbearable to them, and they regard its total loss as the worst of misfortunes. Now these eager and apprehensive men of small property form the class that is constantly increased by the equality of conditions. Hence, in democratic communities, the majority of the people do not clearly see what they have to gain by a revolution, but they continually and in a thousand ways feel that they might lose by one.

I have shown in another part of this work that the equality of conditions naturally drives men into commercial and industrial pursuits, and that it tends to increase and distribute real property. I have also pointed out the means by which it inspires every man with an eager and constant desire to increase his welfare. Nothing is more opposed to revolutionary passions than these things. It may happen that the final result of a revolution is favorable to commerce and manufactures; but its first consequence will almost always be the ruin of manufacturers and merchants, because it must always change at once the general patterns of consumption, and temporarily upset the existing balance between supply and demand. I know of nothing more opposite to revolutionary manners than commercial manners. Commerce is naturally opposed to all the violent passions; it loves to temporize, takes delight in compromise, and carefully avoids provocation. It is patient, insinuating, flexible, and never resorts to extreme measures until forced to by the most absolute necessity. Commerce makes men independent of each other, gives them a lofty notion of their personal importance, leads them to want to manage their own affairs, and teaches them how to manage them well. It therefore prepares men for freedom, but preserves them from revolutions. In a revolution the owners of personal property have more to fear than all others. On the one hand their property is often easy to seize, and on the other it may totally disappear at any moment—a subject of alarm to which the owners of real property are less exposed, since, though they may lose the income of their estates, they can hope to preserve the land itself through the greatest vicissitudes. Hence the former are much more alarmed at the symptoms of revolutionary commotion than the latter. Thus nations are less disposed to make revolutions in proportion as personal property is increased and distributed among them, and as the number of those possessing it grows. Moreover, whatever profession men may embrace, and whatever kind of property they may possess, one characteristic is common to them all: no one is fully content with his present fortune—all are perpetually striving in a thousand ways to improve it. Consider any one of them at any period of his life, and he will be found engaged with some new project for increasing what he has. Talk not to him of the interests and rights of mankind: this small domestic concern absorbs all his thoughts for the time, and inclines him to postpone political excitement to some other season. This not only prevents men from making revolutions; it deters men from desiring them. Violent political passions have little hold on those who have devoted all their faculties to the pursuit of their well-being. The ardor they display in small matters calms their zeal for momentous undertakings.

From time to time, it is true, enterprising and ambitious men will arise in democratic communities, whose unbounded aspirations cannot be satisfied by following the beaten track. Such men love revolutions and hail their approach; but they have great difficulty in bringing them about, unless unusual events come to their aid. No man can struggle with advantage against the spirit of his age and country; and however powerful he may be supposed to be, he will find it difficult to make his contemporaries share feelings and opinions that run counter to all their feelings and desires.

It is a mistake to believe that, once the equality of conditions has become the old and uncontested state of society and has impressed its characteristics on the manners of a nation, men will easily allow themselves to be thrust into perilous risks by an imprudent leader or a bold innovator. Not that they will resist him openly, with well-contrived schemes or a premeditated plan of resistance. They will not struggle energetically against him; sometimes they will even applaud him—but they do not follow him. To his vehemence they secretly oppose their inertia; to his revolutionary tendencies, their conservative interests; their homely tastes to his adventurous passions; their good sense to the flights of his genius; to his poetry, their prose. With immense effort he raises them for an instant, but they quickly escape from him and fall back, as it were, by their own weight. He strains himself to rouse the indifferent and distracted multitude, and finds at last that he is reduced to impotence—not because he is conquered, but because he is alone.

I do not claim that men living in democratic communities are naturally stationary. On the contrary, I think that a perpetual stir prevails in the bosom of those societies, and that rest is unknown there. But I think that men stir themselves within certain limits beyond which they hardly ever go. They are forever varying, altering, and restoring secondary matters; but they carefully abstain from touching what is fundamental. They love change, but they dread revolutions. Although the Americans are constantly modifying or repealing some of their laws, they by no means display revolutionary passions. It is easy to see, from the speed with which they check and calm themselves when public excitement begins to grow alarming, and at the very moment when passions seem most roused, that they dread a revolution as the worst of misfortunes, and that every one of them is inwardly resolved to make great sacrifices to avoid such a catastrophe. In no country in the world is the love of property more active and more anxious than in the United States; nowhere does the majority display less inclination for those principles that threaten to alter, in whatever manner, the laws of property. I have often observed that theories that are revolutionary in nature, since they cannot be put into practice without a complete and sometimes sudden change in the state of property and persons, are much less favorably viewed in the United States than in the great monarchical countries of Europe. If some men profess them, the bulk of the people reject them with instinctive abhorrence. I do not hesitate to say that most of the maxims commonly called democratic in France would be proscribed by the democracy of the United States. This is easily understood: in America men have the opinions and passions of democracy; in Europe we still have the passions and opinions of revolution. If ever America undergoes great revolutions, they will be brought about by the presence of the black race on the soil of the United States—that is to say, they will owe their origin not to the equality, but to the inequality, of conditions.

When social conditions are equal, every man is apt to live apart, centered on himself and forgetful of the public. If the rulers of democratic nations were either to neglect to correct this fatal tendency, or to encourage it on the notion that it weans men from political passions and thus wards off revolutions, they might eventually produce the very evil they seek to avoid, and a time might come when the inordinate passions of a few men, aided by the unintelligent selfishness or the cowardice of the greater number, would ultimately compel society to pass through strange vicissitudes. In democratic communities revolutions are seldom desired except by a minority, but a minority may sometimes bring them about. I do not claim that democratic nations are safe from revolutions; I merely say that the state of society in those nations does not lead to revolutions, but rather wards them off. A democratic people left to itself will not easily embark on great hazards; it is only led into revolutions unawares. It may sometimes undergo them, but it does not make them. And I will add that, when such a people has been allowed to acquire sufficient knowledge and experience, it will not suffer them to be made. I am well aware that in this respect public institutions may themselves do much: they may encourage or repress the tendencies that originate in the state of society. I therefore do not claim, I repeat, that a people is safe from revolutions simply because conditions are equal in the community. But I think that, whatever the institutions of such a people may be, great revolutions will always be far less violent and less frequent than is supposed; and I can easily imagine a state of polity which, when combined with the principle of equality, would make society more stationary than it has ever been in our western part of the world.

The observations I have made here on events may also be applied, in part, to opinions. Two things are surprising in the United States: the mutability of the greater part of human actions, and the singular stability of certain principles. Men are in constant motion; the mind of man appears almost unmoved. Once an opinion has spread over the country and struck root there, it would seem that no power on earth is strong enough to uproot it. In the United States, general principles in religion, philosophy, morality, and even politics do not vary, or at least are only modified by a hidden and often imperceptible process. Even the grossest prejudices are erased with incredible slowness, amid the continual friction of men and things. I hear it said that it is in the nature and habits of democracies to be constantly changing their opinions and feelings. This may be true of small democratic nations, like those of the ancient world, where the whole community could be assembled in a public place and then excited at will by an orator. But I saw nothing of the kind among the great democratic people that dwells on the opposite shores of the Atlantic. What struck me in the United States was the difficulty of shaking the majority from an opinion once held, or of drawing it away from a leader once adopted. Neither speaking nor writing can accomplish it; nothing but experience will do, and even experience must be repeated. This is surprising at first sight, but a more careful investigation explains the fact. I do not think that it is as easy as is supposed to uproot the prejudices of a democratic people—to change its belief—to supersede principles once established by new principles in religion, politics, and morals—in a word, to make great and frequent changes in men's minds. Not that the human mind is at rest there: it is in constant agitation. But it is engaged in endlessly varying the consequences of known principles, and in seeking new consequences, rather than in seeking new principles. Its motion is one of rapid circular revolution, rather than of straightforward impulse by rapid and direct effort; it extends its orbit by small, continual, and hurried movements, but it does not suddenly alter its position.

Men who are equal in rights, in education, in fortune—or, to sum it all up in one word, in their social condition—necessarily have wants, habits, and tastes that are hardly dissimilar. Since they view objects from the same angle, their minds naturally tend to analogous conclusions; and though each of them may deviate from his contemporaries and form opinions of his own, they will involuntarily and unconsciously concur in a certain number of received opinions. The more attentively I consider the effects of equality on the mind, the more I am persuaded that the intellectual anarchy we see around us is not, as many men suppose, the natural state of democratic nations. I think it is rather to be regarded as an accident peculiar to their youth, and that it only breaks out at that period of transition when men have already snapped the former ties that bound them together, but are still amazingly different in origin, education, and manners; so that, having retained opinions, propensities, and tastes of great diversity, nothing any longer prevents men from avowing them openly. The leading opinions of men become similar in proportion as their conditions become similar; such appears to me to be the general and permanent law—the rest is casual and transient.

I believe that it will rarely happen to any man in a democratic community to suddenly frame a system of notions very remote from that which his contemporaries have adopted; and if some such innovator appeared, I think he would have great difficulty finding listeners, and still more in finding believers. When the conditions of men are almost equal, they do not easily allow themselves to be persuaded by each other. Since they all live in close intercourse, since they have learned the same things together, and since they lead the same life, they are not naturally disposed to take one of themselves as a guide and to follow him implicitly. Men seldom take the opinion of their equal, or of a man like themselves, on trust. Not only is confidence in the superior attainments of certain individuals weakened among democratic nations, as I have remarked elsewhere, but the general notion of the intellectual superiority that any man whatever may acquire relative to the rest of the community is soon overshadowed. As men grow more like each other, the doctrine of the equality of the intellect gradually infuses itself into their opinions, and it becomes more difficult for any innovator to acquire or exert much influence over the minds of a people. In such communities sudden intellectual revolutions will therefore be rare; for if we read the history of the world aright, we shall find that great and rapid changes in human opinions have been produced far less by the force of reasoning than by the authority of a name. Observe, too, that since the men who live in democratic societies are not connected with each other by any tie, each of them must be convinced individually; whereas in aristocratic society it is enough to convince a few—the rest follow. If Luther had lived in an age of equality, and had not had princes and potentates for his audience, he would perhaps have found it more difficult to change the face of Europe. Not that the men of democracies are naturally strongly persuaded of the certainty of their opinions, or are unwavering in belief; they often entertain doubts that no one, in their eyes, can remove. It sometimes happens at such times that the human mind would willingly change its position; but since nothing urges or guides it forward, it oscillates back and forth without progressive motion. *a

[Footnote a: If I ask what state of society is most favorable to the great revolutions of the mind, I find that it occurs somewhere between the complete equality of the whole community and the absolute separation of ranks. Under a system of castes, generations succeed each other without altering men's positions; some have nothing more, others nothing better, to hope for. The imagination slumbers amid this universal silence and stillness, and the very idea of change fades from the human mind. When ranks have been abolished and social conditions are almost equalized, all men are in ceaseless excitement, but each of them stands alone, independent and weak. This latter state of things is exceedingly different from the former, yet it has one point of analogy: great revolutions of the human mind seldom occur in it. But between these two extremes of the history of nations there is an intermediate period—a period as glorious as it is agitated—when the conditions of men are not sufficiently settled for the mind to be lulled into torpor, when they are sufficiently unequal for men to exercise a vast power over the minds of one another, and when some few may modify the convictions of all. It is at such times that great reformers rise up, and new opinions suddenly change the face of the world.]

Even when the trust of a democratic people has been won, it is still no easy matter to gain their attention. It is extremely difficult to obtain a hearing from men living in democracies, unless it be to speak to them about themselves. They do not attend to the things said to them, because they are always fully engrossed with the things they are doing. Indeed, few men are idle in democratic nations; life is passed in the midst of noise and excitement, and men are so engaged in acting that little time remains to them for thinking. I would especially note that they are not only busy—they are passionately devoted to their employments. They are always in action, and each of their actions absorbs their faculties. The zeal they display in business puts out the enthusiasm they might otherwise feel for ideas. I think it is extremely difficult to excite the enthusiasm of a democratic people for any theory that does not have a palpable, direct, and immediate connection with the daily occupations of life. Therefore they will not easily abandon their old opinions; for it is enthusiasm that flings the minds of men out of the beaten track, and effects the great revolutions of the intellect as well as the great revolutions of the political world. Thus democratic nations have neither the time nor the taste to go in search of new opinions. Even when those they possess become doubtful, they still retain them, because it would take too much time and inquiry to change them—they retain them, not as certain, but as established.

There are yet other and more cogent reasons that prevent any great change from being easily made in the principles of a democratic people. I have already touched on them at the beginning of this part of my work. If the influence of individuals is weak and hardly perceptible among such a people, the power exercised by the mass upon the mind of each individual is extremely great—I have already shown for what reasons. I would now add that it is wrong to suppose that this depends solely upon the form of government, and that the majority would lose its intellectual supremacy if it were to lose its political power. In aristocracies men often have much greatness and strength of their own. When they find themselves at variance with the greater number of their fellow countrymen, they withdraw to their own circle, where they support and console themselves. Such is not the case in a democratic country; there public favor seems as necessary as the air we breathe, and to live at variance with the multitude is, as it were, not to live. The multitude needs no laws to coerce those who do not think like it: public disapproval is enough. A sense of their loneliness and impotence overtakes them and drives them to despair.

Whenever social conditions are equal, public opinion presses with enormous weight on the mind of each individual; it surrounds, directs, and oppresses him. This arises from the very constitution of society, much more than from its political laws. As men grow more alike, each man feels himself weaker in regard to all the rest. Since he sees nothing by which he is considerably raised above them, or distinguished from them, he mistrusts himself as soon as they assail him. Not only does he mistrust his strength, but he even doubts his right; and he is very close to acknowledging that he is in the wrong when the greater number of his countrymen assert that he is. The majority do not need to constrain him—they convince him. In whatever way, then, the powers of a democratic community may be organized and balanced, it will always be extremely difficult to believe what the bulk of the people reject, or to profess what they condemn.

This circumstance is extraordinarily favorable to the stability of opinions. When an opinion has taken root among a democratic people, and established itself in the minds of the bulk of the community, it afterward subsists by itself and is maintained without effort, because no one attacks it. Those who at first rejected it as false eventually receive it as the general impression, and those who still dispute it in their hearts conceal their dissent; they are careful not to engage in a dangerous and useless conflict. It is true that when the majority of a democratic people change their opinions, they may suddenly and arbitrarily effect strange revolutions in men's minds; but their opinions do not change without much difficulty, and it is almost as difficult to show that they have changed.

Time, events, or the unaided individual action of the mind will sometimes undermine or destroy an opinion, without any outward sign of the change. It has not been openly attacked; no conspiracy has been formed to make war on it; but its followers one by one noiselessly secede—day by day a few of them abandon it, until at last it is only professed by a minority. In this state it will still continue to prevail. Since its enemies remain silent, or only exchange their thoughts in secret, they are themselves unaware for a long time that a great revolution has actually taken place; and in this state of uncertainty they take no steps—they observe each other and are silent. The majority have ceased to believe what they believed before, but they still pretend to believe, and this empty phantom of public opinion is strong enough to chill innovators, and to keep them silent and at a respectful distance. We live at a time that has witnessed the most rapid changes of opinion in the minds of men; nevertheless it may be that the leading opinions of society will before long be more settled than they have been for several centuries in our history. That time is not yet come, but it may perhaps be approaching. As I examine more closely the natural wants and tendencies of democratic nations, I grow persuaded that if ever social equality is generally and permanently established in the world, great intellectual and political revolutions will become more difficult and less frequent than is supposed. Because the men of democracies appear always excited, uncertain, eager, changeable in their wills and in their positions, it is imagined that they are about to suddenly abolish their laws, adopt new opinions, and take on new manners. But if the principle of equality predisposes men to change, it also suggests to them certain interests and tastes that cannot be satisfied without a settled order of things. Equality urges them on, but at the same time it holds them back; it spurs them, but fastens them to earth; it kindles their desires, but limits their powers. This, however, is not perceived at first: the passions that tend to sever the citizens of a democracy are obvious enough, but the hidden force that restrains and unites them is not discernible at a glance.

Amid the ruins that surround me, shall I dare to say that revolutions are not what I most fear for coming generations? If men continue to shut themselves more closely within the narrow circle of domestic interests, and to live on that kind of excitement, it is to be feared that they may ultimately become inaccessible to those great and powerful public emotions that perturb nations—but that also enlarge them and recruit them. When property becomes so fluctuating, and the love of property so restless and so ardent, I cannot but fear that men may arrive at such a state as to regard every new theory as a peril, every innovation as an irksome toil, every social improvement as a stepping-stone to revolution, and so refuse to move at all for fear of being moved too far. I dread, and I confess it, that they may at last give way so entirely to a cowardly love of present enjoyment that they lose sight of the interests of their future selves and of their descendants, and prefer to glide along the easy current of life, rather than to make, when necessary, a strong and sudden effort toward a higher purpose. It is believed by some that modern society will be ever changing its aspect; for my part, I fear that it will ultimately be too invariably fixed in the same institutions, the same prejudices, the same manners, so that mankind will be stopped and circumscribed; that the mind will swing back and forth forever, without producing fresh ideas; that man will waste his strength in futile and solitary trifling; and, though in continual motion, that humanity will cease to advance.

chapters.title: Chapter XXII — Why Democratic Nations Are Naturally Desirous Of Peace, And Democratic Armies Of War
paragraphs: And Democratic Armies Of War

The same interests, the same fears, the same passions that deter democratic nations from revolutions deter them also from war. The spirit of military glory and the spirit of revolution are weakened at the same time and by the same causes. The ever-increasing numbers of men of property—lovers of peace; the growth of personal wealth, which war consumes so rapidly; the mildness of manners, the gentleness of heart, those tendencies to pity produced by equality of conditions; that coolness of understanding that makes men comparatively insensible to the violent and poetical excitement of arms—all these causes combine to quench the military spirit. I think it may be accepted as a general and constant rule that, among civilized nations, the warlike passions will become rarer and less intense in proportion as social conditions become more equal. War is nevertheless something to which all nations are subject, democratic nations as well as others. Whatever taste they may have for peace, they must be ready to repel aggression; in other words, they must have an army.

Fortune, which has conferred so many peculiar benefits on the inhabitants of the United States, has placed them in the midst of a wilderness where they have, so to speak, no neighbors. A few thousand soldiers are enough for their needs; but this is peculiar to America, not to democracy. Equality of conditions, and the manners as well as the institutions that result from it, do not exempt a democratic people from the necessity of standing armies, and their armies always exercise a powerful influence on their fate. It is therefore singularly important to inquire what are the natural propensities of the men of whom these armies are composed.

Among aristocratic nations, especially those in which birth is the only source of rank, the same inequality exists in the army as in the nation. The officer is noble, the soldier is a serf; one is naturally called upon to command, the other to obey. In aristocratic armies, the private soldier's ambition is therefore confined within very narrow limits. Nor does the officer's ambition have an unlimited range. An aristocratic body not only forms part of the scale of ranks in the nation; it also contains a scale of ranks within itself. The members composing it are placed one above another in a particular and unvarying way. Thus one man is born to the command of a regiment, another to that of a company. Once they have reached the utmost object of their hopes, they stop of their own accord and remain content with their lot. There is, besides, a strong cause that, in aristocracies, weakens the officer's desire for promotion. Among aristocratic nations, an officer, independently of his rank in the army, also occupies an elevated rank in society. The former is almost always, in his eyes, only an appendage to the latter. A nobleman who takes up the profession of arms follows it less from motives of ambition than from a sense of the duties imposed on him by his birth. He enters the army to find honorable employment for the idle years of his youth, and to be able to bring back to his home and his peers some honorable recollections of military life; but his principal object is not to obtain by that profession property, distinction, or power, for he possesses these advantages in his own right, and enjoys them without leaving his home.

In democratic armies all soldiers may become officers, which makes the desire for promotion general and immensely extends the bounds of military ambition. The officer, on his part, sees nothing that naturally and necessarily stops him at one grade rather than another; and each grade has immense importance in his eyes, because his rank in society almost always depends on his rank in the army. Among democratic nations it often happens that an officer has no property but his pay, and no distinction but military honors. Consequently, as often as his duties change, his fortune changes, and he becomes, as it were, a new man. What was only an appendage to his position in aristocratic armies has thus become the main point, the basis of his whole condition. Under the old French monarchy, officers were always called by their titles of nobility; they are now always called by the title of their military rank. This little change in the forms of language is enough to show that a great revolution has taken place in the constitution of society and in that of the army. In democratic armies the desire for advancement is almost universal: it is ardent, tenacious, perpetual; it is strengthened by all other desires, and only extinguished with life itself. But it is easy to see that, of all the armies in the world, those in which advancement must be slowest in times of peace are the armies of democratic countries. Since the number of commissions is naturally limited while the number of competitors is almost unlimited, and since the strict law of equality is over all alike, none can make rapid progress—many can make no progress at all. Thus the desire for advancement is greater, and the opportunities for advancement fewer, there than anywhere else. All the ambitious spirits of a democratic army are consequently ardently desirous of war, because war makes vacancies, and justifies the violation of that law of seniority that is the sole privilege natural to democracy.

We thus arrive at this singular conclusion: of all armies, those most ardently desirous of war are democratic armies, and of all nations, those most fond of peace are democratic nations. What makes these facts still more extraordinary is that these contrary effects are produced at the same time by the principle of equality.

All the members of the community, being alike, constantly harbor the wish, and discover the possibility, of changing their condition and improving their welfare. This makes them fond of peace, which is favorable to industry and allows every man to pursue his own small undertakings to their completion. On the other hand, this same equality makes soldiers dream of fields of battle, by increasing the value of military honors in the eyes of those who follow the profession of arms, and by making those honors accessible to all. In either case the restlessness of the heart is the same, the taste for enjoyment as insatiable, the ambition for success as great—only the means of gratifying it differ.

These opposite tendencies of the nation and the army expose democratic communities to great dangers. When a military spirit leaves a people, the profession of arms immediately ceases to be held in honor, and military men fall to the lowest rank of public servants: they are little esteemed and no longer understood. The reverse of what takes place in aristocratic ages then occurs: the men who enter the army are no longer those of the highest, but of the lowest rank. Military ambition is only indulged when no other is possible. Hence arises a cycle of cause and consequence from which it is difficult to escape: the best part of the nation shuns the military profession because that profession is not honored, and the profession is not honored because the best part of the nation has stopped following it. It is then no surprise that democratic armies are often restless, ill-tempered, and dissatisfied with their lot, even though their physical condition is usually far better, and their discipline less strict, than in other countries. The soldier feels that he occupies an inferior position, and his wounded pride either stimulates his taste for hostilities that would make his services necessary, or gives him a turn for revolutions, during which he may hope to win by force of arms the political influence and personal importance now denied him. The composition of democratic armies makes this last danger much to be feared. In democratic communities almost every man has some property to preserve; but democratic armies are generally led by men without property, most of whom have little to lose in civil conflicts. The bulk of the nation is naturally much more afraid of revolutions than in the ages of aristocracy, but the leaders of the army much less so.

Moreover, since among democratic nations (to repeat what I have just remarked) the wealthiest, best educated, and most able men seldom adopt the military profession, the army, taken collectively, eventually forms a small nation by itself, where the mind is less enlarged and habits more rude than in the nation at large. Now this small uncivilized nation has arms in its possession and alone knows how to use them. Indeed, the peaceful temper of the community increases the danger to which a democratic people is exposed from the military and turbulent spirit of the army. Nothing is as dangerous as an army in the midst of an unwarlike nation; the community's excessive love of quiet continually puts its constitution at the mercy of the soldiery. It may therefore be said, generally speaking, that if democratic nations are naturally drawn to peace by their interests and their propensities, they are constantly drawn to war and revolutions by their armies. Military revolutions, which are scarcely ever to be feared in aristocracies, are always to be dreaded among democratic nations. These perils must be reckoned among the most formidable that beset their future fate, and the attention of statesmen should be sedulously applied to finding a remedy for the evil.

When a nation perceives that it is inwardly affected by the restless ambition of its army, the first thought that occurs is to give this troublesome ambition an object by going to war. I speak no ill of war: war almost always enlarges the mind of a people and raises their character. In some cases it is the only check to the excessive growth of certain propensities that naturally spring from the equality of conditions, and it must be considered a necessary corrective to certain inveterate diseases to which democratic communities are liable. War has great advantages, but we must not flatter ourselves that it can diminish the danger I have just pointed out. That peril is only suspended by it, to return more fiercely when the war is over; for armies are much more impatient of peace after having tasted military exploits. War could only be a remedy for a people always athirst for military glory. I foresee that all the military rulers who may arise in great democratic nations will find it easier to conquer with their armies than to make their armies live at peace after conquest. There are two things a democratic people will always find very difficult: to begin a war, and to end it.

Again, if war has some peculiar advantages for democratic nations, on the other hand it exposes them to certain dangers that aristocracies have no cause to fear to an equal extent. I shall point out only two of these. Although war gratifies the army, it embarrasses and often exasperates that countless multitude of men whose smaller passions require peace every day to be satisfied. Thus there is some risk of its causing, under another form, the very disturbance it is meant to prevent. No prolonged war can fail to endanger the freedom of a democratic country. Not, indeed, that after every victory it is to be feared that the victorious generals will seize supreme power by force, in the manner of Sulla and Caesar; the danger is of another kind. War does not always hand democratic communities over to military government, but it must invariably and immeasurably increase the powers of civil government. It must almost compulsorily concentrate the direction of all men and the management of all things in the hands of the administration. If it does not lead to despotism by sudden violence, it prepares men for it more gently by their habits. All who seek to destroy the liberties of a democratic nation ought to know that war is the surest and shortest means to accomplish it. This is the first axiom of the science.

One remedy that appears obvious when the ambition of soldiers and officers becomes the subject of alarm is to augment the number of commissions to be distributed by increasing the army. This affords temporary relief, but it plunges the country into deeper difficulties later on. To increase the army may produce a lasting effect in an aristocratic community, because military ambition there is confined to one class of men, and the ambition of each individual stops, as it were, at a certain limit, so that it may be possible to satisfy all who feel its influence. But nothing is gained by increasing the army among a democratic people, because the number of aspirants always rises in exactly the same ratio as the army itself. Those whose claims have been satisfied by the creation of new commissions are instantly succeeded by a fresh multitude beyond all power of satisfaction; and even those who were just now satisfied soon begin to crave more advancement. The same excitement prevails in the ranks of the army as in the civil classes of democratic society, and what men want is not to reach a certain grade, but to have constant promotion. Though these wants may not be very vast, they are perpetually recurring. Thus a democratic nation, by augmenting its army, only allays for a time the ambition of the military profession, which soon becomes even more formidable, because the number of those who feel it has increased. I am of the opinion that a restless and turbulent spirit is an evil inherent in the very constitution of democratic armies, and beyond hope of cure. The legislators of democracies must not expect to devise any military organization capable by its influence of calming and restraining the military profession. Their efforts would exhaust their powers before the object was attained.

The remedy for the vices of the army is not to be found in the army itself, but in the country. Democratic nations are naturally afraid of disturbance and of despotism; the object is to turn these natural instincts into well-digested, deliberate, and lasting tastes. When men have at last learned to make peaceful and profitable use of freedom, and have felt its blessings—when they have conceived a manly love of order, and have freely submitted themselves to discipline—these same men, if they follow the profession of arms, bring into it, unconsciously and almost against their will, these same habits and manners. The general spirit of the nation, being infused into the spirit peculiar to the army, tempers the opinions and desires produced by military life, or represses them by the mighty force of public opinion. Teach the citizens to be educated, orderly, firm, and free, and the soldiers will be disciplined and obedient. Any law that, in repressing the turbulent spirit of the army, should also tend to diminish the spirit of freedom in the nation, and to overshadow the notion of law and right, would defeat its object: it would do much more to favor than to defeat the establishment of military tyranny.

After all, and in spite of all precautions, a large army in the midst of a democratic people will always be a source of great danger. The most effective means of diminishing that danger would be to reduce the army, but this is a remedy that not all nations have the power to use.

chapters.title: Chapter XXIII — Which Is The Most Warlike And Most Revolutionary Class In Democratic Armies?
paragraphs: It is part of the essence of a democratic army to be very numerous relative to the people it belongs to, as I will show later. On the other hand, people living in democratic times rarely choose a military life. Democratic nations are therefore soon led to give up voluntary recruiting and adopt compulsory enlistment. The necessity of their social condition forces them to the latter, and it is easy to foresee that they will all eventually adopt it. When military service is compulsory, the burden is borne indiscriminately and equally by the whole community. This is another necessary consequence of the social condition of these nations, and of their ideas. The government may do almost whatever it pleases, provided it appeals to the whole community at once: it is the unequal distribution of the weight, not the weight itself, which usually occasions resistance. But since military service is common to all citizens, the obvious consequence is that each remains on active duty for only a few years. So it lies in the nature of things that in democracies the soldier only passes through the army, whereas among most aristocratic nations the military profession is one that the soldier adopts — or that is imposed on him — for life.

This has important consequences. Among the soldiers of a democratic army, some acquire a taste for military life, but the majority, enlisted against their will and always ready to go back to their homes, do not consider themselves seriously engaged in the military profession, and are always thinking of leaving it. Such men do not contract the needs, and only half share the passions, that this mode of life breeds. They adapt themselves to their military duties, but their minds remain attached to the interests and duties that occupied them in civilian life. They do not, therefore, imbibe the spirit of the army — or rather, they infuse the spirit of the community at large into the army, and keep it there. Among democratic nations the private soldiers remain most like civilians: on them the habits of the nation have the firmest hold, and public opinion the greatest influence. It is through the private soldiers especially that it may be possible to infuse into a democratic army the love of freedom and the respect of rights, once these principles have been successfully instilled in the people at large. The reverse happens among aristocratic nations, where the soldiery eventually have nothing in common with their fellow citizens, and live among them as strangers, often as enemies. In aristocratic armies the officers are the conservative element, because the officers alone have kept a strict connection with civil society, and never give up the purpose of resuming their place in it sooner or later. In democratic armies the private soldiers hold this position, and for the same reason.

It often happens, by contrast, that in these same democratic armies the officers acquire tastes and needs wholly distinct from those of the nation — a fact that can be accounted for as follows. Among democratic nations, the man who becomes an officer severs all the ties that bound him to civilian life; he leaves it forever, and has no interest in returning. His true country is the army, since he owes everything he has to the rank he has reached in it; he therefore follows the fortunes of the army, rises or sinks with it, and from then on directs all his hopes to that quarter alone. Since the needs of an officer are distinct from those of the country, he may ardently desire war, or labor to bring about a revolution, at the very moment when the nation most desires stability and peace. There are, nevertheless, some causes that allay this restless and warlike spirit. Though ambition is universal and continual among democratic nations, we have seen that it is seldom great. A man who, born in the lower classes of the community, has risen from the ranks to become an officer, has already taken a prodigious step. He has gained a footing in a sphere above the one he filled in civilian life, and he has acquired rights that most democratic nations will always consider inalienable. *a He is willing to pause after so great an effort and enjoy what he has won. The fear of risking what he has already obtained dampens the desire to acquire what he has not. Having conquered the first and greatest obstacle to his advancement, he resigns himself with less impatience to the slowness of his progress. His ambition will cool more and more as the growing distinction of his rank teaches him that he has more to put at risk. If I am not mistaken, the least warlike — and also the least revolutionary — part of a democratic army will always be its chief commanders. [Footnote a: The position of officers is indeed much more secure among democratic nations than elsewhere; the lower the personal standing of the man, the greater is the comparative importance of his military grade, and the more just and necessary that the enjoyment of that rank be secured by the laws.]

But the remarks I have just made about officers and soldiers do not apply to a numerous class that fills the intermediate space between them in every army — I mean the class of non-commissioned officers. This class of non-commissioned officers, which has never played a part in history until the present century, is, I think, from now on destined to play one of some importance. Like the officers, non-commissioned officers have broken, in their minds, all the ties that bound them to civilian life; like them, they devote themselves permanently to the service, and perhaps make it even more exclusively the object of all their desires. But non-commissioned officers are men who have not yet reached a firm and lofty post where they can pause and breathe more freely before attaining further promotion. By the very nature of his duties, which is invariable, a non-commissioned officer is doomed to lead an obscure, confined, comfortless, and precarious existence. So far he sees nothing of military life but its dangers; he knows nothing of it but its privations and its discipline — harder to bear than dangers. He suffers all the more from his present miseries because he knows that the constitution of society and of the army permits him to rise above them; he may, indeed, at any time obtain his commission, and enter at once into command, honors, independence, rights, and enjoyments. Not only does this object of his hopes appear to him of immense importance, but he is never sure of reaching it until it is actually his own. The grade he holds is by no means irrevocable; he is always entirely at the arbitrary pleasure of his commanding officer, for this is imperiously required by the necessity of discipline. A slight fault, a whim, may at any moment deprive him of the fruits of many years of toil and striving. Until he reaches the grade to which he aspires, he has accomplished nothing; only on reaching that grade does his career seem to begin. A desperate ambition cannot fail to be kindled in a man thus incessantly goaded on by his youth, his wants, his passions, the spirit of his age, his hopes, and his fears. Non-commissioned officers are therefore bent on war — on war always, and at any cost; but if war is denied them, then they desire revolutions that suspend the authority of established regulations, and enable them, aided by the general confusion and the political passions of the time, to get rid of their superior officers and take their places. Nor is it impossible for them to bring about such a crisis, because their common origin and habits give them considerable influence over the soldiers, however different their passions and desires may be.

It would be a mistake to suppose that these various characteristics of officers, non-commissioned officers, and men belong to any particular time or country; they will always occur, at all times, and among all democratic nations. In every democratic army the non-commissioned officers will be the worst representatives of the pacific and orderly spirit of the country, and the private soldiers the best. The latter will carry into military life the strength or weakness of the manners of the nation; they will display a faithful reflection of the community. If that community is ignorant and weak, they will let themselves be drawn by their leaders into disturbances, either unconsciously or against their will; if it is enlightened and energetic, the community will itself keep them within the bounds of order.

chapters.title: Chapter XXIV — Causes Which Render Democratic Armies Weaker Than Other Armies At The Outset Of A Campaign, And More Formidable In Protracted Warfare
paragraphs: Armies At The Outset Of A Campaign, And More Formidable In Protracted Warfare

Any army is in danger of being defeated at the outset of a campaign after a long peace; any army that has long been engaged in warfare has strong chances of victory. This truth is particularly applicable to democratic armies. In aristocracies the military profession, being a privileged career, is held in honor even in time of peace. Men of great talents, great attainments, and great ambition embrace it; the army is in all respects on a level with the nation, and frequently above it. We have seen, on the contrary, that among a democratic people the choicer minds of the nation are gradually drawn away from the military profession to seek, by other paths, distinction, power, and especially wealth. After a long peace — and in democratic ages the periods of peace are long — the army is always inferior to the country itself. In this state it is called into active service; and until war has altered it, there is danger for the country as well as for the army.

I have shown that in democratic armies, in time of peace, the rule of seniority is the supreme and inflexible law of advancement. This is not only a consequence, as I said before, of the constitution of these armies, but of the constitution of the people, and it will always be so. Again, since among these nations the officer derives his position in the country solely from his position in the army, and draws all the distinction and the competency he enjoys from the same source, he does not retire from his profession, or is not superannuated, until near the extreme close of life. The consequence of these two causes is that when a democratic people goes to war after a long interval of peace, all the leading officers of the army are old men. I speak not only of the generals, but of the non-commissioned officers, most of whom have been stationary, or have only advanced step by step. It may be remarked with surprise that in a democratic army after a long peace, all the soldiers are mere boys, and all the superior officers in declining years, so that the former are wanting in experience, the latter in vigor. This is a strong element of defeat, for the first condition of successful generalship is youth; I should not have ventured to say so if the greatest captain of modern times had not made the observation. These two causes do not act in the same way on aristocratic armies: since men are promoted in them by right of birth much more than by right of seniority, there are in all ranks a certain number of young men, who bring to their profession all the early vigor of body and mind. Again, as the men who seek military honors among an aristocratic people enjoy a settled position in civil society, they seldom continue in the army until old age overtakes them. After devoting the most vigorous years of youth to the career of arms, they voluntarily retire and spend at home the remainder of their maturer years.

A long peace not only fills democratic armies with elderly officers, but it also gives all the officers habits both of body and mind that unfit them for actual service. The man who has long lived amid the calm and lukewarm atmosphere of democratic manners can at first ill adapt himself to the harder toils and sterner duties of warfare; and if he has not absolutely lost the taste for arms, he has at least assumed a mode of life that unfits him for conquest.

Among aristocratic nations, the ease of civil life exercises less influence on the manners of the army, because among those nations the aristocracy commands the army; and an aristocracy, however plunged in luxurious pleasures, always has many other passions besides that of its own well-being, and to satisfy those passions more thoroughly its well-being will be readily sacrificed. *a
[Footnote a: See Appendix V.]

I have shown that in democratic armies, in time of peace, promotion is extremely slow. The officers at first bear this state of things with impatience; they grow excited, restless, exasperated; but in the end most of them become resigned to it. Those who have the largest share of ambition and of resources quit the army; others, adapting their tastes and desires to their scanty fortunes, end by looking on the military profession from a civilian point of view. The quality they most value in it is the competency and security that attend it; their whole notion of the future rests on the certainty of this small provision, and all they ask is to enjoy it peacefully. Thus a long peace not only fills an army with old men, but frequently imparts the views of old men to those who are still in the prime of life.

I have also shown that among democratic nations in time of peace the military profession is held in little honor and indifferently followed. This lack of public favor is a heavy discouragement to the army; it weighs down the minds of the troops, and when war breaks out at last, they cannot immediately resume their spring and vigor. No similar cause of moral weakness occurs in aristocratic armies: there the officers are never lowered either in their own eyes or in those of their countrymen, because, independently of their military greatness, they are personally great. But even if the influence of peace operated on the two kinds of armies in the same way, the results would still be different. When the officers of an aristocratic army have lost their warlike spirit and the desire to raise themselves by service, they still retain a certain respect for the honor of their class, and an old habit of being foremost to set an example. But when the officers of a democratic army no longer have the love of war and the ambition of arms, nothing whatever remains to them.

I am therefore of the opinion that when a democratic people engages in a war after a long peace, it incurs much more risk of defeat than any other nation; but it ought not to be easily cast down by its reverses, for the chances of success for such an army are increased by the duration of the war. When a war has at last, by its long continuance, roused the whole community from their peaceful occupations and ruined their minor undertakings, the same passions that made them attach so much importance to the maintenance of peace will be turned to arms. War, after destroying every mode of speculation, becomes itself the great and sole speculation, to which all the ardent and ambitious desires that equality engenders are exclusively directed. Hence it is that the same democratic nations which are so reluctant to engage in hostilities sometimes perform prodigious achievements once they have taken the field. As the war attracts more and more of public attention, and is seen to create high reputations and great fortunes in a short time, the choicest spirits of the nation enter the military profession; all the enterprising, proud, and martial minds, no longer of the aristocracy alone but of the whole country, are drawn in this direction. As the number of competitors for military honors is immense, and war drives every man to his proper level, great generals are always sure to arise. A long war produces on a democratic army the same effects that a revolution produces on a people; it breaks through regulations, and allows extraordinary men to rise above the common level. Those officers whose bodies and minds have grown old in peace are removed, or superannuated, or they die. In their place a host of young men are pressing on, whose frames are already hardened, whose desires are extended and inflamed by active service. They are bent on advancement at all hazards, and perpetual advancement; they are followed by others with the same passions and desires, and after these are others still, unlimited by anything but the size of the army. The principle of equality opens the door of ambition to all, and death provides chances for ambition. Death is constantly thinning the ranks, making vacancies, closing and opening the career of arms.

There is moreover a secret connection between the military character and the character of democracies, which war brings to light. The men of democracies are naturally passionately eager to acquire what they covet, and to enjoy it on easy conditions. For the most part they worship chance, and are much less afraid of death than of difficulty. This is the spirit they bring to commerce and manufactures; and this same spirit, carried with them to the field of battle, induces them willingly to expose their lives in order to secure in a moment the rewards of victory. No kind of greatness is more pleasing to the imagination of a democratic people than military greatness — a greatness of vivid and sudden luster, obtained without toil, by nothing but the risk of life. Thus, while the interests and tastes of the members of a democratic community divert them from war, their habits of mind fit them for carrying on war well; they soon make good soldiers, when they are roused from their business and their enjoyments. If peace is peculiarly hurtful to democratic armies, war secures to them advantages that no other armies ever possess; and these advantages, however little felt at first, cannot fail in the end to give them the victory. An aristocratic nation which, in a contest with a democratic people, does not succeed in ruining the latter at the outset of the war always runs a great risk of being conquered by it.

chapters.title: Chapter XXV — Of Discipline In Democratic Armies
paragraphs: It is a very common opinion, especially in aristocratic countries, that the great social equality prevailing in democracies eventually makes the private soldier independent of the officer, and so destroys the bond of discipline. This is a mistake, for there are two kinds of discipline, and it is important not to confuse them. When the officer is noble and the soldier a serf — one rich, the other poor, the former educated and strong, the latter ignorant and weak — the strictest bond of obedience can easily be established between the two men. The soldier is broken in to military discipline, so to speak, before he ever enters the army. Or rather, military discipline is nothing but an intensification of social servitude. In aristocratic armies the soldier soon becomes insensible to everything but the orders of his superior officers. He acts without reflection, triumphs without enthusiasm, and dies without complaint. In this state he is no longer a man, but he is still a most formidable animal trained for war.

A democratic people must give up hope of ever obtaining from soldiers that blind, minute, submissive, and unvarying obedience which an aristocratic people can impose on them without difficulty. The state of society does not prepare them for it, and the nation might be in danger of losing its natural advantages if it tried artificially to acquire advantages of this particular kind. Among democratic communities, military discipline should not try to annihilate the free spring of the faculties. All that discipline can do is direct it. The obedience thus instilled is less exact, but it is more eager and more intelligent. It has its root in the will of the one who obeys. It rests not only on his instinct but on his reason. And as a result it will often spontaneously become stricter as danger requires. The discipline of an aristocratic army is apt to be relaxed in war, because that discipline is founded on habits, and war disturbs those habits. The discipline of a democratic army, on the contrary, is strengthened in sight of the enemy, because every soldier then clearly sees that he must be silent and obedient in order to conquer.

The nations that have performed the greatest military achievements knew no other discipline than the one I am speaking of. Among the ancients, only freemen and citizens were admitted into the armies. They differed little from one another and were accustomed to treating each other as equals. In this respect the armies of antiquity may be called democratic, even though they came out of the bosom of aristocracy. The result was that in those armies a sort of fraternal familiarity prevailed between the officers and the men. Plutarch's lives of great commanders furnish convincing examples of this: the soldiers were in the constant habit of addressing their general freely, and the general listened to and answered whatever the soldiers had to say. They were kept in order by language and by example, far more than by constraint or punishment. The general was as much their companion as their chief. I do not know whether the soldiers of Greece and Rome ever carried the minutiae of military discipline to the same degree of perfection as the Russians have done. But this did not prevent Alexander from conquering Asia — or Rome, the world.

chapters.title: Chapter XXVI — Some Considerations On War In Democratic Communities
paragraphs: When the principle of equality is developing not just within a single nation but among several neighboring nations at once, as is now the case in Europe, the inhabitants of these different countries — despite their different languages, customs, and laws — nevertheless resemble each other in their equal dread of war and their shared love of peace.*a It is in vain that ambition or anger puts arms in the hands of princes. They are calmed, against their will, by a kind of general apathy and goodwill that makes the sword drop from their grasp, and wars become rarer. As the spread of equality goes on in several countries at once, simultaneously pushing their various inhabitants toward manufactures and commerce, not only do their tastes grow alike but their interests become so mixed and tangled together that no nation can inflict harm on other nations without that harm falling back on itself. In the end all nations regard war as a disaster, almost as severe for the victor as for the vanquished. Thus, on the one hand, it is extremely difficult in democratic ages to draw nations into hostilities. But on the other hand, it is almost impossible for any two of them to go to war without drawing in the rest. The interests of all are so interlaced, their opinions and needs so much alike, that none can remain quiet when the others stir. Wars therefore become rarer, but when they break out they spread over a larger field. Neighboring democratic nations not only grow alike in some respects; they end up resembling each other in almost all.*b This similarity of nations has consequences of great importance for war.

[Footnote a: It is scarcely necessary for me to note that the dread of war shown by the nations of Europe is not solely due to the progress of the principle of equality among them. Apart from this permanent cause, several other accidental causes of great weight could be cited, and first among them the extreme exhaustion left behind by the wars of the Revolution and the Empire.]

[Footnote b: This is not only because these nations share the same social condition; it also arises from the very nature of that social condition, which leads men to imitate and identify with one another. When the members of a community are divided into castes and classes, they not only differ from each other but have no wish or desire to be alike. On the contrary, each tries more and more to keep his own opinions undisturbed, to retain his own distinctive habits, and to remain himself. The characteristics of individuals are very sharply marked. When the state of society among a people is democratic — that is, when there are no longer any castes or classes and all members are roughly equal in education and in property — the human mind moves in the opposite direction. Men are much alike, and they are annoyed, as it were, by any deviation from that likeness. Far from trying to preserve their own distinguishing peculiarities, they try to shake them off so as to identify themselves with the general mass of the people, which is to them the sole representative of right and might. The characteristics of individuals are nearly erased. In the ages of aristocracy even those who are naturally alike strive to create imaginary differences between themselves; in the ages of democracy even those who are not alike seek only to become so and to imitate each other — so strongly is every man's mind carried along by the general impulse of mankind. Something similar may be observed between nations. Two nations sharing the same aristocratic social condition might remain thoroughly distinct and very different, because the spirit of aristocracy is to retain strong individual characteristics. But if two neighboring nations share the same democratic social condition, they cannot fail to adopt similar opinions and manners, because the spirit of democracy tends to assimilate men to one another.]

If I ask why it is that the Helvetic Confederacy made the greatest and most powerful nations of Europe tremble in the fifteenth century, whereas today the power of that country is exactly proportioned to its population, I see that the Swiss have become like all the surrounding communities, and those surrounding communities like the Swiss. So, since numerical strength now forms the only difference between them, victory necessarily goes to the largest army. Thus one of the consequences of the democratic revolution taking place in Europe is to make numerical strength prevail on every field of battle and to compel all small nations either to merge into large states or at least to adopt the policies of the large ones. Since numbers are the decisive cause of victory, every people must of course strive by every means in its power to bring the largest possible number of men into the field. When it was possible to enlist a kind of troops superior to all others, such as the Swiss infantry or the French cavalry of the sixteenth century, it was not thought necessary to raise very large armies. But the case is altered when one soldier is as effective as another.

The same cause that produces this new need also supplies the means of satisfying it; for, as I have already observed, when men are all alike, they are all weak, and the supreme power of the state is naturally much stronger among democratic nations than elsewhere. Thus, while these nations wish to enroll the whole male population in the ranks of the army, they also have the power to do it. The result is that in democratic ages armies seem to grow larger in proportion as the love of war declines. In the same ages, too, the manner of waging war is changed by the same causes. Machiavelli remarks in The Prince "that it is much more difficult to subdue a people led by a prince and his barons than a nation commanded by a prince and his slaves." To avoid offense, let us read "public officials" for "slaves," and this important truth will apply exactly to our own time.

A great aristocratic people cannot either conquer its neighbors or be conquered by them without great difficulty. It cannot conquer them, because all its forces can never be gathered and held together for any long time. It cannot be conquered, because an enemy meets at every step small centers of resistance that check the invasion. War against an aristocracy may be compared to war in a mountainous country: the defeated side has constant opportunities to rally its forces and make a stand in a new position. Exactly the reverse happens among democratic nations. They easily bring their whole available force into the field, and when the nation is wealthy and populous it soon wins. But if it is ever conquered and its territory invaded, it has few resources left. If the enemy takes the capital, the nation is lost. This can be explained easily. Since every member of the community is individually isolated and extremely powerless, no one in the whole body can defend himself or serve as a rallying point for others. Nothing is strong in a democratic country except the state. As the military strength of the state is destroyed by the destruction of the army, and its civil power paralyzed by the capture of the chief city, all that remains is a multitude without strength or government, unable to resist the organized power attacking it. I am aware that this danger may be reduced by the creation of provincial liberties and, consequently, of provincial powers, but this remedy will always be insufficient. After such a catastrophe, not only is the population unable to continue hostilities, but there is reason to fear that it will not even be inclined to try. According to the law of nations accepted in civilized countries, the object of war is not to seize the property of private individuals, but simply to gain political power. The destruction of private property is only occasionally resorted to for the sake of that object. When an aristocratic country is invaded after the defeat of its army, the nobles — who are at the same time the wealthiest members of the community — will continue to defend themselves individually rather than submit. For if the conqueror remains master of the country, he will deprive them of their political power, to which they cling even more than to their property. They therefore prefer fighting to submission, which is to them the greatest of all misfortunes. And they readily carry the people along with them, because the people have long been used to following and obeying them, and moreover have little to risk in the war. Among a nation where equality of conditions prevails, by contrast, each citizen has only a slender share of political power, and often has none at all. On the other hand, all are independent and all have something to lose, so that they are much less afraid of being conquered and much more afraid of war than an aristocratic people. It will always be extremely difficult to persuade a democratic population to take up arms once hostilities have reached its own soil. Hence the necessity of giving such a people the rights and the political character that may impart to every citizen some of those interests that cause the nobles to act for the public welfare in aristocratic countries.

The princes and other leaders of democratic nations should never forget that nothing but the passion and habit of freedom can mount a successful contest against the passion and habit of physical well-being. I cannot imagine anything more prepared for subjection, in case of defeat, than a democratic people without free institutions.

Formerly it was the custom to take the field with a small body of troops, fight in small engagements, and conduct long, regular sieges. Modern tactics consist in fighting decisive battles and, as soon as a line of march is open before the army, rushing on the capital city to end the war at a single stroke. Napoleon, it is said, was the inventor of this new system. But the invention of such a system did not depend on any individual man, whoever he might be. The way in which Napoleon waged war was suggested to him by the state of society in his time. That method was successful because it was admirably suited to that state of society, and because he was the first to use it. Napoleon was the first commander to march at the head of an army from capital to capital, but the road was opened for him by the ruin of feudal society. It may fairly be believed that if that extraordinary man had been born three hundred years earlier, he would not have drawn the same results from his method of warfare — or rather, that he would have had a different method.

I will add only a few words on civil wars, for fear of exhausting the reader's patience. Most of the remarks I have made about foreign wars apply all the more strongly to civil wars. Men living in democracies are not naturally prone to the military character. They sometimes take it on when they have been forced into the field, but to rise as one body and voluntarily expose themselves to the horrors of war — especially civil war — is a course men in democracies are not apt to adopt. Only the most adventurous members of the community agree to run such risks; the bulk of the population stays still. But even if the population were inclined to act, considerable obstacles would stand in its way.
